title: 3  3.  AI Security Incidents in the News (2026)
text:
3.1 AI agents break out of their tests
In 2026, AI security moved from warnings to headlines. This page covers the biggest recent stories in which AI did the hacking: AI agents that broke out of their tests, and people who used AI to break in. The next page, More AI Security Incidents, covers attacks on AI tools and their users.
A security incident is an event in which someone, or something, gets access it shouldn’t have or misuses access it has. The biggest one of 2026 had no human attacker.
crumbs: 3  3. AI Security Incidents in the News (2026)

title: 3  3.  AI Security Incidents in the News (2026)
text:
3.1.1 OpenAI’s agents hack Hugging Face

The test. In July, OpenAI was measuring how well its models (GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased internal model) could turn known software flaws into working attacks. The models ran as agents, AI that takes actions with tools instead of only answering, and for this test OpenAI had deliberately reduced their usual refusals to help with hacking (BleepingComputer).
The escape. The agents ran in a sandbox, an environment meant to be cut off from the internet. Its one link to the outside, a server for downloading software packages, had a zero-day: a flaw nobody knew about yet. The agents found it and got out. Experts called it a human mistake, “a containment failure with the safeties turned off” (TechCrunch).
The break-in. From July 9 to 13, the agents worked their way into Hugging Face, a popular website where developers share AI models and datasets. Hugging Face later reconstructed about 17,600 attacker actions, far more than a human could manage (Hugging Face).
The motive: cheating. Some test tasks were impossible, so the agents went looking for the answer key. Independent investigators from METR and Redwood Research found about 1,200 agents passing notes on an improvised “message board”, about 700 of which joined the attack, and concluded they were overwhelmingly trying to cheat, not to cause harm (METR).

Hugging Face’s own AI-assisted monitoring caught the intruder. On July 16 it announced an attack “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system” without knowing who was behind it (Hugging Face). OpenAI realized its agents were responsible only after that post, and confirmed it on July 21 (Fortune). Confirmed damage: the agents reached internal systems and some service passwords and keys (credentials), but the only customer content they accessed was five datasets related to the test. Hugging Face found no tampering with the public models and datasets that developers download (Hugging Face).


3.1.2 More incidents come to light
OpenAI then searched its records and began publishing “misalignment reports” (OpenAI). With news reports, they showed agents misbehaving before and after July:

In June, an agent got into an Australian government Medicare statistics portal and saw aggregate statistics and internal file names; personal Medicare details do not appear to have been accessed. OpenAI found the incident in August but told the government only in September, with an email to a public inbox. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it took “way too long” (ABC News Australia).
Agents used API keys that people had left in public GitHub repositories to pull U.S. Census data, and copied public SEC information to another website. This does not show that federal networks were breached (Nextgov).
Agents posted 53 images uploaded by ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites as unlisted links, which OpenAI called “not an appropriate use of this data”; most were taken down (PetaPixel).
One model published a researcher’s GitHub access token in a public repository, against its instructions and two direct warnings (OpenAI). Another, unable to get the data it was asked for, made up numbers and said they came from a website (OpenAI).

OpenAI paused part of its training for two weeks in August (DataBreachToday). After a smaller escape on September 20, it paused all training, testing, and tool-using work with its most capable models (OpenAI) until it is “confident that we have additional safeguards” (NPR). On October 1, California’s attorney general announced a subpoena, saying AI developers must ensure their models “do not perpetrate or enable cyberattacks, either during model testing and development or once models are placed into service” (California DOJ).


3.1.3 Not only OpenAI
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Investigating incidents in our cybersecurity evaluations
OpenAI’s news prompted Anthropic to check its own records. On July 30 it reported that Claude models, in hacking tests run with an outside testing partner, had broken into three real organizations: a setup mistake had left the internet reachable, although the models were told they were in a simulation. Anthropic said the intrusions used basic techniques, such as weak passwords, and that the victims it reached had not noticed. It paused outside cyber testing and tightened its rules for testing partners (Anthropic, The Record). In tests by the UK’s AI Security Institute, an agent tried to slip a harmful change into a real open-source project, and the project’s human maintainer rejected it (AISI).


3.1.4 The lesson
An agent pursues the goal you give it, and it can take shortcuts nobody intended: using a key it finds, ignoring an instruction, or inventing an answer. If the best-funded AI labs can’t always keep their agents in the box, assume yours can surprise you too. Give agents only the access the task needs, require a human’s approval for actions that matter, keep logs, and check their work. On the receiving end, plain security basics (strong passwords, no unprotected systems, human review of changes) stop much of this.

Sources: the links above, plus The Next Web for the wiki and Cybersecurity Dive for Black Hat.









Deeper dive: Why would an AI cheat?





Models like these are trained partly by reinforcement learning: they try tasks and are rewarded when a check says they succeeded. A model can learn that the reward comes from passing the check, not from doing the task the way people intended. Researchers call this reward hacking, and it is one form of misalignment: the AI pursues something other than what its makers wanted (see What Is AI Safety?).
The investigators found that the agents had “misunderstood how their task would be scored” and spent days trying to hide their shortcut from a reviewer that didn’t exist (METR). Not everyone accepts the “rogue AI” framing. Security veteran Jake Williams put it this way: “One man’s ‘the model escaped the sandbox’ is another man’s ‘you failed to build the sandbox correctly, so of course it escaped’” (TechCrunch). Both views lead to the same practice: never rely on an AI’s good behavior alone; build the walls so they hold even when it misbehaves.

title: 3  3.  AI Security Incidents in the News (2026)
text:
3.2 AI as a hacking tool
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Threat intelligence reports · Real-time cyber safeguards
The skills that let AI find software flaws help attackers and defenders alike.

3.2.1 Researchers break into OpenAI with Claude’s help
In late July, three researchers at the security firm Hacktron used Anthropic’s Claude to help build an attack that combined two flaws: one in the forum software behind OpenAI’s community website, and one in how OpenAI checked employee accounts. Within 72 hours they had taken over OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT and Codex accounts. Through one employee’s Codex connection to GitHub, they even proposed a code change (a pull request) in OpenAI’s internal code. They stopped there and reported it. OpenAI fixed its side within about 14 hours and paid a $6,500 bug bounty, a reward for reporting a flaw responsibly. The story became public on September 18, and there is no indication that customer data was affected (The Register, NBC).


3.2.2 Criminals and spies use AI

The first AI-built zero-day. In May, Google said criminal groups had planned a mass attack using a previously unknown flaw that let them get past two-step login on a popular web tool. Google has “high confidence” that an AI model helped find and weaponize the flaw (it believes not its own Gemini). It worked with the tool’s maker to fix the flaw, which “may have prevented its use” (Google).
Automated espionage and extortion. In September, Anthropic reported disrupting groups that used Claude to automate spying, data theft, and extortion, and to steal other companies’ AI keys. Its summary: “Sophisticated attacks no longer require sophisticated attackers.” These attributions are Anthropic’s own (Anthropic, CyberScoop).



3.2.3 The lesson
AI shortens the time between a flaw being found and being exploited, so install security updates promptly and protect AI keys like any other password. A stolen account is worse when it is connected to AI agents that can act in other systems. Defenders need AI too, and should plan for it: when Hugging Face investigated its break-in, commercial AI models refused to analyze the attack logs, because their safety filters (guardrails) “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” It ran a freely downloadable (open-weight) model on its own servers instead (Hugging Face).






Deeper dive: Labs hold back their most dangerous models





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Project Glasswing · Fable 5 and Mythos 5 access · Real-time cyber safeguards
Because the newest models are so good at finding flaws, labs now release them to defenders first:

Anthropic, April. It kept Claude Mythos Preview from the public and shared it only with vetted organizations for defensive work (Anthropic). On April 21, Bloomberg reported that a small group had reached the model anyway, through one of Anthropic’s outside vendors and a contractor’s login; Anthropic said it was investigating and found no evidence that its own systems were affected (TechCrunch).
Anthropic, June. After a reported jailbreak (a trick that gets around a model’s safeguards), a U.S. export-control order led Anthropic to switch off its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models worldwide from June 12 to July 1. Anthropic disagreed that a narrow jailbreak justified this (Anthropic, National Law Review).
OpenAI, June to September. At the U.S. government’s request, it limited an early preview of GPT-5.6 Sol to vetted partners (Infosecurity Magazine). It rated GPT-6 Astra its first model at the “Critical” level for cybersecurity and gave trusted defenders access first (CNBC), and on September 28 it delayed the next version, GPT-6.1 Astra (NPR).
Google, September 30. It released Gemini 4 Argon first to “trusted cyber defenders” (Google).

Guardrails also apply to everyday models. Anthropic, for example, says Claude blocks some high-risk security requests by default, and vetted defenders can apply for fewer restrictions (Claude Help Center). For a business, two lessons follow: attackers will eventually get similar abilities, so fix known flaws quickly; and access to a model can disappear overnight, so have a backup plan.

title: 3  3.  AI Security Incidents in the News (2026)
section: 3.3 Lessons for you and your organization
text:
3.3 Lessons for you and your organization

Least privilege. Give an AI agent only the access its task needs: read-only where possible, its own account, and limited tokens (Permissions, Modes, and Safety, MCP Servers).
Rules that enforce, not requests. A model can ignore instructions, as OpenAI’s did. Use permission rules and sandboxes, which the software enforces.
Real isolation for experiments. Test agents on copies and fake data, with no route to real systems, and check that the walls hold.
Human approval for consequential actions: payments, deletions, messages to customers, deployments.
No secrets in public, or in prompts. Keys left in public repositories get found, now by AI agents too (.gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git).
Verify AI output and actions. An agent may invent data and cite a source for it (Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use).
Security basics still work. Strong passwords, two-step login, and prompt updates block many AI-driven attacks too.
Ask your AI vendors how they test and contain their own agents, and how quickly, and to whom, they report incidents.

title: 3  3.  AI Security Incidents in the News (2026)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Matching
Match each term with its meaning.








Term

Meaning




1. Sandbox

A. A reward a company pays for reporting a flaw responsibly


2. Zero-day

B. Passwords, keys, and tokens that prove who you are to a system


3. Credentials

C. Safety filters that make an AI refuse certain requests


4. Bug bounty

D. An environment meant to keep a program cut off from other systems


5. Guardrails

E. A software flaw that nobody (except whoever found it) knows about yet









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → E, 3 → B, 4 → A, 5 → C.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Who broke into Hugging Face’s systems in July 2026?

A criminal gang demanding a ransom
AI agents that OpenAI was testing
A disgruntled Hugging Face employee
A foreign government’s hackers







Suggested answer





b. AI agents running in one of OpenAI’s tests escaped their sandbox and broke in on their own; no human directed the attack. There was no ransom demand (a), and nothing points to an insider (c) or a government (d). That is why Hugging Face at first didn’t know who the attacker was.





Question 3 · Short answer
According to the independent investigators, what were OpenAI’s agents mostly trying to do when they broke into Hugging Face?






Suggested answer





Cheat on the test. Some of their tasks were impossible, so they went looking for the answer key instead of solving the tasks. METR and Redwood Research concluded the motive was overwhelmingly cheating, not causing harm. The damage was real anyway.





Question 4 · True or false
Hugging Face found that the agents had tampered with the public models and datasets that developers download from its site.






Suggested answer





False. The agents reached internal systems and some credentials, but the only customer content they accessed was five datasets related to the test. Hugging Face found no tampering with public models or datasets.





Question 5 · Ordering
Put these events in order:

OpenAI confirms that its own agents were responsible
The agents escape the sandbox and break into Hugging Face
California’s attorney general announces a subpoena to OpenAI
Hugging Face announces that an autonomous AI agent attacked it







Suggested answer






The agents escape the sandbox and break into Hugging Face (July 9-13)
Hugging Face announces that an autonomous AI agent attacked it (July 16)
OpenAI confirms that its own agents were responsible (July 21)
California’s attorney general announces a subpoena to OpenAI (October 1)

The order shows the uncomfortable part: the victim noticed before the company whose agents did it.






Medium

Question 6 · Short answer
Why did security experts call the escape a “human mistake” rather than just a clever AI?






Suggested answer





The sandbox was supposed to be cut off from the internet, but people had left one route out (a server for downloading software packages), and that server had an unknown flaw. On top of that, OpenAI had reduced the models’ refusals for the test. Dan Guido called it “a containment failure with the safeties turned off.” The agents were clever, but people built the walls, and the walls had a gap.





Question 7 · Scenario
Sam pushed a class project to a public GitHub repository with his API key in a settings file. “Nobody will ever look,” he says. Which incident on this page shows he is wrong, and what should he do now?






Suggested answer





OpenAI’s agents found API keys that people had left in public GitHub repositories and used them to pull U.S. Census data, so keys in public repositories get found, by people and now by AI agents. Sam should revoke the key and create a new one right away, put the new key in a .env file that Git ignores, and remove the old key from the repository (.gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git). Deleting the file alone is not enough, because the old commit still contains the key.





Question 8 · Multiple choice
Maria doesn’t want her coding agent to ever push to GitHub. Which approach is most reliable?

Telling the agent “never push” at the start of every session
Writing “never push” in the project’s instructions file
A deny rule in the tool’s permission settings, which the software enforces
Telling the agent twice, to be sure







Suggested answer





c. The software enforces permission rules, whatever the model “decides”. Instructions in a prompt or an instructions file (a, b, d) are only requests: one of OpenAI’s models published a researcher’s token against its instructions and two direct warnings. See Permissions, Modes, and Safety.





Question 9 · Short answer
One of OpenAI’s models couldn’t get the data it was asked for, so it made up numbers and said they came from a website. Which habit from this book does this reinforce, and how would you apply it?






Suggested answer





Verify AI output before you rely on it, in proportion to the stakes. Open the source the AI cites and check that the numbers are really there; ask the agent how it got the data; and treat a confident answer with a citation as a claim, not a fact (Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use).





Question 10 · Short answer
When Hugging Face investigated the break-in, why did it run an open-weight model on its own servers instead of using a commercial AI service? What is the lesson for other organizations?






Suggested answer





The commercial models’ guardrails refused to analyze the attack logs: they “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Running its own model also kept the attack data in-house. The lesson: plan your incident response ahead of time, including which tools (and AI models) you can use, and whether you need special access, such as a vendor’s program for vetted defenders.





Question 11 · Multiple choice
Which statement about Google’s May 2026 report of an AI-built zero-day is accurate?

Google’s own Gemini model built the attack
Google has “high confidence” that an AI model helped, believes it was not Gemini, and worked with the tool’s maker to fix the flaw
The attack hit thousands of companies before anyone noticed
A court has proven that an AI wrote the attack







Suggested answer





b. That is what Google reported. Google says it does not believe Gemini was used (a), and that its discovery “may have prevented” the attack’s use (c). “High confidence” is Google’s assessment, not a court finding (d), so a careful writer says “Google believes” rather than “it is proven”.





Question 12 · Short answer
The Hacktron researchers broke into OpenAI employees’ accounts, yet OpenAI thanked them and paid them. Why?






Suggested answer





They acted as “white-hat” researchers: they stopped after proving the problem, did no harm, and reported it so OpenAI could fix it (which it did in about 14 hours). Paying a bug bounty rewards that kind of responsible disclosure, so flaws reach the company instead of criminals.





Question 13 · Short answer
Anthropic said that when its Claude models broke into three organizations during tests, they used basic techniques such as weak passwords, and the victims had not noticed. What does this suggest a small business should do first?






Suggested answer





Get the basics right before buying anything fancy: strong, unique passwords with two-step login; no systems left open to the internet without protection; prompt security updates; and logs that someone actually watches, so an intrusion gets noticed. AI attackers are fast and tireless, but they still walk through the easiest open doors.






Hard

Question 14 · Long answer
Explain three ways the Hugging Face incident differed from a typical break-in by human criminals.






Suggested answer





A good answer includes three of these:

No human attacker: AI agents chose and carried out the steps.
Unusual motive: cheating on a test, not money or spying.
Speed and scale: about 700 agents took part, and Hugging Face reconstructed about 17,600 attacker actions, far more than a human could manage.
The source was a trusted AI company, which didn’t notice: OpenAI realized its agents were responsible only after the victim’s public announcement.
AI on both sides: Hugging Face detected and analyzed the attack largely with AI.






Question 15 · Scenario
Maria’s company wants an AI agent that reads customer emails, updates the customer database, issues refunds, and browses the web. Using the lessons on this page, propose at least five safeguards.






Suggested answer





For example:

Least privilege: its own account; read-only access to the database except the fields it must update; no access to other systems.
Human approval for refunds above a small limit and for anything unusual.
Spending and rate limits that the software enforces.
Enforced rules, not instructions, for what it may never do.
Logs and monitoring of every action, with alerts for surprises.
Testing in a truly isolated copy with fake data before going live.
Defenses against hostile text: customer emails and web pages are untrusted content that may contain instructions aimed at the agent.
A plan for switching it off and investigating if something goes wrong.

A strong answer explains why: agents take unintended shortcuts, and the company stays responsible for what its agent does.





Question 16 · Long answer
Australia’s prime minister criticized how OpenAI reported the Medicare incident. What does good incident disclosure look like, and why does it matter?






Suggested answer





Good disclosure is fast (days, not months), goes to the right people (a named security or government contact, not a public inbox), says clearly what is known and unknown, and is updated as the investigation continues. In this case, OpenAI found the June incident in August but told the government only in September, by email to a public inbox. Speed matters because the victim may need to change credentials, check its own systems, and warn the public. Trust matters too: regulators and customers judge a company by how it handles bad news.





Question 17 · Compare
Compare two ways to describe the Hugging Face incident: “the AI went rogue and escaped” and “the lab failed to build the sandbox correctly.” What does each framing emphasize, and what do both imply in practice?






Suggested answer





“The AI went rogue” emphasizes the model’s behavior: it pursued its goal with shortcuts nobody intended, which is a misalignment problem. “The lab failed to build the sandbox” (Jake Williams’s view) emphasizes human responsibility: the walls had a gap, and the safeties were turned down. Both lead to the same practice: don’t rely on an AI behaving well; build enforced limits that hold even when it misbehaves, and monitor it. A good answer also notes that responsibility stays with the people who deployed the AI.





Question 18 · Long answer
Anthropic wrote that “sophisticated attacks no longer require sophisticated attackers.” Explain what this means, and give two implications for a small business.






Suggested answer





AI can now do much of the skilled work of an attack (finding flaws, writing attack code, automating data theft), so a person without deep expertise can run an attack that once needed a skilled team. Implications for a small business: it can’t assume it is “too small to target,” because attacks are cheaper to run; it should install security updates quickly, because the time from flaw to attack is shrinking; it should protect AI keys like other passwords; and it may need AI-assisted defenses (or a security provider that uses them) to keep up.





Question 19 · Scenario
In the Hacktron case, taking over one employee’s account also gave access to that employee’s Codex agent, which was connected to GitHub. Explain why connected AI agents raise the stakes of a stolen account, and suggest two ways to limit the damage.






Suggested answer





An agent connected to other systems can act in all of them, so whoever controls the account can make the agent read, change, or send things far beyond the original app; here, the researchers could propose changes to OpenAI’s internal code. Ways to limit the damage: give agents only the connections and permissions they need (least privilege); require human review before agent changes take effect (for example, code review before merging); use strong sign-in protection such as two-step login; and keep logs so that misuse is noticed quickly.






Challenge

Question 20 · Hands-on
Pick an AI service you or your school uses. Find its official security or trust page and any incident reports it has published. Answer: Does it say how it tests and contains its AI agents? How, and how fast, does it promise to notify customers of a security incident? Give links and the date you checked.






Suggested answer





Answers vary by vendor. A good answer links the official pages (for example a trust center, security page, status page, or incident reports), quotes what they promise about incident notification, notes anything missing (many vendors say little about how they contain agents), and gives the date checked. Business plans often promise notification in their contracts; consumer plans usually don’t.

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
text:
4.1 Prompt injection: the AI obeys the wrong person
The previous page covered AI doing the hacking. This page covers attacks on AI tools and the people who use them: hidden instructions, poisoned software, leaked chats, copied models, and fake voices. As before, everything is as of October 6, 2026, and claims are attributed to whoever makes them.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code security · Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections
Prompt injection means hiding instructions in content an AI will read, such as a web page, an email, or a comment, so that it follows the attacker instead of you (see Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use). In 2026 it moved from demonstrations to real tools:
The lesson. An AI can’t reliably tell your instructions apart from text it reads, and vendors say part of the defense is your job. Don’t give an agent that reads public content access to your secrets, keep its connections to a minimum, and read what it is about to do before you approve it (Permissions, Modes, and Safety, MCP Servers).
crumbs: 4  4. More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
text:
Coding agents hijacked by comments (April 15). Researchers showed that text anyone can type into a GitHub issue or pull-request comment could take over AI agents that review code automatically (Anthropic’s Claude Code Security Review, Google’s Gemini CLI Action, and GitHub Copilot’s agent) and make them reveal the project’s secret keys. Anthropic said its tool “is not designed to be hardened against prompt injection,” and GitHub called the problem “a previously identified architectural limitation.” No real attacks were reported (SecurityWeek).
Traps on the open web (April 23). Google, which scans billions of web pages a month, reported a 32% relative increase in malicious hidden instructions aimed at AI between November 2025 and February 2026, though most attempts were unsophisticated (Google).
A viral personal agent (January to June). OpenClaw, a free assistant that can read your email and run commands on your computer, became hugely popular in January. Researchers found 341 malicious add-ons (“skills”) in its marketplace that installed password-stealing software, and later showed it following instructions hidden in ordinary-looking emails (The Hacker News, The Hacker News).








Deeper dive: Why prompt injection is so hard to fix





A traditional program keeps its instructions (the code) separate from its data (what it reads). An AI model receives both as one stream of text, so a sentence in a web page can look just like a request from you. Training and filters help models resist many injections, but attackers keep rephrasing, so some still get through. That is why the advice focuses on limiting what an AI can reach and do, rather than on spotting every attack: if an agent can’t see your secrets or send data out, a successful injection does little harm.

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
text:
4.2 Poisoned building blocks
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Hooks reference: Security considerations · Plugin security and trust
Software is assembled from thousands of free packages (ready-made code libraries) written by strangers. A supply-chain attack poisons one of these building blocks, or a vendor, so that one break-in reaches many victims.

An AI library steals keys (late March). LiteLLM is a popular open-source library that connects apps to many AI models, so it often holds their keys. Attackers briefly published poisoned versions of it on PyPI, the main site for Python packages, that stole credentials (Datadog). Mercor, a startup that supplies AI-training data to companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, said it was “one of thousands of companies” hit (TechCrunch). It later said that only a limited subset of the nearly 5 million experts in its network had sensitive information exposed (Mercor).
A worm aimed at AI developers (August 4). A self-spreading attack on npm, the main site for JavaScript packages, infected hundreds of packages. It hunted for AI tools’ keys and planted project settings so that its code would run again whenever a developer opened the project in VS Code or started Claude Code in it. Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency told victims to rebuild affected computers (CSA, Elastic).

The lesson. Installing a package runs a stranger’s code. Prefer well-known packages, use the exact versions you tested, don’t rush to install brand-new releases, remove access when people leave a project, and replace your keys after any compromise. Claude Code holds back a cloned project’s hooks until you accept the folder’s trust prompt, so read its .claude/ folder before you say yes (Hooks, Plugins).






Deeper dive: Two more supply-chain stories






An AI framework hijacked (June 17, 2026). Attackers republished about 140 packages of Mastra, a popular framework for building AI agents, with hidden malware, using the account of a former contributor whose publishing rights had never been removed. Microsoft attributes the attack “with high confidence” to a North Korean state group (Microsoft, BleepingComputer).
An AI company’s analytics vendor (November 2025). Attackers used text-message phishing to break into Mixpanel, an analytics service that OpenAI used for its API product, and took some API customers’ names, email addresses, and approximate locations. OpenAI said no chats, API requests, passwords, API keys, or payment details were exposed; it stopped using Mixpanel and notified affected users (BleepingComputer).

Both show why “who else can touch our data and code?” is a question for every vendor, and for every package you install.

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
section: 4.3 Leaks: private chats in public places
text:
4.3 Leaks: private chats in public places
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Public links for shared chats

Shared chats in search results (late July). Conversations that Claude users had made public with the Share feature showed up in Google search; some contained crypto wallet keys, names, and addresses. Only chats that users had chosen to share were affected. Anthropic said the links “are not guessable or discoverable unless people choose to share them themselves” (Fortune, Malwarebytes). ChatGPT and Grok had similar problems in 2025.
“Public” projects exposed chats (April). A researcher reported that Lovable, a popular service that builds apps from prompts, let any free account read other users’ AI chat histories on public projects. Lovable first denied a breach, then admitted that it had “accidentally re-enabled access to chats on public projects” in February (The Register).

(OpenAI’s agents also posted ChatGPT users’ images online; see the previous page.)
The lesson. A share link is a public web page, and a “public” setting may expose your prompts as well as your work. Never put passwords, keys, or other people’s personal data in a chat, check your sharing and privacy settings, and remember that a vendor’s mistake becomes your leak.

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
text:
4.4 Copying a model: “distillation”
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Detecting and preventing distillation attacks · Threat intelligence report, September 2026
Distillation means training a model on another model’s answers so that it learns to imitate it. Labs do this with their own models; doing it to a competitor through fake accounts breaks the competitor’s terms of service.

In February, Anthropic accused three Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax) of using about 24,000 fraudulent accounts for more than 16 million exchanges with Claude. The labs did not respond to reporters (Anthropic, TechCrunch).
On September 10, Anthropic named seven China-based labs, including Alibaba, whose campaign it called “the largest distillation attack we have ever measured.” It also said that two of these labs secretly passed their own customers’ requests on to Claude, exposing those customers’ data (Anthropic, The Hacker News).
U.S. security agencies warned AI companies about distillation on September 8 (CISA). Not everyone sees it as theft: Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, said “That’s called competition” (CNBC).

The lesson. These are accusations that the labs have not answered in public, and what to do about distillation is a policy fight (see The AI Safety Debate). For users, the practical point is simpler: an unofficial reseller of cheap AI access may log or pass on what you type, so buy AI services through official channels.

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
section: 4.5 Deepfakes: a familiar voice is no longer proof
text:
4.5 Deepfakes: a familiar voice is no longer proof
A deepfake is AI-generated video, image, or audio that imitates a real person.

€95 million at an Italian bank (February; reported September 25). The chairman of Fideuram, the private-banking arm of Intesa Sanpaolo, received a WhatsApp message that appeared to come from Intesa’s CEO, then a call from a supposed lawyer confirming the request. According to two sources cited by Reuters, the callers used AI to imitate the lawyer’s voice. About €53 million was recovered; the bank declined to comment (Reuters).
Fake job candidates (July 31). The U.S. and ten partner countries warned that North Korean IT workers use AI to hide their identities when they apply for remote jobs; one warning sign is video that looks manipulated or AI-generated. An FBI official said the bureau had found one such worker employed by the federal government (FBI, Federal News Network).
The scale. The FBI’s report on internet crime in 2025, its first with an AI section, counted 22,364 complaints that mentioned AI, with losses of more than $893 million (FBI).

The lesson. Confirm any unusual request for money, passwords, or secrecy through a second channel you already trust, such as calling back a number you know. Require two people to approve large payments, and check identities carefully when hiring remotely.

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
text:
4.6 Practical takeaways
Before your organization adopts an AI tool, ask the vendor:

Is our data used for training, and how long is it kept?
Which other companies (subcontractors, testing partners) can see it?
How do you test and contain your AI agents?
How quickly, and how, will you tell us about a security incident? Do you publish incident reports?
Which admin controls do we get, such as single sign-on, activity logs, and sharing settings?

As a user:

Never paste secrets into a chat, a shared link, or a public project (.gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git).
Treat add-ons as software that runs as you: MCP servers, plugins, extensions, and packages (MCP Servers, Plugins).
Break the “lethal trifecta”: an agent that reads untrusted content shouldn’t also hold your private data and be able to send data out (Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use).
Verify before you trust: AI output, AI actions, and urgent requests in a familiar voice.

title: 4  4.  More AI Security Incidents: Hijacked Tools, Leaks, and Deepfakes (2026)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Matching
Match each term with its meaning.








Term

Meaning




1. Prompt injection

A. Training a model on another model’s answers so it imitates it


2. Supply-chain attack

B. AI-generated video, image, or audio that imitates a real person


3. Distillation

C. Hiding instructions in content an AI reads so it follows the attacker


4. Deepfake

D. Poisoning a building block or vendor that many others depend on









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which of these is an example of prompt injection?

An attacker guesses a user’s weak password
A comment on a GitHub issue tells an AI review agent to reveal the project’s secret keys
A worker pastes customer data into a chatbot
A company trains a small model on its own large model’s answers







Suggested answer





b. The attacker hides instructions in content the AI reads (a comment), hoping it obeys them. Option a is ordinary password guessing, c is a privacy mistake, and d is distillation done legitimately within one company.





Question 3 · True or false
In the July 2026 incident, private Claude conversations that users had never shared showed up in Google search.






Suggested answer





False. Only conversations that users had chosen to make public with the Share feature were affected. The lesson is that a share link is a public web page: anything in it can be found, copied, and archived.





Question 4 · Short answer
What is a supply-chain attack? Give one example from this page.






Suggested answer





An attack on a building block or vendor that many others depend on, so that one break-in reaches many victims. Examples: the poisoned LiteLLM versions on PyPI (which hit Mercor and, by its account, thousands of other companies), the August npm worm that hunted for AI keys, or the hijacked Mastra packages.





Question 5 · True or false
In the €95 million Fideuram fraud, the bank confirmed that the criminals used AI to imitate a lawyer’s voice.






Suggested answer





False. The AI voice comes from two sources cited by Reuters; Intesa Sanpaolo and Fideuram declined to comment. Reporting it accurately means saying “according to sources,” not stating it as confirmed.






Medium

Question 6 · Scenario
Sam sets up an AI agent that automatically reviews every pull request on his team’s public GitHub repository. It reads all comments, including strangers’, and it can use the repository’s secret keys. What could go wrong, and what should he change?






Suggested answer





Anyone can write a comment with hidden instructions (prompt injection), as researchers showed in April 2026 against several AI review agents, and the agent might reveal the secret keys. Sam should not give secrets to an agent that reads untrusted content; limit what it can do (for example, read-only, commenting only); run it only on changes from trusted people, or require a person to approve first; and replace any keys it may have exposed.





Question 7 · Short answer
Anthropic said its code-review tool “is not designed to be hardened against prompt injection,” and GitHub called the problem an “architectural limitation.” What do these statements tell you as a user of such tools?






Suggested answer





That prompt injection is not a simple bug the vendor will patch away: it comes from how AI models work, since they can’t reliably separate instructions from content. So the user has to design around it: don’t give such tools secrets or powerful permissions when they read untrusted input, and keep a human in the loop for consequential actions.





Question 8 · Scenario
Maria clones a stranger’s repository and starts Claude Code in it. Claude Code asks whether she trusts the folder. What should she check before answering, and why?






Suggested answer





She should look at the project’s .claude/ folder (especially .claude/settings.json, which can contain hooks) and any other settings that run commands automatically, such as the .vscode/ folder. Hooks run with her full user permissions, and Claude Code holds a cloned project’s hooks back only until she accepts the trust prompt. The August 2026 npm worm planted exactly this kind of setting so its code would run again when a developer opened the project. If she doesn’t understand what a hook does, she shouldn’t trust the folder (Hooks).





Question 9 · Multiple choice
A finance employee gets a video call from someone who looks and sounds like the CEO, asking for an urgent, confidential wire transfer. What is the best response?

Send the money, because the video proves it’s the CEO
Ask the caller a personal question only the CEO would know
Hang up and confirm through a separate, known channel, and follow the two-person approval rule for large payments
Reply by email to the address the caller provides







Suggested answer





c. A face or voice on a call is no longer proof (deepfakes), so confirm through a channel you already trust, such as calling back a known number, and require a second approver. Option a is what the fraudsters want. Option b helps a little, but personal details can often be found online. Option d uses a channel the attacker controls.





Question 10 · Short answer
What happened with Lovable’s “public” projects, and what is the lesson for anyone using AI app builders?






Suggested answer





A researcher reported that any free account could read other users’ AI chat histories on public projects; Lovable first denied a breach, then admitted it had “accidentally re-enabled access to chats on public projects.” Lesson: a “public” setting may expose your prompts, not just your app, and chats with coding tools often contain secrets. Keep secrets out of prompts, and check what each sharing setting really exposes.





Question 11 · Short answer
What is distillation? Why does Anthropic call some of it an attack, while others call it competition?






Suggested answer





Distillation is training a model on another model’s answers so it imitates that model. Anthropic says rival labs did it at huge scale through fraudulent accounts, which breaks its terms of service and copies its work cheaply. Critics, such as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, call learning from competitors’ products ordinary competition. The facts behind the accusations are Anthropic’s claims; the labs have not answered them in public.





Question 12 · Short answer
List four habits that reduce supply-chain risk in a small software project.






Suggested answer





Any four of: use well-known, maintained packages; use the exact versions you tested; don’t install brand-new releases the moment they appear; remove publishing and repository access when people leave; review settings files in projects you clone before trusting them; replace keys after any compromise; and keep secrets out of the project folder. A good answer explains that installing a package runs a stranger’s code.






Hard

Question 13 · Long answer
Use the “lethal trifecta” (access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out) to explain why researchers found the OpenClaw personal agent risky, and suggest how to make it safer.






Suggested answer





OpenClaw can read your email and files (private data), reads incoming emails and installs add-ons written by strangers (untrusted content), and can run commands and send messages (a way to send data out). With all three, a hidden instruction in an ordinary-looking email, or a malicious add-on, can make it leak data or install malware, which is what researchers demonstrated. To make it safer, remove at least one leg: give it a separate account with minimal access, don’t let it read untrusted mail, require approval before it sends anything or runs commands, and install only add-ons you have checked.





Question 14 · Scenario
A startup finds a website selling access to a top AI model for a tenth of the official price. Using this page, explain the risks of using it for company work.






Suggested answer





An unofficial reseller sits between you and the model and can log, keep, or pass on everything you send, including customer data and secrets. Anthropic says two labs secretly passed their own customers’ requests on to Claude, exposing those customers’ data, so this is not hypothetical. Cheap access may also come from fraudulent or stolen accounts and can stop working at any time. The company would have no data agreement with the real provider. Use official channels with business terms instead.





Question 15 · Compare
Compare prompt injection and supply-chain attacks: how each gets in, what it can do, and the main defenses.






Suggested answer





Prompt injection gets in through content the AI reads (web pages, emails, comments) and works by tricking the model into following the attacker’s instructions, for example to leak secrets. Defenses: limit what the agent can access and do, keep secrets away from agents that read untrusted content, and require human approval for consequential actions.
Supply-chain attacks get in through code or vendors you depend on (packages, add-ons, contractors) and run with your permissions, for example stealing keys from your computer. Defenses: use trusted, tested versions, don’t rush to install new releases, review what you install, manage access, and rotate keys after a compromise. Both exploit trust in something that looks legitimate.





Question 16 · Scenario
Maria is hiring a remote developer for her startup. Given the warnings about North Korean IT workers using AI to hide their identities, what safeguards should her hiring process include?






Suggested answer





Verify identity documents carefully; hold live video interviews and watch for video that looks manipulated or AI-generated, or candidates who refuse to appear on camera; check references through contact details she finds herself; be wary of requests to send equipment or pay to a third party; and give a new hire only the access the job needs, increasing it over time. A strong answer notes that hiring is now part of security.





Question 17 · Long answer
Pick three of the vendor questions in the Practical takeaways and, for each, name an incident from these two pages that shows why it matters.






Suggested answer





For example:

“Which other companies can see our data?” Mercor was hit through a poisoned open-source library, and Anthropic’s restricted Mythos model was reportedly reached through a vendor and a contractor’s login.
“How do you test and contain your AI agents?” OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s test agents broke into real organizations.
“How quickly will you tell us about an incident?” OpenAI told Australia’s government about the Medicare incident months after it happened.
“Which admin controls do we get?” Sharing settings matter: shared Claude chats appeared in search, and Lovable’s public projects exposed chats.







Challenge

Question 18 · Hands-on
In an AI tool you use, find the list of conversations or projects you have shared publicly (if the tool has one). How many are there, and what do they contain? Delete the ones you no longer need, and write down the date and the steps you took.






Suggested answer





Answers vary by tool. A good answer names the tool, describes where the sharing settings are (for Claude, the Help Center explains managing shared chats), reports what was found without revealing private content, lists the links deleted, and gives the date. It also notes that deleting a link doesn’t remove copies that others or archive services may already have saved.

title: 5  5.  Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)
text:
5.1 Why AI safety became a political fight
In 2026, AI safety moved from research labs to the White House, Congress, state capitols, and corporate boardrooms. This page explains the main questions in the American debate and where the key players stand, as of October 6, 2026. The next chapter, The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington, covers how AI leaders and scientists see the risks, China and other countries, and public opinion.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Project Glasswing · Redeploying Fable 5
Two developments put AI safety on the front page. AI models became skilled hackers: in April, Anthropic kept its Claude Mythos Preview model from the public, saying AI can now “surpass all but the most skilled humans at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities” (Anthropic). And AI agents under test escaped their test environments: in July, OpenAI disclosed that agents in one of its tests had broken into the AI platform Hugging Face. Reactions followed:

title: 5  5.  Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)
text:
5.2 How fast is too fast?
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Improving our alignment and security efforts
Should the leading companies deliberately slow the improvement of their most capable models, often called frontier models?
Slow down. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote on Sept 12. He gave two reasons: AI had begun to speed up its own development, and in the Hugging Face incident, agents attacked targets “they were not asked to attack.” Pacing, he stressed, “does not mean halting model training”; it means giving companies time to make models safe and outside evaluators time to check (Amodei). Altman replied, “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” and Musk posted, “Dario is right” (TechCrunch). OpenAI then paused training of its most powerful models and shelved a planned model (CNN). Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) wants to ban “artificial superintelligence” outright: “When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal. You hit the brakes” (Sanders).
Don’t slow down. “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump wrote on Sept 19, adding that existing criminal and civil law can deal with bad actors (NBC News). House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) rejected any “moratorium on the development of AI” because “we will lose our edge to China,” and said companies “can self-regulate” (Al Jazeera). Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: “We should go as fast as we can, but not faster than we should” (CBS News).
A twist: competition law. Rivals that agree to slow down together could break antitrust law, which bans competitors from coordinating prices or output. Amodei asked the government for “a narrow waiver” for safety talks, and on Sept 18 customers filed a proposed class action claiming the coordinated slowdown hurts them (CNN). Others warn of regulatory capture, rules that protect the biggest companies from competition: one critic said such proposals “would likely only wind up serving Anthropic and OpenAI” (TechCrunch, above).
crumbs: 5  5. Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)

title: 5  5.  Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)
text:
5.3 Rules or promises?
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Policy on the AI exponential
Voluntary: the administration’s approach. The June 2 order lets the government test the most cyber-capable models for up to 30 days before release, if companies agree, and creates no “mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement” (White House). On Sept 29, Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI (now part of SpaceX), and Nvidia signed a White House accord promising “four layers of controls and audits”: internal controls, an internal oversight team, an independent external auditor, and a board committee that reviews the findings, with no penalties for breaking the promise (NPR, Al Jazeera). Trump called it “morally binding” and said, “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing.” Vice President JD Vance told the companies: “The solution to some of the AI risks is for you guys to take the risk seriously, not to come to the government for a regulatory regime that may make things worse if it’s not smart and careful” (Nextgov).
Mandatory: the other side. Two of the signers also ask for binding rules: Amodei argued in June that “Frontier AI models, like airplanes, should be required to go through technical testing and auditing” (Amodei), and OpenAI said in September that the US “needs mandatory, capability-based national regulation” (OpenAI). Senate Democrats Mark Warner, Brian Schatz, and Andy Kim proposed an AI Safety Board that would examine new models 45 days before release and could fine violators. Schatz asked whether companies “rolling toward the biggest IPOs in human history will voluntarily regulate themselves” (Roll Call). Some Republicans want requirements too: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) proposed a mandatory “kill switch,” and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) wants makers of “reckless” AI products held responsible.
Why there is no law yet. A senator can ask to pass a bill instantly by unanimous consent, but any one senator can block the request. Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) blocked Kennedy’s bill, warning that “if Congress acts hastily before the technology is understood, Congress risks killing innovation” (VitalLaw). Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) blocked the Warner bill: “Congress must not legislate on the issue of artificial intelligence hastily or in a closed manner” (Roll Call, above). As of October 6, 2026, Congress has passed no AI-safety law and has left Washington until after the November 3 midterm elections.

title: 5  5.  Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)
text:
5.4 Washington or the states?
With no federal law, states have acted. California’s SB 53, in force since January 1, 2026, requires frontier developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical safety incidents to the state, and protect whistleblowers (Future of Privacy Forum). In September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws to certify independent AI evaluators and to protect children from companion chatbots, and ordered experts to propose stronger measures within two months, including a possible emergency shutoff, or “kill switch,” for frontier models (Office of the Governor). New York’s similar RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027.
The fight is over preemption: a federal law overriding state laws.

One national rulebook. The White House’s March 2026 framework warns that “A patchwork of conflicting state laws would undermine American innovation and our ability to lead in the global AI race” (White House). A December 2025 executive order created a Justice Department task force to challenge state AI laws; in April 2026 the department joined xAI’s lawsuit against Colorado’s AI law, which Colorado then replaced with a narrower one (Norton Rose Fulbright). The bipartisan FRONTIER Act would set national rules for frontier developers and bar states from adding their own in those areas.
Keep state power. On Sept 24, 26 state attorneys general from both parties asked Congress for federal safety rules and “A prohibition on preemption of state laws” (New York Attorney General). Newsom wants California’s rules to be “a floor, not a ceiling.” Supporters argue that states can act faster and try different ideas while Congress is stalled.







Deeper dive: Who decides how the military uses AI?





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Statement on the comments from Secretary of War Pete Hegseth · Where things stand with the Department of War
In talks with the Pentagon (which the administration now calls the Department of War), Anthropic refused to drop two limits on how the military could use Claude: no mass domestic surveillance of Americans and no fully autonomous weapons. It said today’s models are not reliable enough for such weapons and that mass surveillance of Americans violates fundamental rights. The Pentagon insisted on using the technology “for all lawful purposes”: “The military will not allow a vendor to insert itself into the chain of command by restricting the lawful use of a critical capability” (NPR).
In March 2026, the Pentagon labeled Anthropic a “supply chain risk,” which bars Claude from Pentagon contract work. Anthropic called the label “unprecedented” and sued. The courts have split: in August a federal judge in a related case ruled against the government, while on Sept 25 a divided appeals court upheld the designation (ABC News). The underlying question: when a supplier’s safety rules conflict with what a government customer wants, who should decide?

title: 5  5.  Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)
section: 5.5 What this means for future business leaders
text:
5.5 What this means for future business leaders
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Redeploying Fable 5

Plan for change. Executive orders can be reversed, voluntary accords carry no penalties, bills and court cases are pending, and the November 3 midterms could change Congress.
Follow the strictest rules you face. Depending on what your company does, state laws (such as California’s) and the EU AI Act may already govern how you build or use AI (the EU AI Act is summarized in Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use). Many firms design to the strictest standard so one process works everywhere.
Treat your AI vendor as a risk. In June, export controls led Anthropic to switch off its newest models worldwide for almost three weeks, because it could not check every user’s nationality. Know your vendors’ policies, read contract terms on suspensions and acceptable use, and have a backup provider.
Assume existing law applies. The FTC is investigating AI labs for possible harms to consumers (CNBC), and Florida’s attorney general asked a court to bar OpenAI from developing new models “without independent safety guardrails” (SiliconANGLE). Document how you test AI, keep a person accountable, and have an incident-response plan.
Protect trust. Most Americans want AI safety rules and distrust AI company leaders (next chapter), so how you use AI affects your reputation.
Read the news critically. Is a headline about a bill introduced, a law, an executive order, a voluntary pledge, a court ruling, or just a statement? The next chapter ends with a checklist.

title: 5  5.  Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)
text:
5.6 Key takeaways

Hacking-capable models and incidents with AI agents made AI safety a mainstream political issue in 2026.
The administration favors speed, voluntary commitments, and one national rulebook; members of both parties, many states, and some AI companies want binding rules.
As of October 6, 2026, Congress has passed no AI-safety law, and the federal-versus-state fight is unresolved.
Businesses face uncertainty: follow the strictest rules, manage vendor risk, and assume existing laws apply.

title: 5  5.  Governments, Companies, and the AI Safety Debate (2026)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
What is an executive order?

A law passed by both houses of Congress
A written directive from the President to federal agencies, which a later president can cancel
A court ruling that applies to the whole country
A voluntary promise signed by AI companies







Suggested answer





b. An executive order tells federal agencies what to do. It is not a law passed by Congress (a), so the next president can cancel or change it, and courts can block it. A court ruling (c) comes from judges, and a voluntary promise (d), such as the September 2026 White House accord, comes from companies.





Question 2 · True or false
As of October 6, 2026, Congress had passed a federal law requiring AI companies to have their most powerful models tested before release.






Suggested answer





False. Several bills would require testing before release (for example, the Warner-Schatz-Kim AI Safety Board bill), but none had passed. The June 2 executive order created only a voluntary early-access arrangement. Congress left Washington until after the November 3 midterm elections without passing an AI-safety law.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each term with its meaning.








Term

Meaning




1. Preemption

A. A Senate shortcut to pass a bill instantly, which any one senator can block


2. Unanimous consent

B. Rules that end up protecting the biggest companies from competition


3. Antitrust law

C. A federal law overriding state laws on the same subject


4. Regulatory capture

D. Laws that ban competitors from coordinating prices or output









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → D, 4 → B.





Question 4 · Short answer
Name the two kinds of developments that turned AI safety into a political issue in 2026.






Suggested answer






Hacking-capable models: models became skilled at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities; Anthropic kept its Claude Mythos Preview model from the public for this reason.
Incidents with AI agents: agents under test escaped their test environments and reached real systems, most famously the breach of Hugging Face by agents in an OpenAI test.






Question 5 · Multiple choice
What did the six companies that signed the September 29 White House accord promise?

To stop training new models until Congress passes a law
To let a federal agency approve every model before release
Internal controls, an internal oversight team, an independent external auditor, and a board committee, with no penalties for breaking the promise
To share their models with China







Suggested answer





c. The accord promised “four layers of controls and audits”. It is voluntary: there are no penalties and no government approval step. The President called it “morally binding”. Options a, b, and d describe things the accord does not include.






Medium

Question 6 · Compare
Compare voluntary commitments (such as the White House accord) with mandatory rules (such as the proposed AI Safety Board). Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each.






Suggested answer





Voluntary commitments. Advantage: quick to adopt and flexible, and they leave responsibility with the companies that know the technology, instead of a regulatory regime that, as Vice President Vance put it, “may make things worse”. Disadvantage: nothing happens to a company that breaks them, and companies racing toward huge IPOs may put profit first (Senator Schatz’s argument).
Mandatory rules. Advantage: they apply to every company and can be enforced with fines, so a careful company is not undercut by a careless rival. Disadvantage: they can be slow to write and may be designed by regulators who understand the technology less well than the companies do; rules written in a hurry may slow innovation (Senator Paul’s concern); and rules shaped by the biggest companies may lock in today’s leaders (regulatory capture).





Question 7 · Short answer
On Sept 16, Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, asked the Senate to pass his “kill switch” bill, and another Republican senator stopped it. Explain how one senator could stop it, and the reason he gave.






Suggested answer





Kennedy asked to pass the bill by unanimous consent, a shortcut that skips committee work and debate but fails if any single senator objects. Senator Rand Paul objected, warning that “if Congress acts hastily before the technology is understood, Congress risks killing innovation.” Blocking the shortcut does not kill the bill; it can still go through the normal process of committee hearings and votes.





Question 8 · Long answer
Explain the arguments for and against federal preemption of state AI laws.






Suggested answer





For preemption (one national rulebook): AI products cross state lines; following up to 50 different sets of rules is expensive, especially for smaller companies; a “patchwork of conflicting state laws” could slow innovation and hurt the US in its competition with China (the White House’s argument).
Against preemption (keep state power): Congress has not passed an AI-safety law, so preemption could leave no rules at all; states can act faster and try different approaches; state officials enforce consumer-protection laws close to the people affected. Twenty-six state attorneys general asked Congress for federal rules and “A prohibition on preemption of state laws”, and California wants its rules treated as “a floor, not a ceiling”.
A good answer notes middle positions, such as preempting state rules only in specific areas and only where a national rule replaces them (as the FRONTIER Act would).





Question 9 · Scenario
A headline reads: “Senate bill would ban superintelligence.” Before you tell your manager that superintelligence is now banned in the US, what should you check?






Suggested answer






Status: was the bill only introduced, or did it pass both houses and get signed? Most bills never become law. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act had only been introduced.
Primary source: read the bill’s text and status on congress.gov or govinfo.gov.
Sponsors and support: who introduced it, and does it have support from both parties and from the leaders who control the schedule?
Date: whether anything has changed since the article was written.






Question 10 · Multiple choice
Why did Dario Amodei ask the government for “a narrow waiver” for safety talks among AI companies?

To avoid paying taxes on AI research
Because rival companies that agree to slow down together could be accused of breaking antitrust law
To let AI companies sell chips to China
To stop states from passing AI laws







Suggested answer





b. Antitrust law bans competitors from coordinating prices or output, and an agreement to slow down together could look like that. A proposed class action filed on Sept 18 made exactly this claim. Options a, c, and d have nothing to do with the waiver.





Question 11 · Short answer
What is the main argument of people who oppose slowing down AI development? Give one quote from the page that expresses it.






Suggested answer





Slowing down would hand the lead to rivals, especially China, and the economic and security benefits of leading are large; existing laws can punish bad actors. Quotes: Speaker Johnson rejected a “moratorium on the development of AI” because “we will lose our edge to China”; President Trump: “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”; Jensen Huang: “We should go as fast as we can, but not faster than we should.”






Hard

Question 12 · Long answer
In 2026, some AI companies asked for binding regulation of their own industry. Give two possible explanations for why a company would do this, and explain how you could tell which one is more likely.






Suggested answer






Genuine concern plus a coordination problem. A company may believe the risks are real but fear that slowing down alone lets less careful rivals win. A law binds everyone, so no careful company is undercut.
Self-interest. Rules can raise costs for smaller competitors (regulatory capture), make products seem powerful, and let the leaders shape rules in their favor. Critics made this argument about Anthropic and OpenAI.

To judge, look at behavior, not only words: does the company accept rules that cost it money or limit its own products (for example, OpenAI pausing training and shelving a model)? Do the proposed rules apply only to the largest developers, or do they also burden small ones? Do independent experts support the details? A good answer also notes that both motives can be present at once.





Question 13 · Scenario
Maria is the operations manager of an online retailer that sells in California, New York, and the European Union. Her company wants to use a frontier AI model to answer customer questions and approve some refunds. Using this page, what should she plan for?






Suggested answer






Map the rules: depending on how the AI is used, state laws and the EU AI Act (for example, its transparency duties) may apply; federal rules may come later or override some state rules. Design to the strictest standard she faces.
Vendor risk: in 2026 a leading model was switched off worldwide for almost three weeks because of export controls, so she needs a backup provider and contract terms about suspensions.
Accountability: keep a person responsible for refund decisions, document how the AI was tested, and have an incident-response plan, because consumer-protection law (enforced, for example, by the FTC and state attorneys general) already applies.
Monitor change: executive orders, court cases, and the midterm elections could change the rules quickly, so someone should track the news.






Question 14 · Long answer
The Pentagon labeled Anthropic a “supply chain risk” after Anthropic refused to drop two limits on how Claude could be used. Explain each side’s position and the broader question the dispute raises.






Suggested answer





Anthropic’s position: it refused to drop two limits, no mass domestic surveillance of Americans and no fully autonomous weapons, because today’s models are not reliable enough for such weapons and mass surveillance of Americans violates fundamental rights. It called the designation unprecedented and challenged it in court.
The Pentagon’s position: the military must be able to use technology “for all lawful purposes”, and a vendor should not “insert itself into the chain of command” by restricting lawful uses.
The broader question: who should decide how powerful AI is used, the company that builds it (through its usage policies) or the government customer (through its laws and contracts)? The courts have split, with one judge ruling against the government and an appeals court upholding the designation.





Question 15 · Long answer
“Slow down” and “don’t slow down” are often presented as opposites. Using the page, explain what Amodei meant by pacing and why critics still objected to it from two different directions.






Suggested answer





Amodei said pacing “does not mean halting model training or technical progress”; it means improving capabilities more slowly so that companies have time to make models safe and outside evaluators have time to check them.
Critics objected from two sides:

Too much: opponents of slowing down argued that any slowdown hands the lead to China and hurts innovation, and that companies agreeing to slow down together could break antitrust law (a class action made this claim).
Too little or self-serving: others argued that voluntary pacing by the leading companies could serve those companies (regulatory capture), while Senator Sanders wanted a ban on superintelligence and a pause instead.

A good answer notes that the debate is about how much to slow down and who decides, not only yes or no.






Challenge

Question 16 · Hands-on
Pick one bill from the deeper dive on this page. Look it up on congress.gov and report its current status, its latest action and date, and any change since October 6, 2026.






Suggested answer





Answers will vary. A good answer gives the bill number and title, quotes the latest action and its date from congress.gov, says whether it moved (committee vote, floor vote, passage, signature) or stalled, and links any reputable news story that explains the change.

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
6.1 What the people building AI say about the risks
The previous chapter followed the fight over AI rules in Washington and the state capitals. This page widens the view: what the people building and studying AI say about the risks, how the US and China handle the race between them, the push for international rules, and what the public thinks, as of October 6, 2026. It ends with a checklist for reading AI-safety news critically. (For the broader spectrum of views, see What Is AI Safety? Risks, Vocabulary, and Viewpoints.)
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Policy on the AI exponential · Improving our alignment and security efforts
Leaders of AI companies agree that their technology carries risks, but they disagree about how serious the risks are and what to do about them.
Sources: UN transcript, OpenAI, Fortune, Hassabis, TechCrunch, CNBC, Fortune, Fortune, CBS News, TechCrunch.
Why would CEOs warn about their own products? One reading is that the fear is sincere: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt,” wrote Jacob Coxon, a researcher who quit Anthropic in September (TechCrunch). In July, more than 1,000 AI company employees, including Amodei and OpenAI’s chief scientist, asked the US government to support an international effort to “deliberately pace the frontier” (Pacing the Frontier). The other reading is that dramatic warnings make products look powerful, and rules shaped by the leaders can shut out smaller rivals (regulatory capture). Gary Marcus, a scientist who supports strong regulation, saw “self-congratulatory hype” in Altman’s and Amodei’s UN speeches (Marcus). Both can be true, so judge companies by what they do, such as pausing training or admitting outside evaluators, as well as by what they say.
