crumbs: 6  6. The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
6.2 Scientists and other voices

Yoshua Bengio, a Turing Award winner who chairs the International AI Safety Report (written by more than 100 experts and backed by more than 30 countries and international organizations), told the UN Security Council: “The dangers are real and imminent.” He wants frontier AI “licensed like other critical technologies,” as in medicine, aviation, and nuclear energy.
Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate, told reporters after a closed-door briefing for lawmakers in September that Congress may have only about one year left to impose safety measures (Fortune).
Focus on today’s harms. The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), a digital-rights group, argued that the most urgent problems “are not about sci-fi scenarios concerning rogue super-intelligence” but “biased algorithmic decision-making,” “AI-powered surveillance,” and “artificially inflated personalized pricing” (EFF).







Deeper dive: An unusual alliance, and religious voices





On Sept 15, progressives such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and conservatives such as former White House strategist Steve Bannon and Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) appeared together at a “Pro-Human Assembly” in Washington to raise alarms about AI’s risks. Sanders: “A super intelligent AI that escapes human control will not simply be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem. It will be humanity’s problem.” Roy: “I don’t think big tech CEOs should be making all the decisions about AI. I don’t think Congress should be making all the decisions about AI” (CNBC).
Religious leaders have joined the debate too. Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical on AI, Magnifica Humanitas (May 2026), calls for “adequate regulatory tools capable of upholding justice and curbing the distorting effects of technological power” (Vatican).
crumbs: 6  6. The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
6.3 The United States and China
The race argument says that whoever leads in AI gains economic and military power, so slowing down could hand the lead to China. After meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump said the US is “not going to be putting on brakes” because “we’re leading China by a lot” (PBS). Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence chosen to lead the new Super Intelligence Force, said: “The risk of not being first is high” (ABC News). Critics answer that the race is a choice: “The race is not a law of nature. It is the product of choices, choices made by the companies themselves,” Bengio told the UN. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella pointed out that China faces the same dangers: “It’s not like they won’t have the same hacking problem” (TechCrunch, above).
The rivals also talk. During Xi’s state visit in late September, the two governments agreed to start a dialogue on AI’s risks and benefits, with the next meeting by November 2026, and to set up a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents, much like a hotline (White House, China’s Foreign Ministry). Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that “moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important” (NBC News). Meanwhile, the US limits sales of advanced AI chips to China with export controls (government limits on selling sensitive technology abroad), although in December 2025 it let Nvidia sell its H200 chips to approved customers in China, with 25% of the sales going to the US government (CNBC).
crumbs: 6  6. The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
6.4 The push for global rules

On Sept 21-22, leaders of 20 countries, including Germany, Canada, Australia, Spain, and Singapore, and the European Commission issued “A Call for Control of Frontier AI Models.” It asks for “mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation” and for UN members to “explore creating an international institution, able to set standards, enable verification, and convene states when capability thresholds are crossed” (Government of the Netherlands). The US, China, the UK, France, India, and Japan did not sign (Al Jazeera).
On Sept 22, Trump told the UN General Assembly that the US “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme of control for the Artificial Intelligence being spoken of so much now” (White House).
On Sept 23, the UN Security Council held a meeting focused on the safety risks of advanced AI (see the deeper dive below).
The UN’s new Independent International Scientific Panel on AI warned in its first brief, on the Hugging Face incident, that “the traditional model of safeguarding is unravelling” (UN News).
Since August 2, 2026, the EU’s AI Office can enforce the AI Act’s rules for general-purpose AI models and fine companies that break them (European Commission). Companies from anywhere that offer such models in the EU must comply (the EU timeline is in Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use).







Deeper dive: Who said what at the UN Security Council (Sept 23, 2026)





France convened the meeting. Highlights from the UN transcript (an automatic transcript, so some wording may be slightly off):

Yoshua Bengio: “The dangers are real and imminent.”
Sam Altman, OpenAI: “This moment calls for extreme care.”
The United States (Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy): the rapid advance of AI “is not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structures” (US Mission to the UN).
The United Kingdom (Foreign Secretary): “we cannot outsource to private companies the first duty of government to protect our people.”
China: asked countries to “support the UN as the main forum of global AI governance” and promoted its new Shanghai-based World AI Cooperation Organization.
Russia: “it is counterproductive to consider the use of AI technologies solely through the lens of risk.”

Other AI company leaders also spoke; their main warnings are in the table at the top of this page.
crumbs: 6  6. The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
6.5 What the public thinks
Polls taken during the September debate show broad support for safety rules:

In a Quinnipiac poll of US adults (Sept 24-27), 86% supported requiring AI companies “to meet independent safety standards, even if it slows down AI development.” Asked about the pace of development, 30% said stop until safety can be evaluated, 47% slow down, 14% keep the current pace, and 5% move faster. And 74% had little or no trust in the leaders of AI companies (Quinnipiac).
The same poll found that 69% think keeping up with China is important and 91% think guardrails are important; 65% hold both views. As the pollster put it, “The public is not neatly divided into a competition camp and a safety camp.”
Worry differs by party. In an Economist/YouGov poll (Sept 18-21), 42% called AI’s risks “very serious,” up from 35% in late August, including 53% of Democrats and 29% of Republicans (YouGov). Among registered voters, 71% said they were more likely to back a candidate who supports stricter AI guardrails, including 52% of Republicans and 86% of Democrats (Quinnipiac).

Wording matters: a question that mentions slowing down, or one that mentions China, can shift the answers.
crumbs: 6  6. The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
6.6 Reading AI-safety news critically
For a business leader, reading this news well shows which rules are coming, which are only talk, and what could disrupt your AI tools. A checklist:

What kind of action is it? A bill introduced, a law, an executive order, a voluntary pledge, a court ruling, or just a statement? Only some of these bind anyone, and most bills never pass.
Read the primary source. The Sept 29 executive order tells agencies to say “Super Intelligence” instead of “Artificial Intelligence,” but it defines super intelligence as the same technologies the law already calls artificial intelligence (White House). It renames today’s AI; it does not mean AI far smarter than humans, the sense used in the chapter on If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.
Compare official accounts. The White House called the new US-China channel the “U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue”; China’s Foreign Ministry called it the “China-U.S. AI Dialogue” and did not mention the new term.
Ask who is speaking and what they gain. CEOs, politicians, and advocacy groups all have interests. That doesn’t make them wrong, but it is a reason to check their claims.
Check how a poll asked its question, and who was asked.
Separate facts from forecasts, and check dates. “OpenAI paused training in September 2026” is a fact; “AI could kill us all by the end of the decade” is a forecast.
Confirm with two reputable sources, and prefer original documents over social-media posts.
crumbs: 6  6. The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
6.7 Key takeaways

AI leaders call the risks serious but split on remedies: binding rules and a slower pace, or market incentives and engineering fixes.
Scientists such as Bengio and Hinton urge fast government action; others stress today’s harms.
The US and China are racing, yet agreed to share AI-incident alerts. Many countries want international rules; the US government rejects global AI governance.
In fall 2026 polls, most Americans favored safety rules, though worry differed by party.
crumbs: 6  6. The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)

title: 6  6.  The AI Safety Debate Beyond Washington (2026)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
What does the White House’s September 29, 2026 executive order on “super intelligence” do?

It announces that AI smarter than all humans now exists
It tells federal agencies to call AI “super intelligence,” defining the term as the same technologies the law already calls artificial intelligence
It bans the development of superintelligence
It creates an international agency to regulate AI







Suggested answer





b. The order is about terminology: agencies must say “Super Intelligence” instead of “Artificial Intelligence,” and the order defines super intelligence as the technologies already covered by the legal definition of artificial intelligence. It does not claim that AI smarter than humans exists (a), it bans nothing (c), and the US government rejects new global AI governance (d).





Question 2 · True or false
The United States and China both signed the September 2026 “Call for Control of Frontier AI Models.”






Suggested answer





False. Twenty countries, including Germany, Canada, Australia, Spain, and Singapore, and the European Commission signed it. The US, China, the UK, France, India, and Japan did not. The US government said at the UN that it rejects a “globalist scheme of control” for AI.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each voice with the position it took in September 2026.








Voice

Position




1. A Turing Award-winning AI scientist (Bengio)

A. Today’s urgent problems are biased decisions, surveillance, and personalized pricing, not “sci-fi scenarios”


2. The CEO of a leading AI chip maker (Huang)

B. Rapid AI progress is no reason to pause or to create new global governance structures


3. A digital-rights group (EFF)

C. Frontier AI should be licensed like medicine, aviation, and nuclear energy


4. The US government at the UN Security Council

D. “Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one”









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 4 · Short answer
What did the US and China agree to during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit in September 2026?






Suggested answer





To start a dialogue on the risks and benefits of AI, with the next meeting by November 2026, and to set up a bilateral communication channel for AI incidents, something like a hotline that lets each side alert the other.





Question 5 · Short answer
What are export controls? Give the AI-related example from this page.






Suggested answer





Export controls are government limits on selling sensitive technology to other countries. The US limits sales of advanced AI chips to China; in December 2025 it allowed Nvidia to sell its H200 chips to approved customers in China, with 25% of the sales going to the US government. (The previous chapter describes export controls that briefly applied to Anthropic’s models in 2026.)






Medium

Question 6 · Long answer
Explain the race argument about AI and China, and give two counterarguments from this page.






Suggested answer





The race argument: whoever leads in AI gains economic and military power, so slowing down could hand the lead to China. President Trump said the US is “not going to be putting on brakes,” and Jay Clayton said, “The risk of not being first is high.”
Counterarguments:

The race is a choice, not a law of nature (Bengio): companies and governments can decide to coordinate.
China faces the same dangers, such as hacking, so both sides have reasons to cooperate on safety (Nadella).
The two governments did agree to talk and to share AI-incident alerts, which shows rivals can cooperate on some risks.






Question 7 · Compare
Compare the view that AI may pose catastrophic risks (for example, Bengio’s) with the EFF’s view. Does accepting one view require rejecting the other?






Suggested answer





Bengio warns that the dangers of advanced AI are “real and imminent” and wants frontier AI licensed like medicine, aviation, and nuclear energy. The EFF says the most urgent problems are already happening: biased automated decisions, surveillance, and personalized pricing.
They are not mutually exclusive. One can worry about future catastrophic risks and today’s harms at the same time. The real disagreement is about priorities: where attention, money, and new laws should go first. A good answer also notes that some measures, such as independent testing and incident reporting, address both concerns.





Question 8 · Scenario
A colleague says: “Polls show 86% of Americans want AI development stopped.” Is that what the Quinnipiac poll found? Correct the claim.






Suggested answer





No. The 86% figure is the share who support requiring AI companies “to meet independent safety standards, even if it slows down AI development.” On a separate question about pace, 30% said stop until safety can be evaluated, 47% slow down, 14% keep the current pace, and 5% move faster. So most respondents favored stopping or slowing until safety can be evaluated, but only 30% chose “stop.” The lesson: quote the exact question and number, with the poll’s date.





Question 9 · Short answer
The White House and China’s Foreign Ministry gave the same US-China agreement different names. What were the names, and what does this teach you about reading the news?






Suggested answer





The White House called it the “U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue”; China called it the “China-U.S. AI Dialogue” and did not mention the new term. Each government describes events in the way that suits it. Compare official accounts from both sides, and other sources, before concluding what was agreed.





Question 10 · Multiple choice
Which statement is a forecast rather than a fact?

OpenAI paused training of its most powerful models in September 2026.
Twenty countries and the European Commission signed a call for an international AI institution.
AI could kill us all by the end of the decade.
Since August 2, 2026, the EU’s AI Office can fine makers of general-purpose AI models that break the AI Act.







Suggested answer





c. It is a prediction about the future that can’t be checked today, however sincerely it is held. Options a, b, and d describe events or rules that can be checked against primary sources.





Question 11 · Long answer
Why would the CEO of an AI company warn that its own technology could be dangerous? Give two readings, and explain how you could judge between them.






Suggested answer






Sincere concern. The people closest to the technology may see risks first. A researcher who quit Anthropic wrote that the fear “is not a marketing stunt,” and more than 1,000 AI company employees signed a call to pace the frontier.
Self-interest. Warnings make products seem powerful, and rules shaped by the leaders can shut out smaller rivals (regulatory capture). Critics such as Gary Marcus saw “hype” in some CEO speeches.

To judge, look at actions as well as words: does the company accept costs or limits, such as pausing training, withholding a model, or letting outside evaluators in? Do the rules it favors also bind itself? Both motives can exist at the same time.






Hard

Question 12 · Long answer
Should the US join an international institution that sets standards for frontier AI? Without taking a side, explain the strongest arguments on each side, using the positions on this page.






Suggested answer





For joining: AI risks cross borders, and no country can manage them alone; shared testing standards, verification, and incident reporting reduce the chance of a race to the bottom (the 20-country Call for Control; Bengio; the UK’s view that governments cannot outsource safety to companies). The US-China incident channel shows that rivals can cooperate.
Against joining: a global regulator could limit national sovereignty, slow American innovation, or be shaped by rivals; national governments and responsible companies can manage risks themselves (the US government’s position at the UN; Trump’s rejection of a “globalist scheme”). Verification is hard, and rivals might not comply.
A strong answer weighs both sides and notes middle options, such as narrow agreements on specific risks or bilateral channels like the one agreed with China.





Question 13 · Scenario
Sam works for a US software company that sells an AI model to businesses in the US, the EU, and Asia. List the international risks from this page that his company should plan for.






Suggested answer






EU rules: since August 2, 2026, the EU’s AI Office can enforce the AI Act’s rules for general-purpose AI models, with fines, so the company must comply in the EU.
More rules to come: 20 countries and the European Commission are pushing for an international institution and mandatory pre-deployment testing.
Geopolitics and export controls: US-China tensions can change which chips and models can be sold where, sometimes suddenly.
Public trust: polls show low trust in AI company leaders and strong support for safety standards, so customers may demand evidence of testing and oversight.

A good answer also says how to respond: track regulations by market, document testing, and plan for sudden changes.





Question 14 · Long answer
In the Quinnipiac poll, 65% of Americans said both that keeping up with China is important and that AI guardrails are important. What does this suggest for politicians and companies?






Suggested answer





The public does not see a simple choice between competing with China and being safe; most people want both. For politicians, a message that frames safety and competitiveness as opposites may not match voters’ views; policies that pursue both (for example, testing requirements that don’t stop development) may have broad support. For companies, being seen as safe and trustworthy is part of competing, not a cost that can be skipped. A good answer adds a caution: poll results depend on wording, and opinions differed by party.





Question 15 · Scenario
A headline reads: “White House declares the era of superintelligence has begun.” Use the checklist on this page to evaluate it.






Suggested answer






Kind of action: an executive order, which directs federal agencies; it is not a law, and a later president can change it.
Primary source: the order renames AI as “super intelligence” for federal agencies and defines the term as the same technologies the law already calls artificial intelligence. It does not say that AI smarter than humans exists.
Who is speaking: the administration, which says the new term better reflects the technology’s “transformative capabilities.” That is its stated reason, not a scientific finding.
Compare accounts: China’s readout of the same week’s agreement kept the term “AI”.
Conclusion: the headline is misleading if readers take “superintelligence” in its usual meaning, AI far smarter than humans.







Challenge

Question 16 · Hands-on
Find the latest news on one story from this page, such as the US-China AI dialogue (its next meeting was due by November 2026) or the UN discussions on an international AI institution. Compare an official source with two news reports.






Suggested answer





Answers will vary. A good answer links the official source (for example, a White House or Chinese Foreign Ministry statement, or a UN page) and two reputable news reports, notes any differences in how they describe the event, separates facts from forecasts, and gives the date of each source.

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
text:
7.1 What counts as “AI”?
AI products change every month, but the big ideas behind them change slowly. This page gives you a quick tour of what AI can do in fall 2026, the vocabulary to talk about it, and one of the year’s biggest business stories: cheap, capable open-weight models from China.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has no single agreed definition. A practical one is: the science of making machines do tasks that we used to think required human intelligence.
That makes AI a moving target. Playing chess well was once a famous AI goal. In 1997, IBM’s chess computer Deep Blue beat the world champion, Garry Kasparov. Soon after, chess programs stopped feeling like “AI” and became “just software”. The same thing happened to spell checkers, spam filters, and turn-by-turn directions.
Most of today’s headline AI is generative AI: systems that create new content (text, images, audio, video, or code) from a request written in plain language. That request is called a prompt.
crumbs: 7  7. What AI Can Do Today

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
text:
7.2 What is an AI model?
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude models overview
An AI model is the trained “engine” inside an AI product. Physically, it is a huge file of numbers called weights (often billions of them) plus the software that runs them. The next chapter explains where those numbers come from.
People often mix up three different things:








Term
What it is
Examples (as of October 2026)




AI company (or “lab”)
Builds and trains models
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Alibaba


Model
The trained engine, with a family name and a version number
GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash


App (or product)
What you actually use; usually lets you choose a model
ChatGPT, the Claude app, the Gemini app, Claude Code



One app usually offers several models (bigger and smarter, or smaller and faster), and one model can power many apps: Microsoft’s Copilot, for example, offers models from both OpenAI and Anthropic (Microsoft, Sept 2026). New model versions appear every few weeks; app names last longer.
A large language model (LLM) is a model trained on enormous amounts of text that reads and writes text (many can also read images). Chat assistants and coding tools such as Claude Code are built on LLMs.
crumbs: 7  7. What AI Can Do Today

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
section: 7.3 A quick tour of what AI can do (October 2026)
text:
7.3 A quick tour of what AI can do (October 2026)
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code overview · Get started with Claude in Chrome






Names change monthly



Treat every product and model name in this section as a snapshot from October 2026. Some will be renamed, replaced, or shut down during this semester. Learn the categories, and look up current names on each company’s own website.



7.3.1 Words, code, and data

Chat assistants answer questions, write text, analyze files, and search the web: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), Grok (xAI), Microsoft Copilot, Meta AI, Perplexity, and the Chinese assistants DeepSeek, Qwen (Alibaba), and Kimi (Moonshot AI).
Reasoning (“thinking”) models work through a problem step by step before answering; you can often choose how hard they think. In May 2026, leading mathematicians confirmed that an OpenAI model had disproved a famous 1946 conjecture by Paul Erdős (arXiv).
Deep research agents search the web for several minutes and write a report with citations (ChatGPT deep research, Gemini Deep Research, Claude Research). They still make factual errors.
Coding agents read a whole software project, write and run code, and fix what fails: Claude Code (this book’s main tool), OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Antigravity. See The AI Coding Tool Landscape.
Agents for office work turn a goal into finished documents, spreadsheets, or slides (ChatGPT Work, Claude’s Cowork features, and the Cowork agent in Microsoft Copilot).



7.3.2 Images, video, voice, and music

Images from a description: ChatGPT Images, Google’s Nano Banana, Midjourney.
Video clips, many now with sound: Google Veo, Kling, ByteDance’s Seedance, Runway. Products come and go: OpenAI shut down its well-known Sora video app in 2026 (NBC News).
Voice and music: real-time spoken conversation in the major chat apps, synthetic voices (ElevenLabs), and complete songs from a prompt (Suno, Udio).



7.3.3 Acting in the world

Computer-use and browser agents operate a browser or desktop for you: they read the screen, click, type, and fill in forms (Claude in Chrome, ChatGPT’s agent features, Gemini in Chrome, Perplexity’s Comet browser).
Robots: humanoid robots are moving into factories. Boston Dynamics began manufacturing its Atlas robot in 2026 for Hyundai and Google DeepMind (Boston Dynamics).
Self-driving cars: Waymo was giving about 500,000 paid driverless rides a week by March 2026 (TechCrunch).



7.3.4 Science, health, and business

Science: AlphaFold predicts the 3-D shapes of proteins; its creators Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared in the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Nobel Prize).
Health: the US FDA has authorized over 1,600 AI-enabled medical devices, for example to support disease detection and diagnosis (FDA).
Finance and business: fraud detection, credit scoring, customer service, and increasingly agents that handle paperwork-heavy back-office work.
crumbs: 7  7. What AI Can Do Today

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
text:
7.4 AI is built into everything
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude for Microsoft 365
More and more often, AI is not a separate app but a feature inside products you already use:

Office software: Copilot inside Word, Excel, and PowerPoint; Claude add-ins for Excel, PowerPoint, and Word; Gemini inside Gmail and Google Docs.
Search and browsers: AI-written answers at the top of search results, and AI helpers built into web browsers.
Messaging and social media: Meta AI inside WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and Messenger.
“Invisible” AI you have used for years: spam filters, fraud alerts from your bank, product and video recommendations, and photo search on your phone.

So you often use AI without noticing, and it pays to ask what data an AI feature can see (Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use). For businesses, AI is becoming a standard feature, the way “having a website” was around 2000, and AI agents are starting to compete with traditional software.






Deeper dive: Why software investors worry about AI agents





Much business software is sold “per seat”: a company pays a monthly fee for each employee who uses it. If AI agents can do part of that work, a company may need fewer seats, or may drop the software entirely. In early February 2026, after Anthropic released industry-specific plug-ins (legal, finance, sales, and others) for its Claude Cowork agent, investors sold software and data stocks heavily. Legal-information company Thomson Reuters fell 18% in one day, and a broad index of software and services stocks lost about $830 billion in market value in a week (ITPro, Feb 2026). Whether those fears turn out to be justified is still an open question.

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
text:
7.5 Open-weight vs. closed models
A closed (or proprietary) model can only be used through its maker’s apps or paid API; the model itself never leaves the company’s servers. An open-weight model is one whose trained weights are published, so anyone can download it, run it on their own hardware, and fine-tune it (train it further on their own data).









Closed models
Open-weight models




Examples (October 2026)
OpenAI’s GPT-6 models, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, Meta’s Muse Spark
DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, and GLM (China); Google’s Gemma, NVIDIA’s Nemotron, OpenAI’s gpt-oss (US); Mistral (France)


How you use them
Through the maker’s app or API
Download and run them yourself, or use a hosting company’s API


Cost
Pay per use, or a subscription
Free to download; you pay for the computers that run them (or for a hosted API, often cheap)


Your data
Sent to the model maker
Can stay on your own machines


Safety and updates
Handled by the maker
Your responsibility


Capability
The very best models are currently closed
Strong, and the gap is narrowing



Open-weight is not the same as open source. The Open Source Initiative’s definition of open-source AI also requires the training code and detailed information about the training data (OSI), which most open-weight releases don’t include. Licenses differ too: some (such as MIT and Apache 2.0) allow almost any use, while others add conditions, for example for very large companies. Read the license before you build a product on a model.
crumbs: 7  7. What AI Can Do Today

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
section: 7.6 The 2026 headline: cheap Chinese open-weight models
text:
7.6 The 2026 headline: cheap Chinese open-weight models
Chinese labs such as DeepSeek, Alibaba (Qwen), Moonshot AI (Kimi), Zhipu (GLM), and MiniMax release strong models as open weights and charge low prices for using them. In 2026 this became one of the biggest stories in the AI business:

Popularity. By spring 2026, Chinese models made up 41% of downloads on Hugging Face (the main site for sharing open models), overtaking US models. On OpenRouter (a service for reaching many models through one account), the six most-used models in mid-2026 were all Chinese open models (TechCrunch).
Quality. Moonshot claims its Kimi K3 (July 2026) competes with Anthropic’s top model of the time (a vendor claim), and it arrived months sooner than analysts expected (Fortune).

Effects on US AI companies:

Price pressure. US labs cut prices in 2026, which the trade press calls a price war with China’s labs (Capacity). OpenAI, for example, launched GPT-6 Sol and Luna at half the price of the models they replaced, crediting efficiency gains (TechCrunch).
US products built on Chinese models. Cursor says its Composer 2.5 coding model is built on Moonshot’s Kimi K2.5 (Cursor), and Cognition’s SWE-2 is “post-trained from Kimi K3” (Cognition).
Security and trust disputes. In February 2026 Anthropic said DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax had used about 24,000 fraudulent accounts to distill Claude: to collect millions of its answers and train their own models on them (Anthropic). Fast Chinese progress also feeds the debate over US export controls on AI.
Different bets in the US. Meta switched its flagship from open Llama models to a closed model, Muse Spark (VentureBeat), although in August 2026 it also released a smaller open-weight model, Muse Glimmer (Meta). Google (Gemma) and NVIDIA (Nemotron) keep releasing open models.

For you, this means more choice and lower prices, but also more homework: before sending company or customer data to any AI service, especially a low-cost one abroad, check where the data goes and what your school’s or employer’s rules allow.
crumbs: 7  7. What AI Can Do Today

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
text:
7.7 Narrow AI vs. AGI

Narrow AI is built for one task: a chess engine, a spam filter, a fraud detector, a self-driving system. It can be superhuman inside its niche and useless outside it.
Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a hypothetical AI that could learn and do essentially any intellectual task a human can, and carry skills over to problems it has never seen. There is no agreed definition or test for it.

Today’s LLMs sit in between. They are far more general than classic narrow AI: one model can write an essay, fix code, and read a chart. But their abilities are uneven, or “jagged”. The same kind of model that helped settle an open math problem can still miscount the letters in a word (How Large Language Models Work) or confidently invent a fact. Whether today’s methods will lead to AGI, and when, is hotly debated.
People also talk about superintelligence: AI far better than the best humans in nearly every field. The first chapter of the AI Safety part looks at the argument that building it could be catastrophic.
crumbs: 7  7. What AI Can Do Today

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
text:
7.8 Key takeaways

Keep the company, the model (the engine), and the app apart.
Learn the categories of AI tools; the product names will keep changing.
Cheap open-weight models, many from China, are reshaping prices and strategies.
Today’s AI is broad but uneven; AGI remains hypothetical and debated.
crumbs: 7  7. What AI Can Do Today

title: 7  7.  What AI Can Do Today
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
Why do people say that “AI” is a moving target? Use the Deep Blue example in your answer.






Suggested answer





A common definition of AI is “making machines do tasks that we used to think required human intelligence.” Once a machine can do such a task reliably, people stop thinking of it as AI. Playing championship chess was once a famous AI goal; after IBM’s Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, chess programs came to be seen as ordinary software. So the boundary of “AI” keeps moving as technology improves.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which statement best describes an AI model?

The app or website you type your questions into
The trained “engine”: a huge set of numbers (weights) plus the software that runs them
The company that builds and sells AI products
A database of facts that the AI looks answers up in







Suggested answer





b. The model is the trained engine inside a product. The app (a) is what you use to reach a model, and one app can offer several models. The company (c) builds models. A model is not a fact database (d): its knowledge is stored indirectly in its weights, which is one reason it can get facts wrong.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each type of AI system with what it does.








Type of AI

What it does




1. Reasoning model

A. Clicks, types, and fills in forms in a browser or desktop for you


2. Coding agent

B. Searches the web for several minutes and writes a report with citations


3. Computer-use agent

C. Works through a problem step by step before answering


4. Deep research agent

D. Reads a software project, edits code, and runs commands and tests









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 4 · True or false
“Open-weight” and “open source” mean exactly the same thing for AI models.






Suggested answer





False. An open-weight model publishes its trained weights so anyone can download and run it. The Open Source Initiative’s definition of open-source AI also requires the training code and detailed information about the training data, which most open-weight releases do not provide. Their licenses also vary, and some add conditions on use.





Question 5 · Short answer
What is generative AI? Name three kinds of content it can create.






Suggested answer





Generative AI is AI that creates new content from a request written in plain language (a prompt). It can create text, images, audio (voices and music), video, and computer code. Any three of these are correct.





Question 6 · Multiple choice
Which of the following is an example of narrow AI?

A spam filter that sorts your email
An AI that could learn any job a human can do, and carry skills to new problems
An AI that is far better than the best humans in nearly every field
Any AI system that runs in the cloud







Suggested answer





a. A spam filter is built for one specific task. Option b describes AGI and option c describes superintelligence; both are hypothetical. Where a system runs (d) has nothing to do with whether it is narrow or general.






Medium

Question 7 · Scenario
A friend says, “I don’t use AI.” Name three places where your friend is probably using AI anyway, and explain what it means that AI is “embedded” in products.






Suggested answer





Examples include: the spam filter in their email, fraud alerts from their bank, recommendations on shopping, video, or music sites, photo search on their phone, AI-written answers at the top of search results, and AI features in office software or messaging apps (for example Meta AI inside WhatsApp or Instagram).
“Embedded” means the AI is a feature inside another product rather than a separate app you open on purpose. You often use it without noticing, which is why it is worth checking what data such a feature can see.





Question 8 · Short answer
A classmate says: “I always use the same chat app, so I’m always using the same AI.” Explain why this is not quite right.






Suggested answer





The app and the model are different things. A chat app usually offers several models (bigger and smarter vs. smaller and faster), may pick one for you depending on your plan or settings, and switches to new model versions every few weeks or months. So the same app can give you different “AIs” over time, and different users of the same app may be using different models. (The reverse is also true: one model can power many different apps.)





Question 9 · Multiple choice
A hospital wants AI to summarize patient notes, but its rules say patient data must never leave its own data center. Which option fits best?

A closed model used through a free consumer chat app
An open-weight model running on the hospital’s own servers
A browser agent that copies the notes into a web form
A deep research agent that searches the web for similar notes







Suggested answer





b. With an open-weight model the hospital can download the weights and run the model on its own machines, so the data stays in-house. In exchange, the hospital must handle the hardware, setup, updates, and safety itself. Option a sends the data to an outside company. Options c and d also send data outside and don’t solve the summarizing task safely.





Question 10 · Compare
Give two advantages of closed models and two advantages of open-weight models.






Suggested answer





Closed models: the very best models are currently closed; nothing to install or run yourself; the maker handles updates and safety; easy to start through an app or API.
Open-weight models: free to download and often much cheaper to use; you can keep data on your own machines; you can fine-tune them on your own data; you are not locked in to one vendor’s service.
(Any two from each list are fine.)





Question 11 · Scenario
A tutorial from last year tells you to use a particular AI video app, but you can’t find it anywhere. Give two possible explanations, and describe how you would find a current alternative.






Suggested answer





Possible explanations: the product was shut down (OpenAI shut down its Sora video app in 2026), it was renamed or merged into another product, or it is no longer offered in your country or on your plan.
To find an alternative, think in terms of the category (here, “AI video generation”), then search for current options and check the companies’ own websites and the dates on articles. Be careful with AI answers about this: a model’s knowledge may be older than the change.





Question 12 · Short answer
In February 2026, Anthropic accused three Chinese labs of a “distillation” campaign. What does distillation mean here, and why would the company that built the original model object?






Suggested answer





Distillation means training your own model on the answers of a stronger model: you send it huge numbers of questions, collect its responses, and use them as training data. Anthropic said the labs used about 24,000 fraudulent accounts to do this with Claude. The original company objects because the copier gets much of the value of an expensive model cheaply, it breaks the terms of service, and (according to Anthropic) the copies may not keep the original model’s safety protections.





Question 13 · Multiple choice
Which statement about open-weight models in 2026 is supported by this page?

US companies stopped releasing open-weight models entirely.
Chinese open-weight models overtook US models in Hugging Face downloads.
Open-weight models are always more capable than closed ones.
Open-weight models can only be used inside China.







Suggested answer





b. By spring 2026, Chinese models made up 41% of Hugging Face downloads, overtaking US models. Option a is wrong: Google, NVIDIA, OpenAI, and Meta have all released open-weight models (although Meta’s flagship, Muse Spark, is closed). Option c is wrong: the very best models are currently closed, although the gap is narrowing. Option d is wrong: anyone can download open weights and run them anywhere (subject to the license).






Hard

Question 14 · Long answer
Explain three ways that cheap, capable Chinese open-weight models are affecting US AI companies. Give an example for each.






Suggested answer





A good answer covers three of these, with examples:

Price pressure. Customers can get “good enough” results much more cheaply, so US labs cut prices (for example, OpenAI launched its GPT-6 Sol and Luna models at half the price of the models they replaced; the trade press calls 2026 a price war).
US products built on Chinese models. Some US companies fine-tune Chinese open-weight models instead of training from scratch (Cursor’s Composer 2.5 is built on Kimi K2.5; Cognition’s SWE-2 is post-trained from Kimi K3).
Security and trust disputes. Anthropic accused DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax of distilling Claude through fraudulent accounts, and the rapid progress feeds the policy debate over export controls.
Different strategies. Some US companies respond by going closed (Meta’s Muse Spark), others by releasing their own open models (Google’s Gemma, NVIDIA’s Nemotron).






Question 15 · Scenario
A startup must choose between (1) a closed frontier model through its maker’s API and (2) a much cheaper open-weight model offered by a hosting company in another country. List at least four factors the founders should weigh, and say how they could decide.






Suggested answer





Factors to weigh:

Quality on their task (the very best models are closed, but a cheaper model may be good enough).
Cost at their expected volume.
Data: what data will be sent, where it is stored, and whether customers, laws, or contracts restrict that (especially for personal data sent abroad).
License terms of the open-weight model (some add conditions for commercial use or for large companies).
Reliability and support of the provider, and the risk of the service changing or disappearing.
Security and trust concerns, and any company or government rules about particular vendors.
Flexibility: open weights let them switch hosts or run the model themselves later.

How to decide: run a small test of both options on real (non-sensitive) examples, compare quality and cost, and check the data and license questions before committing. Many companies use a cheap model for simple tasks and a frontier model for hard ones.





Question 16 · Long answer
Is a modern chat assistant “narrow AI” or “AGI”? Make an argument, using the idea of “jagged” abilities.






Suggested answer





A strong answer says it is neither, at least by most definitions. It is much more general than classic narrow AI: one model can write, translate, summarize, code, and read images, and it can handle tasks nobody trained it for specifically. But it does not meet the usual definition of AGI, because its abilities are uneven (“jagged”): it may help with research-level math yet miscount the letters in a word or confidently invent a fact, and it cannot reliably learn and carry out any intellectual task a human can. Experts disagree on whether today’s methods will eventually lead to AGI, so a good answer acknowledges the debate.





Question 17 · True or false
“An AI model that can help settle an open math problem will also reliably handle simpler tasks, such as counting letters or getting basic facts right.”






Suggested answer





False. AI abilities are “jagged”: a model can be excellent at some very hard tasks and still fail at tasks that look easy to people. How Large Language Models Work explains why counting letters is hard for language models, and Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use explains why they sometimes invent facts. You must check AI output even when the model is impressive elsewhere.





Question 18 · Scenario
Your manager wants to “use AI” for three jobs: (a) summarizing 50 competitors’ web pages into a report with sources, (b) building a small internal web app, and (c) entering the same data into a web form 200 times. Which category of AI tool fits each job, and what is one risk to watch for in each?






Suggested answer







A deep research agent. Risk: factual errors or misread sources, so open and check the citations.


A coding agent (such as Claude Code). Risk: code that looks right but has bugs or security holes, so review and test it.


A computer-use / browser agent. Risk: it takes real actions, so mistakes (wrong data, wrong button) have real effects; web pages can also contain hidden instructions that try to trick it (prompt injection; see Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use). Watch it closely and start with a few entries.








Challenge

Question 19 · Hands-on
Make your own “as of today” snapshot. For three AI companies, find (1) their current main chat app, (2) their newest flagship model, and (3) whether that model is closed or open-weight. Use only each company’s own website or official docs, and record the date and link for each fact. Compare your results with this page: what has changed?






Suggested answer





Answers will vary with the date. A good answer:

uses official sources (for example a company’s models page, docs, or newsroom), not just an AI chat answer or a random blog;
records the date checked and a link for every fact;
correctly separates app names from model names;
notes at least one change since October 2026 (a renamed product, a new model version, a price change, or a shut-down service), or states that nothing changed and how that was verified.






Question 20 · Hands-on
Give the same prompt to two different assistants (or to two different models inside one app), for example: “In three sentences, explain the difference between an open-weight model and a closed model, and give one example of each.” Record which model answered each time, compare the answers, and check every factual claim against this page or an official source.






Suggested answer





Answers will vary. A good write-up names the app and the model used for each answer (not just “ChatGPT” or “Claude”), points out real differences (accuracy, length, examples chosen, how current the examples are), and flags any claim that turned out to be wrong or out of date. Noticing that a model gives an outdated example is a good lead-in to knowledge cutoffs (How Large Language Models Work) and hallucinations (Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use).





Question 21 · Hands-on
Pick one open-weight model on Hugging Face (huggingface.co) and find its license on the model’s page. Is it a standard license such as MIT or Apache 2.0, or a custom one? Could a company use the model in a paid product, and are there any conditions?






Suggested answer





Answers depend on the model. A good answer quotes the license name shown on the model page, opens the actual license text, and summarizes in plain English what it allows and requires (for example: commercial use allowed; attribution required; extra terms above a certain company size or number of users; restrictions on certain uses). It should also note that “open weights” does not automatically mean “anything goes”, which is why companies read the license before building on a model.

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
text:
8.1 Programming vs. training
You don’t need the math to use AI well, but you do need a correct mental model of what a large language model (LLM) does. It explains why LLMs write so fluently, why they sometimes make things up, why they “forget”, and how a coding agent can run commands on your computer.
In classic programming, a person writes the rules, for example a fraud check: if the amount is over $5,000 and the card was used abroad in the last hour, flag it. Machine learning works the other way around: you show the computer many examples with the right answers (thousands of transactions labeled “fraud” or “not fraud”), and it adjusts itself until it gets them right. The rules are learned, not written.

Classic program
Machine-learning model




Who writes the rules?
A programmer
Nobody; they are learned from examples


How do you change its behavior?
Edit the code
Train it on different examples, or give it different instructions


Can you see why it decided something?
Yes, read the code
Only partly; it is largely a “black box”

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
text:
8.2 Neural networks and deep learning
Almost all modern AI uses an artificial neural network, a design loosely inspired by the brain. It is made of many simple units (“neurons”) arranged in layers. Every connection between units has a number, called a weight (or parameter), that sets how strongly one unit influences the next. Training works like this: show the network an example, compare its answer with the correct one, and nudge every weight slightly in the direction that would have made the answer better. Repeat billions of times.
Deep learning means training neural networks with many layers. The largest models now have more than a trillion weights. Nobody sets these numbers by hand, and nobody can fully explain what each one does. Most LLMs use a network design called the transformer (the “T” in GPT), introduced by Google researchers in 2017 (paper).
crumbs: 8  8. How Large Language Models Work

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
section: 8.3 An LLM predicts the next token
text:
8.3 An LLM predicts the next token
A large language model (LLM) is a deep neural network trained on enormous amounts of text to do one thing: given some text, predict what comes next.
Text so far:  "Joe went to the"

The model's guesses for the next word (made-up numbers):
    store         31%
    park          12%
    doctor         6%
    ...
    circus         1%
    intelligent    0.0001%
To write a whole answer, the model repeats this: pick one of the likely next pieces, add it to the text, and predict again.
"The capital of France is"         -> predict ->  " Paris"
"The capital of France is Paris"   -> predict ->  "."
"The capital of France is Paris."  -> predict ->  (end of answer)
That sounds simple, but to predict text well across millions of books, websites, and programs, a model has to pick up grammar, facts, styles, reasoning patterns, and how code works. That’s why LLMs can seem to understand (whether they “really” do is debated).

8.3.1 Tokens
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude models overview
LLMs don’t read letters or whole words. Before the model sees your text, a program called a tokenizer splits it into tokens: a common word is often a single token, while a longer or rarer word is split into pieces. Spaces, punctuation, and digits count too. Each company uses its own tokenizer, so the same text can be a different number of tokens on different models.
As a rule of thumb, Anthropic’s docs say 1 million tokens is roughly 555,000 English words on the newest Claude models (about 750,000 on older ones, such as Claude Haiku 4.5). So in English, a token averages a bit more than half a word. Tokens matter because:

Prices for using models through an API are quoted per million tokens.
Limits, such as how much text a model can consider at once, are counted in tokens.
Quirks: some tasks that are easy for people are hard when you only see tokens.







Deeper dive: Why “how many r’s are in strawberry?” was hard





In 2024, popular chatbots famously answered that “strawberry” has two r’s (it has three) (TechCrunch). The model doesn’t see s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y; it sees a few tokens (something like straw + berry; the exact split depends on the tokenizer), and the letters inside a token are not directly visible to it.
Modern systems can work around this: a reasoning model can first spell the word out one letter at a time (so each letter becomes its own token) and then count, and an agent can run a one-line program that counts. When exact counting, spelling, or arithmetic matters, ask the AI to use a tool, or check the result yourself.





8.3.2 Choosing the next token
The model doesn’t output one word; it outputs a probability distribution: a probability for every token it knows. The software then samples from it: it usually picks a likely token, but not always the single most likely one. That’s why the same question asked twice can get two differently worded answers.






Deeper dive: Temperature





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Glossary · Model deprecations
Temperature is a setting that controls how random the sampling is. At a low temperature the model almost always picks the most likely token, so answers are more predictable. At a high temperature it picks less likely tokens more often, so answers are more varied, but also more likely to go off track. Even at temperature 0, the output is not guaranteed to be identical every time.
Chat apps choose these settings for you. Many developer APIs let you set the temperature, but some newer models no longer allow it: on Anthropic’s newest Claude models, the API rejects non-default temperature values, and Anthropic recommends steering the model through your prompt instead.
crumbs: 8  8. How Large Language Models Work

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
text:
8.4 How an LLM is trained

8.4.1 Pre-training
First, the model reads a gigantic collection of text: public web pages, books, articles, code, and other licensed or collected data, adding up to trillions of tokens. Over and over, it predicts the next token, and its weights are nudged whenever it is wrong. This pre-training takes months on thousands of specialized chips and uses a great deal of electricity.
The result is a base model: an excellent autocomplete, but not yet an assistant. Pretrained models “are not inherently good at answering questions or following instructions” (Anthropic glossary): ask one a quiz question and it might just continue with more quiz questions.


8.4.2 Post-training: from autocomplete to assistant
Post-training turns the base model into a helpful assistant:

Fine-tuning on example conversations teaches it to answer questions and follow instructions.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): people rank several answers to the same prompt, and the model is adjusted to prefer answers like the higher-ranked ones. (Reinforcement learning means learning by trial and error from rewards and penalties.)
Reinforcement learning on checkable tasks: the model practices problems whose answers can be verified automatically (math with a known result, code that must pass tests) and is rewarded for correct results. This is a key way reasoning models are trained (DeepSeek-R1 paper).

Post-training also shapes the model’s personality and what it refuses to do, and it can have side effects, such as a tendency to tell users what they want to hear (see the next chapter).
crumbs: 8  8. How Large Language Models Work

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
text:
8.5 Reasoning (“thinking”) models and effort
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Effort
A reasoning model (or “thinking” model) writes out intermediate steps, called thinking, before its final answer, like working a math problem on scratch paper. Thinking helps on multi-step problems such as math, planning, and debugging. The cost: answers are slower and more expensive, because thinking tokens are billed like other output tokens.
Most current flagship models let you control how much they think. Anthropic calls this dial effort, with five levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, and max; OpenAI and Google offer similar dials. Use low effort for quick, simple tasks and high effort for hard problems where quality matters more than speed.
crumbs: 8  8. How Large Language Models Work

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
text:
8.6 Multimodal models
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude models overview
A multimodal model handles more than one kind of data. All current Claude models accept text and images as input and produce text. Some other models, such as Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash, also accept audio and video. Creating images, video, or speech is usually done by separate, specialized models. As a developer, you can paste a screenshot (an error message, a page that looks wrong, a design sketch) and ask the AI about it.

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
section: 8.7 What a model knows: training data vs. context window
text:
8.7 What a model knows: training data vs. context window
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude models overview · Context windows
An LLM has two very different kinds of “memory”.

8.7.1 Long-term memory: frozen at the knowledge cutoff
What a model learned in training is stored in its weights and stops at the knowledge cutoff, the date its training data ends. Anthropic lists a “reliable knowledge cutoff” for each model: June 2026 for its newest models, February 2025 for Claude Haiku 4.5. A model knows little about later events and software versions, and may confidently describe an old version of a fast-changing tool (including Claude Code itself). Apps work around this with web search or documents you paste in.


8.7.2 Working memory: the context window
The context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider at once. It holds everything for the current request: hidden instructions from the app (the system prompt), the conversation so far, files, tool results, and the model’s own output, including its thinking.



Model (as of October 2026)
Context window
Roughly




Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5
1M tokens
555,000 words


Claude Haiku 4.5
200K tokens
150,000 words



Other frontier models also offer about 1 million tokens. Three things to know:

The model remembers nothing between requests. Its weights don’t change while you chat; each time you send a message, the whole conversation so far is fed to the model again. A new chat starts empty, unless an app’s “memory” feature adds saved notes to the context for you.
When the window fills up, older material must be dropped or summarized (called compaction), and details can get lost.
More context is not automatically better. Anthropic’s docs warn that as the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, which they call context rot. Give the model what it needs, not everything you have.

Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code shows how to manage the context window and effort in Claude Code.

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
section: 8.8 Why LLMs sometimes make things up
text:
8.8 Why LLMs sometimes make things up
An LLM generates the most plausible-sounding continuation; it does not look facts up. When it doesn’t know, a fluent, confident, wrong answer can still sound the most plausible. A 2025 paper by researchers at OpenAI and Georgia Tech argues that training and testing make this worse: “like students facing hard exam questions”, models are rewarded for guessing rather than admitting uncertainty (Kalai et al.). Such invented answers are called hallucinations; the next chapter covers how to catch them.
crumbs: 8  8. How Large Language Models Work

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
section: 8.9 Tools: how an LLM becomes an agent
text:
8.9 Tools: how an LLM becomes an agent
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How tool use works · How Claude Code works
By itself, an LLM can only produce text. A tool is a function that the software around the model lets it ask for: search the web, read a file, edit a file, run a terminal command, query a database. As Anthropic’s docs put it, “The model never executes anything on its own.”
   You: "Fix the failing test"
            |
            v
   +----------------+   1. asks for a tool:       +--------------------+
   |      LLM       | ---- run "npm test" ------> | The app (for       |
   |  (the model)   |                             | example, Claude    |
   |                | <--- the test output ------ | Code) runs it      |
   +----------------+   2. added to the context   +--------------------+
            |
            v
   3. Next step: read a file, edit the code, run the tests again ...
      (loop until the task is done, then reply to you)
The model replies with a structured request (which tool, with what inputs); the app runs the tool, often after asking your permission, and adds the result to the context; the model reads it and decides the next step. Repeating this loop is what makes an agent: an LLM plus tools plus a loop.
Claude Code works exactly this way: the model does the reasoning, and Claude Code (the harness around the model) provides the tools, runs them, and manages the context. That is how it can edit files and run commands for you, and why you must review what it does. See How Claude Code Works; the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard way to plug in more tools, is covered in MCP Servers.
crumbs: 8  8. How Large Language Models Work

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
text:
8.10 Key takeaways

An LLM predicts the next token; prices and limits are counted in tokens.
Pre-training gives knowledge (up to a cutoff); post-training makes an assistant.
The context window is working memory; outside it, the model remembers nothing.
Tools plus a loop turn an LLM into an agent such as Claude Code.

title: 8  8.  How Large Language Models Work
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is the main difference between classic programming and machine learning?






Suggested answer





In classic programming, a person writes the rules and the computer follows them exactly. In machine learning, nobody writes the rules: the computer is shown many examples with the right answers and adjusts itself (its weights) until it gets them right, so the rules are learned from data.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
In a neural network, what are weights (also called parameters)?

The amount of memory the model needs
Numbers on the connections between units that are adjusted during training
The rules a programmer writes for the model
The number of questions a user can ask per day







Suggested answer





b. Weights are the numbers that set how strongly one unit influences the next. Training nudges them, example after example, until the network gives good answers. They are not written by a programmer (c), and they have nothing to do with memory size (a) or usage limits (d), although more weights do mean a bigger model.





Question 3 · True or false
An LLM answers questions by looking them up in a database of facts stored inside it.






Suggested answer





False. An LLM generates text by predicting one token at a time. Its knowledge is spread across billions of weights, not stored as a list of facts it can look up. That is why it can produce a fluent answer that sounds right but is wrong.





Question 4 · Short answer
What is a token? Is a token the same as a word?






Suggested answer





A token is a small piece of text that the model reads and writes. A tokenizer splits text into tokens before the model sees it. A token is not the same as a word: a common word may be one token, but a long or rare word can be split into several tokens, and spaces, punctuation, and digits also count. On average, an English token is a bit more than half a word on the newest Claude models.





Question 5 · Matching
Match each term with its description.








Term

Description




1. Pre-training

A. The date after which the model’s training data ends


2. RLHF

B. Reading trillions of tokens and predicting the next one, over and over


3. Context window

C. People rank answers, and the model is adjusted toward the preferred kind


4. Knowledge cutoff

D. A function the model can ask the app to run


5. Tool

E. The maximum amount of text the model can consider at once









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → E, 4 → A, 5 → D.





Question 6 · Multiple choice
What does the word “deep” in deep learning refer to?

The model understands topics deeply
The neural network has many layers
The training data comes from the “deep web”
The model thinks for a long time before answering







Suggested answer





b. Deep learning means training neural networks with many layers of units. It says nothing about understanding (a), data sources (c), or thinking time (d); “thinking” is a separate feature of reasoning models.






Medium

Question 7 · Calculate
Use the rule of thumb on this page: 1 million tokens is about 555,000 English words on the newest Claude models. Roughly how many tokens is a 300-page book of about 90,000 words? Would it fit in a 200K-token context window? In a 1M-token window?






Suggested answer





A token is about 0.555 words, so 90,000 words ÷ 0.555 ≈ 162,000 tokens. That fits in a 200K-token window, but only just: about 38,000 tokens would be left for instructions, your questions, and the model’s answers (including its thinking). It fits easily in a 1M-token window. (It is only an estimate: the real number depends on the tokenizer and the text. On an older tokenizer, such as Claude Haiku 4.5’s, the same book is closer to 120,000 tokens.)





Question 8 · Short answer
You ask an AI assistant the same question twice, in two new chats, and get two differently worded answers. Why?






Suggested answer





At each step the model produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens, and the software samples from it: it usually picks a likely token, but not always the single most likely one. Small differences early in the answer lead to different wording later. (The app may also use a different model or settings, or the model may have been updated.)





Question 9 · Scenario
You ask an AI chatbot (with web search turned off) how to use a feature that was added to a software tool last month. It confidently describes how the feature worked in an older version. Explain why, and give two ways to get a better answer.






Suggested answer





The model’s knowledge comes from training data that ends at its knowledge cutoff, so it doesn’t know about last month’s change. Because it generates plausible text rather than admitting it doesn’t know, it describes what it learned about the older version.
Better options: turn on web search, paste the relevant part of the official documentation (or the changelog) into the chat so it is in the context window, or check the official docs yourself.





Question 10 · Multiple choice
Which of these happens during post-training?

The model reads trillions of tokens of web pages and books
People rank several answers, and the model is adjusted toward the preferred ones
The tokenizer splits your prompt into tokens
The app adds tool results to the context window







Suggested answer





b. That is RLHF, one part of post-training (along with fine-tuning on example conversations and reinforcement learning on checkable tasks). Option a is pre-training. Options c and d happen every time you use the model, not during training.





Question 11 · Short answer
You start a new chat, and the AI has no idea what you discussed yesterday. Why? And how can an app’s “memory” feature still let it know some things about you?






Suggested answer





The model itself remembers nothing between requests: its weights don’t change while you chat, and it only “knows” what is in its context window for the current request. A new chat starts with an empty conversation. A memory feature works by saving notes about earlier chats and automatically adding them to the context of new chats, so the model can read them.





Question 12 · Ordering
Put these steps of a tool call in the right order.

A. The app runs the tool (after your permission, if needed) and adds the result to the context.
B. The model reads the result and decides what to do next.
C. The model replies with a structured request: which tool to use, with what inputs.
D. You ask the agent to do a task.







Suggested answer





D → C → A → B. Then the loop repeats (more tool calls) until the task is done and the model replies to you. Note that the model never runs anything itself; the app does.





Question 13 · Multiple choice
Why does a reasoning model at high effort usually take longer and cost more?

It uses a larger context window
It writes many thinking tokens before the answer, and those are billed as output
It must search the web before answering
It runs on a different, more expensive tokenizer







Suggested answer





b. Thinking is extra generated text, so it takes time and is billed like other output tokens. Higher effort generally means more thinking. The context window size (a), web search (c), and the tokenizer (d) are not what effort controls.





Question 14 · Short answer
What does multimodal mean? Give one practical way to use it while building a web app.






Suggested answer





A multimodal model handles more than one kind of data, for example text and images. While building a web app, you can paste a screenshot of an error message, of a page that looks wrong in the browser, or of a design sketch, and ask the AI to explain the error, find the layout problem, or build the page.






Hard

Question 15 · Long answer
Explain why counting the letters in a word such as “strawberry” can be hard for an LLM, and describe two ways modern AI systems get around the problem.






Suggested answer





The model doesn’t see individual letters. The tokenizer turns the word into a few tokens (pieces of the word), and the letters inside each token are not directly visible to the model; it only knows them indirectly from training. So it has to “guess” the spelling from memory, which can fail.
Workarounds: (1) reasoning: the model first spells the word out one letter at a time, so each letter becomes its own token, and then counts; (2) tools: an agent writes and runs a tiny program that counts the letters exactly. For important counts and calculations, you can also check the result yourself.





Question 16 · Scenario
Early in a very long session you told an AI assistant, “Always answer in bullet points.” Since then you have pasted a 400-page report and chatted for hours. Now it answers in paragraphs and seems to have forgotten details from the start. Explain what is probably happening, and suggest three remedies.






Suggested answer





Everything (instructions, the report, all the messages) competes for space in the context window. When it fills up, older material is dropped or summarized (compaction), so early instructions and details can be lost. Even before it is full, very long contexts reduce accuracy and recall (context rot).
Remedies: start a fresh chat for a new task and restate the key instructions; give only the relevant parts of the report instead of all 400 pages; repeat important instructions or put them somewhere the app always loads (in Claude Code, a CLAUDE.md file); ask for a summary of the important points, then continue in a new chat from that summary.





Question 17 · Long answer
An LLM can only produce text, yet Claude Code can edit files and run commands on your computer. Explain how this works, and why it makes reviewing the agent’s actions important.






Suggested answer





Claude Code gives the model tools (read a file, edit a file, run a shell command, and so on). The model never runs anything itself: it replies with a structured request to use a tool, Claude Code (the harness) runs the tool, often after asking you for permission, and puts the result back into the context. The model then decides the next step, and the loop repeats until the task is done. LLM + tools + loop = an agent.
Because the tools take real actions (changing files, running commands, possibly deleting things or reaching the internet), a wrong or misled model can cause real damage. That is why you review permission requests and diffs, keep your work in Git, and stay “in the loop”.





Question 18 · Compare
Compare a base model with an assistant model. What does pre-training contribute, what does post-training contribute, and why would a base model alone make a poor chatbot?






Suggested answer





Pre-training (predicting the next token over trillions of tokens of text) gives the model its broad knowledge of language, facts, and code, producing a base model: a powerful autocomplete. Post-training (fine-tuning on example conversations, RLHF, and reinforcement learning on checkable tasks) teaches it to follow instructions, answer helpfully, reason through problems, and refuse harmful requests, producing an assistant model.
A base model alone is a poor chatbot because it simply continues text: given a question, it might continue with more questions or ramble instead of answering.





Question 19 · True or false
“If you set the temperature to 0, the model’s answers will always be correct.”






Suggested answer





False. Temperature only controls how random the choice of the next token is. At temperature 0 the model mostly picks its single most likely token, but the most likely answer can still be wrong (a hallucination is often a confident, “likely” answer). Even at temperature 0, outputs are not guaranteed to be identical every time, and Anthropic’s newest models don’t let you change the temperature at all.





Question 20 · Scenario
You can choose the effort level for each request. Which level would you choose for (a) renaming a variable in one file, (b) tracking down a bug that only happens sometimes and involves many files, and (c) a quick question about what a command does? Explain the trade-off.






Suggested answer






Low effort: a simple, well-defined task. (b) High (or higher) effort: a hard, multi-step problem where careful reasoning pays off. (c) Low effort: a quick lookup.

The trade-off: more effort means more thinking, which usually improves quality on hard problems but is slower and uses more tokens (more cost, or more of your usage limit). On easy tasks, extra thinking mostly wastes time and tokens.






Challenge

Question 21 · Hands-on
Ask an AI assistant: “Which model are you, and what is your knowledge cutoff?” Then look up the same model on its maker’s official documentation. Do the answers match? Explain why they might not.






Suggested answer





Answers vary. A good answer records the app, the model the app says it is using, the assistant’s claims, and the official values with a link and date. They may not match because a model only “knows” about itself what was in its training data or system prompt; it can be unsure or wrong about its own name, version, or cutoff, and the docs may distinguish a “reliable knowledge cutoff” from a broader “training data cutoff”. The official documentation is the source to trust.





Question 22 · Hands-on
Ask an AI assistant to count how many times a given letter appears in a long, unusual word or phrase (for example, the letter “s” in “Mississippi’s assistants”). Then ask it to spell the word out letter by letter first and count again. Compare the two answers and explain any difference.






Suggested answer





Results vary by model. (The correct count for the example: “Mississippi’s” has 5 s’s and “assistants” has 4, so 9 in total.) A good answer reports both attempts and connects any difference to tokens: when the word is spelled out letter by letter, each letter becomes visible to the model as a separate token, so counting gets easier. If the assistant ran code to count, note that this is a tool, which is another reliable workaround.





Question 23 · Hands-on
If an AI app you have access to lets you choose the effort or thinking level, give it the same tricky logic puzzle at the lowest and the highest level. Compare the time it took, the quality of the answer, and (if shown) the amount of thinking.






Suggested answer





Answers vary. A good write-up states the app, model, and levels used; reports the response times; checks whether each answer is actually correct; and draws a conclusion about the trade-off (higher effort is usually slower but more reliable on hard problems, while on easy problems the difference may be small). If the app doesn’t offer an effort setting, say so and describe what it offers instead.

title: 9  9.  Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use
text:
9.1 Limits you will run into
AI tools are powerful and fallible. This page covers where they fail, how to protect your data and your computer, the legal and ethical questions, and what AI means for jobs. One idea runs throughout: you stay responsible for what you do with AI.
A hallucination is a confident, plausible answer that is false. It is not rare: one public database lists more than 2,000 court decisions about filings that relied on AI-invented material, such as fake case citations (AI Hallucination Cases, October 2026). Sycophancy is also well documented: research from Anthropic found that assistants trained with human feedback often match the user’s views over the truth, partly because people rate agreeable answers higher (Sharma et al., 2023). Bias matters most when AI helps make decisions about people, such as hiring or lending, which is why regulators treat those uses as high-risk.

What it looks like
What to do




Hallucination
Invented facts, quotes, or citations; code that calls functions that don’t exist

Describes an old version of a tool; unaware of recent events
Give it current docs; check dates

9.1.1 A verification habit
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Reduce hallucinations

Match your checking to the stakes. A birthday poem needs none; a number in a report, legal or medical advice, or code that touches customer data needs a lot.
Go to the source. Open every citation and confirm it says what the AI claims.
Run it. Run and test code, and read the changes before you accept them.
Make “I don’t know” acceptable. Anthropic’s docs recommend explicitly allowing the model to say it doesn’t know, which reduces hallucinations.
A second AI can spot problems, but agreement between two AIs is not proof.
