title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
12.1 Two ways to talk to a computer: GUI and CLI
Most of the time you control your computer by pointing and clicking. Developers also control computers by typing commands, and AI coding agents do exactly the same. This page explains what the command line is, why it is worth learning, and how to read a command. You will install and open Bash on the next page.
Think of a CLI as texting your computer precise instructions instead of pointing at things. The command line is the line where you type those instructions. In everyday speech, “the command line”, “the CLI” and “the terminal” are often used to mean the same thing.
A GUI is easier to discover: you can see your options. A CLI is faster, more precise, and easy to automate - once you know a few commands.
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
A GUI (graphical user interface) is what you use every day: windows, icons, menus, and a mouse or trackpad. To create a folder, you right-click in Finder or File Explorer and choose “New Folder”.
A CLI (command-line interface) is a text conversation with the computer. You type a command, press Enter, and the computer answers with text. To create a folder named progress-reports, you type:

mkdir progress-reports
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
12.2 Terminal vs. shell
Two programs work together when you use the command line:

The terminal is the app that gives you a window to type in and shows the text that comes back. Examples: the Terminal app on a Mac, the Git Bash window on Windows, Windows Terminal, and the terminal panel inside code editors such as VS Code.
The shell is the program running inside the terminal. It reads each command you type, runs it, and shows you the result.

An analogy: the terminal is a chat window; the shell is who you are chatting with. Different shells understand different “languages” (sets of commands and rules):








Shell
Where you meet it
Notes




Bash
Most Linux computers and servers; Git Bash on Windows; also available on Macs
The shell this book teaches. The name stands for “Bourne Again SHell”: it was written as a free replacement for Stephen Bourne’s older shell.


zsh (“Z shell”)
The default shell on Macs since macOS 10.15 Catalina (2019)
Nearly identical to Bash for the everyday commands in this book.


PowerShell
Built into Windows
Different commands, such as Get-ChildItem to list files.


CMD (Command Prompt)
Built into Windows (the older shell)
Different commands, such as dir to list files.



This book teaches Bash: it is the standard shell on the Linux servers that run most web apps, it comes with Git on Windows, and most tutorials and AI tools assume it. Mac users can type the same commands in zsh.






Windows: PowerShell and CMD are not Bash



PowerShell and CMD are good shells, but their commands and rules are different. PowerShell even accepts a few Bash-looking names such as ls and cd as shortcuts for its own commands, but Bash options such as ls -la then fail with an error. When you follow this book on Windows, use Git Bash (set up on the next page).
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
12.3 Why learn the command line?

Developer tools live there. Git, Python, Node.js and npm are all used by typing commands. Some developer tools have no graphical version at all.
Speed and automation. Suppose a folder project1 holds 100 files and you want to move the 50 whose names contain 2025 into project2. In Finder or File Explorer that means a lot of careful clicking. In Bash it is one line (the * is a wildcard meaning “anything” - see Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching):
mv project1/*2025* project2
Because commands are just text, you can also save them in a file and rerun them whenever you like - a script (see Bash Scripts).
Servers have no GUI. The computers that run websites and apps in the cloud are usually Linux machines without a screen. People manage them by typing commands, very often in Bash.
AI coding agents work in the terminal - see the next section.
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
section: 12.4 The command line in the age of AI
text:
12.4 The command line in the age of AI
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How Claude Code works · Configure permissions
Claude Code, the main AI tool in this course, runs in your terminal: you start it by typing claude. According to its documentation, it can run any command you could run yourself - listing files, running tests, using Git, creating, moving, or deleting files. Depending on its permission mode, it may show you a command such as rm -r old-reports and ask “Do you want to proceed?” before running it, or let an automatic safety check approve routine commands without asking you (details in Permissions, Modes, and Safety).
To answer that question sensibly - and to understand afterwards what an agent did to your files - you must be able to read commands. You don’t need to memorize hundreds of them. You need to recognize the common ones (the next pages cover them) and know how to look up the rest.
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
12.5 Anatomy of a command
A command is like a short sentence. Its words are separated by spaces:
ls -l -a documents
│  └─┬─┘ └───┬───┘
│    │       └── argument: what to work on
│    └────────── options: how to do it
└─────────────── command name: what to do

The command name comes first. It names the program to run (ls lists the contents of a folder).
Options (also called flags) change how the command behaves. They start with a dash:

Short options are one dash and one letter: -l, -a. Several short options can be combined, and their order usually doesn’t matter: ls -la means the same as ls -l -a and ls -a -l.
Long options are two dashes and a word: --all, --help. They are easier to read but longer to type. Not every program supports them.

Arguments tell the command what to act on - usually file or folder names, such as documents.










Command line
Command
Options
Arguments




pwd
pwd
(none)
(none)


ls -l
ls
-l
(none)


ls -la documents
ls
-l and -a
documents


mkdir progress-reports
mkdir
(none)
progress-reports


cp -r website website-backup
cp
-r
website and website-backup



Three rules that save a lot of frustration:

Spaces matter. ls -l works, but ls-l makes Bash look for a command named ls-l, which doesn’t exist (bash: ls-l: command not found).
Capitalization matters. -l and -L are two different options.
Silence is success. Many commands print nothing when they work. If something goes wrong, you get an error message.







Deeper dive: subcommands and options that take a value





Some programs, such as git and npm, have subcommands: git status, git commit, npm install. Some options also take a value:
git commit -m "Fix typo on home page"
Here git is the command, commit is the subcommand, -m is an option meaning “message”, and "Fix typo on home page" is the value of that option. The quotes keep the four words together as one value (quotes have their own pages: Writing to Files and Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes).
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
12.6 The prompt
When the shell is ready for your next command, it shows a prompt: a bit of text ending in a symbol such as $ or %. Prompts look different on different computers, but they work the same way.

MacWindows (Git Bash)Linux


maria@MacBook-Air ~ %
User maria, on a computer named MacBook-Air, currently in her home folder (~). The % at the end is the zsh prompt symbol. If Maria starts Bash instead, the prompt ends with $.


sam@DESKTOP-4F7Q2K1 UCRT64 ~
$
User sam, on the computer DESKTOP-4F7Q2K1, in his home folder (~). The word in the middle is a label for Git Bash’s environment (older versions of Git show MINGW64). The $ on the second line is where Sam types.


maria@laptop:~$
User maria, on the computer laptop, in the home folder (~), followed by the $ prompt symbol.



In this book, commands you should type appear in boxes without a prompt, so you can copy them with the copy button. When we show a command together with its output, we put $ in front of the command, as many websites do:
$ pwd
/Users/maria
Don’t type the $ (or %). It belongs to the prompt, not to the command. (pwd prints the folder you are in; it’s explained in Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd.)
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
12.7 Key takeaways

GUI = point and click. CLI = type commands and read text answers.
The terminal is the window; the shell is the program that interprets your commands. This book uses Bash (Git Bash on Windows; Mac users can use the default zsh).
A command = command name + options + arguments, separated by spaces.
Don’t type the prompt symbol ($ or %).
AI coding agents run shell commands for you - reading those commands is your job.

Next: Getting Bash on Your Computer.
crumbs: 12  12. What Is the Command Line?

title: 12  12.  What Is the Command Line?
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What do the abbreviations GUI and CLI stand for? Give one example of creating a folder with each.






Suggested answer





GUI = graphical user interface; CLI = command-line interface.

GUI: right-click in Finder (Mac) or File Explorer (Windows) and choose “New Folder”.
CLI: type a command such as mkdir progress-reports and press Enter.






Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which statement best describes the difference between a terminal and a shell?

They are two names for exactly the same program.
The terminal is the window you type in; the shell is the program that interprets and runs your commands.
The shell is the window you type in; the terminal runs the commands.
The terminal is only for Mac; the shell is only for Windows.







Suggested answer





b. The terminal is the app that shows the window and text; the shell runs inside it and does the work. Option a is how people speak casually, but they are technically different programs. Option c swaps the roles. Option d is wrong: both Mac and Windows have terminals and shells.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
Which shell is the default on new Mac user accounts (since macOS 10.15 Catalina)?

Bash
PowerShell
zsh
CMD







Suggested answer





c. zsh. Bash was the Mac default before Catalina and is still available. PowerShell and CMD are Windows shells.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each shell with its description.








Shell

Description




1. Bash

A. The older built-in Windows shell; lists files with dir


2. zsh

B. The shell this book teaches; standard on Linux servers and in Git Bash


3. PowerShell

C. The default shell on modern Macs


4. CMD

D. Built into Windows; lists files with Get-ChildItem









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → D, 4 → A.





Question 5 · True or false
When a tutorial shows $ ls -l, you should type the $ too.






Suggested answer





False. The $ (or % in zsh) is the prompt: the shell displays it to show it is ready. You type only ls -l. If you type the $, Bash treats it as the command name and you get an error such as bash: $: command not found.





Question 6 · Short answer
Many commands print nothing at all when you run them. What does that usually mean?






Suggested answer





It usually means the command succeeded. Most commands stay silent when they work and print an error message only when something goes wrong (“no news is good news”).






Medium

Question 7 · Short answer
Identify the command name, the option(s), and the argument(s) in:
ls -l -t projects






Suggested answer






Command name: ls
Options: -l and -t
Argument: projects






Question 8 · Write the command
Rewrite ls -l -a -t as a single combined group of short options. Does the order of the letters matter?






Suggested answer





ls -lat (or ls -alt, ls -tla, …). For simple on/off options like these, the order doesn’t matter - all of these versions mean the same thing.





Question 9 · Multiple choice
Which of these is a long option?

-a
-la
--all
all







Suggested answer





c. Long options start with two dashes followed by a word. -a is a short option, -la is two short options combined, and all without dashes would be treated as an argument (for example, a file named all).





Question 10 · Predict the output
Sam types ls-l (forgetting the space) in Git Bash and presses Enter. What happens, and why?






Suggested answer





He gets an error: bash: ls-l: command not found. Bash splits a command line into words at the spaces. Without a space, the whole thing ls-l is one word, so Bash looks for a program named ls-l, which doesn’t exist.





Question 11 · Fill in the blank
Complete the sentence: “The ______ is the app that shows you a window; the ______ is the program that reads your commands and runs them. In this book we use the ______ shell.”






Suggested answer





“The terminal is the app that shows you a window; the shell is the program that reads your commands and runs them. In this book we use the Bash shell.”





Question 12 · Scenario
A classmate on Windows opens PowerShell, types ls -la, and gets an error. The same command works for you in Git Bash. Explain what is going on and what your classmate should do.






Suggested answer





PowerShell is a different shell with its own commands and rules. It accepts ls as a shortcut for its own Get-ChildItem command, but it doesn’t understand Bash options such as -la, so it reports an error. Your classmate should open Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows) and run the command there.





Question 13 · Short answer
Give three reasons why developers use the command line even though a GUI is easier to learn.






Suggested answer





Any three of:

Many developer tools (Git, npm, Python, Claude Code) are command-line tools, and some have no GUI.
It is faster for many tasks, such as moving all files whose names match a pattern with one command.
Commands can be saved in scripts and rerun (automation).
Servers in the cloud usually have no GUI, so they are managed by typing commands.
AI coding agents run shell commands, and you need to read and understand them.







Hard

Question 14 · Long answer
Some people say “Now that AI can write and run commands for me, I don’t need to learn the command line.” Explain why this course disagrees.






Suggested answer





Agents such as Claude Code run commands on your computer, with your files. Depending on its permission mode, Claude Code may show you a command and ask whether to proceed - you can only make a good decision if you can read the command (for example, recognize that rm -r deletes a folder and everything in it). Even when it runs commands without asking, you are still responsible for the result and need to understand what it did, spot mistakes, and fix problems. You also need the command line to set things up yourself (installing tools, using Git, starting Claude Code with claude). A good answer mentions: agents run real commands, you approve or review them, and you stay responsible.





Question 15 · Scenario
Claude Code shows you this command and asks “Do you want to proceed?”:
rm -r old-reports
Identify the parts of the command. Which part would you double-check before answering, and why?






Suggested answer






Command name: rm (remove, i.e. delete)
Option: -r (“recursive”: delete a folder and everything inside it)
Argument: old-reports (what will be deleted)

Double-check the argument: is old-reports really the folder you want to delete, and is it the one in the current folder (not some other folder with the same name)? Deleting with rm is permanent - there is no trash can (see Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting).





Question 16 · Short answer
Explain in your own words why the single command mv project1/*2025* project2 can save a lot of time compared with Finder or File Explorer. What does each part do?






Suggested answer






mv moves files.
project1/*2025* means “every file in project1 whose name contains 2025” - the * wildcards match any characters before and after 2025.
project2 is the destination folder.

In a GUI you would have to find and select each matching file by hand (easy to miss one). The command selects them all by a rule, in one step, and you can reuse it whenever you need it.





Question 17 · Short answer
In the command below, name the command, the subcommand, the option, and the option’s value. Why are the quotes needed?
git commit -m "Add contact page"






Suggested answer






Command: git
Subcommand: commit
Option: -m (the commit message)
Value: Add contact page

Spaces separate the words of a command. Without quotes, Add, contact and page would be three separate words; the quotes keep them together as one value for -m.





Question 18 · Compare
Maria (Mac) sees the prompt maria@MacBook-Air ~ %. Sam (Windows, Git Bash) sees sam@DESKTOP-4F7Q2K1 UCRT64 ~ with a $ on the next line. What do the two prompts have in common, and what does the ~ tell you in both?






Suggested answer





Both show the user name, the computer name, and the current folder, followed by a prompt symbol (% for zsh, $ for Bash) that says “ready for your next command”. In both, ~ means the user is currently in their home directory. The exact look of a prompt depends on the shell and its settings, but its job is the same everywhere.

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
text:
13.1 Set up your command line
To follow the rest of this book you need a command line that speaks Bash. A Mac has one built in. On Windows you install Git for Windows, which includes Git Bash. This page gets you set up and has you run your first commands. Pick your operating system in the tabs below; the book remembers your choice.
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
text:
MacWindows (Git Bash)


Every Mac comes with the Terminal app - there is nothing to install.

Press Cmd+Space to open Spotlight, type Terminal, and press Enter. (Or, in Finder, open Applications > Utilities and double-click Terminal.)
A window opens with a prompt such as:
maria@MacBook-Air ~ %

The % tells you the shell is zsh, the Mac’s default since macOS 10.15 Catalina. For the commands in this book, zsh and Bash work the same way, so you can stay in zsh (see the deeper dive below for the few differences). If your prompt ends in $ instead, your account is set up to use Bash - also fine.
To try real Bash, type bash and press Enter. macOS first prints this notice:
The default interactive shell is now zsh.
To update your account to use zsh, please run `chsh -s /bin/zsh`.
For more details, please visit https://support.apple.com/kb/HT208050.
Then the prompt changes to bash-3.2$ (the program’s name and version); the $ shows that you are in Bash. The Mac’s built-in Bash is an old version, 3.2, which is fine for this book. Type exit to go back to zsh.
Git itself is set up later, in Installing and Configuring Git.


Windows doesn’t include Bash, so you install Git for Windows. It contains Git (the version-control tool you will use from What Is Version Control? on) and Git Bash, a Bash command line for Windows.

Go to git-scm.com/install/windows and click the link that downloads the latest x64 version. (On a Windows-on-ARM laptop, for example one with a Snapdragon processor, choose Git for Windows/ARM64 Setup instead.)
Run the downloaded installer (Git-...-64-bit.exe). If Windows asks whether to allow the app to make changes, click Yes.
Click Next on each screen to accept the defaults, except on these three screens:







Screen
What to choose




Select Components
Also check Add a Git Bash Profile to Windows Terminal.


Choosing the default editor used by Git
The default, Vim, is hard for beginners. Choose Use Visual Studio Code as Git’s default editor if VS Code is already installed; otherwise choose Use the Nano editor by default.


Adjusting the name of the initial branch in new repositories
Choose Override the default branch name for new repositories and keep main in the box.



On the screen Adjusting your PATH environment, keep the option marked (Recommended): “Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software”.
On the last options screen the button says Install. When installation finishes, check Launch Git Bash and click Finish.

Opening Git Bash later:

Start menu: type Git Bash and press Enter. It opens in your home folder.
From a folder in File Explorer: right-click the folder (or empty space inside it) and choose Open Git Bash here, which opens Git Bash in that folder. On Windows 11, click Show more options first (or press Shift+F10).
In Windows Terminal: click the ⌄ arrow next to the tabs and choose Git Bash. To make Git Bash the default, go to Settings > Startup > Default profile.

The Git Bash prompt takes two lines:
sam@DESKTOP-4F7Q2K1 UCRT64 ~
$
Older versions of Git show MINGW64 instead of UCRT64; it makes no difference for this book.
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
text:
13.2 Your first commands
Type each of these commands and press Enter after each one:
echo hello
whoami
pwd
date
Output:

MacWindows (Git Bash)


hello
maria
/Users/maria
Tue Oct  6 10:42:17 EDT 2026


hello
sam
/c/Users/sam
followed by the current date and time (its format may differ slightly from the Mac’s).




echo prints whatever you give it (more in Writing to Files).
whoami prints your user name.
pwd prints the folder you are in - right now, your home folder (see Files, Folders, and Paths).
date prints the current date and time.

If you see an error such as command not found, check the spelling and the spaces, and make sure you are in the right program (see the next sections).
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
section: 13.3 Copy, paste, and closing the window
text:
13.3 Copy, paste, and closing the window
Copying commands from this book into the terminal saves typing, but the keys differ from what you are used to:










Mac Terminal
Git Bash window
Windows Terminal




Copy
Cmd+C
Just select the text with the mouse (it is copied automatically), or Ctrl+Insert
Ctrl+C while text is selected


Paste
Cmd+V
Shift+Insert, or right-click and choose Paste
Ctrl+V



In a terminal, Ctrl+C normally means “stop the running command”, not “copy”. In the Git Bash window, Ctrl+V doesn’t paste by default either. (You can turn on Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V under Options > Keys.)
To finish, type exit and press Enter: this ends the shell session. Git Bash then closes its window. On a Mac, quit the Terminal app with Terminal > Quit Terminal (Cmd+Q). If you started Bash inside zsh, exit takes you back to zsh.
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
section: 13.4 Windows: make sure you are in Git Bash
text:
13.4 Windows: make sure you are in Git Bash
Windows has two other built-in command lines, and Windows Terminal often opens one of them by default:








Program
Prompt looks like
Lists files with




PowerShell
PS C:\Users\sam>
Get-ChildItem (also accepts ls, but not Bash options such as ls -la)


CMD (Command Prompt)
C:\Users\sam>
dir


Git Bash
sam@DESKTOP-4F7Q2K1 UCRT64 ~ and $ on the next line
ls



The commands in this book are Bash commands, so type them in Git Bash. If a command from this book fails in a window whose prompt starts with PS or looks like C:\...>, you are in the wrong program. (Occasionally an installer has to be run in PowerShell; its instructions say so explicitly.)
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
section: 13.5 Claude Code and Git for Windows
text:
13.5 Claude Code and Git for Windows
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Advanced setup · Terminal guide for new users
Claude Code runs natively on Windows. Its documentation lists Git for Windows as optional but recommended: Git for Windows provides Git Bash, which Claude Code uses for its Bash tool (the tool Claude uses to run shell commands). Without Git for Windows, Claude Code runs shell commands through PowerShell instead. Because this book teaches Bash, install Git for Windows first. Installing Claude Code itself is covered in Installing Claude Code.
Claude Code’s own beginner terminal guide tells you to accept every default in the Git installer. That is enough for Claude Code; the three changes recommended above simply make Git friendlier to use.
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
section: 13.6 WSL: a full Linux inside Windows (optional)
text:
13.6 WSL: a full Linux inside Windows (optional)
The Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) runs a real Linux system (Ubuntu by default) inside Windows, using a lightweight virtual machine. You install it by opening PowerShell as administrator, running wsl --install, and restarting the computer (Windows 10 version 2004 or later, or Windows 11). Inside WSL you can install any Linux software, but it is a separate world: your Windows C: drive appears as /mnt/c, and Linux has its own home folder.
WSL is popular with professional developers, and you may want to explore it later (Microsoft’s WSL install guide). This book uses Git Bash because it installs in minutes, works directly with your normal Windows folders, and also gives you Git.






Deeper dive: zsh vs. Bash on a Mac





For the commands in this book (cd, ls, pwd, mkdir, rm, echo, quotes, variables, export), zsh and Bash use the same syntax. A few differences can still surprise you in zsh:

Comments typed at the prompt. In Bash, everything after a # is a comment and is ignored. In zsh (by default) it is not: pasting ls -l   # long list passes #, long and list to ls, which then complains that they don’t exist. Leave the comment out, or run setopt interactivecomments first.
Wildcards that match nothing. ls *.csv in a folder without CSV files gives zsh: no matches found: *.csv in zsh; Bash passes the pattern on to ls, which reports that the file doesn’t exist (see Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching).
rm * asks first. zsh asks for confirmation before deleting every file in a folder with rm *; Bash doesn’t.
A few quoting and echo details. For example, echo "a\nb" prints two lines in zsh but a\nb in Bash, and zsh doesn’t split unquoted variables at spaces. If an example on the quoting pages behaves differently for you, type bash and try it again.
Settings files. zsh reads ~/.zshrc; Bash reads ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile (see Environment Variables).

If you prefer, chsh -s /bin/bash makes Bash your default shell (chsh -s /bin/zsh switches back). It’s not necessary for this course.









Deeper dive: where are my Windows files in Git Bash?






Your home folder ~ is /c/Users/sam, which is C:\Users\sam (see Files, Folders, and Paths).
The C: drive is /c, the D: drive is /d, and so on.
In Git Bash, / on its own is not your C: drive: it is the folder where Git is installed (C:\Program Files\Git). To get to your files, use cd ~ or cd /c.
If OneDrive backs up your Desktop and Documents folders, those folders live inside your OneDrive folder (whose name starts with OneDrive). Run ls ~ to see where your Documents folder really is.
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 13  13.  Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Which app does a Mac user open to use the command line?

Finder
Terminal
Git Bash
PowerShell







Suggested answer





b. Terminal comes with every Mac. Finder is the Mac’s file browser (a GUI). Git Bash is the Windows program you install with Git for Windows, and PowerShell is a Windows shell.





Question 2 · Short answer
What is Git Bash, and how do Windows users get it?






Suggested answer





Git Bash is a Bash command line for Windows. It is installed together with Git when you install Git for Windows (from git-scm.com/install/windows).





Question 3 · True or false
Mac users must install a Bash program before they can follow this book.






Suggested answer





False. Every Mac has the Terminal app with zsh (the default) and Bash already installed. The commands in this book work the same in zsh.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each prompt with the program that shows it.








Prompt

Program




1. maria@MacBook-Air ~ %

A. PowerShell


2. PS C:\Users\sam>

B. Git Bash


3. C:\Users\sam>

C. zsh in Mac Terminal


4. sam@DESKTOP-4F7Q2K1 UCRT64 ~ (and $ on the next line)

D. CMD (Command Prompt)









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → D, 4 → B.





Question 5 · Short answer
Give two ways to open Git Bash on Windows after installing Git for Windows.






Suggested answer





Any two of:

Search the Start menu for Git Bash.
Right-click a folder in File Explorer and choose Open Git Bash here (on Windows 11, click Show more options first).
In Windows Terminal, choose Git Bash from the ⌄ menu (if you added the Git Bash profile during installation).






Question 6 · Multiple choice
What does the command whoami print?

Your computer’s name
Your user name
The current folder
The shell you are using







Suggested answer





b. For example maria or sam. The current folder is printed by pwd. The computer’s name is part of the prompt, but whoami doesn’t print it.






Medium

Question 7 · Scenario
Sam pastes ls -la into a window whose prompt is PS C:\Users\sam> and gets an error. What is wrong, and what should he do?






Suggested answer





The PS shows that he is in PowerShell, not Bash. PowerShell has its own commands and doesn’t understand Bash options such as -la. He should open Git Bash (Start menu, or the ⌄ menu in Windows Terminal) and run the command there.





Question 8 · Short answer
When installing Git for Windows, which three screens does this book tell you to change, and what do you choose on each?






Suggested answer






Select Components: also check Add a Git Bash Profile to Windows Terminal.
Choosing the default editor used by Git: choose Visual Studio Code (if installed) or Nano instead of the default, Vim.
Adjusting the name of the initial branch in new repositories: choose Override the default branch name and keep main.

Everything else: accept the defaults (including the Recommended PATH option).





Question 9 · Predict the output
Sam (Windows user name sam) opens Git Bash from the Start menu and types whoami and then pwd. What does he see?






Suggested answer





sam
/c/Users/sam
Git Bash opened from the Start menu starts in his home folder, C:\Users\sam, which Git Bash writes as /c/Users/sam.





Question 10 · Scenario
In the Git Bash window, Sam selects a command with the mouse and presses Ctrl+C to copy it, then Ctrl+V to paste it - and nothing is pasted. What should he do instead?






Suggested answer





In the Git Bash window, selecting text already copies it, so no key is needed (or he can press Ctrl+Insert). To paste, he should press Shift+Insert or right-click and choose Paste. Ctrl+C means “stop the running command” in a terminal, and Ctrl+V doesn’t paste in this window unless he enables Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V under Options > Keys.





Question 11 · Short answer
Maria types bash in her Mac’s Terminal. What does she see, how can she tell that she is now in Bash, and how does she get back to zsh?






Suggested answer





macOS prints a notice saying that the default interactive shell is now zsh. Then the prompt changes to bash-3.2$ - the $ at the end shows she is in Bash (zsh shows %). Typing exit takes her back to zsh.





Question 12 · True or false
According to the Claude Code documentation, Claude Code cannot run on Windows unless Git for Windows is installed.






Suggested answer





False. Git for Windows is optional but recommended. With it, Claude Code uses Git Bash for its Bash tool; without it, Claude Code runs shell commands through PowerShell instead.





Question 13 · Short answer
What is WSL, and how do you install it?






Suggested answer





WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) runs a real Linux system (Ubuntu by default) inside Windows, using a lightweight virtual machine. To install it, open PowerShell as administrator, run wsl --install, and restart the computer. This book uses Git Bash instead.






Hard

Question 14 · Compare
Compare Git Bash and WSL: what each one is, where your C: drive appears, and why this book uses Git Bash.






Suggested answer














Git Bash
WSL




What it is
Bash and common command-line tools running as ordinary Windows programs (installed with Git for Windows)
A real Linux system running inside Windows


C: drive
/c
/mnt/c


Home folder
Your Windows home (/c/Users/sam)
A separate Linux home folder



This book uses Git Bash because it is quick to install, works directly with your normal Windows folders, and installs Git at the same time. WSL is more powerful (you can install any Linux software) but adds a separate system to manage.





Question 15 · Find the bug
Maria copies this line from a website into her Mac’s Terminal (zsh):
ls -l   # show details
She gets errors saying that #, show and details don’t exist. Why? Give two ways to avoid the problem.






Suggested answer





In Bash, # starts a comment, so the rest of the line is ignored. In zsh’s default settings, comments typed at the prompt are not recognized, so #, show and details are passed to ls as names of files to list - and those files don’t exist. To avoid it:

paste only the command (ls -l), without the comment, or
run setopt interactivecomments in zsh (or switch to Bash by typing bash).






Question 16 · Scenario
Sam’s Windows Terminal always opens PowerShell. He would like it to open Git Bash instead. What are his options?






Suggested answer






For a single tab: click the ⌄ arrow next to the tabs and choose Git Bash.
Permanently: in Windows Terminal, go to Settings > Startup > Default profile and choose Git Bash.

Both require the Git Bash profile (the Add a Git Bash Profile to Windows Terminal option in the installer). He can also simply open Git Bash from the Start menu.





Question 17 · Long answer
A classmate installed Git for Windows by clicking Next on every screen. What will be different for them compared with someone who followed this page’s three recommendations? Is it a problem?






Suggested answer






Editor: Git will open Vim when it needs a message typed (for example for a commit without -m). Vim is hard to use - even quitting requires a special command.
Branch name: new repositories will start on a branch called master instead of main, while GitHub uses main by default.
Windows Terminal: there will be no Git Bash profile in Windows Terminal (Git Bash still works from the Start menu).

None of this is serious. Git and Git Bash work fine, and the editor and branch name can be changed later with git config (see Installing and Configuring Git), or by running the installer again.





Question 18 · Scenario
In Git Bash, Sam types cd / and then ls. He sees folders such as bin, etc and usr, but none of his own files. Where is he, and how does he get back to his files?






Suggested answer





In Git Bash, / is the folder where Git is installed (C:\Program Files\Git), not his C: drive. His files are in his home folder. cd ~ (or just cd) takes him home, to /c/Users/sam; cd /c takes him to the top of the C: drive.
crumbs: 13  13. Getting Bash on Your Computer (Mac and Windows)

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
14.1 Files and folders (directories)
Before you can move around your computer with Bash, you need a mental map of how the computer organizes files. This page gives you that map. The commands that use the map (pwd, ls, cd, …) are on the next pages.
Because folders can contain folders, two different files can have the same name as long as they are in different folders. For example, projects/website/README.txt and projects/data-analysis/README.txt are two completely separate files.

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
A file holds data: a document, a photo, a program, a spreadsheet.
A folder holds files and other folders. In the command-line world a folder is usually called a directory. The two words mean the same thing.

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
section: 14.2 The file system is a tree
text:
14.2 The file system is a tree
All of the folders on a computer form one big upside-down tree. The folder at the very top is called the root. On Mac and Linux the root is written as a single forward slash: /.
/                         <- the root (top of the tree)
├── Applications
├── Users
│   ├── maria             <- maria's home directory
│   │   ├── Desktop
│   │   ├── Documents
│   │   │   └── notes.txt
│   │   └── Downloads
│   └── sam               <- sam's home directory
└── ...
Windows organizes files by drive (usually C:). Git Bash (the Bash program we use on Windows) shows the C: drive as the folder /c, so the same ideas apply.

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
14.3 Your home directory and ~
Every user account has a personal folder called its home directory. Your Desktop, Documents and Downloads folders live inside it. When you open a new terminal window, you usually start out in your home directory.

MacWindows (Git Bash)Linux


/Users/maria


/c/Users/sam (Windows itself writes this as C:\Users\sam)


/home/maria



(Throughout this book, Maria uses a Mac and Sam uses Windows. Replace maria or sam with your own user name.)
The tilde character ~ is Bash’s shortcut for “my home directory”. These two lines mean exactly the same thing to Maria’s Bash on a Mac:
/Users/maria/Documents/notes.txt
~/Documents/notes.txt
~ is handy because it works for every user on every computer - your ~ is your home directory, my ~ is mine.

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
section: 14.4 Paths: the address of a file
text:
14.4 Paths: the address of a file
A path is the “address” of a file or folder. It lists the folders you pass through to reach it, separated by forward slashes /:
/Users/maria/Documents/notes.txt
Read it left to right: start at the root /, go into Users, then maria, then Documents, and there you will find notes.txt.






Windows users: use forward slashes in Bash



Windows normally writes paths with backslashes (C:\Users\sam). In Bash, always use forward slashes (/c/Users/sam). Bash treats a backslash as a special “escape” character, so backslash paths will not work the way you expect.

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
14.5 Full (absolute) paths vs. relative paths
At every moment, the terminal is “standing” in one folder. That folder is called your current working directory - think of it as the “you are here” marker on a map.
There are two ways to write the path to a file:









Full path (also called absolute path)
Relative path




Starts from…
the root / (or your home ~)
your current working directory


Starts with…
/ or ~
anything else (a name, . or ..)


Example
/Users/maria/Documents/notes.txt
Documents/notes.txt


Works from any folder?
Yes - it always means the same file
No - its meaning depends on where you are



An analogy: a full path is like a complete mailing address (“123 Main St, Springfield”). A relative path is like directions from where you are standing (“two doors down on the left”).
For example, if Maria’s working directory is /Users/maria, the relative path Documents/notes.txt refers to /Users/maria/Documents/notes.txt. If her working directory were /Users/maria/Desktop, the same relative path would point to /Users/maria/Desktop/Documents/notes.txt - a different place (which probably doesn’t exist).

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
14.6 The special names . and ..
Every folder contains two special entries:

. (one dot) means this folder - the current directory.
.. (two dots) means the parent folder - the folder one level up.

You can use them inside relative paths. Using the practice files below, if you are standing in bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes:







Relative path
Means




ideas.txt
the file ideas.txt in the current folder


./ideas.txt
the same file (. = this folder)


..
the parent folder, documents


../reports/annual-summary.txt
go up to documents, then down into reports


../..
two levels up: bash-tutorial-files


../../music/song1.mp3
up two levels, then down into music

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
14.7 Hidden files (dot files)
Files and folders whose names start with a dot, such as .gitignore, .env, or .claude, are hidden. The plain ls command and the Mac’s Finder normally don’t show them. (Windows File Explorer shows most of them; it hides only items specially marked as hidden, such as Git’s .git folder.) Programs use hidden files to store settings. You will meet several important ones later: Git keeps its history in a hidden .git folder, and Claude Code keeps its settings in .claude folders.

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
section: 14.8 Tips for naming files and folders
text:
14.8 Tips for naming files and folders

Avoid spaces. quarterly-report.txt or quarterly_report.txt is much easier to type in Bash than quarterly report.txt. If a name does contain spaces, you must put quotes around it, e.g. "My Documents/notes.txt". (Quotes get their own pages later.)
Treat names as case-sensitive. Linux treats Notes.txt and notes.txt as two different files. Mac and Windows usually don’t, but code you write often ends up running on Linux servers, so it’s best to be consistent.







Deeper dive: Windows paths in Git Bash





Git Bash translates Windows drives into folders under /:



Windows writes
Git Bash writes




C:\Users\sam\Documents
/c/Users/sam/Documents


D:\photos
/d/photos



If you ever need the Windows-style version of your current location (for example, to paste into File Explorer’s address bar), Git Bash’s pwd -W command prints it (e.g. C:/Users/sam/Documents). File Explorer accepts forward slashes too.









Deeper dive: ~ is expanded by Bash, not by the computer





~ is not a real folder name. Bash replaces ~ with your home directory’s full path before running a command. This only happens when ~ appears at the start of a word and is not inside quotes. For example, ls ~/Documents works, but ls "~/Documents" looks for a folder literally named ~. This is one reason to avoid unnecessary quotes around paths that start with ~.

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
14.9 Practice files
Download the practice files and unzip them into the Documents folder in your home directory, so that you have the folder ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files (the next pages assume this location): Download the practice files (zip)






Windows: is your Documents folder inside OneDrive?



If OneDrive backs up your Documents folder, the “Documents” you see in File Explorer is actually inside your OneDrive folder (whose name starts with OneDrive), not at ~/Documents. If cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files later says “No such file or directory”, run ls ~ to find the OneDrive folder and look for Documents/bash-tutorial-files inside it (see Getting Bash on Your Computer).


bash-tutorial-files/
├── README.txt
├── documents/
│   ├── notes/
│   │   ├── ideas.txt
│   │   └── meeting-notes.txt
│   └── reports/
│       ├── annual-summary.txt
│       └── quarterly-report.txt
├── music/
│   ├── song1.mp3
│   └── song2.mp3
├── pictures/
│   ├── family.jpg
│   └── vacation.jpg
└── projects/
    ├── data-analysis/
    │   ├── analysis.py
    │   └── data.csv
    └── website/
        ├── index.html
        └── styles.css
The practice questions below assume this tree is located at /Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files (Maria is using a Mac).

title: 14  14.  Files, Folders, and Paths
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is another name for a “folder”?






Suggested answer





A directory. The two words mean the same thing.





Question 2 · Short answer
What is the name of the folder at the very top of the file system, and how is it written on Mac and Linux?






Suggested answer





It is called the root, and it is written as a single forward slash: /.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
What does ~ stand for in Bash?

The root of the file system
The current working directory
Your home directory
The parent of the current directory







Suggested answer





c. ~ is shorthand for your home directory (for example /Users/maria). The root is / (a), the current directory is . (b), and the parent directory is .. (d).





Question 4 · Matching
Match each symbol with its meaning.



Symbol

Meaning




1. / (by itself)

A. the parent folder


2. .

B. your home directory


3. ..

C. the root of the file system


4. ~

D. the current folder









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 5 · True or false
Two different files can have exactly the same name as long as they are stored in different folders.






Suggested answer





True. A file is identified by its full path, not just its name. projects/website/README.txt and projects/data-analysis/README.txt are two different files.





Question 6 · Short answer
What is the “current working directory”?






Suggested answer





It is the folder the terminal is currently “standing in” - the “you are here” marker. Relative paths are interpreted starting from this folder.






Medium

Question 7 · Multiple choice
Which of the following is a full (absolute) path?

documents/notes/ideas.txt
../reports/annual-summary.txt
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/README.txt
./README.txt







Suggested answer





c. It starts with /, the root, so it means the same file no matter where you are. Options a, b and d are relative paths: they start with a name, .. or ., so their meaning depends on the current working directory.





Question 8 · Write the path
Maria’s working directory is /Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files. Write the relative path to quarterly-report.txt.






Suggested answer





documents/reports/quarterly-report.txt
(./documents/reports/quarterly-report.txt is also correct.)





Question 9 · Write the path
Write the full path to song2.mp3 in two different ways: once starting with / and once starting with ~.






Suggested answer






/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/music/song2.mp3
~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/music/song2.mp3

Both are full paths because ~ always means Maria’s home directory, /Users/maria.





Question 10 · Write the path
Maria’s working directory is .../bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes. Write the shortest relative path to annual-summary.txt.






Suggested answer





../reports/annual-summary.txt
.. goes up from notes to documents; from there, go down into reports.





Question 11 · Short answer
Starting in .../bash-tutorial-files/projects/website, which folder does the relative path ../.. refer to?






Suggested answer





bash-tutorial-files. The first .. goes up from website to projects; the second goes up from projects to bash-tutorial-files.





Question 12 · Convert
A Windows user named Sam sees this path in File Explorer: C:\Users\sam\Documents\budget.xlsx. How should Sam type this path in Git Bash?






Suggested answer





/c/Users/sam/Documents/budget.xlsx (or ~/Documents/budget.xlsx). The drive C: becomes the folder /c, and backslashes become forward slashes.





Question 13 · Short answer
Why are files such as .gitignore and .env not shown by a plain ls command or by the Mac’s Finder? What are such files usually used for?






Suggested answer





Their names start with a dot, which makes them hidden files. Programs usually use hidden files and folders to store settings and configuration (for example Git’s .git folder or Claude Code’s .claude folder).






Hard

Question 14 · Predict
Maria’s working directory is /Users/maria/Desktop. She refers to the relative path Documents/notes.txt. Which file does that path point to, and why might she get a “No such file or directory” error?






Suggested answer





It points to /Users/maria/Desktop/Documents/notes.txt, because relative paths start from the current working directory (the Desktop). Her Documents folder is actually /Users/maria/Documents, not inside the Desktop, so the file is probably not there. She could use ~/Documents/notes.txt or ../Documents/notes.txt instead.





Question 15 · Simplify
Simplify the relative path documents/notes/../reports/./annual-summary.txt (working directory: bash-tutorial-files).






Suggested answer





documents/reports/annual-summary.txt.
documents/notes/.. goes into notes and right back out to documents, and ./ means “this folder”, so it adds nothing.





Question 16 · Short answer
A script uses the relative path data.csv. It works when Maria runs it from projects/data-analysis but fails when she runs it from her home directory. Explain why, and give one way to make it work from anywhere.






Suggested answer





A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. From projects/data-analysis, data.csv refers to the file in that folder; from the home directory it refers to ~/data.csv, which doesn’t exist. Using a full path, such as ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/projects/data-analysis/data.csv, works from any folder (or she can first move into the right folder).





Question 17 · Long answer
Give two reasons why it is a good idea to avoid spaces in file and folder names when you work with the command line, and explain what you must do if a name does contain a space.






Suggested answer






Bash uses spaces to separate the pieces of a command, so a name such as quarterly report.txt looks like two separate names (quarterly and report.txt).
Names without spaces are faster to type and less error-prone (and the same goes for code, URLs and servers, where spaces often cause problems).

If a name does contain a space, put the whole path in quotes, for example "quarterly report.txt" (or put a backslash before the space: quarterly\ report.txt).





Question 18 · True or false
The command ls "~/Documents" lists the contents of your Documents folder.






Suggested answer





False. Bash only replaces ~ with your home directory when the ~ is not inside quotes. With the quotes, Bash looks for a folder literally named ~. Use ls ~/Documents instead.

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
15.1 Where am I? pwd
Three commands do most of the work of getting around in Bash: pwd shows where you are, ls shows what is there, and cd moves you somewhere else. This page walks through them with the practice files from Files, Folders, and Paths.
To follow along, open Bash (Terminal on a Mac, Git Bash on Windows - see Getting Bash on Your Computer) and unzip the practice files into your Documents folder, so that you have the folder ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files: Download the practice files (zip). The outputs below come from Maria’s Mac; Git Bash shows the same information with small differences, which are pointed out along the way.
pwd stands for print working directory. It prints the full path of your current working directory - the “you are here” marker. A new terminal window usually starts in your home directory:
Output:
Whenever you are unsure where you are, run pwd. Many beginner mistakes come from running a command in the wrong folder.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
pwd


MacWindows (Git Bash)


/Users/maria


/c/Users/sam
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
15.2 What’s here? ls
ls (short for list) shows the contents of the current folder:
ls
Output (Maria’s home folder):
Desktop         Downloads       Movies          Pictures
Documents       Library         Music           Public
Your list will be different. On Windows you will see more entries, including a few system files such as NTUSER.DAT - leave those alone.

15.2.1 Look inside another folder without moving
Give ls a path as an argument, and it lists that folder instead. A relative path (starting from where you are, the home folder):
ls Documents/bash-tutorial-files
Output:
README.txt      documents       music           pictures        projects
A full path, starting with ~, works no matter where you are:
ls ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/music
Output:
song1.mp3       song2.mp3






Git Bash looks slightly different




Git Bash puts a / after every folder name (documents/), because it is set up to run ls -F whenever you type ls (-F is explained below).
ls arranges names in columns that fit your window, so the layout varies. The order can vary too: a Mac lists capitalized names such as README.txt first; Git Bash may list it last.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
15.3 Moving around: cd
cd (change directory) makes another folder your current working directory. Like most commands, it prints nothing when it works. From your home folder, go into the practice files (a relative path) and check where you are:
cd Documents/bash-tutorial-files
pwd
Output:
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
Now go two levels down and look around:
cd documents/notes
pwd
ls
Output:
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes
ideas.txt               meeting-notes.txt

15.3.1 Going up with ..
.. means “the parent folder” (one level up). You can use it alone or inside a longer relative path:
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/documents
$ cd ../projects/website
$ pwd
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/projects/website
$ cd ../..
$ pwd
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
../projects/website means “up one level (to bash-tutorial-files), then down into projects/website”. ../.. means “up two levels”.


15.3.2 Full paths, home, and back again







Command
Takes you to




cd /Users/maria/Documents
A full path - works from anywhere. (Sam would type cd /c/Users/sam/Documents.)


cd ~/Documents
The same folder, using ~ for the home folder.


cd ~
Your home folder.


cd (nothing after it)
Also your home folder.


cd -
Back to the folder you were in just before; the shell prints its path.



$ cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/pictures
$ cd
$ pwd
/Users/maria
$ cd -
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/pictures
In zsh (the Mac’s default shell), cd - shows the same path written with ~: ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/pictures.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
15.4 More ls options
These examples run inside ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files.







Option
Meaning




-F
Add a symbol that shows the type: / after folders (and * after programs).


-a
Show all items, including hidden ones whose names start with a dot.


-l
Long format: one item per line, with details.


-t
Sort by time last modified, newest first.


-r
Reverse the sort order.


-h
With -l, show sizes in human-readable units (4.0K, 2.4M, 1.1G) instead of bytes.



Short options can be combined in any order: ls -la, ls -lh, ls -ltr.

15.4.1 ls -F: which names are folders?
ls -F
Output:
README.txt      documents/      music/          pictures/       projects/


15.4.2 ls -a: show hidden items
ls -a
Output:
.               README.txt      music           projects
..              documents       pictures
. is the current folder and .. is its parent. Any hidden files would appear here too. On a Mac you may also see .DS_Store, a hidden file that Finder creates to remember how a folder is displayed. It is harmless.


15.4.3 ls -l: the long listing
ls -l
Output:
total 0
-rw-r--r--  1 maria  staff    0 Oct 22  2025 README.txt
drwxr-xr-x  4 maria  staff  128 Oct 22  2025 documents
drwxr-xr-x  4 maria  staff  128 Oct 22  2025 music
drwxr-xr-x  4 maria  staff  128 Oct 22  2025 pictures
drwxr-xr-x  4 maria  staff  128 Oct 22  2025 projects
Here is how to read the README.txt line:








Part
Example
Meaning




First character
-
- = a regular file, d = a directory (folder).


Next nine characters
rw-r--r--
Permissions: who may read, change, or run it (see the deeper dive below).


Number
1
Number of links. You can ignore it.


Owner and group
maria staff
The user who owns the item, and a group of users.


Size
0
Size in bytes (the practice files are empty). For a folder, this is not the size of what is inside.


Date
Oct 22  2025
When it was last modified. Recent changes show the time of day instead of the year (anything older than about six months shows the year).


Name
README.txt
The file or folder name.



You can ignore the total line. Your dates will differ - they depend on when and how you unzipped the files. On a Mac you might see an @ right after the permissions (-rw-r--r--@): it means macOS has attached extra information to the file, for example that it was downloaded from the internet. In Git Bash the columns are the same, but the owner and group may look different.


15.4.4 -t, -r, and -h

ls -lt lists the most recently changed items first. Add -r to reverse that: ls -ltr puts the newest item at the bottom, right above your next prompt - handy in a folder with many files.
ls -lh shows sizes such as 2.4M instead of a long number of bytes.

The practice files are empty and all have the same date, so -t and -h change little there. Try them on your Downloads folder instead: ls -lth ~/Downloads.






Deeper dive: reading permissions (rwxr-xr-x)





The nine permission characters are three groups of three: what the owner may do, what the group may do, and what everyone else may do. In each group, r means read, w means write (change or delete), and x means execute (run it as a program; for a folder, x means you may enter it). A dash means “not allowed”.

-rw-r--r--: a file that the owner can read and change, and that everyone else can only read.
drwxr-xr-x: a folder; the owner can do everything, others can list it and enter it but cannot change it.

You will give a file the x permission with chmod +x in Bash Scripts. In Git Bash these letters are only an approximation of Windows’ own permission system.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
15.5 When cd or ls fails
Run from inside bash-tutorial-files, these two commands fail:
$ cd notes
bash: cd: notes: No such file or directory
$ cd README.txt
bash: cd: README.txt: Not a directory

No such file or directory: nothing with that name exists here. Check for a typo, and check where you are with pwd and ls. In this case, notes is inside documents, so you need cd documents/notes.
Not a directory: you tried to cd into a file. You can only cd into folders.

In zsh (the Mac default) the same errors read cd: no such file or directory: notes and cd: not a directory: README.txt. ls complains about a missing name too: ls: musik: No such file or directory on a Mac, or ls: cannot access 'musik': No such file or directory in Git Bash.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
section: 15.6 Work faster: Tab, the up arrow, and clear
text:
15.6 Work faster: Tab, the up arrow, and clear

Tab completion. Type the first few letters of a file or folder name and press Tab - the shell fills in the rest. In your home folder, typing cd Doc and pressing Tab gives cd Documents/. If several names match, the shell completes as much as it can and can list the choices: in Git Bash, press Tab a second time; zsh on a Mac shows the list right away (more in Getting Help and Working Faster). Tab completion saves typing and prevents typos, including wrong capitalization.
Command history. Press the up arrow (↑) to bring back earlier commands, and the down arrow (↓) to go forward again. Edit a command with ← and →, then press Enter to run it.
clear (or Ctrl+L) wipes the screen. It doesn’t change any files.

More shortcuts are in Getting Help and Working Faster.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
15.7 Getting help for ls
ls has many more options. In Git Bash, ls --help lists them all. On a Mac, ls --help doesn’t work: the Mac’s ls is a different version (the “BSD” version), which doesn’t understand --help or most other long options. Use man ls instead (scroll with the arrow keys, press q to quit). Git Bash, in turn, does not include man.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
15.8 Command summary







Command
What it does




pwd
Print the full path of the current folder.


ls / ls path
List the current folder / list another folder.


ls -F, ls -a, ls -l
Mark folders with /; include hidden items; long format.


ls -ltr, ls -lh
Oldest first (newest at the bottom); human-readable sizes.


cd path
Go to a folder (relative or full path).


cd .., cd ../..
Go up one level, two levels.


cd, cd ~
Go to your home folder.


cd -
Go back to the previous folder.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 15  15.  Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd
text:
Practice Questions
Unless a question says otherwise, Maria’s practice files are in /Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files (see the tree on Files, Folders, and Paths).

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What does pwd stand for, and what does it print?






Suggested answer





Print working directory. It prints the full path of the current working directory - the folder the terminal is “standing in”, for example /Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which command moves you to the parent of the current folder?

cd .
cd ..
cd ~
cd -







Suggested answer





b. .. means the parent folder. cd . “moves” to the current folder (so nothing changes), cd ~ goes to your home folder, and cd - goes back to the folder you were in before.





Question 3 · True or false
Typing cd with nothing after it does nothing.






Suggested answer





False. cd on its own takes you to your home directory, exactly like cd ~.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each ls option with what it does.



Option

Effect




1. -a

A. reverse the sort order


2. -l

B. sizes like 4.0K or 2.4M (with -l)


3. -t

C. show hidden items too, including . and ..


4. -r

D. mark folders with a trailing /


5. -h

E. sort by time modified, newest first


6. -F

F. long format with details









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → F, 3 → E, 4 → A, 5 → B, 6 → D.





Question 5 · Short answer
What does cd - do? What does it print?






Suggested answer





It takes you back to the folder you were in just before your last cd, and it prints the path of that folder so you can see where you landed (Bash prints the full path; zsh writes your home folder as ~).





Question 6 · Multiple choice
In the output of ls -l, what does a line that starts with d describe?

A deleted file
A directory (folder)
A document
A hidden file







Suggested answer





b. The first character shows the type: d for a directory, - for a regular file. Deleted files don’t appear at all, documents are just regular files (-), and hidden files are recognized by a name starting with a dot, not by the first character of the line.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
Maria is in bash-tutorial-files. Write one command that lists the contents of projects/website without changing her current folder.






Suggested answer





ls projects/website
Giving ls a path lists that folder; Maria stays where she is. (A full path such as ls ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/projects/website also works.)





Question 8 · Predict the output
Maria is in bash-tutorial-files and runs:
cd documents/reports
cd ../notes
pwd
What does pwd print?






Suggested answer





/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes
cd documents/reports goes down two levels. ../notes goes up to documents and then down into notes.





Question 9 · Write the command
Maria is in documents/notes. Using a relative path, write one command that takes her to projects/data-analysis.






Suggested answer





cd ../../projects/data-analysis
../.. goes up from notes to documents and then to bash-tutorial-files; from there, go down into projects/data-analysis.





Question 10 · Write the command
Sam (Windows, Git Bash) unzipped the practice files into C:\Users\sam\Documents. Write two different commands that take him to the bash-tutorial-files folder from anywhere.






Suggested answer





cd /c/Users/sam/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
Both are full paths, so they work from any folder. In Git Bash, the C: drive is written /c, and ~ is /c/Users/sam.





Question 11 · Compare
What is the difference between ls -lt and ls -ltr? Which one shows the most recently changed file at the bottom of the list?






Suggested answer





Both show the long format sorted by modification time. ls -lt puts the newest item first. ls -ltr reverses the order, so the oldest comes first and the newest is at the bottom - right above your next prompt, where it’s easy to see.





Question 12 · Short answer
Read this line from ls -l:
drwxr-xr-x  4 maria  staff  128 Oct 22  2025 projects
Is projects a file or a folder? Who owns it? Does 128 mean the files inside it take up 128 bytes?






Suggested answer





It is a folder (the line starts with d). It is owned by the user maria (group staff). No: for a folder, the size column is not the size of its contents - it only describes the folder’s own bookkeeping, so you can ignore it.





Question 13 · Multiple choice
Which command shows hidden files such as .gitignore?

ls -h
ls -a
ls -l
ls -F







Suggested answer





b. -a (“all”) includes names that start with a dot. -h is a common trap: it means human-readable sizes, not “hidden”. -l adds details and -F marks folders, but neither shows hidden files.





Question 14 · Fill in the blank
Maria is in bash-tutorial-files.

cd pictures/family.jpg fails with the error “______”, because family.jpg is a file.
cd picture (missing the s) fails with the error “______”.







Suggested answer






Not a directory - you can only cd into folders.
No such file or directory - nothing named picture exists in the current folder.







Hard

Question 15 · Find the bug
Maria opens a new terminal window and types:
cd bash-tutorial-files
She gets a “No such file or directory” error, although the folder definitely exists. Explain why, and give two commands that work.






Suggested answer





A new terminal starts in her home folder, /Users/maria. The relative path bash-tutorial-files is looked up there, but the folder is inside Documents. Either of these works:
cd Documents/bash-tutorial-files
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
(The second is a full path, so it works from any folder.) Running pwd and ls first would have shown the problem.





Question 16 · Scenario
Sam (Git Bash) types ls in bash-tutorial-files and sees documents/, music/ and so on, with slashes. Maria types the same command on her Mac and sees no slashes. Who is right, and why the difference?






Suggested answer





Both are right - they see the same folders. Git Bash is set up so that typing ls actually runs ls -F, which adds a / after each folder name. Maria can get the same display by typing ls -F herself.





Question 17 · Predict the output
Maria runs these four commands. What appears on the screen?
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/music
cd ../pictures
cd -
pwd






Suggested answer





/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/music
/Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/music
The two cd commands print nothing. cd - jumps back to the previous folder (music) and prints its path; then pwd prints the same path again. That is what Bash shows. In zsh, the Mac’s default shell, cd - writes the path with ~, so the first line reads ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/music.





Question 18 · Scenario
Maria types ls --help on her Mac and gets an error instead of a help text. Sam types man ls in Git Bash and gets command not found. Explain both and say what each of them should do instead.






Suggested answer





The Mac comes with the BSD version of ls, which doesn’t understand the long option --help; Maria should use man ls (and press q to quit). Git Bash comes with the same ls as Linux (the GNU version), which does support ls --help, but Git Bash does not include the man command; Sam should use ls --help. Either of them can also search online or ask an AI - saying which operating system and shell they use.





Question 19 · Compare
From bash-tutorial-files, compare:


ls documents


cd documents followed by ls


Do they show the same names? What is different afterwards?






Suggested answer





Both list the same names (notes and reports). The difference is where you end up: after (A) you are still in bash-tutorial-files; after (B) your current working directory is bash-tutorial-files/documents, so relative paths in your next commands start from there.





Question 20 · Ordering
Maria is in her home folder. Put these commands in an order that (1) goes to documents/notes, (2) shows a long listing including hidden items, (3) returns to the home folder, and (4) confirms where she is.

pwd
ls -la
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes
cd







Suggested answer





cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes
ls -la
cd
pwd
The last command prints /Users/maria.





Question 21 · Long answer
Why is it a good habit to run pwd (and often ls) before running a command that creates, moves, or deletes files - whether you type the command yourself or an AI agent suggests it?






Suggested answer





Relative paths are interpreted from the current working directory, so the same command does different things in different folders. A command such as “delete reports” might hit the wrong reports folder - or fail - if you are not where you think you are. pwd confirms the folder; ls confirms that the files you expect are really there. Commands suggested by an AI are written for a particular folder, so checking your location before running them prevents surprises.
crumbs: 15  15. Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.1 Set up a playground
So far you have only looked around. This page covers the commands that change things: mkdir and touch create, cp copies, mv moves and renames, and rmdir and rm delete. You will practice in a new folder called playground inside the practice files, and delete it at the end.
As on the previous page, the outputs come from Maria’s Mac (with her practice files in ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files). Where Git Bash words an error message differently, both versions are shown.
Experimenting in a throwaway folder is a good habit: if something goes wrong, nothing important is affected.
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
mkdir playground
cd playground
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.2 Creating folders: mkdir
mkdir (make directory) creates one or more folders. With the -p option (parents), it also creates any missing folders along the path:
mkdir reports
mkdir -p archive/2026/october
ls -F
Output:
archive/        reports/
ls archive/2026
Output:
october
Without -p, mkdir refuses to create a folder inside a folder that doesn’t exist yet. It also refuses to create a folder that already exists:
$ mkdir backups/2026
mkdir: backups: No such file or directory
$ mkdir reports
mkdir: reports: File exists
Git Bash words these as mkdir: cannot create directory followed by the name and the same reason. mkdir -p never complains about a folder that already exists.
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.3 Creating empty files: touch
touch creates an empty file - or several at once. If a file already exists, touch leaves its contents alone and only updates its “last modified” time.
touch todo.txt notes.txt
ls
Output:
archive         notes.txt       reports         todo.txt
Usually you create files with an editor or a program; touch is just a quick way to make an empty one. To put text into a file from the command line, see Writing to Files: echo, >, >>, and cat.
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.4 Copying: cp
cp source destination copies a file. The destination can be a new name, or an existing folder (then the copy keeps its name):
cp todo.txt todo-backup.txt
cp ../documents/notes/ideas.txt .
ls
Output:
archive         notes.txt       todo-backup.txt
ideas.txt       reports         todo.txt
The first command makes a copy with a new name. The second copies ideas.txt from the practice files into . - the current folder.
To copy a folder and everything in it, add -r (recursive: “and everything inside, all the way down”):
cp -r ../projects/website website-copy
ls website-copy
Output:
index.html      styles.css
Without -r, cp refuses to copy a folder:
$ cp ../projects/website website-copy
cp: ../projects/website is a directory (not copied).
(Git Bash: cp: -r not specified; omitting directory '../projects/website'.)






cp and mv overwrite without asking



If a file with the destination name already exists, cp and mv replace it silently - its old contents are gone. Add -i (interactive) to be asked first, for example cp -i todo.txt notes.txt. Answer y to overwrite or n to keep the existing file.
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.5 Moving and renaming: mv
mv (move) does two jobs, because moving and renaming are really the same operation: giving a file a new path (a new folder, a new name, or both). Unlike cp, it moves folders without needing -r.
mv todo-backup.txt old-todo.txt
mv old-todo.txt archive
mv notes.txt archive/2026/october/october-notes.txt
mv website-copy archive
ls -F
Output:
archive/        ideas.txt       reports/        todo.txt
ls -F archive
Output:
2026/           old-todo.txt    website-copy/
Line by line, the four mv commands:

rename todo-backup.txt to old-todo.txt (same folder, new name);
move old-todo.txt into the existing folder archive;
move and rename notes.txt in one step: it ends up in archive/2026/october as october-notes.txt;
move a whole folder, website-copy, into archive.

The rule for both cp and mv: if the last argument is an existing folder, the item goes inside it and keeps its name; otherwise the last argument is the new name.
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.6 Deleting: rmdir and rm

16.6.1 rmdir: remove an empty folder
rmdir reports
This works because reports is empty. rmdir refuses to delete a folder that contains anything - a built-in safety check:
$ rmdir archive
rmdir: archive: Directory not empty
(Git Bash: rmdir: failed to remove 'archive': Directory not empty.)


16.6.2 rm: remove files
rm ideas.txt
rm (remove) deletes files immediately. Add -i to be asked first:
$ rm -i todo.txt
remove todo.txt? y
Type y and press Enter to delete, or n to keep the file. (Git Bash asks rm: remove regular empty file 'todo.txt'?.)


16.6.3 rm -r: remove a folder and everything in it
On its own, rm refuses to delete a folder:
$ rm archive
rm: archive: is a directory
(Git Bash: rm: cannot remove 'archive': Is a directory.) With -r, it deletes the folder and every file and folder inside it, all the way down:
rm -r archive
ls
This time ls prints nothing: the playground is empty.






rm is forever




There is no Trash or Recycle Bin. Files deleted with rm do not go to the Mac Trash or the Windows Recycle Bin. There is no undo.
-f means “force”: never ask, and stay quiet about missing files. You will often see rm -rf in instructions and AI answers. It deletes a folder and everything in it without a single question, so use it only when you are sure.
One typo can be a disaster. rm -rf ~ /old-stuff (do not type this) has a stray space after ~, so it means “delete my entire home folder, and also /old-stuff”. Never run an rm -rf you don’t fully understand - whether it comes from a website, a classmate, or an AI.
Habits that help: run pwd and ls first; use rm -i when in doubt; name exactly the files you mean; and keep your projects in Git (see What Is Version Control?), so that committed work can be recovered.





16.6.4 When an AI agent deletes files
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Checkpointing · Choose a permission mode
Claude Code can run rm, mv, and cp too. Depending on its permission mode, it asks you first, lets an automatic safety check review the command, or - in the mode that auto-accepts edits - runs commands such as rm and mv inside your project without asking. Its checkpoints let you rewind changes it made with its own file-editing tools, but its documentation states that they do not undo file changes made by shell commands like these. Permission modes and Claude Code’s other safeguards are covered in Permissions, Modes, and Safety.
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.7 Names with spaces need quotes
Back in the (now empty) playground, try to create a folder called new folder:
$ mkdir new folder
$ ls -F
folder/         new/
Bash splits a command line at spaces, so mkdir received two names and created two folders. Remove them both and try again with quotes:
$ rmdir new folder
$ mkdir "new folder"
$ ls -F
new folder/
The quotes turn new folder into a single argument. You need them every time you use that name: cd "new folder", rmdir "new folder". (Git Bash displays the name as 'new folder'/; the quotes in the listing just show that it is one name.) Tab completion helps: it types a backslash before the space for you (new\ folder/), which works too. Quotes are explained fully in Writing to Files and Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes. The simplest fix is to avoid spaces in names you create.
Finally, clean up. The last rmdir works because the playground is empty again:
rmdir "new folder"
cd ..
rmdir playground
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
16.8 Command summary







Command
What it does




mkdir name
Create a folder.


mkdir -p a/b/c
Create nested folders; no error if they already exist.


touch file
Create an empty file (or update its “last modified” time).


cp file new-name / cp file folder
Copy a file to a new name / into a folder.


cp -r folder new-folder
Copy a folder and everything in it.


mv old-name new-name
Rename a file or folder.


mv item folder
Move a file or folder into a folder.


rmdir folder
Delete an empty folder.


rm file
Delete a file - permanently.


rm -r folder
Delete a folder and everything in it - permanently.


-i (with cp, mv, rm)
Ask before overwriting or deleting.
crumbs: 16  16. Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting

title: 16  16.  Creating, Copying, Moving, and Deleting
text:
Practice Questions
