title: 19  19.  Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes
section: 19.2 The difference: $ works only inside double quotes
text:
19.2 The difference: $ works only inside double quotes

Inside double quotes, the shell still looks for $. It replaces $NAME (or ${NAME}) with the variable’s value, and $(command) with the output of that command. Everything else is kept as typed.
Inside single quotes, nothing is changed. The text is literal: exactly what you typed, character for character.

Here is Maria on her Mac:
echo "Home: $HOME"
echo 'Home: $HOME'
Output:
Home: /Users/maria
Home: $HOME
price=20
echo "Price: $price dollars"
echo 'Price: $price dollars'
Output:
Price: 20 dollars
Price: $price dollars
$(command) is called command substitution: the shell runs the command and puts its output into the text. It also works only inside double quotes (or with no quotes at all):
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
echo "I am in $(pwd)"
echo 'I am in $(pwd)'
Output:
I am in /Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
I am in $(pwd)
A simple way to remember: single quotes mean “say exactly this”; double quotes mean “say this, but fill in the variables first.”









"double quotes"
'single quotes'




Keep spaces and >, ;, *, ~ … as plain text
yes
yes


$NAME and ${NAME}
replaced with the variable’s value
kept as typed


$(command)
replaced with the command’s output
kept as typed


A backslash \ before $ or "
makes it a plain character
kept as typed
crumbs: 19  19. Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes

title: 19  19.  Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes
text:
19.3 When a $ should stay a $
Money amounts are a classic surprise:
echo "The total is $5"
Output:
The total is
The shell read $5 as a variable (a special one that scripts use, see Bash Scripts). It’s empty here, so it disappeared. Two fixes:
echo 'The total is $5'
echo "The total is \$5"
Output:
The total is $5
The total is $5
Inside double quotes, a backslash (\) in front of $ “escapes” it: it tells the shell to treat the next character as an ordinary character. The same rule matters for Git commit messages you will write later: use git commit -m 'Fix $10 discount bug', not double quotes.
crumbs: 19  19. Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes

title: 19  19.  Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes
text:
19.4 Quotes inside quotes

To include an apostrophe, use double quotes: echo "It's Maria's laptop"
To include double quotes, use single quotes: echo 'He said "hi"'
To include a double quote and a $ inside double quotes, escape them with backslashes:

echo "She said \"wow\" and paid \$20"
Output:
She said "wow" and paid $20
A single quote can never appear inside single quotes (not even with a backslash), so switch to double quotes when your text contains an apostrophe.






Stuck at a >, quote>, or dquote> prompt?



If your quotes don’t match, as in echo 'It's raining' (three single quotes), the shell waits for you to close the quote. Git Bash shows a > prompt; zsh on a Mac shows quote> or dquote>. Press Ctrl+C to cancel, then retype the command with matching quotes: echo "It's raining".
crumbs: 19  19. Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes

title: 19  19.  Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes
text:
19.5 No quotes: spaces, wildcards, and ~
Without quotes, the shell does more work before it runs a command:

it splits the line into separate words at the spaces,
it expands wildcards such as * into matching file names (see Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching),
it replaces a ~ at the start of a word with your home directory.

Quotes (of either kind) turn all of this off. In the notes practice folder:
echo Files: *.txt
echo "Files: *.txt"
Output:
Files: ideas.txt meeting-notes.txt
Files: *.txt

19.5.1 Always quote variables that hold file names
In Bash, even the value of an unquoted variable is split at spaces. Suppose a folder contains a file named Q3 report.txt:
file="Q3 report.txt"
cat $file

MacWindows (Git Bash)


zsh (the Mac’s default shell) does not split variables this way, so this unquoted command happens to work at the Mac prompt. It fails as soon as the same command runs in Bash, for example inside a Bash script, which is why you should quote anyway.


Output:
cat: Q3: No such file or directory
cat: report.txt: No such file or directory
Bash split the value into two words, so cat looked for two files, Q3 and report.txt.



The fix works everywhere: put the variable in double quotes, cat "$file". Double quotes keep the value together while still filling it in.


19.5.2 ~ doesn’t work inside quotes
ls "~/Documents" fails with “No such file or directory”, because inside quotes ~ is just a character (see Files, Folders, and Paths). To combine your home folder with a name that contains spaces, use $HOME inside double quotes, or leave the ~/ outside the quotes:
ls "$HOME/My Projects"
ls ~/"My Projects"
crumbs: 19  19. Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes

title: 19  19.  Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes
text:
19.6 Rules of thumb

Text that must stay exactly as typed (prices, commit messages, passwords in examples, search patterns): use single quotes. They are the safe choice for anything containing $, !, `, or \.
Text that should include a variable or a command’s output: use double quotes: echo "Backup of $HOME finished".
Always put variables that hold file names or paths in double quotes: "$file", "$HOME/My Projects".
Don’t put ~ inside quotes. Use "$HOME/..." instead.
Not sure what the shell will do? Put echo in front of the command to see the words it would receive.
crumbs: 19  19. Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes

title: 19  19.  Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes
section: 19.7 Why this matters when AI writes your commands
text:
19.7 Why this matters when AI writes your commands
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How Claude Code works
Claude Code runs shell commands as part of its work (for example to run tests or use Git), and chat assistants give you commands to paste. Quotes decide what those commands actually do, so read them carefully. For example, here is the >> technique from Environment Variables, used to add a PATH line to your startup file:
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
The outer single quotes make everything inside literal, so the file receives exactly export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH", with the $ signs still in it. The variables are filled in later, each time a new terminal reads the file, which is what you want. (With outer double quotes, the inner double quotes would end the text early, and $HOME and $PATH would be filled in right away.)
Quoting rules are also one reason commands don’t move freely between shells: PowerShell and CMD on Windows quote differently from Bash and zsh. When you ask an AI for a command, say which shell you use (“zsh on a Mac” or “Git Bash on Windows”).






Deeper dive: ! and “event not found”





When you type commands interactively, Bash and zsh treat ! as a shortcut for recalling earlier commands (history expansion; for example, !! means “the previous command”). This happens even inside double quotes; only single quotes reliably protect a !.

Git Bash: echo "Hello!" works, because a ! right before the closing quote or a space is left alone. But echo "Wow!Great" fails with bash: !Great: event not found.
Mac (zsh): echo "Hello!" leaves you at a dquote> prompt (press Ctrl+C), and echo "Wow!Great" fails with zsh: event not found: Great.
Both: echo 'Hello!' and echo 'Wow!Great' work.

Scripts are not affected: history expansion only happens in commands you type at the prompt. (Putting a backslash before the ! inside double quotes behaves differently in Bash and zsh, so single quotes are the simple, reliable fix.)
crumbs: 19  19. Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes

title: 19  19.  Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · True or false
Both single quotes and double quotes keep multiple spaces between words.






Suggested answer





True. Both kinds of quotes keep the text inside them together as one piece, spaces included. Their difference is in how they treat $.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
In which of these commands is $HOME replaced by the path of your home directory?

echo '$HOME'
echo "$HOME"
echo '"$HOME"'
None of them







Suggested answer





b. Inside double quotes, $HOME is replaced by its value. In a, the single quotes make it literal. In c, the outer quotes are single quotes, so everything inside, including the double quotes, is printed as typed: "$HOME".





Question 3 · Predict the output
What does echo 'Hello $USER' print?






Suggested answer





Hello $USER, exactly as typed. Single quotes make the text literal, so the shell does not replace $USER.





Question 4 · Fill in the blank
Inside ______ quotes, the shell changes nothing: every character, including $, is kept exactly as typed.






Suggested answer





single quotes.





Question 5 · Multiple choice
Which command prints It's raining correctly?

echo 'It's raining'
echo "It's raining"
echo 'It\'s raining'
echo It's raining







Suggested answer





b. An apostrophe is fine inside double quotes. In a and c, the apostrophe ends the single-quoted text early (a backslash doesn’t help inside single quotes), and in d the apostrophe starts a quote that never ends. Each of those leaves the shell waiting at a > or quote> prompt.






Medium

Question 6 · Predict the output
Sam (Git Bash, home folder /c/Users/sam) runs:
echo "My home is $HOME"
echo 'My home is $HOME'
What does he see?






Suggested answer





My home is /c/Users/sam
My home is $HOME





Question 7 · Predict the output
item="laptop"
echo "Item: $item"
echo 'Item: $item'
echo "Item: ${item}s"






Suggested answer





Item: laptop
Item: $item
Item: laptops
The braces in the last line mark where the variable name ends, so the s is added after the value.





Question 8 · Find the bug
echo "The ticket costs $5" prints The ticket costs with no price. Why? Give two ways to fix it.






Suggested answer





Inside double quotes the shell treats $5 as a variable (a special one used by scripts), which is empty here, so it disappears. Fixes: echo 'The ticket costs $5' (single quotes) or echo "The ticket costs \$5" (escape the $ with a backslash).





Question 9 · Write the command
Write two different echo commands that print exactly:
She said "yes"






Suggested answer





echo 'She said "yes"'
echo "She said \"yes\""
Single quotes keep the double quotes as plain characters; inside double quotes you escape each " with a backslash.





Question 10 · Write the command
The command date +%A prints the day of the week (for example Tuesday). Use command substitution to print a line such as Today is Tuesday.






Suggested answer





echo "Today is $(date +%A)"
$(date +%A) runs the command and puts its output into the text. Double quotes (or no quotes) are needed; with single quotes you would just see Today is $(date +%A).





Question 11 · Find the bug
Maria types ls "~/Documents" and gets “No such file or directory”, even though her Documents folder exists. Explain, and give two commands that work.






Suggested answer





~ is replaced by the home folder only when it is not inside quotes. Here, ls looks for a folder literally named ~. Working versions: ls ~/Documents and ls "$HOME/Documents" ($HOME is filled in inside double quotes).





Question 12 · Find the bug
In Git Bash, Sam types:
cd $HOME/My Projects
He gets an error. What’s wrong, and how should he type it?






Suggested answer





Without quotes, the space splits the path into two words, $HOME/My and Projects, so cd doesn’t receive the full folder name (Bash reports an error such as “too many arguments”). Quote the whole path with double quotes, so that $HOME is still filled in:
cd "$HOME/My Projects"
(cd ~/"My Projects" also works.)





Question 13 · Predict the output
In the notes practice folder (which contains ideas.txt and meeting-notes.txt), what do these print?
echo *.txt
echo '*.txt'






Suggested answer





ideas.txt meeting-notes.txt
*.txt
Without quotes, the shell expands the wildcard *.txt into the matching file names. Quotes turn wildcard expansion off.






Hard

Question 14 · Scenario
An AI assistant suggests this command for a commit message:
git commit -m "Update prices: now $9.99"
What message will actually be saved, and how should the command be written?






Suggested answer





Inside double quotes, $9 is treated as a (special, empty) variable, so the message becomes Update prices: now .99. Use single quotes so that the text is literal:
git commit -m 'Update prices: now $9.99'
(Escaping also works: "Update prices: now \$9.99".)





Question 15 · Long answer
Explain why this command uses single quotes around the whole export ... line, and what would go wrong if you used double quotes on the outside instead.
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc






Suggested answer





The goal is to write the line exactly as shown into ~/.zshrc, including the $HOME and $PATH variable names and the inner double quotes. Single quotes make everything inside literal, so that’s what happens. The variables are then filled in each time a new terminal reads the file, using the PATH of that moment.
With outer double quotes, the inner " characters would end the quoted text early, and $HOME and $PATH would be replaced immediately with their current values. The file would get one long, fixed list of folders (and no quotes around it), instead of a line that builds on whatever PATH is when the terminal starts.





Question 16 · Scenario
A Bash script contains:
file="Q3 report.txt"
cat $file
It prints two “No such file or directory” errors, although Q3 report.txt exists. Maria says the same two lines work fine when she types them into her Mac’s Terminal. Explain both observations and give the fix.






Suggested answer





Bash splits the value of an unquoted variable at spaces, so cat receives two arguments, Q3 and report.txt, and neither file exists. Maria’s Terminal runs zsh, which does not split variable values this way, so the unquoted version happens to work there. The fix works in every shell: cat "$file". Always put variables that hold file names in double quotes.





Question 17 · Scenario
On her Mac, Maria types echo "Deployment done!". The terminal shows dquote> and waits. What is going on, how does she get out, and what should she type instead?






Suggested answer





In zsh, ! is special (history expansion) even inside double quotes, and the combination !" messes up the quoting, so zsh thinks the double quote was never closed and waits for more input. She should press Ctrl+C to cancel and then use single quotes, which always protect !: echo 'Deployment done!'.





Question 18 · Long answer
Give three rules of thumb for choosing between single quotes, double quotes, and no quotes, each with a short example.






Suggested answer





A good answer includes three of these:

Use single quotes for text that must stay exactly as typed, especially if it contains $, !, or \: git commit -m 'Fix $10 discount bug'.
Use double quotes when the text should include a variable or a command’s output: echo "Backup of $HOME finished".
Always double-quote variables that hold file names or paths: cat "$file", cd "$HOME/My Projects".
Leave ~ and wildcards unquoted when you want the shell to expand them: ls ~/Documents/*.txt, and quote them when you don’t: echo '*.txt'.






Question 19 · Predict the output
name="Sam"
echo "Hi $name, it's \$10 for 'Pro'"






Suggested answer





Hi Sam, it's $10 for 'Pro'
Inside double quotes, $name is filled in, the backslash turns \$ into a plain $, and single quotes and apostrophes are ordinary characters.
crumbs: 19  19. Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
text:
20.1 Built-in help: --help and man
Nobody memorizes every command and option. This page shows how to look things up from the terminal, how to ask the web or an AI effectively, and the keyboard shortcuts that make working at the command line much faster.
Most commands come with built-in help, but this is one place where the Mac and Git Bash really differ:
Here are the first lines of ls --help in Git Bash:
Output:
In a usage line, square brackets [ ] mean “optional” and ... means “you can give more than one”. So ls takes zero or more options and zero or more files. Short options have one dash (-a), long options have two (--all).
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
text:
MacWindows (Git Bash)



man ls opens the manual page (“man page”) for ls. It works like less: arrow keys or Space to scroll, /word to search, q to quit.
Many basic commands on a Mac, such as ls and cp, don’t understand --help (see Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd). Use man for those.
Newer tools do support --help, for example git --help and python3 --help.




The commands in Git Bash support --help. ls --help prints a summary of all its options.
Git Bash does not include man. Use --help, or search online for “man ls”.
For commands that are built into Bash itself, such as cd, use help: help cd.
git help commit (or git commit --help) opens Git’s manual page in your web browser.





ls --help

Usage: ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...
List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
section: 20.2 Asking the web or an AI
text:
20.2 Asking the web or an AI
Searching online for “bash how to count lines in a file” usually finds an answer quickly. AI assistants are even faster, and they can explain a command piece by piece. To get answers that work for you:

Say which system and shell you use. Otherwise you may get a PowerShell command, which won’t work in Bash or zsh.
Paste the exact error message, not a summary of it.
Ask for an explanation of each part of the command before you run it (more on using AI safely in Bash Scripts).

For example:
I'm on Windows 11 using Git Bash. How do I find all .csv files in my
Documents folder and its subfolders? Explain each part of the command.
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
section: 20.3 More from Tab and your command history
text:
20.3 More from Tab and your command history
Moving Around: pwd, ls, and cd introduced Tab completion and the ↑/↓ arrow keys. A few more details make them even more useful:

Tab works for commands too, not just files and folders, and it adds the backslashes needed for names that contain spaces. If Tab completes nothing, that’s a hint that the file isn’t where you think it is.
When several names fit, the shell can list them. In Git Bash, press Tab twice. zsh on a Mac shows the list after the first Tab (pressing Tab again there starts cycling through the choices). In bash-tutorial-files, cd p could mean pictures or projects: once you see both, type one more letter (r) and press Tab again.
history prints a numbered list of your recent commands. (In zsh on a Mac, plain history shows only the last 16; history 1 shows them all.)
Ctrl+R searches your history. Press Ctrl+R, then type part of an old command, such as nano. The most recent match appears. Press Ctrl+R again for older matches, Enter to run the one shown, or Ctrl+C to cancel.

Your history is saved in a hidden file in your home folder (~/.zsh_history on a Mac, ~/.bash_history in Git Bash). That’s convenient, and it is one more reason never to type passwords or API keys directly into a command.
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
text:
20.4 Keyboard shortcuts







Keys
What they do




Tab
complete a file, folder, or command name


Tab Tab
list the possible completions (zsh on a Mac: one Tab)


↑ / ↓
previous / next command from your history


Ctrl+R
search your command history


Ctrl+C
stop the running command, or cancel the line you’re typing


Ctrl+L
clear the screen (same as the clear command)


Ctrl+A / Ctrl+E
jump to the beginning / end of the line


Ctrl+U
erase the line you’re typing


Ctrl+D
on an empty line: end the shell session, just like exit



These use the Ctrl key on a Mac too, not Cmd. On a Mac, Cmd+K also clears the Terminal window, including everything you could scroll back to.






Ctrl+C stops things; it doesn’t copy



In a terminal, Ctrl+C interrupts the command that is running. Use it whenever a command runs too long, or seems frozen. A common case: you forgot to give a command its file name (for example grep budget with no file), so it sits waiting for you to type input. Press Ctrl+C and try again.
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
text:
20.5 Copy, paste, and dragging files
Copying and pasting works a little differently in each terminal; the keys are listed in Getting Bash on Your Computer.
To enter a long path without typing it, drag a file or folder from Finder or File Explorer into the Mac Terminal or Git Bash window: its full path appears on the command line (Git Bash writes it Bash-style and adds quotes if the name contains spaces). For example, type cd (with a space), drag a folder into the window, and press Enter.
On a Mac you can also copy a path from Finder: right-click a file or folder, hold down the Option key, and choose Copy “…” as Pathname.
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
section: 20.6 Opening folders and files from the terminal
text:
20.6 Opening folders and files from the terminal
The opposite direction is handy too: opening the folder you’re in, in the graphical file browser.

MacWindows (Git Bash)



open . opens the current folder in Finder (. means “this folder”).
open ideas.txt opens a file in its default app.




explorer . opens the current folder in File Explorer.




If you have VS Code installed, code . opens the current folder in VS Code. The Windows installer sets this up automatically. On a Mac, do it once: in VS Code, press Cmd+Shift+P, type shell command, and choose Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH. Then open a new Terminal window.
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
text:
20.7 Running several commands: ; and &&
You can put several commands on one line:

; runs the commands one after the other, no matter what.
&& runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded.

mkdir reports-2026 && cd reports-2026
Here cd runs only if mkdir worked. && really matters when something goes wrong. With a typo in the folder name, cd projetcs && ls prints a “No such file or directory” error and stops. cd projetcs ; ls prints the same error and then runs ls anyway, in the wrong folder. That’s harmless for ls, but imagine cd old-files ; rm *.txt: if the cd fails, rm deletes the .txt files in whatever folder you’re in.
You will often see && in installation instructions and in commands written by AI tools, for example npm install && npm run dev.
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 20  20.  Getting Help and Working Faster
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What happens when you type the first few letters of a file name and press Tab?






Suggested answer





The shell completes the name for you (tab completion). If several names fit, pressing Tab twice lists the choices (in zsh on a Mac, one Tab already lists them).





Question 2 · Multiple choice
A command has been running for a long time and you want to stop it. Which key do you press?

Ctrl+C
Ctrl+D
Esc
q







Suggested answer





a. Ctrl+C interrupts the running command (it is not “copy” in a terminal). Ctrl+D means “end of input” and, on an empty prompt, ends the shell session. Esc doesn’t stop shell commands, and q quits only viewers such as less and man.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
You’re reading man ls on a Mac. How do you get back to the prompt?

Press Esc
Press q
Type exit
Press Ctrl+D twice







Suggested answer





b. Man pages are shown in a viewer that works like less, and q quits it. The other choices don’t leave the viewer, because it treats your keys as viewer commands, not shell commands (for example, Ctrl+D scrolls down).





Question 4 · Matching
Match each shortcut with what it does.



Keys

What it does




1. Ctrl+R

A. jump to the beginning of the line


2. Ctrl+L

B. end the shell session (on an empty line)


3. Ctrl+A

C. search your command history


4. Ctrl+D

D. clear the screen









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 5 · Short answer
Which command prints a numbered list of the commands you typed earlier?






Suggested answer





history. (In zsh on a Mac, history 1 shows the whole list; plain history shows only the most recent commands.)





Question 6 · Multiple choice
Which command opens the current folder in Finder on a Mac?

open .
explorer .
cd .
ls .







Suggested answer





a. open . opens the current folder (.) in Finder. explorer . is the Git Bash equivalent on Windows. cd . stays in the same folder, and ls . lists the folder’s contents in the terminal.






Medium

Question 7 · Scenario
Maria opens man grep on her Mac to find out how to search through folders. How can she search the manual page for the word recursive, jump to the next place it appears, and then leave the page?






Suggested answer





Man pages work like less. She types /recursive and presses Enter to jump to the first match, presses n to go to the next match, and presses q to quit and return to the prompt.





Question 8 · Scenario
Sam types man grep in Git Bash and gets command not found. Give two other ways he can learn about grep’s options.






Suggested answer





Git Bash doesn’t include man. He can:

run grep --help (Git Bash’s commands support --help), or
search online for “man grep”, or ask an AI, saying that he uses Git Bash on Windows.






Question 9 · Predict the output
The folder projetcs doesn’t exist (it’s a typo for projects). What happens with each line?
cd projetcs && ls
cd projetcs ; ls






Suggested answer





Both lines print a “No such file or directory” error for the cd.

With &&, ls does not run, because cd failed.
With ;, ls runs anyway and lists the files of the current folder, which is not the folder you meant.






Question 10 · Write the command
Write one line that creates the folder club-site and then moves into it, but only if creating the folder worked.






Suggested answer





mkdir club-site && cd club-site





Question 11 · Scenario
Yesterday Sam typed a long git commit -m "..." command. Today he wants to run it again (with a small change). What is the fastest way to get it back?






Suggested answer





Press Ctrl+R and type part of the command, such as commit. The most recent matching command appears; press Ctrl+R again for older matches. Then edit it if needed and press Enter. (Pressing ↑ several times also works if the command was recent.)





Question 12 · Short answer
In bash-tutorial-files, Maria types cd p and presses Tab once. The name isn’t completed. Why not, and what should she do?






Suggested answer





Two folders start with p (pictures and projects), so the shell can’t choose. On her Mac, zsh lists both choices right after that Tab (in Git Bash you would press Tab a second time to see them). She can type one more letter (i or r) and press Tab again to complete the name.





Question 13 · Write the command
Write the command that opens the current folder in VS Code. What one-time setup does a Mac need before it works?






Suggested answer





code .
On a Mac, open VS Code, press Cmd+Shift+P, and run Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH, then open a new Terminal window. (This puts the code command in a folder on the PATH.) The Windows installer does this automatically.





Question 14 · Scenario
Sam typed grep budget and pressed Enter. Nothing happens and his prompt doesn’t come back. What’s going on, and what should he do?






Suggested answer





He didn’t give grep a file name, so grep is waiting for him to type the text it should search. Press Ctrl+C to stop it, then run it with a file, for example grep budget meeting-notes.txt.






Hard

Question 15 · Scenario
A classmate’s cleanup instructions say:
cd old-reports ; rm *.txt
Explain the risk, and rewrite the line to be safer.






Suggested answer





If old-reports doesn’t exist (a typo, or you’re in the wrong folder), the cd fails, but ; runs rm *.txt anyway, deleting the .txt files in your current folder, with no undo. Use && so that rm runs only if the cd succeeded:
cd old-reports && rm *.txt
Even better, first check what would be deleted: cd old-reports && ls *.txt.





Question 16 · Long answer
Write a good prompt asking an AI for a command that renames every .jpeg file in a folder to end in .jpg. Explain what makes your prompt good.






Suggested answer





Example prompt:
I'm on a Mac using zsh in Terminal. In my current folder I have about 50
.jpeg files. Give me a command that renames each one to end in .jpg instead.
Explain each part of the command, and show me how to preview the changes
before anything is renamed.
It’s good because it states the operating system and shell (so the answer won’t be a PowerShell command), describes the exact goal and files, asks for an explanation so you understand the command before running it, and asks for a preview, a safe way to check the result first.





Question 17 · Scenario
On her Mac, Maria wants to find a long curl command she ran last week, but history shows only her last 16 commands. Give two ways she can find it.






Suggested answer






Run history 1, which in zsh lists her whole saved history, not just the last 16 commands.
Press Ctrl+R, type curl, and press Ctrl+R repeatedly to step back through older matches.

(After the next page she could also run history 1 | grep curl.)





Question 18 · Short answer
Why is it risky to type a real API key directly into a command such as export WEATHER_API_KEY=abc123...?






Suggested answer





The shell saves the commands you type in a history file in your home folder (~/.zsh_history or ~/.bash_history). The key would be stored there in plain text, where anyone or any program that can read the file could find it, and it can also show up on screen (for example when you press ↑ or run history while sharing your screen). Keep keys in a protected file such as a git-ignored .env file instead.





Question 19 · Scenario
Sam needs to cd into a folder named OneDrive - My University/Course Files and keeps making typos in the long path. Give two ways to get the path right without typing it all.






Suggested answer






Type cd (with a space), then drag the folder from File Explorer into the Git Bash window. Git Bash inserts the full path, with quotes because it contains spaces. Press Enter.
Use tab completion: type the first few letters of each folder name and press Tab, which completes the name and adds the backslashes needed for the spaces.
crumbs: 20  20. Getting Help and Working Faster

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
text:
21.1 Wildcards: matching many file names
This page covers three things that make the command line powerful: wildcards (work with many files at once), pipes (connect commands to each other), and search commands (find files, and find text inside files). The examples use the practice files from Files, Folders, and Paths.
A wildcard is a special character that stands for other characters in a file name. A name pattern that contains wildcards is often called a glob.
echo shows what a wildcard matches:
Output:
Wildcards work with every command. Remember the example from What Is the Command Line?: moving every file with 2025 in its name takes one command. Try it with two new folders:
Output:

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
text:
Wildcard
Matches
Example
Matches in the practice files




*
any number of characters (even none)
music/*.mp3
song1.mp3, song2.mp3


?
exactly one character
music/song?.mp3
song1.mp3, song2.mp3


[abc]
exactly one of the listed characters
pictures/[fg]*
family.jpg (names starting with f or g)




cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
echo music/*.mp3
echo music/*1*
echo documents/reports/*.txt

music/song1.mp3 music/song2.mp3
music/song1.mp3
documents/reports/annual-summary.txt documents/reports/quarterly-report.txt

mkdir project1 project2
touch project1/budget-2025.xlsx project1/budget-2026.xlsx project1/sales-2025.docx
mv project1/*2025* project2
ls project2

budget-2025.xlsx  sales-2025.docx

21.1.1 The shell expands wildcards, not the command
The shell replaces a wildcard pattern with the list of matching names before it runs the command. When you type ls *.txt, ls never sees the *; it receives the file names. That’s why echo is a safe way to preview what a pattern will match.
When nothing matches, for example ls *.pdf in a folder without PDF files, the Mac and Git Bash behave differently:

MacWindows (Git Bash)


zsh stops with an error and doesn’t run the command at all:
zsh: no matches found: *.pdf
(This also happens if you paste a web address containing ? without quotes. Put quotes around addresses.)


Bash passes the pattern unchanged, so ls looks for a file literally named *.pdf:
ls: cannot access '*.pdf': No such file or directory



Two more details:

Quotes turn wildcards off. echo "*.txt" prints *.txt. You need this when you want to hand the pattern itself to a command, as with find below.
* doesn’t match hidden files, whose names start with a dot.







Preview before you delete



rm *.tmp deletes every matching file instantly, with no Trash. Run ls *.tmp first to see exactly what matches. Watch out for stray spaces: rm * .tmp means “delete everything, and also a file named .tmp.” (zsh on a Mac asks “sure you want to delete all … files?” before running a command like that; Bash does not ask.)

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
text:
21.2 Pipes: connecting commands
A pipe, the | character, sends the output of one command into the next command as its input, like an assembly line:







Pipeline
What it does




ls -l | less
shows a long file listing one screen at a time


history | grep cd
shows only the past commands that contain cd


cat data.csv | wc -l
counts the lines in data.csv



Compare pipes with redirection: > sends output into a file, while | sends it into another command.

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
text:
21.3 Searching inside files: grep
grep prints the lines of a file that contain a word or phrase. First, give the notes some content (this replaces what you wrote on earlier pages):
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes
echo "Budget review on Monday" > meeting-notes.txt
echo "Action: Maria updates the budget" >> meeting-notes.txt
echo "Action: Sam books the room" >> meeting-notes.txt
echo "Idea: a budget tracker app" > ideas.txt
grep budget meeting-notes.txt
Output:
Action: Maria updates the budget
grep is case-sensitive, so it skipped Budget. These options change that and more:








Option
Meaning
Example




-i
ignore upper/lower case
grep -i budget meeting-notes.txt


-n
show line numbers
grep -n Action meeting-notes.txt


-r
search all files in a folder and its subfolders
grep -r budget .



grep -i budget meeting-notes.txt
grep -n Action meeting-notes.txt
Output:
Budget review on Monday
Action: Maria updates the budget
2:Action: Maria updates the budget
3:Action: Sam books the room
When grep searches several files, it puts the file name in front of each match. Options can be combined. From the documents folder:
cd ..
grep -r -i -n budget .
Output (the files may be listed in a different order):
./notes/meeting-notes.txt:1:Budget review on Monday
./notes/meeting-notes.txt:2:Action: Maria updates the budget
./notes/ideas.txt:1:Idea: a budget tracker app
Always tell grep -r which folder to search (. means the current folder). If grep finds nothing, it prints nothing.

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
text:
21.4 Finding files by name: find
find searches a folder and all of its subfolders for names that match a pattern. From bash-tutorial-files:
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
find . -name "*.css"
Output:
./projects/website/styles.css
The . means “start searching here”. Put the pattern in quotes so the shell passes it to find unchanged instead of expanding it first. find matches folder names too; add -type f to list only files:
find . -name "*report*"
find . -name "*report*" -type f
Output:
./documents/reports
./documents/reports/quarterly-report.txt
./documents/reports/quarterly-report.txt
The first command found the folder reports and the file inside it; the second found only the file. (Use -iname instead of -name to ignore upper/lower case.)

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
section: 21.5 Counting and sorting: wc, sort, head, tail
text:
21.5 Counting and sorting: wc, sort, head, tail
Create a small data file:
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/projects/data-analysis
echo "East,500" > data.csv
echo "West,750" >> data.csv
echo "North,320" >> data.csv
echo "South,610" >> data.csv
echo "East,410" >> data.csv



Command
What it does




wc -l data.csv
counts the lines (wc = “word count”; without -l it also counts words and characters)


sort data.csv
prints the lines in alphabetical order (-r reverses, -n sorts numbers by value)


head -n 3, tail -n 3
the first / last lines (see Writing to Files)



wc -l data.csv
sort data.csv
Output:
5 data.csv
East,410
East,500
North,320
South,610
West,750
(On a Mac, wc puts some spaces in front of the number.)
These small commands become powerful in pipelines. How many rows are for the East region? Which two rows come first alphabetically?
grep East data.csv | wc -l
sort data.csv | head -n 2
Output:
2
East,410
East,500

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
text:
21.6 Saving results to a file
Pipes and searches combine with redirection (>) from Writing to Files, so you can keep the results:
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files/documents/notes
grep -n Action meeting-notes.txt > action-items.txt
cat action-items.txt
Output:
2:Action: Maria updates the budget
3:Action: Sam books the room
Other examples: find . -name "*.jpg" > photo-list.txt saves a list of photos, and history | grep git > git-commands.txt saves your past Git commands.

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
section: 21.7 How Claude Code searches your files
text:
21.7 How Claude Code searches your files
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Tools reference
When Claude Code needs to find something in your project, it uses exactly these ideas. On a Mac (and on Linux), it searches by running find and grep commands through its Bash tool (using its own built-in versions of these programs), so commands like the ones on this page are literally what you’ll see it run. On Windows, it has two built-in tools for this instead: Glob, which finds files whose names match a wildcard pattern such as **/*.js (all .js files in any subfolder), and Grep, which searches inside files. You’ll meet Claude Code’s tools in How Claude Code Works.

title: 21  21.  Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Which file names does the pattern *.csv match?

Only a file literally named *.csv
Every name that ends in .csv
Every name that contains exactly one character before .csv
Every file in the folder







Suggested answer





b. * matches any number of characters, so *.csv matches data.csv, sales-2026.csv, and so on. Option a is what happens when the pattern is in quotes ("*.csv"), c describes ?.csv, and d describes * on its own.





Question 2 · Short answer
What does the wildcard ? match? Give an example.






Suggested answer





Exactly one character. For example, song?.mp3 matches song1.mp3 and song2.mp3, but not song10.mp3 (two characters) or song.mp3 (none).





Question 3 · True or false
When you type ls *.txt, the ls command itself searches the folder for names that match *.txt.






Suggested answer





False. The shell expands *.txt into the list of matching file names before running ls. ls only receives the names; it never sees the *.





Question 4 · Short answer
What does the pipe character | do in history | grep cd?






Suggested answer





It sends the output of the first command (history, the list of past commands) into the second command (grep cd) as its input. The result shows only the past commands that contain cd.





Question 5 · Matching
Match each command or option with its meaning.



Command or option

Meaning




1. grep -i

A. search all files in a folder and its subfolders


2. grep -n

B. find files whose names match a pattern


3. grep -r

C. ignore upper/lower case


4. find . -name

D. show line numbers









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 6 · Short answer
What does wc -l report.txt tell you?






Suggested answer





The number of lines in report.txt (followed by the file name).






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
Write a command that lists only the .csv files in the current folder.






Suggested answer





ls *.csv





Question 8 · Predict the output
In bash-tutorial-files, what do these commands print?
echo pictures/*.jpg
echo music/song?.mp3
echo "music/*.mp3"






Suggested answer





pictures/family.jpg pictures/vacation.jpg
music/song1.mp3 music/song2.mp3
music/*.mp3
The quotes in the last command turn off wildcard expansion.





Question 9 · Write the command
Search all files in the current folder and its subfolders for the word invoice, ignoring upper/lower case and showing line numbers.






Suggested answer





grep -r -i -n invoice .
(grep -rin invoice . is the same thing, with the options combined.)





Question 10 · Write the command
Give two different commands that count the lines in sales.csv.






Suggested answer





wc -l sales.csv
cat sales.csv | wc -l
The first gives the file name to wc directly; the second pipes the file’s contents into wc. (The second prints only the number.)





Question 11 · Write the command
Write a command that finds all .jpg files in the current folder and all of its subfolders.






Suggested answer





find . -name "*.jpg"
The quotes make sure find, not the shell, handles the *.





Question 12 · Write the command
Save every line of meeting-notes.txt that contains Action into a new file action-items.txt, then display the new file.






Suggested answer





grep Action meeting-notes.txt > action-items.txt
cat action-items.txt





Question 13 · Write the pattern
A folder contains song1.mp3, song2.mp3, and song3.mp3. Write an ls command whose pattern matches song1.mp3 and song2.mp3, but not song3.mp3.






Suggested answer





ls song[12].mp3
[12] matches exactly one character that is either 1 or 2. (song?.mp3 would also match song3.mp3.)





Question 14 · Predict the output
A folder contains no PDF files. What happens when you run ls *.pdf on a Mac (zsh), and in Git Bash?






Suggested answer






Mac (zsh): zsh: no matches found: *.pdf. zsh stops and doesn’t run ls at all.
Git Bash: Bash passes the unmatched pattern unchanged, so ls looks for a file literally named *.pdf and reports ls: cannot access '*.pdf': No such file or directory.







Hard

Question 15 · Find the bug
Sam wanted to delete his backup files and typed rm * .bak (with a space before .bak). What does this command do in Git Bash? What did he mean to type, and what should he have done first?






Suggested answer





Because of the space, * and .bak are two separate words. * matches every (non-hidden) file in the folder, so rm deletes them all, and then complains that there is no file named .bak. There is no undo. He meant rm *.bak. He should first have run ls *.bak to preview exactly which files match. (zsh on a Mac would have asked for confirmation because of the lone *, but Bash does not.)





Question 16 · Scenario
In bash-tutorial-files, Maria forgets the quotes and types find . -name *.txt. It prints only ./README.txt, even though the documents subfolders contain several more .txt files. Explain why.






Suggested answer





Without quotes, the shell expands *.txt before find runs, using the files in the current folder. The only match there is README.txt, so the command that actually runs is find . -name README.txt, which finds only files named exactly README.txt. With quotes, find . -name "*.txt", the pattern reaches find unchanged, and find applies it in every subfolder. (In a folder with several .txt files, the unquoted version fails with an error instead.)





Question 17 · Long answer
Using the data.csv file from this page, explain what each part of this pipeline does and what it prints:
sort -t, -k2 -n data.csv | tail -n 1






Suggested answer






sort -t, -k2 -n data.csv sorts the lines using the comma as the separator between columns (-t,), by the second column (-k2), as numbers (-n), smallest first.
| sends that sorted list to the next command.
tail -n 1 keeps only the last line, which is the row with the largest number.

It prints West,750: the region with the highest sales.





Question 18 · Short answer
Why does find . -name "*report*" list ./documents/reports in addition to quarterly-report.txt? How do you list only files?






Suggested answer





find checks the names of folders as well as files, and the folder name reports contains report. Add -type f to keep only regular files: find . -name "*report*" -type f.





Question 19 · Write the command
Write one pipeline that counts how many times you have run git commit according to your shell history.






Suggested answer





history | grep "git commit" | wc -l
history lists your past commands, grep keeps the lines containing git commit, and wc -l counts them. (In zsh on a Mac, use history 1 instead of history to include the whole history. The count may also include the pipeline itself, since it contains git commit too.)





Question 20 · Scenario
While working on Maria’s Mac, Claude Code runs this command:
grep -rn "checkout" src
What is it doing, and why is it useful for you to be able to read it?






Suggested answer





It searches every file in the src folder and its subfolders (-r) for the text checkout, and prints each matching line with its file name and line number (-n). It’s a read-only search, so it doesn’t change anything. On a Mac, Claude Code searches your project by running ordinary find and grep commands like this one; being able to read them lets you follow what it’s doing and spot a command that does something you didn’t expect.

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
text:
22.1 What is a script?
When you find yourself typing the same commands again and again, you can save them in a file and run the file instead. This page covers the basics of Bash scripts, and how to use AI safely when it writes commands and scripts for you.
A script is a text file that contains commands. When you run it, the shell executes the commands from top to bottom, exactly as if you had typed them one by one. Bash scripts usually have names ending in .sh.
Scripts let you repeat a task with one command (for example, setting up the folders for a new project, or backing up your files), share that task with others, and keep a record of exactly what you did.
crumbs: 22  22. Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
text:
22.2 Your first script
Open a new file in nano (any text editor works; see Writing to Files):
cd ~/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
nano hello.sh
Type these lines, then save (Ctrl+O, Enter) and exit (Ctrl+X):
#!/bin/bash
# hello.sh: my first script
echo "Hello from a script"
echo "You are in $(pwd)"
Run the script by handing it to Bash:
bash hello.sh
Output:
Hello from a script
You are in /Users/maria/Documents/bash-tutorial-files
The second line of the script is a comment: Bash ignores everything from a # to the end of the line. Comments are notes for people who read the script, such as what it does and how to use it. (Comments work inside script files. Typed at the zsh prompt on a Mac, they don’t, by default; see Getting Bash on Your Computer.)
crumbs: 22  22. Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
text:
22.3 The shebang line
The first line, #!/bin/bash, is called the shebang (“hash” + “bang”, the nicknames of # and !). It tells the operating system which program should run the script when you run the file directly, as in the next section. You will also see #!/usr/bin/env bash, which finds bash by searching your PATH.
On a Mac this means that the script runs in Bash, even though your Terminal uses zsh. (The Mac’s built-in Bash is an old version, 3.2, which is fine for simple scripts like these.)
crumbs: 22  22. Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
section: 22.4 Running a script like a command: chmod +x and ./
text:
22.4 Running a script like a command: chmod +x and ./
chmod +x hello.sh
./hello.sh

chmod +x (“change mode: add execute permission”) marks the file as a program that may be run. Without it, a Mac answers permission denied. (In Git Bash, a script that starts with #! usually runs even without chmod +x, but running it does no harm.)
./hello.sh means “the file hello.sh in this folder.” If you type just hello.sh, the shell looks for it only in the folders on your PATH, and your current folder isn’t one of them, so you get command not found. This rule protects you from accidentally running a program just because it happens to sit in the current folder.
crumbs: 22  22. Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
text:
22.5 Variables and arguments
Scripts become really useful when they take input. Here is a script that sets up a starter folder for a new project:
#!/bin/bash
# new-project.sh: create a starter folder for a new project
# Usage: bash new-project.sh PROJECT-NAME

project="$1"
mkdir -p "$project/docs" "$project/src"
echo "# $project" > "$project/README.md"
echo "Created $project with docs/, src/ and README.md"
bash new-project.sh club-site
Output:
Created club-site with docs/, src/ and README.md

$1 is the first argument: the first word you typed after the script’s name (club-site). $2 is the second one, and so on. (That’s why $5 vanished on the quotes page.)
project="$1" stores the argument in a variable with a readable name.
The double quotes around "$project" keep a name that contains spaces in one piece.
echo "# $project" > "$project/README.md" writes a heading into a new README file. This # is inside quotes, so it’s ordinary text, not a comment.

Run it again with another name, such as bash new-project.sh budget-app, and you get a second, identical setup in seconds. That’s the point of a script.
crumbs: 22  22. Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
section: 22.6 Using AI safely at the command line
text:
22.6 Using AI safely at the command line
AI assistants are very good at writing commands and scripts, and they are sometimes confidently wrong. You are responsible for what runs on your computer. A good routine:

Tell the AI your system and shell: “Mac, zsh in Terminal” or “Windows, Git Bash”.
Ask it to explain each part of a command before you run it.
Check where you are with pwd; most commands act on the current folder.
Preview first. Run ls with the same wildcard before an rm or mv, and test new scripts on a copy of your files.
Ask for comments in any script the AI writes, and read the script before you run it.

Never run commands like these unless you understand exactly what they will do:







Pattern
Why it’s risky




rm -rf ...
deletes files and whole folders permanently, without asking


sudo ...
(Mac and Linux) runs the command with administrator rights, so it can change or break anything on the computer


curl … | bash
downloads a script from the internet and runs it immediately, before anyone has read it


... > important-file
replaces everything in the file



Some official installers do work this way: Homebrew’s installer for the Mac, for example, downloads a script with curl and runs it with Bash. That’s acceptable when you copied the command from the official website yourself, not when it comes from a forum post or an AI’s suggestion.
A good request looks like this:
I'm on a Mac using zsh. Write a Bash script that copies every .csv file in
the current folder into a new folder named backup. Add a comment to each
line, and tell me how to test it safely first.
crumbs: 22  22. Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
section: 22.7 Preview: Claude Code runs commands for you
text:
22.7 Preview: Claude Code runs commands for you
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Choose a permission mode · Advanced setup · Interactive mode
Claude Code doesn’t just suggest commands: it can run them itself, through its Bash tool. (On Windows, the Bash tool uses Git Bash, so it needs Git for Windows; without it, Claude Code runs commands through a PowerShell tool instead.) Whether it asks you first depends on its permission mode. In Manual mode, it asks before running shell commands. In auto mode, which recent versions normally start in, a separate safety check reviews most actions instead of you and blocks the risky ones. Either way, you can review the commands it ran (for example in its transcript view, opened with Ctrl+O), and they are the same kind of Bash commands you learned in this part of the book. Permission modes are covered in Permissions, Modes, and Safety.
crumbs: 22  22. Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)

title: 22  22.  Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a Bash script?






Suggested answer





A text file containing shell commands. When you run it, Bash executes the commands from top to bottom, as if you had typed them yourself. Script names usually end in .sh.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
What does the first line #!/bin/bash of a script do?

Nothing; it’s a comment
It tells the operating system to run the script with Bash when you run the file directly
It deletes the previous version of the script
It makes the script executable







Suggested answer





b. This is the shebang line. It looks like a comment (a), but on the first line #! has a special meaning: it names the program that should run the script. Making a file executable (d) is the job of chmod +x.





Question 3 · True or false
In a script, Bash runs the lines that start with # (after the first line) as commands.






Suggested answer





False. Those lines are comments: Bash ignores everything from # to the end of the line. Only the special #! on the very first line has a meaning.





Question 4 · Short answer
What does chmod +x backup.sh do?






Suggested answer





It gives backup.sh execute permission, so that it can be run directly as a command (./backup.sh).





Question 5 · Multiple choice
You run bash greet.sh Maria Lopez. Inside the script, what is the value of $2?

greet.sh
Maria
Lopez
Maria Lopez







Suggested answer





c. $1 is the first argument after the script name (Maria), and $2 is the second (Lopez). To pass Maria Lopez as one argument, put it in quotes: bash greet.sh "Maria Lopez".






Medium

Question 6 · Write the command
Write the two commands that make report.sh executable and then run it from the current folder.






Suggested answer





chmod +x report.sh
./report.sh





Question 7 · Short answer
hello.sh is in the current folder and is executable, but typing hello.sh gives command not found, while ./hello.sh works. Why?






Suggested answer





A plain command name is looked up only in the folders listed in PATH, and the current folder is not on the PATH. ./hello.sh gives an explicit path (“hello.sh in this folder”), so no search is needed.





Question 8 · Predict the output
greet.sh contains:
#!/bin/bash
name="$1"
echo "Hello, $name. Welcome to the course."
What do these two commands print?
bash greet.sh Sam
bash greet.sh "Maria Lopez"






Suggested answer





Hello, Sam. Welcome to the course.
Hello, Maria Lopez. Welcome to the course.
The quotes make Maria Lopez a single argument, so it all ends up in $1.





Question 9 · Find the bug
The script total.sh contains these lines:
#!/bin/bash
total = 5
echo "Total: $total"
Running it prints total.sh: line 2: total: command not found and then Total:. What’s wrong?






Suggested answer





Variable assignments must not have spaces around =. With the spaces, Bash thinks total is a command to run. The line should be total=5; then the script prints Total: 5.





Question 10 · Write the script
Write a script backup-notes.sh that copies meeting-notes.txt to meeting-notes-backup.txt and then prints Backup saved. Include a shebang and a comment. Show how to run it.






Suggested answer





#!/bin/bash
# backup-notes.sh: make a backup copy of the meeting notes
cp meeting-notes.txt meeting-notes-backup.txt
echo "Backup saved"
Run it with bash backup-notes.sh, or with chmod +x backup-notes.sh once and then ./backup-notes.sh. It must be run in the folder that contains meeting-notes.txt, because the script uses relative paths.





Question 11 · Matching
Match each command pattern with its risk.








Pattern

Risk




1. rm -rf old-site

A. downloads a script and runs it before anyone has read it


2. sudo ...

B. replaces the contents of a file


3. curl -fsSL https://example.com/x.sh | bash

C. permanently deletes a folder and everything in it, without asking


4. echo "" > notes.txt

D. runs a command with administrator rights









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 12 · Short answer
List four things you should tell or ask an AI assistant when you want it to write a command for you.






Suggested answer





For example:

Your operating system and shell (“Windows, Git Bash” or “Mac, zsh”).
Exactly what you want to achieve, and which files or folders are involved.
A request to explain each part of the command.
A request for a safe way to preview or test it first (and comments, if it writes a script).







Hard

Question 13 · Scenario
Maria runs bash new-project.sh but forgets to type a project name. The script prints errors about /docs, /src, and /README.md. What happened, and how could the script protect itself?






Suggested answer





Without an argument, $1 is empty, so project is empty and "$project/docs" becomes /docs: the script tries to create folders and a file at the very top of the file system (the root /). Luckily, normal users aren’t allowed to write there, so the commands fail with errors such as “Permission denied” or “Read-only file system”. With a command like rm -rf "$project"/*, an empty variable could be a disaster.
A script should check its input before doing anything, for example:
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
  echo "Usage: bash new-project.sh PROJECT-NAME"
  exit 1
fi
(-z tests whether the text is empty, and exit 1 stops the script.)





Question 14 · Scenario
While you’re trying to fix an error, a forum post suggests:
curl -fsSL https://fix-my-setup.example.net/repair.sh | bash
Explain what this would do and what you should do instead.






Suggested answer





curl downloads the file repair.sh from that website, and | bash sends it straight into Bash, which runs it immediately with your permissions. Nobody (including you) reads the script first, and it could delete files, steal secrets such as API keys, or install malware. Instead: don’t run it. Find the official documentation for the tool you’re fixing, or download the script without running it (for example curl -fsSL URL -o repair.sh), read it, and ask an AI to explain it line by line, before deciding.





Question 15 · Scenario
An AI assistant says: “To fix this, run sudo rm -r /usr/local/lib/node_modules.” Sam is on Windows with Git Bash; Maria is on a Mac. What does the command do, and how should each of them respond?






Suggested answer





sudo runs the command as an administrator (after asking for your password), and rm -r deletes the folder /usr/local/lib/node_modules and everything in it, permanently. Deleting system-wide folders as an administrator can break other programs.

Maria should not run it until she understands why that folder must go: ask the AI to explain the cause of the error and whether there is a safer fix that doesn’t need sudo, and check what the folder contains first.
Sam shouldn’t run it either: it’s a Mac/Linux command (Git Bash doesn’t include sudo, and /usr/local/lib/node_modules is a Mac/Linux path). The AI gave a command for the wrong system, a sign that he should tell it he uses Git Bash on Windows and ask again.






Question 16 · Long answer
Claude Code can run shell commands for you, and in auto mode a safety check approves most of them without asking. Why is it still important that you can read Bash commands?






Suggested answer





A good answer mentions several of these points:

You remain responsible for what happens to your files and accounts; an automatic check reduces risk but can’t know everything you intend.
Reading the commands (for example in the transcript view) lets you notice mistakes early, such as the wrong folder, a dangerous wildcard, or a file being overwritten.
In Manual mode you must decide whether to approve each command, and that decision is only meaningful if you understand it.
Understanding the commands helps you learn, debug problems, and give the AI better instructions.






Question 17 · Ordering
Put these steps in order to create and run a new script:

Run ./tidy.sh and check the output.
Type the commands into the file, starting with #!/bin/bash.
Run chmod +x tidy.sh.
Open a new file with nano tidy.sh.
Save with Ctrl+O, Enter, and exit with Ctrl+X.







Suggested answer





d → b → e → c → a. Create the file, write the commands, save and exit, make it executable, then run it.

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
text:
23.1 The problem: report_final_v2_ACTUAL.docx
Every software project, from a student website to Google Search, keeps its files under version control. This page explains what version control is, why it matters even more when an AI agent edits your code, and the difference between Git and GitHub. The next pages put it into practice.
You have probably seen (or created) a folder like this:
Which one is the latest? What changed between v2 and ACTUAL? Can you get back the paragraph you deleted last Tuesday? Who changed the numbers in section 3? Now imagine a project with 200 files that changes every day.
Version control is a system that records changes to a set of files over time, so you can see what changed, when, by whom, and why, and go back to any earlier version. You keep one copy of each file with its real name (report.docx), and the version control system remembers all the older versions for you.

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
section: 23.2 Snapshots: save points for your project
text:
23.2 Snapshots: save points for your project
With version control, you take a snapshot of your project whenever you reach a good point: “the home page works”, “fixed the typo in the menu”. In Git, a snapshot is called a commit. Think of a commit as a save point in a video game: if something goes wrong later, you can always go back to it.
Each commit records:

the state of all the project’s files at that moment,
a short message describing the change,
the author and the date,
a unique ID (a “hash” such as 4293e1d).

The list of all commits is the project’s history:
  ffd1f1f                    b90f840                     4293e1d
  "Add starter files   --->  "Describe planned    --->   "Add intro and contact
   for portfolio site"        pages in README"            email to home page"
  Oct 6, 10:15               Oct 6, 10:22                Oct 7, 14:05
                                                         (newest)
Here is the same history as Git prints it. You’ll create this exact project yourself on the next pages:
4293e1d (HEAD -> main) Add intro and contact email to home page
b90f840 Describe planned pages in README
ffd1f1f Add starter files for portfolio site
What you get from version control:



Benefit
What it means for you




History
See what changed, when, and why, line by line.


Undo
Throw away a bad change, or bring back an old version of a file or of the whole project.


Safe experiments
Try a risky idea. If it fails, go back to the last commit.


Backup
Keep a copy of the whole history online (for example on GitHub). If your laptop dies, your work survives.


Collaboration
Several people can work on the same project without emailing files around. This is covered later, in the part Git and GitHub: Working with Others.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
text:
23.3 Git vs. GitHub
These two names confuse almost everyone at first.

Git is a free, open-source version control program that runs on your computer. It was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds (the creator of Linux) and is by far the most widely used version control system today. Git works offline and doesn’t need an account.
GitHub (github.com) is a website (owned by Microsoft) that stores copies of Git projects online and adds tools for sharing them and working on them together. GitLab and Bitbucket are popular alternatives that do the same job.





Git
GitHub




What it is
A program
A website / online service


Where it runs
On your computer
In the cloud


Needs internet?
No
Yes


Needs an account?
No
Yes (free accounts are available)


Alternatives
(rarely needed; Git dominates)
GitLab, Bitbucket



An analogy: Git is like your phone’s camera, which takes the photos (the snapshots). GitHub is like an online photo album where you upload copies to keep them safe and share them. You can take photos without ever uploading them, but the album is handy for backup and sharing.

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
section: 23.4 Key words: repository, commit, and the .git folder
text:
23.4 Key words: repository, commit, and the .git folder

A repository (or repo) is a project folder whose history Git keeps track of.
Git stores the entire history inside a hidden folder named .git at the top of the repository. You never edit it by hand. Because its name starts with a dot, plain ls doesn’t show it; ls -a does (see Files, Folders, and Paths).

git-tutorial-project/     <- the repository (your project folder)
├── .git/                 <- Git's database: every commit, the whole history
├── README.md             <- your files, which you edit normally
├── css/
│   └── style.css
└── src/
    └── index.html
If you delete the .git folder, your files stay, but the history is gone and the folder is no longer a repository.
Git also thinks of your project in three areas. You’ll use them on the next pages; for now, just notice that saving a snapshot is a two-step process:
 working directory   ---git add--->   staging area   ---git commit--->   repository
 (the files you see                   (changes you                      (the saved commits,
  and edit)                            picked for the                    stored in .git)
                                       next commit)

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
text:
23.5 What Git is good at
Git works with any kind of file, but it shines with plain text files: code, HTML, CSS, Markdown, CSV. For text files it can show you exactly which lines changed. For binary files such as Word documents, Excel workbooks, or images, Git can store each version but can’t show you what changed inside them. That is one more reason programmers write code in text editors, not word processors (see Writing to Files). Git is also not designed for very large files such as videos.

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
section: 23.6 Why Git matters even more with AI coding agents
text:
23.6 Why Git matters even more with AI coding agents
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How Claude Code works · Checkpointing
An AI agent such as Claude Code can change dozens of files in a minute. Sometimes the result is great; sometimes it breaks something in a way you don’t notice right away. Git is your safety net:

Commit before you let the agent work. Afterwards, Git shows you exactly which files and lines the agent changed, and you can undo all of it.
Claude Code can run Git for you. It can run any command you could run in the terminal, including git. It also sees your Git state (current branch, uncommitted changes, recent commits) and commits changes when you ask. You still need to understand Git to check what it did (see Working Effectively with Claude Code).
Claude Code’s checkpoints don’t replace Git. Claude Code can rewind its own file edits within a session, but its docs say checkpoints are not a replacement for version control. For example, they don’t capture files changed by shell commands that Claude runs (such as rm). Use Git for permanent history.







Deeper dive: Git is “distributed”





Older version control systems kept the history on one central server; you had to be online to save a version. Git is a distributed version control system: every copy of a repository (your laptop, GitHub, a second computer) holds the complete history. That is why you can commit on a plane, and why a copy on GitHub is a real backup rather than just a list of files.









Deeper dive: what is a commit ID?





A commit ID is a hash: a 40-character code (letters a-f and digits) that Git calculates from the commit’s contents, for example 4293e1d6b36575de7e70186a7c2900f518313af0. If anything in the commit changed, even one character, the hash would be different. Because the full hash is long, Git usually shows only the first 7 characters (4293e1d), which is enough to identify a commit within a project.

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
text:
23.7 Key takeaways

Version control records snapshots (commits) of your project, so you can see the history and go back to any earlier version.
Git is the program on your computer; GitHub is a website that hosts copies of Git repositories (alternatives: GitLab, Bitbucket).
A repository is a project folder tracked by Git; its history lives in the hidden .git folder.
With AI agents editing your code, Git is your safety net: commit first, review the changes, undo if needed.

title: 23  23.  What Is Version Control? (Git vs. GitHub)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
In one or two sentences, what is version control?






Suggested answer





A system that records changes to a set of files over time, so you can see what changed, when, by whom, and why, and go back to any earlier version.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which statement about Git and GitHub is correct?

Git and GitHub are two names for the same program.
Git is a program on your computer; GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories.
GitHub is a program on your computer; Git is the website where you upload it.
You must install GitHub before you can install Git.







Suggested answer





b. Git is the version control program that runs on your computer. GitHub is an online service that stores copies of Git repositories and adds sharing and collaboration tools. They are not the same thing (a), the roles in (c) are reversed, and Git works fine without GitHub (d).





Question 3 · Matching
Match each term with its meaning.








Term

Meaning




1. repository

A. a snapshot of the project with a message, author, date and ID


2. commit

B. the hidden folder where Git stores the whole history


3. .git

C. a website that hosts Git repositories


4. GitHub

D. a project folder whose history Git tracks


5. working directory

E. the files you actually see and edit









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → A, 3 → B, 4 → C, 5 → E.





Question 4 · True or false
You need a GitHub account to use Git.






Suggested answer





False. Git is a program that runs on your own computer and works offline without any account. You only need a GitHub (or GitLab, Bitbucket) account if you want to store a copy of your repository online.





Question 5 · Short answer
Name two websites other than GitHub that host Git repositories.






Suggested answer





GitLab and Bitbucket.





Question 6 · Short answer
List the four pieces of information that every commit records.






Suggested answer






The state (snapshot) of the project’s files at that moment.
A message describing the change.
The author and the date.
A unique ID (hash), such as 4293e1d.







Medium

Question 7 · Multiple choice
Which of the following is not something version control does for you?

Lets you see which lines of a file changed between two versions
Lets you go back to an earlier version of your project
Automatically finds and fixes bugs in your code
Lets you keep a backup copy of the whole history on another computer or website







Suggested answer





c. Version control records and restores versions; it does not understand or fix your code. Showing line changes (a), going back (b), and keeping a backup copy of the history elsewhere (d) are all core benefits.





Question 8 · Scenario
Your team folder contains budget.xlsx, budget_final.xlsx, budget_final_v2.xlsx and budget_final_v2_ACTUAL.xlsx. Explain how a version control system would organize this differently.






Suggested answer





There would be just one file, budget.xlsx. Each time it reaches a good state, you make a commit with a message such as “Add Q3 forecast”. The version control system stores all the earlier versions in its history, with the date, the author and the message, so you can always see or restore an older version without keeping extra copies with confusing names.





Question 9 · Short answer
Git can store every version of a Word document, but it can’t show you what changed inside it. Why? What kind of file does Git handle best?






Suggested answer





A Word document is a binary file, not plain text, so Git can’t compare it line by line. Git works best with plain text files (code, HTML, CSS, Markdown, CSV), where it can show exactly which lines were added, removed, or changed.





Question 10 · Multiple choice
Where does Git store the history of a repository?

On GitHub only
In a hidden folder named .git at the top of the repository
Inside each file, at the bottom
In a file named history.txt in your home directory







Suggested answer





b. All commits are stored in the hidden .git folder. GitHub (a) is only an optional online copy; Git never adds history to your files (c); and there is no history.txt file (d).





Question 11 · Ordering
Put these steps in the order a change travels through Git’s three areas:

A. The change is saved as a snapshot in the repository.
B. You edit a file in the working directory.
C. You choose the change for the next commit (it goes to the staging area).







Suggested answer





B → C → A. You edit files in the working directory, use git add to put the changes you want into the staging area, and then use git commit to save them as a snapshot in the repository. (You’ll practice this in Your First Repository.)





Question 12 · Short answer
Maria runs ls in her repository and doesn’t see a .git folder. Is something wrong? How can she check that it’s there?






Suggested answer





Nothing is wrong. .git starts with a dot, so it is a hidden folder and plain ls doesn’t list it. ls -a shows hidden files and folders, including .git.





Question 13 · True or false
If you delete the .git folder of a repository, all your project files are deleted too.






Suggested answer





False. Your current files stay where they are, but the history (all the commits) is lost, and the folder is no longer a Git repository. Never delete .git unless you really want to throw away the history.






Hard

Question 14 · Scenario
You asked Claude Code to “clean up the styling”. It changed 12 files and now the website looks broken. Explain how Git helps in this situation, and what you should have done before asking Claude Code to start.






Suggested answer





Before: commit your working project, so you have a known-good snapshot.
After: because the last commit is a known-good state, Git can show you exactly which files and lines the agent changed since then, so you can review them, keep the good parts, and undo the rest, or throw away all the changes and go back to the commit. Without a commit before the agent started, there is no clean point to compare against or return to.





Question 15 · True or false
“Claude Code has checkpoints that can rewind its edits, so I don’t need Git.”






Suggested answer





False. Checkpoints are meant for quick undo within a Claude Code session. The Claude Code docs say they are not a replacement for version control. For example, they don’t capture files changed by shell commands that Claude runs (such as deleting a file with rm). Git gives you permanent history, backups (with GitHub), and collaboration.





Question 16 · Compare
A classmate says: “I don’t need Git. My project folder is in a cloud drive (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive), and it keeps old versions of my files.” Give two things Git gives you that a cloud drive’s version history does not.






Suggested answer





Any two of:

Snapshots of the whole project with a message. A commit records all files together at a meaningful moment (“Add contact page”), not just automatic saves of individual files.
Line-by-line comparison of any two versions of your code.
You decide when to save a version, so each commit is a working, meaningful state rather than every half-finished edit.
Tools built for code: undoing a single change, viewing an old version of the whole project, and (later) collaborating with branches and pull requests.

A good answer contrasts meaningful, project-wide, described snapshots with automatic copies of individual files.





Question 17 · Long answer
Maria works alone and never plans to share her code. Give three reasons why she should still use Git (and GitHub).






Suggested answer






Undo: she can go back to a working version after a bad change, whether she made it or an AI agent did.
History: she can see what changed, when, and why, which helps her find out when a bug appeared.
Backup: a copy on GitHub survives a lost or broken laptop.
Working from two computers: she can move her work between a laptop and a lab PC through GitHub (Cloning and Pulling).
Portfolio: employers often look at GitHub profiles.

Any three of these, explained, make a good answer.





Question 18 · Short answer
Git is called a distributed version control system. What does that mean, and why does it make a copy on GitHub a real backup?






Suggested answer





Every copy of a Git repository holds the complete history, not just the latest files. So the copy on GitHub contains every commit, and if your laptop is lost you can recover the whole project, history included. It also means you can commit while offline.
