title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
text:
24.1 Is Git already installed?
Before you can use Git, it has to be installed, and you have to tell it who you are. This takes about ten minutes, and you do it once per computer.
Open your terminal (Terminal on a Mac, Git Bash on Windows) and type:
Output (your version number will be different):
If you see a version number, Git is installed. Any reasonably recent version works for this book. On a Mac or on Windows the line may have a little extra text after the number, such as (Apple Git-...) or .windows.2.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
text:
git --version

git version 2.56.0
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
text:
24.2 Installing Git

MacWindows (Git Bash)


Option 1 (easiest): Apple’s Command Line Tools. Type git --version in Terminal. If Git isn’t installed yet, macOS offers to install Apple’s Command Line Tools, a free package of developer tools that includes Git. Accept, wait for the download to finish, and run git --version again. (You can also start this install yourself with xcode-select --install.)
Option 2: Homebrew. If you use Homebrew (a popular “package manager” for installing developer tools on a Mac), this installs the newest version of Git:
brew install git
Apple’s Git is usually a few versions behind the newest one. That doesn’t matter for this book.


You already have Git. Git for Windows, which you installed in Getting Bash on Your Computer to get Git Bash, is Git. Open Git Bash and run git --version to check.
The installer asked several questions about Git. These four matter most:







Installer screen
Recommended choice




Choosing the default editor used by Git
Visual Studio Code (if it’s installed), otherwise Nano. Not Vim, the default.


Adjusting the name of the initial branch in new repositories
“Override the default branch name for new repositories”, with main


Choose the default behavior of git pull
Merge (the default)


Choose a credential helper
Git Credential Manager (the default)



If you skipped these screens (for example, if you installed with winget, which accepts every default), just run the configuration commands below. They fix everything.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
text:
24.3 Tell Git who you are
Every commit records an author: a name and an email address. Set yours once:
git config --global user.name "Maria Lopez"
git config --global user.email "maria@example.com"
These commands print nothing when they succeed. Use your real name (or the name you want others to see), with quotes around it because it contains a space.

--global means “for my user account on this computer”, so the setting applies to every repository you create or copy here.
Use the same email as your GitHub account, so GitHub can link your commits to your profile. Anyone who can see your repository can see this email. To keep your address private, GitHub gives you a noreply address: on github.com go to Settings > Emails, turn on Keep my email addresses private, and use the address shown there. It looks like ID+USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
text:
24.4 Three recommended settings
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "nano"
git config --global pull.rebase false

init.defaultBranch main: the name of the first branch in every new repository. Plain Git still calls it master and prints a long hint about it; GitHub uses main. (Some installations, such as Apple’s Git, already use main. Setting it yourself is harmless and makes every computer behave the same.)
core.editor: the text editor Git opens when it needs you to type something, for example a commit message when you forget -m. Nano is a simple editor that runs inside the terminal: type your text, save with Ctrl+O then Enter, and exit with Ctrl+X. If you prefer VS Code, use git config --global core.editor "code --wait" instead (on a Mac, first open VS Code’s Command Palette and run “Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH”).
pull.rebase false: tells git pull what to do when both your computer and GitHub have new commits: merge them. Without any setting, Git stops with an error in that situation (you’ll meet it in Cloning and Pulling). The Windows installer usually sets this already; on a Mac you need this line.







Stuck in Vim?



If Git ever opens a screen full of ~ symbols that doesn’t respond normally, you’re in Vim, a powerful but tricky editor. To get out: press Esc, type :wq, and press Enter (this saves and quits). Then set core.editor as shown above so it doesn’t happen again.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
text:
24.5 Check your settings
git config --global --list
Output:
user.name=Maria Lopez
user.email=maria@example.com
init.defaultbranch=main
core.editor=nano
pull.rebase=false
(Git shows setting names in lowercase, such as init.defaultbranch; they’re not case-sensitive.) To check a single setting, give its name:
git config user.name
Output:
Maria Lopez
If git config --global --list prints an error such as fatal: unable to read config file '/Users/maria/.gitconfig': No such file or directory, you haven’t set anything yet.
On Windows, the choices you made in the installer are stored in a different (system-wide) file, so they don’t appear in this list. To see every setting and the file it comes from, run git config --list --show-origin.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
section: 24.6 Commit messages and other Git files are plain text
text:
24.6 Commit messages and other Git files are plain text
Commit messages, .gitignore files, and code are all plain text. Always write them in a text editor (nano, VS Code, Notepad, TextEdit in plain-text mode), never in a word processor such as Word or Pages. See Writing to Files for the difference.






Deeper dive: where Git stores your settings





--global settings live in a plain text file in your home folder, ~/.gitconfig:
cat ~/.gitconfig
Output:
[user]
    name = Maria Lopez
    email = maria@example.com
[init]
    defaultBranch = main
[core]
    editor = nano
[pull]
    rebase = false
Git actually reads settings at three levels:









Level
Applies to
Stored in
Set with




system
every user on the computer
a file in Git’s install folder
(the installer)


global
you, in all your repositories
~/.gitconfig
git config --global ...


local
one repository only
.git/config inside the repository
git config ... (no --global), run inside the repository



When the same setting appears at several levels, the most specific one wins: local beats global, and global beats system. For example, running git config user.email "maria@company.com" inside one work repository changes the email for that repository only.









Deeper dive: line endings on Windows





Windows ends each line of a text file with two invisible characters (CRLF); Mac and Linux use one (LF). Git for Windows is normally set up (core.autocrlf=true) to convert between them automatically. That’s why Windows users sometimes see warnings like:
warning: in the working copy of 'README.md', LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it
These warnings are harmless. You can ignore them.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 24  24.  Installing and Configuring Git
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Write the command
Write the command that shows whether Git is installed, and which version.






Suggested answer





git --version
It prints something like git version 2.56.0. If Git isn’t installed, you get an error instead (or, on a Mac, an offer to install the Command Line Tools).





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Sam uses Windows and installed Git for Windows in Getting Bash on Your Computer. What does he need to do to install Git?

Download Git separately from Git for Windows
Nothing: Git for Windows is Git (plus Git Bash)
Install Homebrew and run brew install git
Install the Apple Command Line Tools







Suggested answer





b. Git for Windows installs Git together with Git Bash, so Git is already there; he can check with git --version. Options c and d are Mac methods.





Question 3 · Short answer
Why does Git need your name and email address?






Suggested answer





Every commit records its author (name and email). Git uses your user.name and user.email settings for that, and GitHub uses the email to link your commits to your GitHub account.





Question 4 · True or false
You must run git config --global user.name "..." again in every new repository.






Suggested answer





False. --global settings apply to all repositories for your user account on that computer. You set them once per computer.





Question 5 · Matching
Match each setting with what it controls.








Setting

Controls




1. user.name

A. the editor Git opens for messages


2. user.email

B. what git pull does when both sides have new commits


3. init.defaultBranch

C. the author name recorded in commits


4. core.editor

D. the name of the first branch in new repositories


5. pull.rebase

E. the author email recorded in commits









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → D, 4 → A, 5 → B.





Question 6 · Short answer
In nano, how do you save the file and how do you exit?






Suggested answer





Save with Ctrl+O and then Enter (to confirm the file name); exit with Ctrl+X.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
Write the commands Sam should run to set his name to Sam Chen, his email to his GitHub noreply address 12345678+samchen@users.noreply.github.com, and the default branch name to main.






Suggested answer





git config --global user.name "Sam Chen"
git config --global user.email "12345678+samchen@users.noreply.github.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main





Question 8 · Predict the output
On a brand-new Mac account, Maria runs only these two commands:
git config --global user.name "Maria Lopez"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
What does git config --global --list print?






Suggested answer





user.name=Maria Lopez
init.defaultbranch=main
Only the settings she made, in the order she made them, with the setting name shown in lowercase (defaultbranch).





Question 9 · Scenario
Maria wants to make commits in public GitHub repositories without showing her personal email address. What should she do?






Suggested answer





On github.com, go to Settings > Emails, turn on Keep my email addresses private, and copy the noreply address shown there (it looks like ID+USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com). Then set it in Git:
git config --global user.email "ID+USERNAME@users.noreply.github.com"
(using her own address). Her commits are still linked to her GitHub account.





Question 10 · Short answer
What does --global mean in git config --global ...? What happens if you run git config user.email "..." without --global inside a repository?






Suggested answer





--global stores the setting for your user account on this computer (in ~/.gitconfig), so it applies to all your repositories. Without --global, inside a repository, the setting is stored only for that repository (in .git/config) and overrides the global value there.





Question 11 · Read the output
Maria runs git config --global --list and sees:
fatal: unable to read config file '/Users/maria/.gitconfig': No such file or directory
What does it mean, and what should she do?






Suggested answer





The file where global settings are stored doesn’t exist yet, which means she hasn’t set any global settings. She should run the git config --global commands for user.name, user.email, init.defaultBranch, core.editor, and pull.rebase. The first one creates the file.





Question 12 · Scenario
Sam typed git commit without -m, and his terminal filled with ~ symbols. Typing doesn’t seem to work normally. What happened, how does he get out, and how can he prevent it next time?






Suggested answer





Git opened its editor, and on his computer that’s Vim. To get out, he presses Esc, types :wq, and presses Enter. (To write a message first, he presses i, types the message, then Esc, :wq, Enter.) To prevent it, he sets an easier editor:
git config --global core.editor "nano"
or always uses git commit -m "message".





Question 13 · Short answer
Why is pull.rebase false useful even for someone who works alone?






Suggested answer





Working alone from two computers (or editing on github.com) can still leave new commits on both sides. Without a pull setting, git pull then stops with “fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.” With pull.rebase false, Git merges the two sides automatically (see Cloning and Pulling).






Hard

Question 14 · Find the bug
Maria typed:
git config --global user.name Maria Lopez
There was no error, but her commits show the author as just Maria. Why? How does she fix it?






Suggested answer





Without quotes, Bash splits the name into two separate words, so Git receives Maria as the value and Lopez as an extra, unrelated argument. Only Maria is stored. Fix it with quotes:
git config --global user.name "Maria Lopez"
Commits she makes from now on show the full name. (Existing commits keep the old name.)





Question 15 · Scenario
Sam’s commits on GitHub show the author name, but they aren’t linked to his GitHub profile (no profile picture). git config user.email prints sam@laptop.local. What’s wrong, and how does he fix it?






Suggested answer





GitHub links a commit to an account by its email, and sam@laptop.local isn’t an address on his GitHub account. He should set an email that is on his account (or his GitHub noreply address):
git config --global user.email "12345678+samchen@users.noreply.github.com"
New commits will be linked to his profile. Commits he already made keep the old email.





Question 16 · Compare
Explain the difference between system, global, and local Git settings, and which one wins if the same setting appears in more than one.






Suggested answer






System: for every user on the computer (for example, the choices made in the Git for Windows installer).
Global: for your user account, in all your repositories (~/.gitconfig, set with --global).
Local: for one repository only (.git/config, set without --global inside the repository).

The most specific level wins: local overrides global, which overrides system.





Question 17 · Short answer
If you use VS Code as Git’s editor, the setting is code --wait, not just code. What could go wrong without --wait?






Suggested answer





Without --wait, the code command opens the file and returns immediately, so Git thinks you’ve finished editing before you’ve typed anything. For a commit, Git then finds an empty message and cancels the commit (“Aborting commit due to empty commit message”). --wait makes Git wait until you close the file’s tab in VS Code.





Question 18 · Scenario
Sam installed Git for Windows with winget, which accepts every installer default. When he runs git init in a new project, Git prints a long hint about the branch name master. Explain why, and what he should run so that this computer behaves like the rest of the class.






Suggested answer





The installer’s default for the initial branch name is “Let Git decide”, which means master, and its default editor is Vim. Because winget skipped the installer screens, neither was changed. He should run the configuration commands from this page:
git config --global user.name "Sam Chen"
git config --global user.email "sam@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "nano"
git config --global pull.rebase false
(For the repository he just created, git branch -M main renames the branch to main.)

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
text:
25.1 The three areas
On this page you turn a folder into a Git repository and save your first snapshots. You’ll learn the four commands you will type more than any others: git init, git status, git add, and git commit.
Before you start, make sure Git is installed and configured (see Installing and Configuring Git).
Git thinks of your project in three areas:
An analogy: the staging area is a shopping cart. You put items in the cart (git add), you can take some out again, and nothing is final until you check out (git commit). The cart lets you commit some of your changes and leave others for later. For example, you can commit a finished fix to README.md while a half-done change to index.html waits for another commit.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
text:
WORKING DIRECTORY               STAGING AREA                  REPOSITORY (.git)
  the files you see     ------>   the changes you      ------>  the saved commits
  and edit               git add  picked for the     git commit (the history)
                                  next commit

The working directory is your normal project folder. You edit files here with any text editor.
The staging area (also called the index) is a waiting area for the changes you want in your next commit.
The repository holds the commits: the snapshots you’ve saved. It lives in the hidden .git folder.

text:
25.2 Get the practice project
Download the Git practice project (zip) and unzip it into your Documents folder. You get this small website project:
git-tutorial-project/
├── .gitignore        <- hidden file: tells Git which files to ignore (see the .gitignore chapter)
├── README.md
├── css/
│   └── style.css
├── docs/             <- an empty folder
└── src/
    └── index.html
Open a terminal and move into the project folder:
cd ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
section: 25.3 Step 1: git init creates the repository
text:
25.3 Step 1: git init creates the repository
git init
Output:
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/maria/Documents/git-tutorial-project/.git/
git init creates the hidden .git folder, and from now on this folder is a repository. You run git init once per project, never again. Check that .git is there with ls -a:
ls -a
Output:
.  ..  .git  .gitignore  README.md  css  docs  src
(Git Bash adds a / after folder names, such as .git/ and css/.)






Run git init in the project folder, not your home folder



Always cd into the project folder first. Running git init in your home directory turns your whole home folder (Desktop, Documents, …) into one giant repository. If you ever do that by mistake, see Question 16 below.

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
section: 25.4 Step 2: git status tells you what’s going on
text:
25.4 Step 2: git status tells you what’s going on
git status is the command you’ll use most. Run it whenever you’re unsure what state your project is in.
git status
Output:
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .gitignore
    README.md
    css/
    src/

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
How to read it:

On branch main: main is the name of your project’s main line of history (branches come later, in Branches and Merging).
No commits yet: no snapshots have been saved.
Untracked files: Git sees these files, but isn’t tracking them yet.
The lines in parentheses are hints that tell you what to do next.
docs/ is missing because it’s empty. Git does not track empty folders (more below).
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own
25  25. Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
section: 25.5 Step 3: git add puts changes in the staging area
text:
25.5 Step 3: git add puts changes in the staging area
Add one file:
git add README.md
git status
Output:
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
    new file:   README.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .gitignore
    css/
    src/
README.md moved to Changes to be committed: it’s in the staging area. You can list several files (git add README.md src/index.html), or add everything at once with ., which means “this folder and everything in it”:
git add .
git status
Output:
On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached <file>..." to unstage)
    new file:   .gitignore
    new file:   README.md
    new file:   css/style.css
    new file:   src/index.html
On Windows, git add may also print warnings such as warning: in the working copy of 'README.md', LF will be replaced by CRLF the next time Git touches it. They’re about invisible line-ending characters and are harmless (see Installing and Configuring Git).






Check before you add everything



git add . stages every change in the folder that isn’t ignored. Run git status first, so you don’t commit something you didn’t mean to (such as a file with a password; see .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git).

25  25. Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
section: 25.6 Step 4: git commit saves the snapshot
text:
25.6 Step 4: git commit saves the snapshot
git commit -m "Add starter files for portfolio site"
Output:
[main (root-commit) ffd1f1f] Add starter files for portfolio site
 4 files changed, 39 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 create mode 100644 README.md
 create mode 100644 css/style.css
 create mode 100644 src/index.html

-m stands for message: the text in quotes describes the commit.
main is the branch; root-commit means this is the first commit.
ffd1f1f is the start of the commit’s ID. Yours will be different, because the ID depends on your name, the date, and the time.
4 files changed, 39 insertions(+): four new files with 39 lines in total. (create mode 100644 just means “new regular file”; you can ignore it.)

If you forget -m, Git opens your text editor so you can type the message. Type it, save, and close the editor (in nano: Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).
Now the working directory matches the last commit:
git status
Output:
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
section: 25.7 Step 5: edit, add, commit (the everyday loop)
text:
25.7 Step 5: edit, add, commit (the everyday loop)
Add a line to the end of README.md (in your text editor, or with >>, which appends to a file):
echo "It will have a home page and a contact page." >> README.md
git status
Output:
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   README.md

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Git noticed that a tracked file was modified. Stage it and commit:
git add README.md
git commit -m "Describe planned pages in README"
Output:
[main b90f840] Describe planned pages in README
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
Your project now has two snapshots. git log --oneline lists them, newest first (the next page covers history in detail):
git log --oneline
Output:
b90f840 (HEAD -> main) Describe planned pages in README
ffd1f1f Add starter files for portfolio site
This is the loop you’ll repeat all day:
edit files  -->  git status  -->  git add  -->  git commit  -->  (repeat)

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
text:
25.8 Writing good commit messages
Your future self (and anyone else who reads the history) will rely on these messages.

Write a short summary, about 50 characters or less.
Start with a verb in the imperative: “Add”, “Fix”, “Update”, “Remove”. A handy test: the message should complete the sentence “If applied, this commit will …”.
Say what changed (and why, if it isn’t obvious).
Make each commit one logical change, and commit often.




Good
Bad




Add contact form to home page
stuff


Fix broken link to style.css
changes


Update README with setup steps
asdf

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
text:
25.9 Git doesn’t track empty folders
The empty docs/ folder never appeared in git status and isn’t in the commit. Git tracks files; a folder is included only when it contains at least one tracked file. If you want to keep an empty folder in a repository, the usual trick is to put an empty placeholder file in it. Many people name it .gitkeep (a convention, not a Git feature):
touch docs/.gitkeep
After this, git status lists docs/ as untracked, and you can add and commit it like any other file.






Deeper dive: shortcuts you’ll see (git add -A, git commit -a)






git add -A stages all changes in the whole repository, even when you are in a subfolder. git add . stages the changes in the current folder and below. From the top folder of the repository they do the same thing.
git commit -a -m "message" (or git commit -am "message") stages every modified or deleted tracked file and commits in one step. It does not include new (untracked) files, which still need git add.

These save typing, but they also make it easier to commit something by accident. While you’re learning, git status, git add, git commit is the safer habit.









Deeper dive: what does (HEAD -> main) mean?





main is a branch: a name that points to the newest commit in a line of history. HEAD means “where you are now”. HEAD -> main says you are on the main branch, and that branch points to commit b90f840. When you commit, main moves forward to the new commit, and HEAD moves with it.

title: 25  25.  Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
What does git init do?

Downloads a project from GitHub
Creates a new repository by adding a hidden .git folder to the current folder
Saves a snapshot of all files
Installs Git on your computer







Suggested answer





b. git init turns the current folder into a repository by creating the hidden .git folder. Downloading a project is git clone (a), saving a snapshot is git commit (c), and git init doesn’t install anything (d).





Question 2 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. git init

A. saves the staged changes as a new commit


2. git status

B. lists the commits, one per line


3. git add README.md

C. turns the current folder into a repository


4. git commit -m "..."

D. shows which files are untracked, modified, or staged


5. git log --oneline

E. puts the changes in README.md into the staging area









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → E, 4 → A, 5 → B.





Question 3 · Short answer
Name Git’s three areas and say in a few words what each one holds.






Suggested answer






Working directory: the files you see and edit.
Staging area (index): the changes you’ve chosen for the next commit.
Repository: the saved commits (the history), stored in .git.






Question 4 · True or false
You should run git init every time you start working on your project.






Suggested answer





False. git init is run once, to create the repository. After that you just cd into the folder and use git status, git add, and git commit.





Question 5 · Fill in the blank
In git add ., the . means ________.






Suggested answer





The current folder (and everything inside it). So git add . stages all changes in the current folder and its subfolders, except ignored files.





Question 6 · True or false
Git tracks empty folders, so an empty docs/ folder is included in your first commit.






Suggested answer





False. Git tracks files, not folders. An empty folder is never committed. To keep it, put a placeholder file in it (commonly named .gitkeep) and commit that file.






Medium

Question 7 · Predict the output
Maria’s working tree is clean. She creates a new file with touch contact.html and runs git status. Which section of the output lists contact.html?






Suggested answer





Untracked files. The file is new, and Git hasn’t been told to track it yet. The output ends with nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track).





Question 8 · Write the command
Write the commands to stage only README.md and css/style.css and then commit them with the message Update README and page styles.






Suggested answer





git add README.md css/style.css
git commit -m "Update README and page styles"





Question 9 · Read the output
Which files will be included if Maria runs git commit -m "Update site" now?
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
    modified:   README.md

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   src/index.html

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    notes.txt






Suggested answer





Only README.md, because it is the only file under Changes to be committed (the staging area). src/index.html is modified but not staged, and notes.txt is untracked. Neither is included unless she runs git add on them first.





Question 10 · Multiple choice
Which commit message is the best?

updates
I changed some things in the CSS file because it looked bad
Fix overlapping menu on small screens
asdfgh







Suggested answer





c. It is short, starts with an imperative verb, and says what changed. (a) and (d) say nothing useful. (b) is long, vague (“some things”), and not written in the imperative style.





Question 11 · Read the output
Explain each part of this output:
[main (root-commit) ffd1f1f] Add starter files for portfolio site
 4 files changed, 39 insertions(+)






Suggested answer






main: the branch the commit was made on.
root-commit: this is the first commit in the repository.
ffd1f1f: the start of the new commit’s unique ID.
Add starter files for portfolio site: the commit message.
4 files changed, 39 insertions(+): the commit added four files containing 39 lines in total.






Question 12 · Scenario
Maria finished a fix in README.md but is halfway through a change in src/index.html. She wants to commit only the README fix. What should she type?






Suggested answer





git add README.md
git commit -m "Fix typo in README"
Because only README.md is staged, the commit contains only the README fix. The change to src/index.html stays in the working directory for a later commit. This is exactly what the staging area is for. (Avoid git add . here, because it would stage both files.)





Question 13 · Short answer
What happens if you type git commit without -m "..."?






Suggested answer





Git opens your configured text editor (for example nano) so you can type the commit message. When you save and close the editor, the commit is created. (If you close it without writing a message, Git cancels the commit.)






Hard

Question 14 · Find the bug
Maria created contact.html and typed:
git commit -m "Add contact page"
Git printed a status listing contact.html under Untracked files, ending with:
nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
What went wrong, and how does she fix it?






Suggested answer





She skipped the staging step. git commit only saves what’s in the staging area, and contact.html was never added. Fix:
git add contact.html
git commit -m "Add contact page"





Question 15 · Find the bug
Sam opens Git Bash and types git status. He gets:
fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git
Give two possible reasons and how to fix each one.






Suggested answer






He is in the wrong folder. A new terminal starts in the home directory, not in the project. Fix: cd into the project folder (for example cd ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project) and run git status again.
The folder isn’t a repository yet. Fix: cd into the project folder and run git init (only once).

pwd and ls -a help him check where he is and whether a .git folder exists.





Question 16 · Scenario
Sam accidentally ran git init in his home directory. Now git status lists Desktop/, Documents/, Downloads/ and more as untracked. What happened, and how can he undo it? What must he be careful about?






Suggested answer





git init turned his whole home directory into a repository by creating ~/.git. To undo it, he deletes only that hidden folder:
rm -rf ~/.git
He must type this exactly: rm -rf deletes without asking and there is no trash can. Deleting ~/.git removes only the accidental repository; his files are not touched. (If he had already been using a real repository directly in his home folder, its history would be lost too. That’s one more reason to keep each project in its own folder.)





Question 17 · Long answer
Why does Git have a staging area instead of committing every change automatically? Give an example where it helps.






Suggested answer





The staging area lets you decide exactly what goes into each commit, so every commit can be one clean, logical change with a clear message. Example: you fixed a typo in README.md and are halfway through redesigning src/index.html. You stage and commit only README.md (“Fix typo in README”), and the unfinished redesign stays out of the history until it works. It also gives you a chance to review (with git status) before saving, and to leave out files that should never be committed.





Question 18 · Scenario
Maria committed her whole project, including an empty images/ folder. Later she copies the repository to another computer and the images/ folder is missing. Explain why, and how she could have kept the folder.






Suggested answer





Git doesn’t track empty folders, so images/ was never part of any commit. She could have created a placeholder file in it (for example touch images/.gitkeep), then run git add images/.gitkeep and committed. A folder that contains a tracked file is recreated wherever the repository is copied.





Question 19 · Predict the output
Maria adds the line line A to the end of README.md and runs git add README.md. Then she adds another line, line B, and runs git commit -m "Add line A" (without running git add again). Which of the two lines are in the commit? What will git status show afterwards?






Suggested answer





Only line A is in the commit. git add stages the file as it is at that moment; later edits are not staged automatically. Before the commit, git status would even list README.md twice: under “Changes to be committed” and under “Changes not staged for commit”. After the commit, git status shows README.md as modified under “Changes not staged for commit”, because line B is still only in the working directory. She needs another git add and git commit to save it.






Challenge

Question 20 · Hands-on
Create a brand-new repository from scratch: make a folder named recipes, turn it into a repository, and make three commits (for example: add README.md; add pancakes.txt; add a line to pancakes.txt). Use git status before every git add and git commit. Finish with git log --oneline.






Suggested answer





One possible solution:
cd ~/Documents
mkdir recipes
cd recipes
git init
echo "# My recipes" > README.md
git status
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
echo "Pancakes: flour, milk, eggs" > pancakes.txt
git status
git add pancakes.txt
git commit -m "Add pancake recipe"
echo "Cook 2 minutes per side" >> pancakes.txt
git status
git add pancakes.txt
git commit -m "Add cooking time to pancake recipe"
git log --oneline
git log --oneline should list three commits, newest first, with your own commit IDs.





Question 21 · Hands-on
In the practice project, make Git keep the empty docs/ folder. Use git status to check each step, and finish with git log --oneline.






Suggested answer





cd ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project
touch docs/.gitkeep
git status
git add docs/.gitkeep
git commit -m "Keep empty docs folder"
git log --oneline
After touch, git status lists docs/ under Untracked files. The commit output includes create mode 100644 docs/.gitkeep, and the new commit appears at the top of git log --oneline.





Question 22 · Hands-on
Starting from a clean working tree, make git status show all three sections at once: “Changes to be committed”, “Changes not staged for commit”, and “Untracked files”. Write down the commands you used and explain why each file ended up in its section. Then commit only the staged change.






Suggested answer





One possible solution:
echo "More details soon." >> README.md
git add README.md
echo "/* footer styles */" >> css/style.css
touch todo.txt
git status
git commit -m "Add note to README"

README.md is under Changes to be committed because it was added.
css/style.css is under Changes not staged for commit because it is tracked and was modified, but not added.
todo.txt is under Untracked files because Git has never tracked it.

The commit contains only the README change. Afterwards git status still shows the other two files.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own
25  25. Your First Repository: init, status, add, commit

title: 26  26.  Viewing History and Undoing Changes
text:
26.1 Viewing history: git log
Commits are only useful if you can look back at them and use them to undo mistakes. This page shows you how to read the history, see exactly what changed, and undo changes safely. It continues with the practice project from Your First Repository, which has two commits so far.
Output:
Each entry shows the full commit ID (hash), the author, the date, and the message. The newest commit is at the top. (HEAD -> main) marks where you are now: on the main branch, at its latest commit.
When the history is longer than your window, Git shows it in a scrollable viewer: use the arrow keys or Space to scroll, and press q to quit.
Some useful variations:

title: 26  26.  Viewing History and Undoing Changes
text:
26.2 Seeing what changed: git diff
Open src/index.html in your text editor and replace the line <p>Under construction!</p> with these two lines, then save:
    <p>Hi, I'm Maria. I study business and build websites.</p>
    <p>Contact: maria@example.com</p>
Before you commit, ask Git what you changed:
git diff
Output:
diff --git a/src/index.html b/src/index.html
index ad87688..390be80 100644
--- a/src/index.html
+++ b/src/index.html
@@ -6,6 +6,7 @@
 </head>
 <body>
     <h1>Welcome to My Portfolio</h1>
-    <p>Under construction!</p>
+    <p>Hi, I'm Maria. I study business and build websites.</p>
+    <p>Contact: maria@example.com</p>
 </body>
 </html>

26.2.1 How to read a diff

--- a/src/index.html is the old version, +++ b/src/index.html the new one.
Lines starting with - were removed (red in the terminal); lines starting with + were added (green). Lines starting with a space are unchanged context, shown to help you find your place.
A changed line appears as a removed line followed by an added line.
@@ -6,6 +6,7 @@ says where you are in the file: the snippet starts at line 6 and is 6 lines long in the old version, and starts at line 6 and is 7 lines long in the new version. Sometimes Git adds a nearby line of the file after the second @@ as a landmark.
You can ignore the index ... line; it contains Git’s internal IDs.



26.2.2 git diff vs. git diff --staged
Stage the file and run git diff again:
git add src/index.html
git diff
This time there is no output. That’s because git diff compares your working directory with the staging area, and they are now the same. To see what you are about to commit, compare the staging area with the last commit:
git diff --staged
It prints the same diff as before. A diagram:
 working directory  <-- git diff -->  staging area  <-- git diff --staged -->  last commit
Now commit:
git commit -m "Add intro and contact email to home page"
Output:
[main 4293e1d] Add intro and contact email to home page
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
The history now has three commits:
git log --oneline
Output:
4293e1d (HEAD -> main) Add intro and contact email to home page
b90f840 Describe planned pages in README
ffd1f1f Add starter files for portfolio site

section: 26.3 Looking at one commit: git show
text:
26.3 Looking at one commit: git show
git show followed by a commit ID prints that commit’s details and its diff. You only need the first few characters of the ID:
git show b90f840
Output:
commit b90f840eb88afb1f49b39e019d369b3c837a311a
Author: Maria Lopez <maria@example.com>
Date:   Tue Oct 6 10:22:00 2026 -0400

    Describe planned pages in README

diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 512dd88..9af11fc 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -5,3 +5,4 @@ This is a simple website project to learn Git!
 ## What it does

 A personal portfolio website.
+It will have a home page and a contact page.
git show without an ID shows the latest commit. (In Git, HEAD is a name for “the commit you are on now”, so git show HEAD does the same.)

26  26. Viewing History and Undoing Changes

title: 26  26.  Viewing History and Undoing Changes
text:
26.4 Undoing changes
Which command you need depends on where the mistake is:








Situation
Command
Can you lose work?




Throw away uncommitted changes to a file
git restore <file>
Yes: those changes are gone for good


Unstage a file but keep your changes
git restore --staged <file>
No


Fix the last commit (message or a forgotten file)
git commit --amend
No, but only do it before you push


Undo a commit that is already in the history
git revert <commit>
No: it adds a new commit


Look at an old version of the whole project
git switch --detach <commit>
No (return with git switch main)




26.4.1 Throw away changes in a file: git restore
Maria wanted to add a line to README.md, but typed > instead of >>. The > overwrote the whole file:
echo "Contact page coming soon" > README.md
git diff
Output:
diff --git a/README.md b/README.md
index 9af11fc..b373488 100644
--- a/README.md
+++ b/README.md
@@ -1,8 +1 @@
-# My Awesome Project
-
-This is a simple website project to learn Git!
-
-## What it does
-
-A personal portfolio website.
-It will have a home page and a contact page.
+Contact page coming soon
Because the file was committed, Git can put it back:
git restore README.md
git status
Output:
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean






git restore <file> can’t be undone



It replaces the file with the version in the staging area (which is usually the same as the last commit). Any uncommitted changes in that file are gone for good, because they were never saved in Git.




26.4.2 Unstage a file: git restore --staged
Maria writes a personal to-do list in notes.txt and, out of habit, runs git add .:
echo "call the bank, buy milk" > notes.txt
git add .
git status
Output:
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
    new file:   notes.txt
She doesn’t want it in the project, so she takes it out of the staging area:
git restore --staged notes.txt
git status now lists notes.txt under Untracked files again. The file itself is untouched. Maria then deletes it with rm notes.txt, because it doesn’t belong in the project folder. (To keep files like this out of git status for good, see .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git.)


26.4.3 Fix the last commit: git commit --amend
In css/style.css, Maria changes the h1 rule’s color: #333; to color: navy;, then commits with a typo in the message, and fixes it right away:
git add css/style.css
git commit -m "Make headng navy"
git commit --amend -m "Make heading navy"
Output (of the last command):
[main cb793da] Make heading navy
 Date: Wed Oct 7 14:20:00 2026 -0400
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
--amend replaces the last commit with a new one; notice the new ID. If you forgot to include a file, git add it and run git commit --amend --no-edit (which keeps the message).
Only amend commits you haven’t pushed to GitHub yet (pushing is covered in Putting Your Repository on GitHub). The online copy still has the old commit, and the two copies would disagree.


26.4.4 Undo a commit safely: git revert
Maria decides she doesn’t like the navy heading after all. git revert makes a new commit that does the exact opposite of an earlier one:
git revert --no-edit HEAD
Output:
[main fc2bb9b] Revert "Make heading navy"
 Date: Wed Oct 7 14:30:00 2026 -0400
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
HEAD means the latest commit; you can also give any commit ID, such as git revert cb793da. --no-edit accepts the ready-made message; without it, Git opens your editor so you can edit the message first. Both commits stay in the history, so nothing is lost, and it is safe even after you’ve pushed:
git log --oneline
Output:
fc2bb9b (HEAD -> main) Revert "Make heading navy"
cb793da Make heading navy
4293e1d Add intro and contact email to home page
b90f840 Describe planned pages in README
ffd1f1f Add starter files for portfolio site

section: 26.5 Viewing an old version: git switch --detach
text:
26.5 Viewing an old version: git switch --detach
To see what the whole project looked like in an earlier commit, switch to it:
git switch --detach ffd1f1f
Output:
HEAD is now at ffd1f1f Add starter files for portfolio site
Your files now look exactly as they did in that commit: src/index.html says Under construction! again. git status reports HEAD detached at ffd1f1f. Detached HEAD means you are looking at a commit directly instead of being on a branch. Look around, run the site, but don’t make commits here.
Don’t panic if git log now shows only one commit: it lists history only up to where you are. The newer commits are safe. To return:
git switch main
Output:
Previous HEAD position was ffd1f1f Add starter files for portfolio site
Switched to branch 'main'
(git switch - also works: it goes back to the branch you were on before.)






Deeper dive: older commands you’ll see online (checkout, reset)





Older tutorials, Stack Overflow answers, and AI tools often use older commands. git switch and git restore were added in 2019 (Git 2.23) to split up the jobs of git checkout, which did too many things.



Older command
Modern equivalent




git checkout -- README.md
git restore README.md


git reset HEAD README.md
git restore --staged README.md


git checkout ffd1f1f
git switch --detach ffd1f1f


git checkout main
git switch main



Be very careful with git reset --hard. git reset --hard HEAD throws away all uncommitted changes in every file at once. git reset --hard HEAD~1 also deletes the latest commit from the branch (HEAD~1 means “one commit before HEAD”). If you’ve already pushed that commit, this causes trouble. If an AI suggests git reset --hard, make sure you understand exactly what it will throw away; git revert is usually the safer choice.









Deeper dive: getting back one file from an old commit





To bring back an old version of a single file without moving the whole project, use git restore with --source:
git restore --source=ffd1f1f src/index.html
The old version replaces the file in your working directory, and git status shows the file as modified. Commit it if you want to keep it, or run git restore src/index.html to go back to the current version.

title: 26  26.  Viewing History and Undoing Changes
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Which command lists the commits compactly, one line per commit?

git status
git log --oneline
git diff
git show







Suggested answer





b. git log --oneline prints a short ID and the message for each commit. git status (a) shows the state of your files, git diff (c) shows uncommitted changes, and git show (d) shows one commit in detail.





Question 2 · True or false
git log lists the oldest commit first.






Suggested answer





False. The newest commit is at the top.





Question 3 · Short answer
Your project has 200 commits. You run git log and the output fills the screen in a viewer. How do you scroll, and how do you get back to the prompt?






Suggested answer





Scroll with the arrow keys or Space, and press q to quit the viewer and return to the prompt.





Question 4 · Short answer
In the output of git diff, what do lines starting with +, -, and a space mean?






Suggested answer






+: a line that was added.
-: a line that was removed.
a space: an unchanged line, shown as context.

A changed line appears as a - line followed by a + line.





Question 5 · Matching
Match each situation with the right command.








Situation

Command




1. Throw away my uncommitted changes to README.md

A. git revert <commit>


2. Take notes.txt out of the staging area

B. git commit --amend -m "..."


3. Fix a typo in the last commit’s message (not pushed yet)

C. git restore README.md


4. Undo an older commit with a new commit

D. git switch --detach <commit>


5. Look at the whole project as it was in an old commit

E. git restore --staged notes.txt









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → B, 4 → A, 5 → D.





Question 6 · True or false
git restore --staged notes.txt deletes the file notes.txt.






Suggested answer





False. It only takes the file out of the staging area. The file and its contents stay in your working directory; if it’s a new file, it simply becomes untracked again.






Medium

Question 7 · Read the diff
Describe in plain words what changed:
--- a/css/style.css
+++ b/css/style.css
@@ -4,5 +4,5 @@ body {
 }

 h1 {
-    color: #333;
+    color: navy;
 }






Suggested answer





In css/style.css, the h1 rule’s color changed from #333 (dark gray) to navy. One line was removed and one added, which is how a diff shows a changed line. The rest are unchanged context lines.





Question 8 · Predict the output
Maria edits src/index.html and runs git add src/index.html. What do git diff and git diff --staged show now?






Suggested answer






git diff shows nothing: it compares the working directory with the staging area, and they now match.
git diff --staged shows her change to src/index.html: it compares the staging area with the last commit, so it shows what she is about to commit.






Question 9 · Read the output
A diff contains the line @@ -10,4 +10,6 @@. What does it tell you?






Suggested answer





The snippet starts at line 10 in both versions. It is 4 lines long in the old version and 6 lines long in the new version, so the change added two lines (overall) in that area.





Question 10 · Write the command
Write the command that shows the details and the diff of commit 4293e1d.






Suggested answer





git show 4293e1d





Question 11 · Write the command
Maria just committed with the message Fix typo in hedaer. She hasn’t pushed. Write the command to change the message to Fix typo in header.






Suggested answer





git commit --amend -m "Fix typo in header"
The last commit is replaced by a new one with the corrected message (and a new ID). This is fine because the commit hasn’t been pushed.





Question 12 · Multiple choice
A commit that broke the site was pushed to GitHub yesterday. Which is the safest way to undo it?

git commit --amend
git revert <commit>
git restore <file>
Delete the .git folder and start over







Suggested answer





b. git revert adds a new commit that reverses the bad one, without rewriting history, so it’s safe after pushing. --amend (a) only changes the latest commit and rewrites it, which you shouldn’t do after pushing. git restore (c) only discards uncommitted changes. Deleting .git (d) destroys the whole history.





Question 13 · Ordering
Put these commands in order to look at the project as it was in commit ffd1f1f and then go back to normal work:

A. git switch main
B. git log --oneline (to find the commit ID)
C. git switch --detach ffd1f1f
D. look at the files (for example cat src/index.html)







Suggested answer





B → C → D → A. Find the ID, switch to the old commit, look around, and switch back to main.





Question 14 · Scenario
Maria runs echo "New intro" > README.md, meaning to type >>. She hasn’t run git add or git commit since. How can she recover the file, and what will happen to the line New intro?






Suggested answer





git restore README.md
This brings back the last committed version of README.md. The line New intro is thrown away (she can add it again, this time with >>). The recovery works only because the earlier contents had been committed.






Hard

Question 15 · Scenario
Same mistake as in the previous question, but this time Maria also ran git add . after overwriting README.md. She runs git restore README.md, but the file still says New intro. Why? How does she get the committed version back?






Suggested answer





git restore README.md copies the file from the staging area, and the staging area now contains the bad version (she staged it with git add .). She must first unstage it, then restore it:
git restore --staged README.md
git restore README.md
(git restore --staged --worktree README.md does both in one command.) Now both the staging area and the working directory match the last commit.





Question 16 · Short answer
Why should you not use git commit --amend on a commit you’ve already pushed to GitHub?






Suggested answer





--amend doesn’t edit the commit; it replaces it with a new commit that has a new ID. GitHub still has the old commit, so your local history and the online history no longer match, and Git will refuse a normal push. Fixing this requires more advanced (and risky) commands. After pushing, use git revert or simply make a new commit with the fix.





Question 17 · Scenario
Maria ran git switch --detach ffd1f1f. Now git log --oneline shows only one commit, and her contact email is gone from src/index.html. She thinks she has lost a week of work. Explain what’s going on and what she should do.






Suggested answer





Nothing is lost. She is in detached HEAD state, looking at the old commit ffd1f1f. Her files show that old version, and git log only lists history up to where she is. All the newer commits are still in the repository. Running git switch main (or git switch -) brings back the latest version of every file and the full history.





Question 18 · Compare
Compare git restore <file> and git revert <commit>: what does each one undo, does it change the history, and can you lose work?






Suggested answer














git restore <file>
git revert <commit>




Undoes
uncommitted changes in a file
a change that is already committed


History
not touched
a new commit is added; nothing is removed


Risk
the discarded changes are gone for good
none: both the old commit and its reversal stay in the history








Question 19 · Find the bug
An AI chatbot told Maria: “To undo your last commit, run git reset --hard HEAD~1.” Her last commit is already on GitHub, and she also has unsaved (uncommitted) work in css/style.css. What would this command do? What should she use instead?






Suggested answer





git reset --hard HEAD~1 would:

remove the last commit from her main branch (rewriting history that GitHub already has, so her next normal push would be refused), and
throw away all uncommitted changes in every file, including her work in css/style.css, which can’t be recovered with Git.

Safer: commit (or otherwise save) her work in css/style.css first, then run git revert <commit> with the bad commit’s ID from git log --oneline (after her new commit, the bad commit is no longer HEAD). This undoes the bad commit by adding a new commit.





Question 20 · Long answer
Explain the difference between git diff, git diff --staged, and git show. When would you use each one in your everyday workflow?






Suggested answer






git diff: working directory vs. staging area, i.e. changes you haven’t staged yet. Use it while working, to review your edits (or an AI’s edits) before git add.
git diff --staged: staging area vs. last commit, i.e. exactly what the next commit will contain. Use it right before git commit.
git show <commit>: one commit that is already in the history, with its message and diff. Use it to understand what an earlier commit did.

27.1 What should not be committed
Some files should never go into a repository: clutter your computer creates, folders you can always re-create, and above all secrets such as passwords and API keys. This page shows you how to make Git ignore files and what to do if a secret slips through anyway.
node_modules/ is the folder where npm downloads the packages a JavaScript project uses; it can hold thousands of files (see Web Frameworks and Meta-Frameworks).

27  27. .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git

title: 27  27.  .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git
text:
27.2 The .gitignore file
A .gitignore file is a plain text file, usually in the top folder of the repository, that lists patterns of file and folder names Git should ignore. The practice project from the previous pages already has one:
cat .gitignore
Output:
# Operating system files
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Editor files
*.swp
*.swo
*~

# Build artifacts
build/
dist/
*.log
The most useful pattern rules:







Pattern
What it ignores




.DS_Store
every file with exactly this name, in any folder


*.log
every file whose name ends in .log (* matches any characters)


build/
every folder named build, and everything inside it (the trailing / means “folders only”)


node_modules/
the node_modules folder (and everything inside it)


.env
every file named exactly .env


# Secrets
nothing: a line starting with # is a comment; blank lines are ignored too


!.env.example
an exception: a ! re-includes a file that an earlier pattern ignored



Commit the .gitignore file itself, so the rules travel with the project to every computer that gets a copy.

27  27. .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git

title: 27  27.  .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git
text:
27.3 Checking that it works
Create a log file and ask for the status:
touch debug.log
git status
Output:
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
debug.log doesn’t appear at all, because it matches *.log. Two commands help when you’re not sure why a file is (or isn’t) ignored:
git check-ignore -v debug.log
Output:
.gitignore:13:*.log debug.log
This reads: “line 13 of .gitignore, the pattern *.log, ignores debug.log”. If a file is not ignored, git check-ignore prints nothing. git status --ignored adds an Ignored files section to the normal status.

27  27. .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git

title: 27  27.  .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git
section: 27.4 Keeping a .env file out of Git
text:
27.4 Keeping a .env file out of Git
Maria wants to add a weather widget to her site, and the weather service gave her an API key (a secret code that identifies her account; see APIs, API Keys, and Third-Party Services). Instead of typing the key into her code, she stores it in a .env file, a plain text file of NAME=value lines that programs load as environment variables (see Environment Variables):
echo "WEATHER_API_KEY=abc123-fake-key-for-practice" > .env
git status
Output:
On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .env

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)
This is dangerous: her next git add . would put the key into the history. So she opens .gitignore in her text editor and adds an empty line and then these two lines at the end:
# Secrets: never commit these
.env
Now git status lists only modified: .gitignore. The .env file has disappeared from the status, so git add . can no longer pick it up.
Next she creates a .env.example file: a template with the same variable names but fake values. It’s safe to commit, and it tells anyone who copies the project (including Maria on another computer) which values they need to fill in:
echo "WEATHER_API_KEY=your-key-goes-here" > .env.example
git add .gitignore .env.example
git commit -m "Ignore .env and add .env.example template"
Output:
[main 736e88f] Ignore .env and add .env.example template
 2 files changed, 4 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .env.example
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own
27  27. .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git

title: 27  27.  .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git
section: 27.5 Ignoring a file that is already tracked
text:
27.5 Ignoring a file that is already tracked
.gitignore only affects untracked files. If a file was committed before you added it to .gitignore, Git keeps tracking it and keeps showing its changes.
Sam made exactly this mistake: his first commit in his weather-app project included his .env file. To stop tracking it without deleting it from his computer:
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git rm --cached .env
git status
Output:
rm '.env'
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
    deleted:    .env

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .gitignore
git rm --cached removes the file from the repository (the staging area, and so from the next commit) but leaves it on disk; “deleted” here means “deleted from Git’s tracking”. He then commits:
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"






The secret is still in the history



New commits no longer contain .env, but the old commit still does. Anyone with a copy of the repository can see it, for example with git show HEAD~1:.env, which prints the old file’s contents. If that commit was ever pushed to GitHub, treat the key as leaked (next section).
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own
27  27. .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git

title: 27  27.  .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git
text:
27.6 If you leak a secret

Revoke or rotate the key immediately. Log in to the service that issued it, delete the old key, and create a new one. This is the only fix that really works: once revoked, the leaked key is useless.
Then clean up your project. Put the new key in .env (which is ignored), and remove the secret from any tracked file.
Don’t count on deleting it from GitHub. Removing the file, the commit, or even the repository doesn’t remove copies that already exist in clones and forks, and anyone (or any automated tool) may already have copied it. GitHub’s docs recommend rotating the secret first; rewriting the history is a lot of work and often unnecessary once the key is revoked.

GitHub also has two safety nets on github.com:

Push protection for your account is turned on by default. It blocks a push to a public repository if the push contains a secret in a format GitHub recognizes.
Secret scanning runs automatically on public repositories. For keys from GitHub’s partner services, GitHub notifies the service, which can then revoke the key.

These only catch known kinds of secrets, so they don’t replace good habits. The best protection is that the secret never gets committed in the first place.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own
27  27. .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git

title: 27  27.  .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git
text:
27.7 Secrets and Claude Code
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Settings · Permissions · API key best practices

Anthropic’s help center warns about this exact mistake. It says one of the most frequent causes of leaked API keys is accidental exposure in public code repositories, such as keys committed to public GitHub repositories. It compares an API key to a credit card number: whoever has it can run up charges on your account. It also says to add .env files to .gitignore.
Keep secrets out of your prompts too. Don’t paste a real key into a chat with Claude Code (or any AI tool). Put it in .env, and ask Claude to write code that reads it from an environment variable.
Claude Code can read files in your project, including .env. If you don’t want it to, a deny rule such as Read(./.env) in Claude Code’s settings blocks its file tools from reading that file (see The .claude Folders and Settings Files).
Claude Code’s personal settings file stays out of Git. .claude/settings.local.json holds your personal settings for one project. The first time Claude Code writes this file in a Git repository, it adds it to your global Git ignore file (see the deeper dive below), so it stays out of your commits. If you create the file by hand, add it to .gitignore yourself.







Deeper dive: other places Git looks for ignore rules






Your global ignore file, by default ~/.config/git/ignore, applies to every repository on your computer. It’s a good place for your own clutter, such as .DS_Store on a Mac. It’s not shared with anyone. (A different file can be chosen with the core.excludesFile setting.)
.git/info/exclude works like .gitignore but only in this one repository, and is never committed.
Templates: GitHub maintains a collection of ready-made .gitignore files for many languages and tools at github.com/github/gitignore.










Deeper dive: a few more pattern rules






A pattern without a slash (like *.log or .env) matches in any folder. A leading slash anchors it to the folder of the .gitignore file: /build/ ignores only the top-level build folder.
** matches any number of folders: logs/**/*.txt matches .txt files anywhere under logs.
A ! exception can’t rescue a file whose folder is ignored: with build/ ignored, !build/keep.txt has no effect.
A common pair for environment files: .env* (ignore .env, .env.local, …) followed by !.env.example (but keep the template).

27  27. .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git

title: 27  27.  .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a .gitignore file?






Suggested answer





A plain text file (usually in the top folder of a repository) that lists patterns of file and folder names Git should ignore. Ignored files don’t show up as untracked in git status, and git add . doesn’t stage them.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which of these files should not be committed?

README.md
.env containing STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=...
src/index.html
.gitignore







Suggested answer





b. A .env file holds secrets, so it belongs in .gitignore. The README (a) and the web page (c) are normal project files, and the .gitignore file itself (d) should be committed so that its rules travel with the project.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each .gitignore line with its meaning.








Line

Meaning




1. *.log

A. a comment; Git ignores this line


2. build/

B. every file whose name ends in .log


3. # Secrets

C. don’t ignore this file, even if an earlier pattern matched it


4. !.env.example

D. every file named exactly .DS_Store


5. .DS_Store

E. every folder named build and everything inside it









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → E, 3 → A, 4 → C, 5 → D.





Question 4 · True or false
As soon as you add a file’s name to .gitignore, Git stops tracking it, even if it was committed earlier.






Suggested answer





False. .gitignore only affects untracked files. A file that is already tracked stays tracked until you run git rm --cached <file> and commit.





Question 5 · Short answer
What is a .env.example file, and why is it safe (and useful) to commit it?






Suggested answer





It’s a template of the .env file: the same variable names with fake values (for example WEATHER_API_KEY=your-key-goes-here). It contains no secrets, so it’s safe to commit, and it tells anyone who copies the project (including you on another computer) which values they must fill in.





Question 6 · Short answer
You accidentally pushed a real API key to GitHub. What is the first thing you should do?






Suggested answer





Revoke or rotate the key immediately: log in to the service that issued it, delete the old key, and create a new one. Cleaning up the repository comes after that, because copies of the old key may already exist.






Medium

Question 7 · Predict the output
The practice project’s .gitignore contains *.log, and the working tree is clean. Maria runs:
touch error.log
git status
What does git status print? What would git check-ignore -v error.log print?






Suggested answer





git status prints nothing to commit, working tree clean (after On branch main), because error.log is ignored. git check-ignore -v error.log prints the rule that ignores it, for example .gitignore:13:*.log    error.log (file, line number, pattern, path).





Question 8 · Write the file
Write a .gitignore for a small JavaScript project that ignores: the node_modules folder, all .log files, Mac .DS_Store files, and the .env file. Include a comment above the secrets line.






Suggested answer





node_modules/
*.log
.DS_Store

# Secrets: never commit these
.env
The order of the lines doesn’t matter here, and comments are optional (but helpful).





Question 9 · Write the command
config/secrets.json was committed by mistake. Write the commands to stop tracking it (keeping the file on disk), make sure it stays ignored, and commit the change.






Suggested answer





echo "config/secrets.json" >> .gitignore
git rm --cached config/secrets.json
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Stop tracking config/secrets.json"
--cached removes the file from Git’s tracking only; the file stays on disk. (If it contains real secrets that were pushed, rotate them too.)





Question 10 · Multiple choice
What does git rm --cached .env do?

Deletes .env from your computer and from Git
Removes .env from Git’s tracking (starting with the next commit) but keeps the file on your computer
Removes .env from every old commit in the history
Adds .env to .gitignore







Suggested answer





b. --cached means “only in Git, not on disk”. Without --cached (a), git rm would also delete the file. It does not change old commits (c): the file is still in the history. And it doesn’t edit .gitignore (d); you add that line yourself.





Question 11 · Predict the output
Sam’s .env was committed in his first commit. Later he adds .env to .gitignore and commits that, then changes the key inside .env. What does git status show, and why?






Suggested answer





It shows modified:   .env under Changes not staged for commit. .env is still a tracked file, and .gitignore has no effect on tracked files. He needs git rm --cached .env and a commit to stop tracking it (and, since the old key is in the history, he should rotate it if it was pushed).





Question 12 · Scenario
Maria copies her project to her lab computer and finds that .env is missing, so the weather widget doesn’t work. Why is it missing? What should she do?






Suggested answer





.env is in .gitignore, so it was never committed and isn’t part of the repository. That’s exactly what she wanted. On the lab computer she should create it from the template and fill in the real key:
cp .env.example .env
then edit .env in a text editor. The key itself should be brought over in a safe way (for example, typed in again or copied from the service’s website), never through the repository.





Question 13 · Read the output
Explain this output:
$ git check-ignore -v .env
.gitignore:16:.env  .env






Suggested answer





The file .env is ignored because of line 16 of the .gitignore file, whose pattern is .env. (If the file weren’t ignored, the command would print nothing.)






Hard

Question 14 · Scenario
An hour ago Sam pushed a commit containing his API key to a public GitHub repository. He has since deleted the key from the file, committed, and pushed again. Is he safe? What should he do, in which order?






Suggested answer





He is not safe. The key is still in the earlier commit, which is part of the history on GitHub, and it may already have been copied (by clones, forks, or automated tools that scan public repositories). Order:

Revoke/rotate the key now on the service’s website and create a new one. This makes the leaked key useless.
Put the new key in a .env file that is listed in .gitignore (and use git rm --cached if .env was tracked).
Check the service’s usage or billing page for activity he didn’t cause.

Rewriting the Git history is optional and complicated; GitHub’s docs say it is often unnecessary once the key has been revoked.





Question 15 · True or false
“GitHub’s push protection means I can never accidentally leak a secret, so I don’t need .gitignore for .env.”






Suggested answer





False. Push protection for your account only covers pushes to public repositories on github.com and only recognizes known secret formats. A password or a key from a less common service may not be detected, and a private repository can become public later. It’s a safety net; .gitignore and .env files are still your main protection.





Question 16 · Find the bug
Sam created his ignore file in Windows Notepad and saved it in his project folder, but git status still lists .env as untracked. ls -a shows:
.  ..  .env  .git  .gitignore.txt  app.py
What went wrong, and how can he fix it?






Suggested answer





Notepad saved the file as .gitignore.txt, and Git only reads a file named exactly .gitignore. Rename it:
mv .gitignore.txt .gitignore
git status
Now .env disappears from git status. (In Notepad, choose “All files” as the file type when saving to avoid the extra .txt.)





Question 17 · Long answer
Explain why deleting a commit (or even the whole repository) on GitHub is not enough once a secret has been pushed, and what the real fix is.






Suggested answer





Once the secret has been pushed, copies can exist outside your control: in other people’s clones and forks, in GitHub’s cached views, and in the hands of anyone (or any automated tool) who saw it. Deleting the commit on GitHub can’t remove those copies, and every copy still works as long as the key is valid. The real fix is to revoke or rotate the secret, so the leaked value no longer works. Cleaning the history afterwards is optional extra work.





Question 18 · Scenario
Maria asks Claude Code to add the weather widget to her site. List three things she should do (or avoid) to keep her API key safe during this work.






Suggested answer





Any three of:

Don’t paste the real key into the chat; keep it in .env.
Make sure .env is listed in .gitignore before anything is committed, and commit a .env.example with a fake value instead.
Ask Claude to write code that reads the key from an environment variable, not code with the key typed into it.
Optionally add a Read(./.env) deny rule so Claude Code’s file tools don’t read the file.
Review git status and git diff --staged before every commit (including commits Claude Code makes for her) to check that no key ended up in a tracked file.






Question 19 · Short answer
Maria notices that .claude/settings.local.json never shows up in git status, even though it isn’t listed in her project’s .gitignore. Why?






Suggested answer





The first time Claude Code wrote that file in her Git repository, it added it to her global Git ignore file (by default ~/.config/git/ignore), which applies to every repository on her computer. So Git ignores it even though the project’s .gitignore doesn’t mention it. (If she had created the file by hand, she would need to add it to .gitignore herself.)





Question 20 · Short answer
A teammate’s .gitignore contains build/ followed by !build/keep.txt, but build/keep.txt is still ignored. Why?






Suggested answer





build/ ignores the whole folder, and Git doesn’t look inside an ignored folder, so a ! exception can’t re-include a file in it. One fix is to ignore the folder’s contents instead (build/*) and then add !build/keep.txt.

28.1 Step 1: Create a GitHub account
So far your repository exists only on your computer. On this page you put a copy on GitHub. That gives you an online backup, a way to reach your work from other computers (Cloning and Pulling), and something you can show others. The steps: create an account, create an empty repository, let Git sign in to GitHub, then connect and push.
Go to github.com and sign up. A few tips:

Choose a professional username. It appears in all your repository addresses (https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/...), and future employers may look at your profile.

section: 28.2 Step 2: Create an empty repository on GitHub
text:
28.2 Step 2: Create an empty repository on GitHub

In the upper-right corner of any GitHub page, click +, then New repository.
Repository name: git-tutorial-project (letters, digits, ., - and _ only).
Choose Public or Private (see the table below). Private is a safe choice for coursework.
Don’t add a README, a .gitignore, or a license. Your project already has its own files. If GitHub creates files too, GitHub’s copy and yours start with different histories, and your first push is rejected.
Click Create repository.

GitHub then shows a Quick Setup page with the repository’s address (URL), for example https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git, and the commands for pushing an existing repository. You’ll use them in Step 4.









Public repository
Private repository




Who can see it
everyone on the internet
only you and the people you invite


Good for
portfolio projects, open source
coursework, work in progress



Either way, never commit secrets (see .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git): a private repository can be made public later, or shared with someone.
