title: 28  28.  Putting Your Repository on GitHub
section: 28.3 Step 3: Let Git sign in to GitHub
text:
28.3 Step 3: Let Git sign in to GitHub
When you push, GitHub has to know it’s really you. Your GitHub password doesn’t work for this: GitHub removed password sign-in for Git commands. GitHub recommends a tool that signs you in through your web browser and then remembers you. The simplest choice depends on your computer:

MacWindows (Git Bash)


Use the GitHub CLI (gh), GitHub’s official command-line tool. With Homebrew installed:
brew install gh
gh auth login
gh auth login asks a few questions. Answer:

where you use GitHub: GitHub.com
preferred protocol for Git operations: HTTPS
authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials: Yes
how to authenticate: Login with a web browser

It then shows a one-time code. Copy it, press Enter to open the browser, paste the code, and approve. Your login is saved in the Mac’s keychain, so you won’t be asked again. Check with gh auth status.
No Homebrew? Use a personal access token instead (see the deeper dive below).


Nothing to install. Git for Windows includes Git Credential Manager (the installer’s default credential helper). The first time you push (Step 4), a window opens and asks you to sign in to GitHub in your browser, and you may be asked to authorize the app. After that, Windows remembers your login.
(If you prefer, you can also use the GitHub CLI: install it from cli.github.com and run gh auth login as described in the Mac tab.)









Deeper dive: the four ways to sign in, compared













Method
How it works
Good to know




GitHub CLI (gh auth login)
Browser sign-in once; gh stores the login and hands it to Git.
Recommended by GitHub; also gives you handy commands like gh repo create.


Git Credential Manager
Browser sign-in the first time Git needs it; stored in Windows Credential Manager or the Mac keychain.
Included with Git for Windows; a separate install on a Mac.


Personal access token (PAT)
A long, random password-like code you create on GitHub (Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens) and paste when Git asks for a password.
GitHub recommends fine-grained tokens. On a Mac, Apple’s and Homebrew’s Git remember it in the keychain. Treat it like a password: it’s a secret.


SSH key
A key pair: the private key stays on your computer, and you upload the public key to GitHub.
Needs git@github.com:... style addresses instead of https://.... More setup steps; many developers use it long term.

title: 28  28.  Putting Your Repository on GitHub
section: 28.4 Step 4: Connect your repository and push
text:
28.4 Step 4: Connect your repository and push
In the terminal, go to your project and add GitHub as a remote, a named link to another copy of your repository:
cd ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git
git remote -v
Output:
origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git (push)
Replace YOUR-USERNAME with your GitHub username (or simply copy the URL from GitHub’s Quick Setup page). origin is just a nickname for that long URL; it’s the conventional name for the main remote. The two lines say the same URL is used to download (“fetch”) and upload (“push”).
Now push:
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
Output:
Enumerating objects: 24, done.
Counting objects: 100% (24/24), done.
Delta compression using up to 8 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (19/19), done.
Writing objects: 100% (24/24), 2.51 KiB | 2.51 MiB/s, done.
Total 24 (delta 5), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
To https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
(Your numbers will differ, and GitHub may add a few lines that start with remote:. On Windows, this is when the sign-in window appears the first time.)

git branch -M main renames your current branch to main. If it’s already called main, as it is if you followed Installing and Configuring Git, it changes nothing. GitHub’s Quick Setup page includes it for computers where the first branch is still called master.
git push -u origin main uploads your main branch (all its commits) to origin. The -u (short for --set-upstream) links your local main to origin/main, its upstream. That’s what the last line of the output says.
origin/main is Git’s record of where main is on GitHub.

Because of -u, Git now knows where to push, and git status compares your branch with GitHub’s copy:
git status
Output:
On branch main
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

nothing to commit, working tree clean
From now on, the routine is: commit as usual, then upload with a plain git push (no -u origin main needed). If there’s nothing new to upload, Git says Everything up-to-date.

28  28. Putting Your Repository on GitHub

title: 28  28.  Putting Your Repository on GitHub
section: 28.5 Step 5: Look at your repository on GitHub
text:
28.5 Step 5: Look at your repository on GitHub
Reload your repository’s page on GitHub. You’ll see your folders and files, the number of commits (click it to browse the history), and below the file list, your README.md displayed as formatted text. Notice what’s missing: .env (it’s ignored) and the empty docs/ folder. That’s exactly what you want.
You can also edit files directly on github.com. Each edit there is saved as a commit on GitHub, which you then bring to your computer with git pull (Cloning and Pulling).

28.5.1 README.md and Markdown
A README is the front page of a repository: what the project is, how to use it, who made it. README.md is written in Markdown (.md), a simple way to format plain text:



You type
You get




# My Portfolio
a big heading


## Features
a smaller heading


- Home page
a bullet point


1. Install
a numbered list item


**important**
bold text


[my site](https://example.com)
a link


`git status`
code



For example, this README.md:
# Maria Lopez - Portfolio

A personal portfolio website, built while learning Git.

## Pages

- Home page
- Contact page (coming soon)

Run it by opening `src/index.html` in a browser.
shows on GitHub as a heading, a paragraph, a “Pages” subheading with a bullet list, and a sentence with src/index.html in code font.

title: 28  28.  Putting Your Repository on GitHub
text:
28.6 Shortcut: gh repo create
If you use the GitHub CLI, one command run inside your project folder can replace Steps 2 and 4. It creates the repository on GitHub, adds the remote, and pushes:
gh repo create git-tutorial-project --private --source=. --remote=origin --push

--private (or --public): the visibility.
--source=.: use the repository in the current folder (.).
--remote=origin: the name of the remote to add.
--push: push your commits right away.

28  28. Putting Your Repository on GitHub

title: 28  28.  Putting Your Repository on GitHub
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Why should you create the GitHub repository without a README when you plan to push an existing project?

GitHub doesn’t allow READMEs in private repositories
Your project already has its own history; files created on GitHub start a different history, so your first push is rejected
A README makes the repository public
README files can only be created with git commit







Suggested answer





b. If GitHub creates a README (or .gitignore or license), GitHub’s copy has a commit your computer doesn’t have, and the two histories don’t fit together, so git push is rejected. Private repositories can have READMEs (a), a README doesn’t change visibility (c), and you can add a README any time later (d).





Question 2 · True or false
When git push asks you to sign in, you can use your GitHub account password.






Suggested answer





False. GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git commands. Use browser sign-in through the GitHub CLI or Git Credential Manager, or a personal access token (or an SSH key).





Question 3 · Short answer
What is origin in git remote add origin https://github.com/...?






Suggested answer





A nickname for the remote repository’s URL. origin is the conventional name for the main remote (here, your repository on GitHub), so you can type origin instead of the long URL.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. git remote add origin <url>

A. lists the remotes and their URLs


2. git remote -v

B. renames the current branch to main


3. git branch -M main

C. uploads new commits to the upstream branch


4. git push -u origin main

D. adds a remote named origin


5. git push

E. first push: uploads main and sets origin/main as its upstream









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → A, 3 → B, 4 → E, 5 → C.





Question 5 · Compare
Who can see a public repository, and who can see a private one?






Suggested answer





A public repository can be seen by everyone on the internet. A private repository can be seen only by you and the people you explicitly give access to.





Question 6 · Short answer
What does the -u in git push -u origin main do, and why is it useful?






Suggested answer





-u (--set-upstream) links your local main branch to origin/main (its upstream). Afterwards, plain git push and git pull know where to go, and git status can tell you whether you’re ahead of or behind GitHub. You only need -u on the first push.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
Sam created an empty GitHub repository at https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/budget-app.git. His local repository ~/budget-app already has commits on main. Write the commands to connect it and push for the first time.






Suggested answer





cd ~/budget-app
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/budget-app.git
git push -u origin main
(Adding git branch -M main before the push is harmless.)





Question 8 · Read the output
Explain the last two lines of this push output:
 * [new branch]      main -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.






Suggested answer






* [new branch] main -> main: GitHub didn’t have a main branch yet; your local main was uploaded and created there.
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.: because of -u, your local main now has origin/main as its upstream, so future git push and git pull commands need no extra arguments.






Question 9 · Find the bug
Maria added the remote but ran plain git push for her first push. Git answered:
fatal: The current branch main has no upstream branch.
To push the current branch and set the remote as upstream, use

    git push --set-upstream origin main
What does it mean, and what should she type?






Suggested answer





Her main branch isn’t linked to a branch on GitHub yet, so plain git push doesn’t know where to push. She should run the first push with the upstream option:
git push -u origin main
(-u is the short form of --set-upstream.) After that, git push alone works.





Question 10 · Write the file
Write a README.md for a project called “Club Events” with: a top-level heading, one sentence describing it, a “Features” subheading with two bullet points, and a link to https://example.com.






Suggested answer





# Club Events

A web app where students sign up for club events.

## Features

- Browse upcoming events
- Sign up with one click

More information: [project site](https://example.com)





Question 11 · Scenario
After her first push, Maria looks at her repository on GitHub. Her .env file and her empty docs/ folder are missing. Did the push fail?






Suggested answer





No, this is correct. .env is listed in .gitignore, so it was never committed, which is exactly what keeps her API key off GitHub. Empty folders are never committed by Git. A push uploads commits, so only files that are in her commits appear on GitHub.





Question 12 · Multiple choice
Sam (Windows) installed Git for Windows with the default choices. What does he need to do so that git push can sign in to GitHub?

Nothing: Git Credential Manager will open a browser sign-in the first time he pushes
Install Homebrew and the GitHub CLI
Type his GitHub password when asked
Create an SSH key; nothing else works on Windows







Suggested answer





a. Git Credential Manager comes with Git for Windows (it’s the installer’s default credential helper) and handles the browser sign-in. Homebrew (b) is a Mac tool. Passwords (c) aren’t accepted for Git. SSH (d) works, but it’s optional.





Question 13 · Write the command
Using the GitHub CLI, write one command that, run inside the project folder, creates a public GitHub repository named recipes, adds it as the remote origin, and pushes the existing commits.






Suggested answer





gh repo create recipes --public --source=. --remote=origin --push






Hard

Question 14 · Find the bug
Maria runs git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/portfolio.git and gets error: remote origin already exists. Why? How can she check what origin points to, and how can she fix it if the URL is wrong?






Suggested answer





Her repository already has a remote named origin (she added one earlier, or the repository was cloned). She can check it with:
git remote -v
If the URL is wrong, she changes it instead of adding a second origin:
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/portfolio.git





Question 15 · Scenario
Sam created his GitHub repository with a README. His first push is rejected with ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first), and git pull origin main says fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories. Explain what’s going on and give the simplest fix for a beginner.






Suggested answer





GitHub’s repository has its own first commit (the README), which has nothing in common with Sam’s local history: the two histories are unrelated. Git refuses to overwrite GitHub’s commit when pushing, and refuses to combine unrelated histories when pulling.
Simplest fix, since the GitHub repository contains nothing he needs: delete it on GitHub (repository Settings, “Danger Zone”, Delete this repository), create it again empty, and push again with git push -u origin main.
(It is possible to combine them with git pull --no-rebase --allow-unrelated-histories origin main, but if both sides have a README.md, Git reports a merge conflict to resolve first; see Merge Conflicts.)





Question 16 · Scenario
A classmate suggests: “Just make your repository private, then you can commit your .env file with the API key.” Give two reasons why this is a bad idea.






Suggested answer





Any two of:

A private repository can be made public later, or shared with collaborators (and their computers), exposing the key.
Once committed, the key stays in the history forever, even if you delete the file later.
Anyone who gets access to the repository, now or later, can use the key and run up charges or misuse your account.
.env files exist precisely so that secrets stay out of Git; the code can be shared safely, and each computer gets its own .env.






Question 17 · Long answer
Describe, step by step, what happens when Maria runs git push -u origin main for the first time on her Windows lab account (with Git Credential Manager).






Suggested answer






Git looks up the remote origin and finds its URL.
GitHub needs to know who she is. Git Credential Manager opens a browser sign-in (first time only), and the login is stored for later.
Git uploads every commit (and file version) on main that GitHub doesn’t have yet; for a new repository, that’s the whole history.
GitHub creates the main branch (* [new branch] main -> main).
Because of -u, Git links local main to origin/main (branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.), so future pushes and pulls need no arguments.






Question 18 · Compare
Compare signing in with a personal access token and with browser sign-in (GitHub CLI or Git Credential Manager). Which would you recommend to a beginner, and why?






Suggested answer






Personal access token: you create a long secret code on GitHub and paste it when Git asks for a password. It works everywhere, but you must create it, choose its permissions, store it safely (it’s a secret, like a password), and replace it when it expires.
Browser sign-in: you log in to GitHub in your browser once, and the tool stores and manages the credentials for you.

For a beginner, browser sign-in (Git Credential Manager on Windows, GitHub CLI on a Mac) is simpler and safer: there’s no token to copy around or accidentally leak. A token is a good fallback when those tools aren’t available.

28  28. Putting Your Repository on GitHub

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
text:
29.1 git clone: copy a repository to a computer
Once your repository is on GitHub, you can get a copy of it on any computer with git clone, and keep the copies in sync with git push and git pull. This page is about one person (you) using two computers, for example your laptop and a computer-lab PC, or making a quick edit on github.com. Working with other people is covered later, in Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks.
GitHub is the meeting point: each computer pushes its new commits there and pulls the other computer’s commits from there.
In the examples, Maria pushed her practice project to GitHub on the previous page. Now she is at a Windows PC in the computer lab, using Git Bash. First she copies the repository’s URL from GitHub: on the repository’s page, she clicks the Code button and copies the HTTPS URL. Then:
Output:
git clone:
Output:
The same six commits, with the same IDs, as on her laptop. Two things are not in the clone, because they were never committed: the ignored .env file and the empty docs/ folder. Maria re-creates .env from the template (see .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git):
and then types her real key into .env with a text editor.
A few more facts about cloning:
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own
29  29. Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
text:
cd ~/Documents
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git

Cloning into 'git-tutorial-project'...
remote: Enumerating objects: 24, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (24/24), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (19/19), done.
remote: Total 24 (delta 5), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
Receiving objects: 100% (24/24), done.
Resolving deltas: 100% (5/5), done.


creates a new folder named after the repository (git-tutorial-project),
downloads all the files and the complete history,
remembers where the copy came from, as a remote named origin, and connects the local main branch to origin/main,
so you do not run git init or git remote add in a cloned folder.

cd git-tutorial-project
git log --oneline

736e88f (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Ignore .env and add .env.example template
fc2bb9b Revert "Make heading navy"
cb793da Make heading navy
4293e1d Add intro and contact email to home page
b90f840 Describe planned pages in README
ffd1f1f Add starter files for portfolio site

cp .env.example .env



Each computer needs Git installed and configured (Installing and Configuring Git). To clone a private repository or to push, you must also be signed in to GitHub on that computer (Putting Your Repository on GitHub). On a shared lab computer, don’t leave your login saved: if you signed in with the GitHub CLI, gh auth logout removes it when you’re done. If Git Credential Manager signed you in (the Windows default), open Windows’ Credential Manager, choose Windows Credentials, and remove the entry git:https://github.com.
Anyone can clone a public repository without signing in. For example, GitHub’s practice repository: git clone https://github.com/octocat/Spoon-Knife.git. You can change your copy, but you can’t push to someone else’s repository.
To use a different folder name, add it at the end: git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git portfolio.
Clone into a normal folder such as ~/Documents, not inside another repository.

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
text:
29.2 Push from the second computer
At the lab PC, Maria adds a status line to the README and commits it, exactly as on her laptop:
echo "Status: home page done, contact page next." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add project status to README"
git status
Output (of git status):
On branch main
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit.
  (use "git push" to publish your local commits)

nothing to commit, working tree clean
“Ahead by 1 commit” means this computer has a commit that GitHub doesn’t have yet. Because git clone connected main to origin/main, a plain git push is enough:
git push
Output:
Enumerating objects: 5, done.
Counting objects: 100% (5/5), done.
Delta compression using up to 8 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (3/3), done.
Writing objects: 100% (3/3), 340 bytes | 340.00 KiB/s, done.
Total 3 (delta 2), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
To https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git
   736e88f..647a9b5  main -> main
The last line says GitHub’s main moved from commit 736e88f to 647a9b5.

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
section: 29.3 git pull: bring your copy up to date
text:
29.3 git pull: bring your copy up to date
Back home, Maria opens her laptop. Watch out: git status there still says Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'. That message only reflects what the laptop knew the last time it talked to GitHub; it doesn’t check GitHub. To actually get the new commit:
git pull
Output:
remote: Enumerating objects: 5, done.
remote: Counting objects: 100% (5/5), done.
remote: Compressing objects: 100% (3/3), done.
remote: Total 3 (delta 2), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
Unpacking objects: 100% (3/3), 320 bytes | 320.00 KiB/s, done.
From https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project
   736e88f..647a9b5  main       -> origin/main
Updating 736e88f..647a9b5
Fast-forward
 README.md | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
git pull downloads the new commits from GitHub and adds them to your branch. Fast-forward means the laptop had no new commits of its own, so Git simply moved main forward to include the downloaded ones; there was nothing to combine.
Edits you make on github.com (for example, editing README.md in the browser) are ordinary commits on GitHub. You bring them to your computer the same way, with git pull.

29  29. Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
text:
29.4 The daily routine
1. git pull                     <- start: get the latest version
2. edit files                   <- (by hand, or with an AI agent)
3. git status  /  git diff      <- review what changed
4. git add <files>
5. git commit -m "..."
6. git push                     <- finish: upload it for your other computer
A rule of thumb: pull when you sit down, push when you get up.

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
section: 29.5 If you forget to pull: the push is rejected
text:
29.5 If you forget to pull: the push is rejected
One evening Maria fixed the README title on github.com. Later, on her laptop, she changed css/style.css and committed it without pulling first. Now GitHub and her laptop each have a commit the other one doesn’t have:
git push
Output:
To https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing to
hint: the same ref. If you want to integrate the remote changes, use
hint: 'git pull' before pushing again.
hint: See the 'Note about fast-forwards' in 'git push --help' for details.
Nothing is broken. Git refuses to push because that would throw away the commit on GitHub. The fix is the hint’s advice: pull, then push.
git pull
Because both sides have new commits, git pull creates a merge commit that combines them. Git opens your text editor with a ready-made message (Merge branch 'main' of https://github.com/...); just save and close it (in nano: Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X). The output ends with:
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 README.md | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
Now git push works, and GitHub has both changes.






“fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches”



If git pull stops with this message (after several hint: lines), Git doesn’t know whether to merge or do something else. Set the beginner-friendly default once (see Installing and Configuring Git), then pull again:
git config --global pull.rebase false
git pull


Two other things can stop a pull:

Uncommitted changes to the same files. Git prints error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge: and does nothing. Commit your changes (or discard them with git restore), then pull again.
The same lines were changed on both computers. Git can’t decide which version to keep and reports a merge conflict, which you resolve by hand. See Merge Conflicts. Pulling before you start work is the best way to avoid conflicts.







Deeper dive: what the merge looks like in the history





git log --oneline --graph draws the history as a graph. After the merge above, Maria’s laptop shows:
*   c0d14e5 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'main' of https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project
|\
| * 0b2c2b7 (origin/main) Update README.md
* | b25b21a Increase line spacing
|/
* 647a9b5 Add project status to README
The two lines of work split after 647a9b5 (the web edit on one side, the laptop’s CSS commit on the other) and come back together in the merge commit. After git push, origin/main points to the merge commit too.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working on Your Own
29  29. Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
text:
29.6 Forking vs. cloning
Cloning copies a repository to your computer. You can clone any public repository, but you can push only to repositories you own or have been given access to. A fork is a copy of someone else’s repository made on GitHub, in your own account (using the Fork button). Because the fork belongs to you, you can clone it and push to it. People fork projects to build their own version or to propose changes to the original. The full-stack tutorial starts this way (Fork the repo and clone it), and Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks explains forks in detail.

29  29. Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)

title: 29  29.  Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
What does git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git do?

Uploads your local project to GitHub
Creates a folder git-tutorial-project with all the files and the full history, and sets up origin
Copies only the latest version of the files, without history
Creates an empty repository on GitHub







Suggested answer





b. Cloning downloads the files and the complete history into a new folder and remembers the URL as the remote origin. Uploading is git push (a). A clone always includes the history (c). Creating a repository on GitHub (d) happens on github.com (or with gh repo create).





Question 2 · True or false
After cloning a repository, you need to run git init and git remote add origin ... in the new folder.






Suggested answer





False. The cloned folder is already a repository, and origin is already set to the URL you cloned from. Check with git remote -v.





Question 3 · Short answer
In one sentence, what does git pull do?






Suggested answer





It downloads the commits that are on GitHub (the remote) but not yet on your computer, and adds them to your current branch.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each term with its meaning.








Term

Meaning




1. git clone

A. upload your new commits to GitHub


2. git pull

B. the usual name for the remote your copy came from


3. git push

C. download a repository (files and history) for the first time


4. origin

D. a copy of someone else’s repository in your own GitHub account


5. fork

E. get new commits from GitHub into your existing copy









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → A, 4 → B, 5 → D.





Question 5 · Fill in the blank
Rule of thumb for working from two computers: “________ when you sit down, ________ when you get up.”






Suggested answer





“Pull when you sit down, push when you get up.” Start each session with git pull and end it with git push, so the next computer you use can pull your work.





Question 6 · True or false
You can clone a public GitHub repository without signing in to GitHub.






Suggested answer





True. Public repositories can be cloned by anyone. You need to sign in to clone a private repository, and to push.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
Write the command that clones https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git into a folder named portfolio instead of the default name.






Suggested answer





git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git portfolio





Question 8 · Read the output
What does this git status output mean, and what should Maria do next?
On branch main
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits.
  (use "git push" to publish your local commits)






Suggested answer





Her computer has two commits that GitHub doesn’t have yet. She should run git push to upload them, so her other computer can pull them later.





Question 9 · Ordering
Put the daily routine in order:

A. git push
B. edit files
C. git pull
D. git commit -m "..."
E. git status and git diff
F. git add <files>







Suggested answer





C → B → E → F → D → A: pull, edit, review, stage, commit, push.





Question 10 · Short answer
Maria pushed a commit from the lab PC an hour ago. On her laptop, git status says Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'. Is the laptop really up to date? Explain.






Suggested answer





No. git status doesn’t contact GitHub; it compares with what the laptop learned the last time it talked to GitHub, which was before the lab-PC push. git pull downloads the new commit and actually brings the laptop up to date.





Question 11 · Find the bug
Sam runs git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git in his Documents folder and gets:
fatal: destination path 'git-tutorial-project' already exists and is not an empty directory.
What does this mean, and what are his options?






Suggested answer





A folder named git-tutorial-project already exists there (probably an earlier clone or the unzipped practice files). Options:

If it’s already a clone of this repository, don’t clone again: cd into it and run git pull.
Clone into a different folder name: git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git portfolio.
Clone from a different location (another parent folder).






Question 12 · Read the output
The output of git pull contains the word Fast-forward. What does that tell you?






Suggested answer





Your computer had no new commits of its own, so Git only had to move your main branch forward to include the downloaded commits. Nothing needed to be combined, so no merge commit was created.





Question 13 · Scenario
Maria clones her repository on the lab PC and runs git remote -v. What does she see, and why didn’t she have to add the remote herself?






Suggested answer





origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git (push)
git clone automatically records the URL it cloned from as the remote named origin, used for both fetching (pulling) and pushing.






Hard

Question 14 · Scenario
Maria edited the README on github.com, then (without pulling) committed a CSS change on her laptop. git push prints ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first). Explain why the push was rejected, and list the commands to fix it. What happens during the fix?






Suggested answer





GitHub has a commit (the web edit) that her laptop doesn’t have. Pushing would replace GitHub’s history and lose that commit, so Git refuses. Fix:
git pull
git push
git pull downloads the web edit and, because both sides have new commits, creates a merge commit that combines them (Git opens the editor with a ready-made message: save and close). Then git push succeeds. If both edits had changed the same lines, she would have to resolve a merge conflict first.





Question 15 · Find the bug
In the same situation, Sam’s git pull prints several hint: lines and ends with:
fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.
Why, and how does he fix it?






Suggested answer





His Git has no setting that says how git pull should combine diverged branches (merge, rebase, or fast-forward only), so it refuses to guess. Set the merge behavior once and pull again:
git config --global pull.rebase false
git pull
(The Git for Windows installer normally sets this for you; it’s mostly Mac users who need this line.)





Question 16 · Scenario
Maria starts editing README.md on her laptop before pulling. When she runs git pull, Git prints error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge: followed by README.md, and Aborting. What happened, and what can she do?






Suggested answer





The commits she is pulling also change README.md, and Git won’t overwrite her uncommitted edits, so it stopped without changing anything. She can:

keep her edits: git add README.md and git commit, then git pull (which may create a merge commit, or a conflict if the same lines changed), then git push; or
throw her edits away: git restore README.md, then git pull.

Next time, pull before starting to edit.





Question 17 · Compare
Compare cloning and forking: where does the copy live, and can you push to it?






Suggested answer














Clone
Fork




Where the copy lives
on your computer
on GitHub, in your account


Made with
git clone <url>
the Fork button on github.com


Can you push?
only if you own the original or were given access
yes, it’s your repository



They are often used together: fork someone’s project on GitHub, then clone your fork to your computer.





Question 18 · Scenario
Maria clones a classmate’s public repository, improves the README, and commits. git push fails with a “permission denied” error. Why? What could she do instead?






Suggested answer





Anyone can clone a public repository, but only the owner (and people they give access to) can push to it. She could fork the repository on GitHub and push to her fork, or ask the classmate to add her as a collaborator. Both are covered in Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks.





Question 19 · Long answer
Maria works on her project from a laptop, a lab PC, and sometimes github.com. Describe a routine that keeps all copies in sync, and explain what can go wrong if she doesn’t follow it.






Suggested answer





A good answer includes:

Start every session with git pull (on the computer she’s using).
Work in small commits: git status/git diff, git add, git commit.
End every session with git push, so the next computer can pull.
After editing on github.com, pull on each computer before working there.

What can go wrong: if she forgets to pull, her push is rejected and she must pull (creating a merge commit) before pushing. If she edits the same lines in two places without syncing, she gets a merge conflict. If she forgets to push, her other computer doesn’t have the latest work. And uncommitted edits can block a pull.

29  29. Cloning and Pulling (Working from Two Computers)

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
text:
30.1 Clients and servers
Every time you open a web page, two programs have a short conversation: your browser asks for something and a web server answers. This page explains who is talking, what they say to each other (HTTP), and how you will run a web server on your own computer while you build apps.
A website “lives” on a computer that is connected to the Internet and is always on. That computer is called a server. A program running on it, the web server program, waits for requests and answers them.
Your browser (Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox…) is a client: a program that asks a server for something. When you visit a site, the browser asks the web server for the page, and the server sends back the files needed to show it: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images (see HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Browser Developer Tools). The browser then draws the page on your screen.
Think of a restaurant: you (the client) order, the kitchen (the server) prepares exactly what you asked for, and one kitchen serves many tables at once. Note that “server” means both the computer and the program running on it; context tells you which.
crumbs: 30  30. Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
text:
Your computer                            A computer on the Internet
 +-----------------+                       +---------------------------+
 |  Browser        |  ---- request ---->   |  Web server program       |
 |  (the client)   |  <--- response ----   |  (the server)             |
 +-----------------+                       +---------------------------+
crumbs: 30  30. Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
text:
30.2 Front end and back end
Developers split an app into two halves:

The front end (also called the client side) is everything that runs in the user’s browser: the screens, buttons and forms.
The back end (also called the server side) is everything that runs on servers: storing data, checking passwords, applying business rules, charging credit cards.

You will see these terms constantly, often used loosely:








Term
Means
Example




client
a program that asks for something
your browser, a phone app, curl


server
a program that answers requests (or the computer it runs on)
the program that runs amazon.com


front end / client side
the part of an app that runs in the browser
HTML, CSS, JavaScript


back end / server side
the part of an app that runs on servers
the code that saves your order


full stack
front end and back end together
“a full-stack web app”
crumbs: 30  30. Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
section: 30.3 HTTP: how browsers and servers talk
text:
30.3 HTTP: how browsers and servers talk
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules - a protocol - that browsers and web servers follow when they talk. Every exchange is one request followed by one response.
A request contains:

a method - what you want to do. The two you will see most:

GET: “please send me this” (loading a page, clicking a link).
POST: “here is some data for you” (submitting a sign-up form, uploading a photo).

a path - which page or file, e.g. /about.
headers - extra information, such as which site you want and which browser you are using.
sometimes a body - the data being sent (for example, the form fields of a POST).

A simplified request looks like this:
GET /about HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Accept: text/html
The response starts with a status code (did it work?), then headers (for example, what kind of content follows), then the body (the content itself):
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html>
  ...the page...
</html>
One page usually needs many requests. The first response is the HTML. The browser reads it, sees which CSS files, JavaScript files, images and fonts it needs, and requests each of those too. A busy shopping site can make more than a hundred requests to show a single page.

30.3.1 Status codes








Code
Name
Meaning




200
OK
Success: here is what you asked for


201
Created
Success: a new item was created (common after a POST)


301, 302
Moved
Redirect: go to this other URL instead


400
Bad Request
The request didn’t make sense (for example, missing data)


401
Unauthorized
You need to log in (or your key is missing or invalid)


403
Forbidden
The server knows who you are, but you are not allowed to do this


404
Not Found
Nothing exists at this path


429
Too Many Requests
Slow down: you hit a rate limit


500
Internal Server Error
The server’s code crashed or failed


503
Service Unavailable
The server is overloaded or down for maintenance



The first digit tells you the family: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the client asked for something wrong, 5xx the server failed. When something breaks, that digit tells you where to look first: a 404 usually means a wrong link or path; a 500 means a bug or crash in the back end.


30.3.2 See HTTP for yourself with curl
curl is a command-line client: it sends HTTP requests from the terminal and prints the response. It comes with macOS and with Git Bash. The -i option (“include”) prints the status line and headers before the body:
curl -i https://example.com
Output (shortened - yours will differ a little):
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
server: cloudflare
...

<!doctype html><html lang=en><head>...<title>Example Domain</title>...

HTTP/2 200 means HTTP version 2, status 200 (OK). You might see HTTP/1.1 200 OK instead - an older version of HTTP with the same meaning.
content-type: text/html says the body is an HTML page.
After a blank line comes the body: the HTML your browser would have drawn. curl just prints it as text.

To see only the status line and headers, use a capital -I instead.
crumbs: 30  30. Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
text:
30.4 HTTPS: HTTP with encryption
Plain HTTP travels as readable text, so anyone along the way (for example, whoever runs the public Wi-Fi you are on) could read or change it. HTTPS is HTTP sent through an encrypted connection. It:

encrypts the traffic, so passwords, card numbers and cookies can’t be read or altered in transit, and
proves the server’s identity with a certificate issued by a trusted authority, so you know you are really talking to amazon.com.

Today nearly every site uses HTTPS. Browsers mark plain-HTTP pages as “Not secure”, and many sites automatically redirect http:// addresses to https://. Hosting services set up HTTPS for you (see Hosting and Deployment).
HTTPS protects the connection, not the content: a scam site can have perfectly valid HTTPS.
crumbs: 30  30. Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
text:
30.5 One server or thousands?
A small website can run on one web server program on one computer. Large sites such as Google or Amazon run on thousands of computers in data centers around the world, yet your browser still sees “one website”. For learning and for building small apps, the one-server picture is all you need.






Deeper dive: How big sites look like one server






A load balancer is a “front door” that receives every request and passes it to one of many identical servers behind it. If one server fails, the others keep answering.
A CDN (content delivery network) keeps copies of files - images, videos, CSS, JavaScript, sometimes whole pages - on servers in many cities. You get them from a nearby copy, which is faster. Cloudflare, Akamai, Amazon CloudFront and Fastly are well-known CDNs.
A cache is a saved copy of something, kept so the same work doesn’t have to be repeated. CDNs, servers and your own browser all cache.

This is why a big site’s address often leads to a computer owned by a CDN company, as you will see with ping and nslookup in URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS.
crumbs: 30  30. Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
section: 30.6 localhost: a server on your own computer
text:
30.6 localhost: a server on your own computer
While you build an app, you run the web server on your own computer. The browser and the server are then on the same machine.

localhost is a special name that always means “this computer”. Only you can reach it; it is not on the public Internet.
A port is a number that tells the computer which program should receive a request. One computer can run many server programs at once, each listening on its own port. If the computer’s address is a building’s street address, the port is the apartment number.
Public websites use port 443 (HTTPS) or 80 (HTTP). Those are the defaults, so you never type them. Development servers use other ports, which you do type: http://localhost:3000 (Next.js), http://localhost:5173 (Vite), http://localhost:8000 (Python’s built-in server).

Things that will save you time later:

A development server runs inside a terminal window and keeps running (you don’t get your prompt back). Press Ctrl+C in that window to stop it.
If the server isn’t running - for example, you closed its terminal window - the browser says something like “This site can’t be reached”.
Only one program can listen on a port at a time. Some tools then pick the next free port (for example 3001); others stop with an “address already in use” error.
A localhost link only works on your own computer. To share your app, deploy it (see Hosting and Deployment).


30.6.1 Try it: run a tiny web server (optional)
This needs Python, which you may have from a programming course. First create a folder with one web page in it:
mkdir -p ~/hello-server
cd ~/hello-server
echo "<h1>Hello from my own computer</h1>" > index.html
Then start Python’s built-in web server in that folder:

MacWindows (Git Bash)


python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1
If macOS offers to install the “command line developer tools”, accept: they include python3 (and Git).


python -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1
If you get an error (or the Microsoft Store opens), try py instead of python. If neither works, Python isn’t installed - just read along.



The command keeps running. Open http://localhost:8000 in your browser and you will see your heading. The terminal prints one line for each request it receives, something like this:
127.0.0.1 - - [06/Oct/2026 10:29:01] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 -
127.0.0.1 - - [06/Oct/2026 10:29:01] code 404, message File not found
127.0.0.1 - - [06/Oct/2026 10:29:01] "GET /favicon.ico HTTP/1.1" 404 -
The request came from 127.0.0.1 (your own computer), it was a GET for the path /, and the server answered 200. Many browsers also ask for /favicon.ico (the little icon in the tab); this folder has none, so the answer is a harmless 404. Try http://localhost:8000/nope.html to cause another 404. Finally, press Ctrl+C in the terminal (or close the window) and reload the page: the browser can no longer connect.






Only share what you mean to share



This server hands out every file in the folder where you start it, so start it only inside a project folder - never in your home folder. The --bind 127.0.0.1 part makes it reachable only from your own computer; without it, other people on the same network might be able to connect.
crumbs: 30  30. Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP

title: 30  30.  Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
When you visit a website, which program is the client and which is the server?






Suggested answer





Your browser is the client: it asks for the page. The web server program running on a computer somewhere on the Internet is the server: it answers the request and sends back the files needed to show the page.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
What is HTTP?

A programming language for building web pages
The set of rules browsers and web servers follow to exchange requests and responses
A program that stores a website’s data
The address of a website







Suggested answer





b. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a protocol: the rules for the request/response conversation. HTML, not HTTP, is the language for pages (a); data is stored by a database (c); a website’s address is its URL (d).





Question 3 · Matching
Match each status code with its meaning.



Code

Meaning




1. 200

A. The server’s code crashed or failed


2. 301

B. Nothing exists at this path


3. 404

C. Success


4. 500

D. Redirect: the page has moved to another URL









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → B, 4 → A.





Question 4 · True or false
The word “server” can mean either a computer or a program running on that computer.






Suggested answer





True. People say “server” for both the server computer and the web server program that runs on it. Context tells you which one is meant.





Question 5 · Multiple choice
Which of these is part of the front end of an online store?

The code that charges the customer’s credit card
The database table that stores all orders
The product page and “Add to cart” button shown in the browser
The code that checks whether a password is correct







Suggested answer





c. The front end is what runs in the user’s browser: the screens, buttons and forms. Charging cards (a), storing orders (b) and checking passwords (d) happen on servers, so they are part of the back end.





Question 6 · Short answer
What does localhost mean, and who can open a localhost address?






Suggested answer





localhost always means “this computer”. Only the person using that computer can open a localhost address; it is not reachable from the public Internet.





Question 7 · Short answer
Name two things HTTPS adds compared to plain HTTP.






Suggested answer






Encryption: data in transit (passwords, card numbers, cookies) can’t be read or changed by others on the network.
Proof of identity: the server shows a certificate from a trusted authority, so you know you are talking to the real site.







Medium

Question 8 · Multiple choice
A user fills in a club sign-up form and clicks “Submit”. Which HTTP method is the browser most likely to use?

GET
POST
200
HTTPS







Suggested answer





b. POST is used to send data to the server, such as form fields. GET (a) asks for something without sending a body. 200 (c) is a status code, not a method, and HTTPS (d) is the encrypted version of HTTP, not a method.





Question 9 · Predict the output
Maria runs this command:
curl -I https://github.com/this-page-does-not-exist-xyz
What number do you expect to see on the first line of the output, and why?






Suggested answer





404 (the first line will look like HTTP/2 404). The server is up and answered, but nothing exists at that path. -I prints only the status line and headers.





Question 10 · Scenario
Your app shows an error page. In one case the status code is 404; in another it is 500. For each, say whether the problem is more likely on the client side (the request) or on the server side, and what you would check first.






Suggested answer






404 (4xx): the request asked for something that doesn’t exist. Check the link or URL path for a typo, or whether the page/route was ever created.
500 (5xx): the server failed while handling a valid request. Check the back-end code and the server’s logs for the error.






Question 11 · Short answer
Explain each part of the address http://localhost:5173.






Suggested answer






http:// - use plain HTTP (fine for a development server on your own computer).
localhost - the server is on this computer.
5173 - the port: the request goes to whichever program is listening on port 5173 (Vite’s development server uses this port by default).






Question 12 · Read the output
While Python’s web server is running, the terminal prints:
127.0.0.1 - - [06/Oct/2026 10:31:12] "GET /about.html HTTP/1.1" 404 -
What happened?






Suggested answer





A browser on the same computer (127.0.0.1) sent a GET request for the path /about.html. The server answered 404 Not Found because there is no about.html file in the folder it is serving.





Question 13 · Multiple choice
Which statement about HTTPS is true?

A site that uses HTTPS is guaranteed to be honest and safe to buy from.
HTTPS encrypts the data travelling between your browser and the server.
HTTPS makes pages load without any requests.
HTTPS is only needed on pages that show images.







Suggested answer





b. HTTPS protects the connection. It says nothing about whether the site’s owner is honest (a) - scam sites use HTTPS too. Pages still need requests (c), and HTTPS matters for every page, especially ones with logins or payments (d).





Question 14 · Short answer
Why does loading a single web page usually involve many HTTP requests?






Suggested answer





The first response is just the HTML. As the browser reads the HTML, it finds references to other files - CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts - and sends a separate request for each one.






Hard

Question 15 · Scenario
Maria starts her app’s development server, which says the app is available at http://localhost:3000. The app works. Later she closes that terminal window, reloads the page, and the browser says “This site can’t be reached”. What happened, and how does she fix it?






Suggested answer





The development server was a program running inside that terminal window. Closing the window stopped it, so nothing is listening on port 3000 any more and the browser can’t connect. She needs to open a terminal, cd into the project folder and start the server again (and leave that window open while she works).





Question 16 · Scenario
Sam texts his friend the link http://localhost:3000 so she can try his new app. She gets an error. Explain why, and what Sam would need to do instead.






Suggested answer





localhost means “this computer” - on the friend’s phone it refers to her own phone, where Sam’s server isn’t running. A localhost address only works on the computer running the server. To share the app, Sam must deploy it to a server on the Internet (a hosting service) and send her that public URL.





Question 17 · Long answer
A site like Amazon handles millions of visitors at once, yet your browser behaves as if it talks to “one server”. Explain, in plain English, two techniques that make this possible.






Suggested answer






Load balancers: one “front door” receives the requests and spreads them across many identical servers. If one server fails, the others keep answering, so visitors don’t notice.
CDNs (content delivery networks): copies of files such as images, CSS and JavaScript are stored on servers in many cities, and each visitor gets them from a nearby copy. This is faster and takes load off the main servers.

A good answer may also mention caching (saved copies so work isn’t repeated) and many data centers in different regions.





Question 18 · Scenario
Sam already has one project’s development server running on port 3000. He starts a second project that also wants port 3000. What can happen, and what are two ways to deal with it?






Suggested answer





Only one program can listen on a port at a time. Depending on the tool, the second server either picks the next free port automatically (for example 3001 - read the terminal output to see which) or stops with an “address already in use” error. Sam can stop the first server with Ctrl+C in its terminal window, or start the second server on a different port.





Question 19 · Read the output
Sam runs curl -I http://amazon.com (note: http, not https) and sees, among other lines:
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://amazon.com/
What is the server telling him, and why do sites do this?






Suggested answer





301 is a redirect: “this address has moved permanently”, and the Location header says where to go instead - the same site over HTTPS. A browser follows the redirect automatically and requests https://amazon.com/; curl only shows it (add -L to make curl follow redirects). Sites do this so that anyone who types or clicks a plain http:// address still ends up on the encrypted version.





Question 20 · Hands-on
Run the tiny Python web server from this page. While it is running, open a second terminal window and run curl -i http://localhost:8000/ and then curl -i http://localhost:8000/missing.html. Compare the first line of each response and the log lines that appear in the server’s window. Then stop the server and run the first curl command again. What changes?






Suggested answer






The first request returns a status line with 200 and your HTML as the body; the second returns 404. (Python’s simple server answers with HTTP/1.0, an older version of HTTP.)
Each request adds a log line in the server window, showing the method, the path and the status code - the same conversation seen from the server’s side.
After you stop the server, curl fails with a “connection refused”-style error (“Failed to connect”), because no program is listening on port 8000.

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
31.1 Anatomy of a URL
A web address tells the browser exactly what to fetch and from which server. This page takes web addresses apart, then follows the human-friendly name (like www.amazon.com) to the numeric address computers actually use - with the help of DNS, the Internet’s phone book.
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the full address of something on the web. Here is one with all the common parts:
Now a real one, from Amazon’s toy department:
The scheme is https://, the domain is www.amazon.com, the path is /toys/b, and the query string holds two parameters: ie=UTF8 and node=165793011 (an ID Amazon uses for the toys category). There is no port (so 443) and no fragment.
A few more things worth knowing:
crumbs: 31  31. URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
https://www.example.com:443/products/shoes?color=red&size=9#reviews








Part
In the example
What it means




scheme
https://
How to talk to the server: here, HTTPS


domain name (host)
www.example.com
Which server to contact


port
:443
Which program on that server. Usually left out: https means 443 and http means 80


path
/products/shoes
Which page or resource on that server (like a file path)


query string
?color=red&size=9
Extra settings as name=value pairs, after a ? and separated by &


fragment
#reviews
A spot within the page. The browser handles it; it is not sent to the server




https://www.amazon.com/toys/b?ie=UTF8&node=165793011



Other schemes exist. When you double-click an HTML file on your own computer, the address bar shows a file:///... URL: the browser reads the file straight from your disk, with no server involved.
Development URLs have the same anatomy: http://localhost:3000/events?club=chess has a scheme, a host (localhost), a port (3000), a path and a query string.
Spaces and some other characters aren’t allowed in URLs, so they are encoded: a space becomes %20 (or + inside a query string).







Put URLs in quotes on the command line



& and ? are special characters in the shell: & runs a command in the background and ? is a wildcard. When you paste a URL with a query string into a command, wrap it in quotes: curl "https://www.example.com/search?q=shoes&page=2". (See Single Quotes vs. Double Quotes and Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching.)
crumbs: 31  31. URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
31.2 Domain names
A domain name is a human-friendly name for a server (or a group of servers). Read it from right to left, from the most general part to the most specific:
     www   .   amazon   .   com
      |          |           |
  subdomain   the name    top-level domain (TLD)
              Amazon
              registered

The top-level domain (TLD) is the last part: .com, .org, .edu, .gov, country codes such as .uk or .ca, and newer ones such as .app or .dev.
The name to its left, together with the TLD, is the domain someone registered (rented): amazon.com. (Some countries add a level: in bbc.co.uk, the registered domain is bbc.co.uk.)
Anything further left is a subdomain, which the domain’s owner can create freely: www.amazon.com, docs.github.com, mail.google.com.

Domain names are not case-sensitive: AMAZON.com and amazon.com are the same. (The path part of a URL can be case-sensitive, depending on the server.)
crumbs: 31  31. URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
31.3 IP addresses
Computers don’t actually find each other by name. Every device on the Internet is reached through a numeric IP address (Internet Protocol address) - think of it as the computer’s phone number. There are two kinds:

IPv4: four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, such as 23.197.45.160. There are only about 4.3 billion of these - not enough for all the world’s devices - so the newer version was created.
IPv6: much longer, written in hexadecimal with colons, such as 2600:141b:1c00:27a3::3bd4 (:: is shorthand for a run of zeros).

Both are in use today. One special address you have already met is 127.0.0.1 (IPv6: ::1), which always means “this computer” - it is the address behind localhost.
Why have names at all? Names are easy to remember; the numbers behind a name can change (when a company moves to a new host) without anyone noticing; and one name can lead to many servers, just as one server can host many names.
crumbs: 31  31. URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
31.4 DNS: the Internet’s phone book
DNS (the Domain Name System) translates domain names into IP addresses. When you type www.amazon.com and press Enter:
 1. Browser:  "What is the IP address of www.amazon.com?"
        |      (checks its own memory first)
        v
 2. DNS resolver (run by your Internet provider or campus network,
    or a public one such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8)
        |      asks other DNS servers if it doesn't already know
        v
 3. Answer:   "www.amazon.com is at 23.197.45.160"
        |
        v
 4. Browser connects to 23.197.45.160 and sends: GET / ...
Answers are remembered (cached) for a while at each step, so most lookups take a few milliseconds. The flip side: when a domain is pointed at a new server, some people may keep seeing the old one until the cached answers expire - from minutes to hours.
crumbs: 31  31. URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
31.5 Try it: nslookup and ping
Both commands work in Mac Terminal and in Git Bash (on Windows they run Windows’ own versions).

31.5.1 nslookup: ask DNS directly
nslookup www.amazon.com
Output (shortened - your names and numbers will differ):
Server:     192.168.1.1
Address:    192.168.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
www.amazon.com  canonical name = tp.47cf2c8c9-frontier.amazon.com.
tp.47cf2c8c9-frontier.amazon.com    canonical name = www.amazon.com.edgekey.net.
www.amazon.com.edgekey.net  canonical name = e15316.dsca.akamaiedge.net.
Name:   e15316.dsca.akamaiedge.net
Address: 23.197.45.160
...

Server is the DNS resolver your computer asked.
“Non-authoritative answer” means the answer came from a resolver, not from Amazon’s own DNS servers.
Each canonical name line is an alias: www.amazon.com is another name for a name that is another name for… a server run by Akamai, a CDN company (see the deeper dive in Browsers, Web Servers, and HTTP). Amazon uses more than one CDN, so your chain may end somewhere else - for example at a name starting with cf. and ending in amazon.com, which belongs to CloudFront, Amazon’s own CDN.
Address lines give the IP addresses (you may also see long IPv6 ones).

On Windows the same information appears in a different layout, with the aliases listed at the end.


31.5.2 ping: is that computer answering?
ping sends small “are you there?” messages to a computer and reports each reply and how long it took (in milliseconds). It also shows which IP address the name turned into. The Mac and Windows versions behave differently:

MacWindows (Git Bash)


ping www.amazon.com
Mac’s ping keeps going until you press Ctrl+C. Output (yours will differ):
PING e15316.dsca.akamaiedge.net (23.197.45.160): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 23.197.45.160: icmp_seq=0 ttl=55 time=12.104 ms
64 bytes from 23.197.45.160: icmp_seq=1 ttl=55 time=11.387 ms
64 bytes from 23.197.45.160: icmp_seq=2 ttl=55 time=13.020 ms
^C
--- e15316.dsca.akamaiedge.net ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.387/12.170/13.020/0.669 ms
To send a fixed number of pings, use -c (count): ping -c 4 www.amazon.com.


ping www.amazon.com
In Git Bash, ping runs Windows’ own ping program, which sends 4 pings and stops by itself. Output (yours will differ):
Pinging e15316.dsca.akamaiedge.net [23.197.45.160] with 32 bytes of data:
Reply from 23.197.45.160: bytes=32 time=12ms TTL=55
Reply from 23.197.45.160: bytes=32 time=11ms TTL=55
Reply from 23.197.45.160: bytes=32 time=13ms TTL=55
Reply from 23.197.45.160: bytes=32 time=12ms TTL=55

Ping statistics for 23.197.45.160:
    Packets: Sent = 4, Received = 4, Lost = 0 (0% loss),
Approximate round trip times in milli-seconds:
    Minimum = 11ms, Maximum = 13ms, Average = 12ms
Use -n to choose how many: ping -n 10 www.amazon.com. Use -t to keep going until you press Ctrl+C.



Three things to notice:

The name in the first line may differ from the one you typed - that is the alias chain from nslookup at work.
Depending on your network you may see an IPv6 address instead of an IPv4 one.
No reply (“Request timed out”) does not always mean a site is down: many servers are configured to ignore pings while still serving web pages.

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
31.6 Getting your own domain
You don’t buy a domain forever; you register (rent) it, usually a year at a time, from a registrar such as Namecheap, Porkbun, Cloudflare or GoDaddy (many hosting services sell domains too). Prices depend on the TLD, and you must keep renewing the registration or lose the domain.
You don’t need your own domain to get started: hosting services give you a free address on their domain, such as yourname.github.io or your-app.vercel.app - a subdomain they create for you. Connecting a domain you bought to your hosting service is covered in Hosting and Deployment.






Deeper dive: DNS records





A domain’s DNS settings are a short list of records. The common types:








Type
Points a name to…
Typical use




A
an IPv4 address
example.com → 203.0.113.10


AAAA
an IPv6 address
example.com → 2001:db8::10


CNAME
another name (an alias)
www.example.com → my-site.hosting-provider.example


MX
the servers that receive email
where mail for @example.com goes


TXT
a piece of text
proving to a service that you own the domain



(The addresses and names above are reserved for examples.) When a hosting service says “add a CNAME record for www pointing to …”, you log in to your registrar (or DNS provider), add that record, and wait for DNS caches to pick up the change. Each record also has a TTL (time to live): how many seconds resolvers may cache it.
crumbs: 31  31. URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS

title: 31  31.  URLs, Domain Names, IP Addresses, and DNS
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
Label the parts of this URL: scheme, domain name, path, query string and fragment.
https://shop.example.com/cart?item=42&qty=2#summary






Suggested answer






scheme: https://
domain name: shop.example.com
path: /cart
query string: ?item=42&qty=2 (two parameters: item=42 and qty=2)
fragment: #summary

There is no port, so the default for HTTPS (443) is used.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
What does DNS do?

Encrypts the connection between your browser and a server
Translates domain names into IP addresses
Stores the files of a website
Sends “are you there?” messages to a computer







Suggested answer





b. DNS works like a phone book: name in, IP address out. Encryption (a) is what HTTPS does, storing files (c) is the web server’s job, and (d) describes ping.





Question 3 · True or false
The fragment part of a URL (for example #reviews) is sent to the server along with the path.






Suggested answer





False. The fragment stays in the browser, which uses it to jump to a spot within the page. The server only receives the path and the query string.





Question 4 · Short answer
Which of these addresses is IPv4 and which is IPv6? 2001:db8::10 and 203.0.113.10.






Suggested answer





203.0.113.10 is IPv4 (four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots). 2001:db8::10 is IPv6 (hexadecimal groups separated by colons; :: stands for a run of zeros).





Question 5 · Fill in the blank
In docs.github.com, the top-level domain is ______, the registered domain is ______, and ______ is a subdomain.






Suggested answer





The TLD is .com, the registered domain is github.com, and docs is a subdomain (so the full name docs.github.com is a subdomain of github.com).





Question 6 · Short answer
What special IP address means “this computer”, and which name do you usually use for it?






Suggested answer





127.0.0.1 (or ::1 in IPv6). Its name is localhost.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
Write a command that sends exactly 4 pings to www.wikipedia.org, first for Maria (Mac) and then for Sam (Git Bash on Windows).






Suggested answer





Maria (Mac):
ping -c 4 www.wikipedia.org
Sam (Git Bash, which runs Windows’ ping) - plain ping www.wikipedia.org already sends 4, or explicitly:
ping -n 4 www.wikipedia.org





Question 8 · Predict
Maria (Mac) and Sam (Git Bash on Windows) both type ping www.amazon.com and then do nothing. What does each of them see after a minute?






Suggested answer






Maria: replies keep scrolling, one per second, because Mac’s ping runs until she presses Ctrl+C (then it prints a summary).
Sam: four replies and a summary, then his prompt is back - Windows’ ping stops after 4 by default.






Question 9 · Short answer
In the URL https://www.amazon.com/toys/b?ie=UTF8&node=165793011, list the query parameters as name/value pairs. Which part of the URL tells Amazon’s server which page you want?






Suggested answer





Two parameters: name ie with value UTF8, and name node with value 165793011. The path, /toys/b, tells the server which page; the query string adds settings (here, the category ID).





Question 10 · Find the bug
Sam pastes this into Git Bash and gets strange results (the command seems to run “in the background” and the server complains that a parameter is missing):
curl https://www.example.com/search?q=shoes&page=2
What went wrong, and how should he write it?






Suggested answer





The shell treats & as “run the command before it in the background”, so the command is cut at the &: curl only receives https://www.example.com/search?q=shoes, and page=2 is treated as a separate shell command. (On a Mac with zsh, the ? can also cause a “no matches found” error, because ? is a wildcard.) Put the URL in quotes:
curl "https://www.example.com/search?q=shoes&page=2"





Question 11 · Scenario
A club moves its website to a new hosting service and updates its DNS records. An hour later, some members see the new site and others still see the old one. Why?






Suggested answer





DNS answers are cached by resolvers (and by browsers and operating systems) for a while - up to each record’s TTL. Members whose resolvers still hold the old answer are sent to the old server until that cached answer expires. Waiting (minutes to hours) fixes it.





Question 12 · Multiple choice
Which of these is a subdomain of github.com?

github.io
docs.github.com
github.com/docs
mygithub.com







Suggested answer





b. docs is added to the left of github.com. github.io (a) and mygithub.com (d) are different registered domains, and in github.com/docs (c) the /docs part is a path, not a subdomain.





Question 13 · Short answer
Give two reasons why the web uses domain names instead of making people type IP addresses.






Suggested answer





Any two of:

Names are easy for people to remember; numbers are not.
The IP address behind a name can change (new server, new host) without users having to learn a new address.
One name can lead to many servers (big sites, CDNs), and one server can host many names.







Hard

Question 14 · Scenario
ping www.example-store.com prints “Request timed out” for every attempt, but the site loads fine in your browser. Is the site down? Explain.






Suggested answer





No. The browser proves the server is answering web (HTTP/HTTPS) requests. Many servers and firewalls are set to ignore ping messages, which are a different kind of traffic. “Request timed out” only means no ping replies came back. To test a web server, use the browser or curl -I instead.





Question 15 · Scenario
nslookup www.amazon.com shows a chain of canonical name lines ending in e15316.dsca.akamaiedge.net. What does this tell you about how Amazon delivers its home page to you?






Suggested answer





www.amazon.com is an alias (CNAME) for other names, ending at a name that belongs to Akamai, a CDN company. So your browser is not connecting to “Amazon’s one computer” but to a nearby server in a content delivery network that Amazon uses to serve visitors quickly around the world.





Question 16 · Long answer
Describe, step by step, what happens between typing https://www.example.com/about into the address bar and seeing the page. Use the terms DNS, IP address, HTTPS, request and response.






Suggested answer






The browser takes the domain name www.example.com from the URL.
It asks DNS (its cache, then the resolver) for the IP address behind that name.
It connects to that IP address on port 443, because the scheme is HTTPS, and sets up an encrypted connection (checking the server’s certificate).
It sends an HTTP request: GET /about.
The server sends a response: status 200 plus the HTML of the page.
The browser reads the HTML and sends more requests for the CSS, JavaScript and images it mentions, then draws the page.






Question 17 · Scenario
You bought the domain myclubapp.com. Your hosting service tells you: “Add a CNAME record for www pointing to xyz.hosting-provider.example.” What will this record do, and where do you add it?






Suggested answer





It makes www.myclubapp.com an alias for the hosting service’s name. When someone looks up www.myclubapp.com, DNS follows the alias to the hosting service’s servers, so visitors reach your app there. You add the record in the DNS settings at your registrar (or wherever your domain’s DNS is managed), then wait for caches to pick up the change.





Question 18 · Compare
For http://localhost:3000/events?id=7#details, name each part. Which parts reach the development server, and which part never leaves the browser?






Suggested answer





Scheme http://, host localhost, port 3000, path /events, query string ?id=7, fragment #details. The scheme, host and port decide where the request goes (the program on port 3000 on this computer). The server receives the path and the query string (/events?id=7). The fragment #details never leaves the browser.





Question 19 · Long answer
Your club wants its own domain for its website. Explain to the club officers, in plain English, the difference between registering a domain and hosting a website, and why you need both (or neither, at first).






Suggested answer






Registering a domain rents the name (for example myclubapp.com) from a registrar, usually for a year at a time. It doesn’t store any website.
Hosting means a server somewhere actually stores and serves the website’s files and code.
DNS records connect the two: they point the registered name at the hosting service’s servers.

At first you need neither a paid domain nor paid hosting: many hosting services give you a free address on their own domain (such as yourclub.github.io). A custom domain is an optional upgrade that makes the address shorter and more professional - and its registration must be kept up (usually renewed every year).





Question 20 · Scenario
A teammate claims: “Domain names are case-sensitive, so https://WWW.Example.com/About and https://www.example.com/about are definitely different pages.” Is that right? Explain.






Suggested answer





Partly wrong. The domain name is not case-sensitive, so WWW.Example.com and www.example.com are the same server. The path (/About vs /about) may or may not be case-sensitive - that depends on the server. Many servers (especially on Linux) treat them as different, so the two URLs might lead to different pages, but not because of the domain.





Question 21 · Hands-on
Run nslookup for three sites you use (for example www.wikipedia.org, www.google.com and your school’s website). For each one, note: does it have canonical name (alias) lines? How many addresses come back? Do you see any IPv6 addresses? Then ping one of them a few times and compare the times with a friend on a different network.






Suggested answer





Results vary - that is the point. Typical observations: big sites often return several addresses (and IPv6 ones), some names are aliases that end at a CDN, and smaller sites may return a single address with no aliases. Ping times depend on how far away (in network terms) the answering server is, so a friend on another network may see different addresses and different times for the same name.

title: 32  32.  HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Browser Developer Tools
text:
32.1 Three languages, three jobs
When a web server answers, it sends the browser code written in three languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. This page shows what each one does with a tiny three-file website, then shows you how to look inside any web page with the browser’s built-in developer tools - a skill you will use constantly when an AI writes code for you.
Think of a house: HTML is the walls and rooms, CSS is the paint and furniture, and JavaScript is the wiring that makes things respond when you flip a switch. The lines blur in practice - JavaScript can change the HTML and CSS on the fly - but this is the right mental model. Whatever tools a developer uses (including the frameworks on Web Frameworks and Meta-Frameworks), in the end the browser receives HTML, CSS and JavaScript (plus media files such as images and fonts).
crumbs: 32  32. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Browser Developer Tools

title: 32  32.  HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Browser Developer Tools
text:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) holds the content and structure: headings, paragraphs, lists, links, images, buttons, forms. It is written with tags such as <h1> and </h1>. An opening tag, its content and the closing tag together form an element: <h1>Hello</h1>.
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls the appearance: colors, fonts, spacing, layout, and how the page adapts to a phone screen.
JavaScript (JS) adds behavior: reacting to clicks, changing the page without reloading it, and talking to servers in the background. (Despite the name, it has nothing to do with Java.)
