title: 36  36.  Hosting and Deployment: Getting Your App Online
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is the difference between development and production?






Suggested answer





Development is where you build and test, usually on your own computer (localhost) with test data and test keys. Production is the real, public version that real users rely on, with real data, live keys and an optimized build, running on a hosting service.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
What does “deploying” an app mean?

Writing the app’s code
Building the app for production and putting it on servers where users can reach it
Buying a domain name
Running npm run dev on your laptop







Suggested answer





b. Deployment builds the app, copies it to the hosting service and switches visitors to the new version. Writing code (a) comes first, a domain (c) is optional, and npm run dev (d) runs a development server only on your own computer.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each service with the kind of hosting it is best known for.



Service

Kind




1. GitHub Pages

A. Backend-as-a-service


2. Render

B. Big cloud provider


3. Supabase

C. Static hosting


4. AWS

D. App platform









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 4 · True or false
GitHub Pages can run a Node.js back end that saves sign-ups to a database.






Suggested answer





False. GitHub Pages serves static files only (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images). Server code needs an app platform, a backend-as-a-service or another kind of hosting.





Question 5 · Fill in the blank
CI stands for ______ and means ______. CD stands for ______.






Suggested answer





CI = continuous integration: every push automatically runs checks such as building and testing. CD = continuous delivery (or deployment): code that passes the checks is released automatically.





Question 6 · True or false
As of October 2026, a small business may run its online store on Vercel’s free Hobby plan.






Suggested answer





False. Vercel’s Hobby plan is for personal, non-commercial use. A business would need a paid plan (or another host). Always check the current terms, since free plans change.






Medium

Question 7 · Scenario
Maria’s app works perfectly with npm run dev. After deploying it to Vercel, the login page shows an error saying the Supabase URL is missing. What is the most likely cause, and how does she fix it?






Suggested answer





Her environment variables live in .env.local, which is (correctly) not in Git, so Vercel never received them. She must add the same variables (for example the Supabase URL and publishable key) in the project’s Environment Variables settings on Vercel, then redeploy.





Question 8 · Ordering
Put the steps of a first deployment in order: (a) click Deploy, (b) push the project to GitHub, (c) enter the environment variables, (d) import the repository on the hosting service, (e) open the public address and test.






Suggested answer





b → d → c → a → e.





Question 9 · Choose
Suggest a suitable kind of hosting for each: (a) a static portfolio site, (b) a Next.js app with logins and a database, (c) a small Python FastAPI back end.






Suggested answer






Static hosting such as GitHub Pages or Netlify. (b) An app platform such as Vercel or Netlify for the Next.js app, plus a backend-as-a-service such as Supabase for the database and logins.
An app platform that runs Python servers, such as Render or Railway (or a container on a platform that runs containers).






Question 10 · Scenario
Sam changed an environment variable in his host’s dashboard, but the live site still uses the old value. Why, and what should he do?






Suggested answer





On many hosts, environment variable changes apply only to new deployments; the running deployment was built with the old value. He should redeploy (trigger a new deployment, for example by pushing a commit or using the dashboard’s redeploy option).





Question 11 · Short answer
What is a preview deployment, and why is it useful?






Suggested answer





A separate, automatically built copy of the app, with its own address, created for a branch or pull request (services such as Vercel and Netlify do this). It lets you and your teammates test a change on a real server before merging it into the main branch and releasing it to users.





Question 12 · Scenario
Sam pushes a commit and the build on his hosting service fails. Is his live site now down? What should he do next?






Suggested answer





No - a failed build is not published, so the live site keeps running the last successful version. He should open the build log, find the first error message (and, if needed, paste the log into Claude Code for an explanation), fix the problem locally (for example run npm run build to reproduce it), then commit and push again.





Question 13 · Short answer
List the steps to put an app on your own domain with HTTPS.






Suggested answer






Register the domain with a registrar.
Add the domain in the hosting service’s dashboard.
Create the DNS records the host shows you (usually an A and/or CNAME record) at the registrar.
Wait for DNS to update. The host then obtains and renews the HTTPS certificate automatically.







Hard

Question 14 · Scenario
Your team’s API runs on a free Render web service. During your class demo, the first request takes almost a minute, but later ones are fast. Explain, and give two ways to avoid it.






Suggested answer





Free Render web services go to sleep after 15 minutes without traffic, and the next request has to wait while the service wakes up (as of October 2026). Options: open the app a few minutes before the demo to wake it up; move to a paid instance that stays on; or host on a service whose free plan doesn’t sleep in the same way. (Read the current free-plan limits before relying on any of them.)





Question 15 · Compare
Compare a virtual server, an app platform and serverless functions for a student team. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each.






Suggested answer






Virtual server: full control over everything; but you must install, update and secure the whole machine yourself.
App platform: push to deploy, little setup, HTTPS and scaling handled for you; but less control, and costs or limits set by the platform.
Serverless functions: no server to manage, scale automatically, pay per use; but you work within the platform’s limits (for example how long a function may run), and costs can be harder to predict at high volume.

For most student teams, an app platform (plus a backend-as-a-service) is the easiest starting point.





Question 16 · Long answer
Why should a payment-taking app use different keys and databases for development, previews and production? Describe how you would set this up.






Suggested answer





So that testing can never touch real money or real customers’ data, and so a leaked development key can be revoked without breaking the live app. Setup: use Stripe sandbox (test) keys and a separate development database in .env.local and in the host’s Preview environment variables; use live keys and the production database only in the host’s Production environment variables. Then a bug in a preview can’t charge real cards or delete real sign-ups.





Question 17 · Scenario
Your app uses a free Supabase project. Nobody used it during spring break, and on demo day it doesn’t respond. What probably happened, and how could you have avoided the surprise?






Suggested answer





As of October 2026, Supabase pauses free projects after a week of inactivity, so the database stopped answering. The owner can restore (unpause) it from the Supabase dashboard, which takes some time. To avoid the surprise: check the free plan’s rules in advance, open the app a day before the demo, and consider a paid plan for anything that must stay available.





Question 18 · Short answer
What problem do containers solve, and what are a Dockerfile and an image?






Suggested answer





Containers solve “it works on my machine”: the app is packaged with everything it needs (runtime, libraries, settings), so it runs the same way on any computer or hosting platform. A Dockerfile is the recipe that says how to build the package; the image is the resulting package that platforms run.





Question 19 · Hands-on
Publish your hello-site (from HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Browser Developer Tools) with GitHub Pages. Push it to a public GitHub repository, then in the repository go to Settings → Pages, under “Build and deployment” choose Deploy from a branch, select your main branch and the / (root) folder, and click Save. After a minute or two, find your site’s address on the same page. Then change the heading, commit and push: how long until the live site shows the change?






Suggested answer





The site appears at an address like https://<your-username>.github.io/<repository-name>/. Because index.html is in the root of the branch, GitHub Pages serves it as the home page. Each push triggers a new build and deployment (you can watch it in the repository’s Actions tab); the change usually appears within a minute or two - this is push-to-deploy in action. If you see a 404, check that the repository is public, that you chose the right branch and folder, and that the file is named exactly index.html.

37.1 The idea: a club event sign-up app
This page pulls the whole “How the Web Works” part together. You will take a product idea, break it into the building blocks from the previous pages, draw the architecture, and use Claude Code as a design partner - before writing a single line of code.
Student clubs run events, and sign-ups are messy: spreadsheets, group chats, no-shows, nobody knows who is on the waitlist. The idea, “ClubHub”:
Two kinds of users with different permissions, data that must be stored and shared, logins, money and an AI feature: a typical small business app.

37.4 Start small: the MVP
An MVP (minimum viable product) is the smallest version that real users can try. For ClubHub, version 1 could be: log in with Google, see upcoming events, sign up and cancel, and let officers create events. The waitlist, payments, emails and AI drafts come later, one at a time.
Starting small means less to build and debug, feedback from real members sooner, fewer accounts, keys and bills at first - and an AI makes far fewer mistakes on small, well-defined steps than on “build the whole app”.

text:
37.5 Designing with Claude Code
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Best practices for Claude Code · Permission modes (plan mode) · How Claude remembers your project
An AI coding agent is a fast, well-read partner for architecture - if you lead the conversation:

Describe the problem, not the technology. Who are the users, what must they be able to do, and what are your constraints: budget, deadline, team skills, “members log in with school Google accounts”.
Discuss in plan mode. In plan mode, Claude Code reads files and proposes a plan but doesn’t edit your files. Press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows plan mode, or start with claude --permission-mode plan (details in Permissions, Modes, and Safety).
Ask for options and trade-offs, not just one answer: two or three possible architectures compared on cost, complexity, free-plan limits and risks.
Ask it to explain every piece in plain English - what it does, why it is needed, what happens if it fails - until you could explain the diagram to someone else.
Let it interview you, then write a spec. Claude Code’s best-practices guide suggests asking Claude to interview you about the feature and then write the result to a file such as SPEC.md (writing a file means leaving plan mode). Good specs say what is out of scope and how you will check that it works. Then start a fresh session to build from the spec.
Record lasting decisions in CLAUDE.md, the file Claude Code reads at the start of every session: the stack, the commands to run, required environment variables, conventions (see CLAUDE.md and Memory).
Verify claims. Prices, free plans and library versions change faster than AI training data. Check the official pricing and documentation pages, or ask Claude to look up the current docs and show you its sources.
Watch costs and secrets. List every paid service and its limits, keep keys in .env files and host settings only, and never paste a real key into the chat.

A first prompt might look like this:
I'm planning a web app for student clubs (feature list below).
Constraints: three business students, beginner coders, $0 budget,
must be live in 6 weeks, members log in with school Google accounts.

Don't write any code yet.
1. Propose 2-3 possible architectures (front end, back end, database,
   login, hosting, email, payments) and compare them in a table:
   monthly cost at 100 and at 5,000 members, complexity, free-plan
   limits, and risks.
2. Recommend one and explain each piece in plain English.
3. Define a minimal first version (MVP) we can build in two weeks.
4. List the accounts, API keys and environment variables we will need.
For the spec, the best-practices guide offers this interview prompt (AskUserQuestion is the built-in tool Claude uses to ask you multiple-choice questions):
I want to build [brief description]. Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool.

Ask about technical implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs. Don't ask obvious questions, dig into the hard parts I might not have considered.

Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.

section: 37.6 Checklist: questions to answer before coding
text:
37.6 Checklist: questions to answer before coding
Users and features

Who are the users, and what roles do they have (member, officer, admin)?
What are the 3-5 must-have features of the MVP? What is explicitly out of scope?

Data and permissions

What data will you store (tables and columns)? What is personal or sensitive?
Who may see and change each kind of data? Where is that enforced (it must be the back end or database rules, not only the front end)?

Architecture and services

Which front end, back end, database and login approach - and why?
Which third-party services will you use? Which cost money, what are their free-plan limits, and what happens when you exceed them?

Secrets and costs

Which keys exist, where are they stored in development and in production, and who has access? Are spending limits set?

Operations

Where will development, previews and production run, and how do you deploy (push to GitHub)?
How will you check that it works: a manual test checklist, automated tests, Claude testing it in a browser?
What if a free plan pauses or sleeps before demo day? Who owns each account?

To see an app of this shape built step by step, work through the full-stack tutorial.

title: 37  37.  Putting It Together: Architecting a Web App with AI
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is an MVP, and why start with one?






Suggested answer





A minimum viable product: the smallest version of the product that real users can try. Starting with one means less to build and debug, earlier feedback from users, fewer services, keys and costs at first, and smaller, clearer steps for the AI to get right.





Question 2 · Matching
Match each ClubHub need with the building block that handles it.








Need

Building block




1. Remember who signed up for which event

A. Payment service (Stripe)


2. “Log in with Google”

B. Email service


3. Pay for the ski trip

C. Database


4. Reminder the day before

D. Authentication (OAuth)









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 3 · True or false
The best first step with Claude Code is to describe your idea in one sentence and ask it to build the whole app right away.






Suggested answer





False. First clarify requirements and constraints, ask for options and trade-offs, agree on a plan (for example in plan mode), and write a short spec. Then build a small MVP step by step. Jumping straight to code often solves the wrong problem.





Question 4 · Multiple choice
What does Claude Code do in plan mode?

It writes and runs code without asking
It reads files and proposes a plan, but doesn’t edit your files
It only answers questions about Claude’s pricing
It deploys your app to production







Suggested answer





b. Plan mode separates thinking from doing: Claude explores and writes a plan, and edits wait until you approve it. It is the opposite of (a), and it has nothing to do with pricing (c) or deployment (d).






Medium

Question 5 · Scenario
Events have a capacity of 30. Where must the “no more than 30 confirmed sign-ups” rule be enforced, and what should happen to the 31st person?






Suggested answer





In the back end (and ideally backed up by database rules), because front-end checks can be bypassed and two people may click at the same moment. When the event is full, the back end saves the 31st sign-up with status waitlist instead of confirmed (or refuses it, if there is no waitlist), and the front end shows the result.





Question 6 · Long answer
Write a prompt asking Claude Code for architecture options for your own app idea, without code. What must a good prompt include?






Suggested answer





A good prompt includes: who the users are and what they need to do; the constraints (budget, deadline, team skills, required logins or data rules); an explicit “don’t write code yet”; a request for 2-3 options compared in a table (cost, complexity, limits, risks); a request to explain each piece in plain English; and a request for an MVP and a list of the accounts, keys and environment variables needed. The sample prompt on this page is a model answer.





Question 7 · Compare
ClubHub has both a SPEC.md and a CLAUDE.md. What belongs in each?






Suggested answer






SPEC.md: the plan for what to build - features, user roles, screens, data, what is out of scope, and how to check that it works.
CLAUDE.md: short, lasting facts Claude should know in every session - the chosen stack and architectural decisions, the commands to run and test the app, required environment variables (names, not values), and conventions.






Question 8 · Ordering
Put these steps in a sensible order: (a) build the MVP in small steps, (b) describe users, needs and constraints, (c) write a spec, (d) compare architecture options and pick one, (e) record the key decisions in CLAUDE.md.






Suggested answer





b → d → c → e → a. (Writing CLAUDE.md alongside the spec, or updating it as you build, is also fine - the point is that understanding and planning come before building.)





Question 9 · Scenario
Claude tells you that a hosting service “has a generous free tier with unlimited projects”. What should you do before relying on it?






Suggested answer





Check the service’s official pricing page today (or ask Claude to fetch the current page and quote it). Free plans change often, and the AI’s training data may be out of date - some hosts that once had free plans no longer do. Also note the limits that matter to you: commercial use, sleeping or pausing, usage caps.





Question 10 · Short answer
Name the four main tables (or the three core ones) you would need for ClubHub, and what links a sign-up to a member and an event.






Suggested answer





The core tables are members, events and signups (a fourth, such as payments, can come later). Each row in signups stores a member_id and an event_id, which point to rows in members and events, plus the sign-up’s status (confirmed or waitlist).






Hard

Question 11 · Scenario
Describe how the “AI drafts the event description” feature should work in this architecture: who calls the Claude API, where the key lives, and how you keep the cost under control.






Suggested answer





The officer’s browser sends the bullet points to ClubHub’s back end, which checks that the user is an officer, calls the Claude API with the key from its environment variables (.env.local in development, the host’s settings in production), and returns the draft. The key never reaches the browser. Cost control: only officers can use the feature, limit how often they can, keep the prompt and output short, use a smaller model if it is good enough, and set a monthly spend limit in the Claude Console.





Question 12 · Compare
For a beginner team, compare using Supabase (database and logins as a service) with writing your own Express API and PostgreSQL database on Render. Give one advantage of each.






Suggested answer






Supabase: much less code to write and secure - logins (including Google), the database and its API are ready-made, with a free plan to start. The trade-off: you must learn its rules (such as Row Level Security) and accept its limits, such as pausing inactive free projects.
Own Express API on Render: full control and a deeper understanding of how a back end works; nothing hidden. The trade-off: you must build and secure logins, permissions and every endpoint yourself, which is slower and riskier for beginners (and Render’s free databases expire).

For most beginner teams, Supabase (or a similar service) is the safer start.





Question 13 · Long answer
Identify three risks in the ClubHub architecture and how you would reduce each.






Suggested answer





Any three well-explained risks, for example:

Leaked secret keys (Stripe, Claude, database): keep them in .env files and host settings only, never in Git or front-end code; rotate immediately if exposed.
Unexpected costs (AI calls, emails, a bug in a loop): set spending limits and alerts, limit who can trigger paid actions and how often.
Free-plan surprises (projects pausing or sleeping, commercial-use restrictions): read the terms, test before demos, budget for a paid plan if needed.
Privacy: members’ emails and payment status are personal data; only officers should see sign-up lists, enforced on the back end; collect only what you need.
Payment mistakes: use Stripe’s test mode until launch; separate development and production keys.






Question 14 · Scenario
A classmate proposes a shortcut: no back end and no database - each browser saves sign-ups in localStorage. What breaks?






Suggested answer





localStorage lives in one browser on one device. Officers couldn’t see who signed up, members couldn’t see the count or the waitlist, capacity couldn’t be enforced across members, the data would vanish when someone clears their browser or switches devices, and there would be no real login. Shared data needs a server-side database, and rules need a back end.





Question 15 · Scenario
Version 1 is live. Now officers want paid events. What changes in the architecture, and how would you develop it safely?






Suggested answer





Add Stripe: the back end creates the payment (for example a Stripe checkout) with the secret key, the browser sends the member to pay, and after a successful payment the back end marks the sign-up as paid (a new payments table or a column on signups). Develop it on a branch with a preview deployment, using Stripe’s test (sandbox) keys and test cards, keep the live secret key only in the production environment variables, and update the spec and CLAUDE.md with the new decisions.





Question 16 · Hands-on
Pick your own app idea. Start Claude Code in an empty folder in plan mode (claude --permission-mode plan) and use the first prompt on this page to get 2-3 architecture options. Then leave plan mode (press Shift+Tab), so that Claude may create files, and use the interview prompt to have it write SPEC.md. Review the result against this page’s checklist: which questions does the spec still not answer?






Suggested answer





Answers vary. A strong result has: a clear user and role list; an MVP with 3-5 features and an explicit out-of-scope list; a data model; a diagram or description of front end, back end, database, logins and third-party services; a list of keys and environment variables; a hosting and deployment plan; and a way to check that the MVP works. Commonly missing items are permissions (“who may see what”), cost limits, and what happens when a free plan pauses - add them before you start building.

38.1 One name, four meanings
“Claude” is the name of an AI model, a chat app, a coding tool, and a developer platform. This page is a map of all of them: what each piece is, where it runs, and who it is for. Later pages cover the pieces this course uses most, especially Claude Code.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Models overview · What interfaces can I use to access Claude?
When someone says “Claude”, they can mean four different things:
Think of the model as an engine and the rest as vehicles built around it. Each vehicle adds its own controls and tools, so the same model can act differently in each (see How Claude Code Works).

38.3 The Claude apps: web, desktop, and mobile
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Install Claude Desktop · Claude Cowork and chat are one Claude

claude.ai works in any browser, on every plan including Free.
Claude Desktop is the installed app for Mac and Windows (Linux is in beta). Besides chat, it can work with folders on your computer, connect to local tools, and has a Code tab that runs Claude Code with buttons and panels instead of a terminal (paid plans).
Claude mobile (iPhone and Android) offers chat, spoken conversations (voice mode, in beta), and a way to check on longer tasks. Its Code tab connects to Claude Code sessions (see Claude Code Beyond the Terminal).


38.3.1 Cowork is becoming plain “Claude” (rolling out)
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Cowork and chat are one Claude · Cowork is now Claude
Cowork was a separate mode for handing Claude a longer, multi-step job, such as research, a report, a spreadsheet, or a slide deck. It is built on the same technology as Claude Code, but for work that isn’t coding. On September 16, 2026, Anthropic started merging chat and Cowork into one conversation: you just ask, and Claude decides whether you need a quick answer or a longer task that keeps running in the cloud after you close your laptop.
The change is rolling out in stages, starting with Pro and Max. If your message box still shows separate “Chat” and “Cowork” options, you have the older experience. Either way, the Desktop Code tab stays where it was.

title: 38  38.  The Claude Product Family
text:
38.4 Features inside the apps
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: What are projects? · What are artifacts? · What are skills?



Feature
In one sentence




Projects
A workspace that keeps related chats together with uploaded files and standing instructions (Free plan: up to 5 projects).


Artifacts
Something Claude makes that you would show to someone, such as a document, deck, design, dashboard, or small interactive tool; it opens beside the chat, and you can share it by link.


Claude Design, Slides, Docs
Artifact templates (beta, paid plans) for designs and mockups, presentations (export to PowerPoint or PDF), and “living documents” that you edit together with Claude and your teammates.


Memory
Claude remembers useful context across chats; you can view and edit what it remembers in Settings.


Connectors
Links to apps such as Google Drive, Gmail, or GitHub, built on the open Model Context Protocol (MCP) (see MCP Servers).


Skills
Folders of instructions that teach Claude a repeatable task; Claude loads a skill only when it’s relevant (see Skills).


Research
A research agent that runs many web searches and writes a report with sources (paid plans).

title: 38  38.  The Claude Product Family
text:
38.5 Claude inside other apps
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Get started with Claude in Chrome · Claude for Microsoft 365 · Claude in Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides · What is Claude Tag?

Claude in Chrome: a Chrome extension with a side panel. Claude reads the page you’re on and can click, type, and fill in forms. Paid plans (the side panel is in beta). Anthropic warns about prompt injection: a web page can hide instructions aimed at Claude (see Limits, Risks, and Responsible Use).
Claude for Microsoft 365: add-ins for Excel, PowerPoint, and Word (generally available on paid plans) and Outlook (beta). Claude works directly in the open workbook, deck, document, or inbox.
Claude for Google Workspace: the same idea for Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides (beta, paid plans). This is different from the Google Drive connector, which lets claude.ai search your Drive while you chat.
Claude Tag: tag @Claude in a Slack channel, and it does the work in the open as your organization’s shared teammate, for coding and non-coding tasks. Team and Enterprise plans (beta); channel work is billed to the organization.

title: 38  38.  The Claude Product Family
section: 38.6 Claude Code: one agent, many places
text:
38.6 Claude Code: one agent, many places
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code overview · Platforms and integrations
Claude Code is an agent: you describe a goal, and it reads your files, edits code, runs commands, and checks the result. Its permission mode decides which actions need your approval first (see Permissions, Modes, and Safety). It is included in every paid plan (not Free), and you can also pay for it per use with a developer (Console) account. The same engine runs in several places:

Terminal (CLI): the claude command. It is the most complete version and the one this course uses (see Installing Claude Code).
Code editors: extensions for VS Code (and editors built on it, such as Cursor) and for JetBrains editors such as PyCharm (the JetBrains plugin is still labeled beta).
Desktop app: the Code tab.
Cloud: sessions started at claude.ai/code run on Anthropic’s computers and keep going after you disconnect.
Phone: the mobile app’s Code tab, which can also steer a session running on your own computer (Remote Control).

Claude Code Beyond the Terminal compares these surfaces.

title: 38  38.  The Claude Product Family
text:
38.7 The Claude Developer Platform
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Platform docs · Agent SDK overview · Managed Agents overview
For people who build Claude into their own software:

Claude API: your program sends Claude a request and gets a reply back. You pay per token (a chunk of text, roughly part of a word; see How LLMs Work). This is billed separately from any app subscription (see APIs, API Keys, and Third-Party Services).
Claude Console (platform.claude.com): the website where developers create API keys, test prompts, and see usage and bills.
Client SDKs: official libraries for Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, and other languages that make calling the API easier.
Agent SDK: “Claude Code as a library”: the same tools and agent loop that power Claude Code, inside your own Python or TypeScript program.
Managed Agents (beta): Anthropic hosts the whole agent for you, including a cloud sandbox where it runs.

Companies can also buy Claude models through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry.

title: 38  38.  The Claude Product Family
section: 38.8 Names that are easy to mix up
text:
38.8 Names that are easy to mix up
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code in Slack · Projects in Claude Code · Share session output as artifacts







These two…
…differ like this




claude.ai vs. Claude Console
claude.ai is the chat app. The Console (platform.claude.com) is the developer dashboard for API keys and API bills. A paid claude.ai plan does not include API usage.


Claude Tag vs. Claude Code in Slack
Both answer @Claude in Slack. Claude Tag is the organization’s shared teammate (Team and Enterprise). Claude Code in Slack is the earlier version: it starts a cloud coding session under your own account (Pro and Max), and only in Slack workspaces that are not connected to Claude Tag.


Projects in claude.ai vs. the new Projects
A classic project is a folder of chats, files, and instructions. The new Projects (public beta, rolling out to some Pro and Max users, starting with Claude Code) is one conversation in which Claude runs many parallel cloud sessions for you. Existing projects keep working.


Artifacts in chat vs. artifacts from Claude Code
The same idea. Claude Code can publish its work (for example, an annotated list of code changes) as a live page on claude.ai that stays private until you share it.


Claude Desktop vs. Claude Code Desktop
The same app; “Claude Code Desktop” means its Code tab.


Claude in Chrome vs. Claude Code’s Chrome integration
The same extension, used on its own or driven by Claude Code.









Deeper dive: Specialized Claude products





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Science overview · Use Claude Security · Claude Fable and Mythos 5.1

Claude Science (beta): a separate desktop app that pairs Claude with a sandboxed analysis environment (Python, R, shell) and connectors to scientific databases. On for Pro and Max; Team and Enterprise owners must turn it on.
Claude Security (beta, Enterprise only): scans a codebase for security weaknesses and proposes fixes for a person to review.
Claude for Government: a version of Claude for government agencies.
Claude Mythos 5.1: an invitation-only model for vetted cybersecurity and biology research groups. Claude Fable 5.1 is the same underlying model with extra safeguards, so everyone else can use it.

38.9 Key takeaways

“Claude” can mean the model, the apps, Claude Code, or the API.
The Free plan does not include Claude Code, and no subscription includes API usage.
Names and plans change quickly: check the date badges and official links.

title: 38  38.  The Claude Product Family
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Which description fits Claude Code?

A website where you chat with Claude about any topic
An agent that reads your project, edits files, and runs commands to complete coding tasks
A dashboard for creating API keys and viewing API bills
A Slack app that acts as your organization’s shared teammate







Suggested answer





b. Claude Code is Anthropic’s coding agent. Option a describes claude.ai, option c describes the Claude Console, and option d describes Claude Tag.





Question 2 · Short answer
The word “Claude” can refer to four different things. Name them.






Suggested answer






The model: the AI itself (the Fable, Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku models).
The Claude apps: claude.ai, Claude Desktop, and the mobile apps.
Claude Code: the coding agent.
The Claude API (part of the Claude Developer Platform): how programs use Claude, paid per use.






Question 3 · True or false
The Free plan includes Claude Code.






Suggested answer





False. Claude Code is included in the paid plans (Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise). You can also pay for it per use with a Console (API) account. The Free plan includes chat, artifacts, connectors, and more, but not Claude Code.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each product with its description.








Product

Description




1. claude.ai

A. Developer dashboard for API keys and API bills


2. Claude Desktop

B. @Claude as a shared teammate in Slack channels


3. Claude in Chrome

C. Chat website that works in any browser


4. Claude Tag

D. Browser extension that reads and acts on web pages


5. Claude Console

E. Installed app for Mac and Windows with a Code tab









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → D, 4 → B, 5 → A.





Question 5 · Multiple choice
Where do you use Claude Tag?

In Slack
In Excel
In VS Code
In the Claude Console







Suggested answer





a. Claude Tag puts @Claude into Slack channels as a shared teammate (Team and Enterprise plans). Excel has Claude for Microsoft 365, VS Code has the Claude Code extension, and the Console is the developer dashboard.





Question 6 · True or false
“Claude for Google Workspace” and the Google Drive connector are two names for the same feature.






Suggested answer





False. Claude for Google Workspace puts Claude in a sidebar inside Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides, where it edits the open file. The Google Drive connector works the other way around: while you chat at claude.ai, Claude can search and read files in your Drive.






Medium

Question 7 · Scenario
Maria keeps her budget in an Excel workbook. She wants Claude to fix formulas directly in the workbook, without copying data into a chat window. Which Claude product fits best, and what kind of plan does she need?






Suggested answer





Claude for Microsoft 365, specifically the Excel add-in. It opens Claude in a sidebar inside Excel and works on the open workbook. It requires a paid plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise).





Question 8 · Scenario
Sam has a Pro plan. His student club chats in a Slack workspace that is not connected to any Claude organization. He wants to type @Claude with a bug report and get back a pull request.

Which Claude product can he use, and under whose account does the work run?
Why can’t he use Claude Tag?







Suggested answer






Claude Code in Slack (the earlier Slack integration). It starts a Claude Code cloud session under Sam’s own Claude account and plan.
Claude Tag is only available on Team and Enterprise plans; it acts as an organization’s shared teammate. A Pro plan doesn’t include it.






Question 9 · Short answer
For each product, say where you use it: in a web browser, in an installed app or program, inside another app, or from your own code.

claude.ai
Claude Desktop
The Claude Code CLI
Claude for Microsoft 365
The Claude API







Suggested answer






Web browser.
Installed app (Mac, Windows; Linux in beta).
Installed program that you run in a terminal.
Inside another app (Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Outlook).
From your own code (your program sends requests to Anthropic).

Note: in all five cases the model itself runs on Anthropic’s servers. What differs is where you interact with Claude and what Claude can reach (for example, the CLI can read and edit files on your computer).





Question 10 · Multiple choice
In claude.ai, what is a classic project?

A Git repository that Claude creates for you
A workspace that groups chats with uploaded files and standing instructions
A paid add-on that unlocks the Opus models
A Claude Code session that runs in the cloud







Suggested answer





b. A project is a workspace with its own chats, files (its knowledge), and instructions. It is not a Git repository (a), not a paid add-on (Free users can create up to 5 projects) (c), and not a cloud session (d). The new Projects beta does coordinate cloud sessions, but it is a different, newer feature.





Question 11 · Short answer
What is an artifact? Give two examples, and name the three artifact templates.






Suggested answer





An artifact is something Claude makes for you that you would put in front of someone else. It opens beside the conversation, you can edit it and come back to it, and you can share it by link. Examples: a document, a slide deck, a design or mockup, a dashboard, a small interactive tool. The templates are Claude Design, Claude Slides, and Claude Docs (beta, paid plans). Claude Code can also publish artifacts.





Question 12 · Short answer
What happened to Cowork in September 2026, and how can you tell whether your account has the new experience yet?






Suggested answer





Anthropic began merging chat and Cowork into one “Claude” conversation. You no longer choose a mode: Claude decides whether a request needs a quick answer or a longer task, which can keep running in the cloud. The change is rolling out in stages (Pro and Max first). If your message box still shows separate “Chat” and “Cowork” options, you still have the older experience.





Question 13 · Matching
Match each part of the Claude Developer Platform with its description.








Part

Description




1. Claude API

A. Website for API keys, prompt testing, and bills


2. Claude Console

B. Claude Code’s tools and agent loop as a library for your own program


3. Agent SDK

C. Anthropic hosts the whole agent and its cloud sandbox


4. Managed Agents

D. Your program sends requests and pays per token









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → A, 3 → B, 4 → C.






Hard

Question 14 · Find the bug
A classmate says: “I already pay for Claude Pro, so the Python app I’m building can call the Claude API for free.” What is wrong with this reasoning, and what would the classmate actually need?






Suggested answer





A Claude subscription and the Claude API are separate products. Pro covers the Claude apps and Claude Code (within usage limits), but it does not include API usage. To call the API from a program, the classmate needs a Claude Console account (platform.claude.com), an API key, and API credit; the app is then billed per token.





Question 15 · Scenario
A small-business owner wants three things:

A weekly summary of the sales spreadsheets she keeps on her computer.
An assistant her six employees can tag in their shared Slack channels.
A chatbot on her company website that answers customer questions.

Recommend a Claude product for each, and explain why.






Suggested answer






The Claude apps, for example Claude Desktop, which can work with files on her computer and can repeat the task on a schedule (the app must be open when a task uses local files), or Claude for Excel if the work happens inside one workbook. These need a paid plan.
Claude Tag: it acts as a shared @Claude teammate in Slack channels. It requires a Team or Enterprise plan.
The Claude API (Claude Developer Platform): a website chatbot is her own software calling Claude, so it needs an API key from the Console and is billed per token. A subscription cannot be embedded in a website.

A good answer matches each need to a product and notes the plan or billing model it requires.





Question 16 · Compare
How is the Claude in Chrome extension related to Claude Code’s Chrome integration? Why should you be careful when letting Claude control your browser?






Suggested answer





They use the same extension. You can use Claude in Chrome on its own (in the side panel), or let Claude Code drive your browser through it, for example to test a web app you are building.
Be careful because Claude acts in your real browser with your logins, so it can do anything you could do on those sites. Also, web pages can contain prompt injection: hidden text that tries to give Claude instructions. Keep an eye on what it does, especially on sites with money, email, or private data.





Question 17 · Short answer
A friend says, “Claude Code is just a website.” Correct this. Name at least four places where you can use Claude Code, and say which one this course uses.






Suggested answer





Claude Code is an agent that runs in many places: the terminal (the claude command), code editors (VS Code and JetBrains extensions), the Desktop app’s Code tab, the cloud (sessions at claude.ai/code), and the mobile app’s Code tab (including Remote Control of a session on your computer). There is a web version, but it is only one surface. This course uses the terminal version.





Question 18 · Long answer
Two students argue about “Projects”. One says a project is a folder of chats and files with instructions; the other says a project is a conversation where Claude runs many coding sessions in parallel. Explain how both can be right, and why the date badges on Claude pages matter for questions like this.






Suggested answer





Both describe real features. The classic claude.ai project is a workspace with chats, uploaded files, and instructions. The new Projects (public beta, rolling out to some Pro and Max users, starting with Claude Code) is one conversation in which Claude starts and tracks many parallel cloud sessions. Existing classic projects keep working.
Anthropic renames, merges, and redesigns products often (Cowork merging into chat is another example). A description is only correct as of a certain date, so check the “As of” badge, follow the official link, and compare with what you see in your own account.





Question 19 · Hands-on
Sign in to claude.ai (any plan is fine) and find:

Your current plan (in Settings).
Whether your message box shows separate “Chat” and “Cowork” options.
Whether you can see a “Code” entry anywhere in the app.
Where your projects and artifacts are listed.

Compare what you find with the map on this page. Write down anything that has changed since October 6, 2026.






Suggested answer





Answers depend on your account and the date. A good answer:

names the plan (for example Free or Pro);
says whether the account has the older (separate Chat and Cowork) or newer (one conversation) experience (on the Free plan you won’t see Cowork at all, because it is a paid feature);
notes whether Code appears (it requires a paid plan);
explains where Projects and Artifacts appear (in the sidebar or an Artifacts tab);
lists at least one difference from this page, or states that nothing differs, with the date you checked.

39.1 The current models
Which Claude model should you use? What does each plan include? And why do you sometimes see “limit reached”? This page answers those three questions (the products themselves are mapped in The Claude Product Family). Models and prices change often, so treat every number here as a snapshot from October 6, 2026.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Models overview · Choosing the right model
Claude is a family of models. The most capable models are slower and more expensive; the fastest ones are cheaper.

Names: the family name tells you the tier (from fastest to most capable: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, Fable), and the number is the version. Fable 5.1 is Anthropic’s most capable model available to everyone.
Context window: how much text the model can work with at once. 1M (one million) tokens is roughly 555,000 words (see How LLMs Work).
Knowledge cutoff: Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and Sonnet 5.5 have reliable knowledge through June 2026; Haiku 4.5 through February 2025. A model knows about anything newer only if it searches the web or reads it in your files.
Model IDs and aliases: programs name a model by its ID, such as claude-opus-5-5. Claude Code also accepts short aliases such as opus, sonnet, haiku, and fable, which point to the current version (details in Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code).
Claude Code’s default on paid plans is Opus 5.5. Fable is never the default; you choose it yourself, for example with /model fable.

title: 39  39.  Claude Models, Plans, and Usage Limits
text:
39.2 Effort: how hard Claude thinks
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Effort · Change the model, effort, and thinking settings · Model configuration
Effort is a dial for how much work Claude puts into each response. The levels, from least to most, are low, medium, high, xhigh (shown as “Extra high”), and max.

Higher effort means more careful reasoning and more checking of its own work, but it is slower and uses more tokens. That costs more on the API and uses up your plan’s limits faster.
Lower effort gives quicker answers and uses less, which is fine for routine work you will review anyway.
Each model has its own default. In Claude Code, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 start at medium. Haiku 4.5 has no effort setting.
Anthropic’s advice: tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.

In the Claude apps, effort is in the model menu next to the send button. In Claude Code, use /effort (details).

As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: API pricing · Why do I pay separately for the API? · Authentication

The two are separate: a Pro plan does not include API usage, and API credit does not give you a Pro plan. API prices on October 6, 2026, in US dollars per million tokens:



Model

For example, a request that sends Sonnet 5.5 100,000 tokens and gets 10,000 tokens back costs 0.1 × $2 + 0.01 × $10 = $0.30. Notice that output costs five times as much as input for every model in the table. Batch requests (answered later, in bulk) are half price, and input that is sent again and again can be cached at a discount.






Watch out for ANTHROPIC_API_KEY



If the environment variable ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set, Claude Code asks whether to use that key, and once you approve it, Claude Code uses the key instead of your subscription, billed at API rates. To go back to your subscription, remove the variable (for example unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, and delete it from your shell startup file), then check /status to see which sign-in is active. See Environment Variables.

title: 39  39.  Claude Models, Plans, and Usage Limits
text:
39.5 Usage limits in plain English
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How do usage and length limits work? · Manage usage credits · What is a limit reset?
A subscription does not give you a fixed number of messages. Instead you get an allowance of work, measured in tokens:

Two clocks. Every plan has a limit that resets on a rolling 5-hour window. Paid plans also have a weekly limit that resets at a fixed day and time for your account (shown in Settings > Usage on claude.ai).
One shared pool. claude.ai, the desktop and mobile apps, and Claude Code all draw from the same limits.
What uses it up faster: long conversations, big files, bigger models (Fable fastest), higher effort, tools such as Research and web search, multi-step agent tasks, and several sessions running in parallel.
Usage limit vs. length limit. The usage limit is about how much you use Claude over time. The length limit is the context window: how long a single conversation can get. They are different limits.

When you hit a usage limit, you can:

Wait for the reset (the message tells you when).
Upgrade to a bigger plan.
Turn on usage credits (paid plans): pay as you go at API rates, with a monthly spending cap that you choose.
Use a free limit reset if Anthropic has given you one (Settings > Usage, on the web or in Claude Desktop).

text:
39.6 Checking your usage with /usage
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Manage costs effectively · Commands
Inside a Claude Code session, type:
/usage

A Session block shows this session’s token counts and an estimated cost at API prices. It matters if you pay through the API (your real bill is in the Console); on a subscription, that dollar figure is not what you pay.
On a subscription, you also see usage bars for your plan’s limits (the current session and the week), each with its reset time, plus a breakdown of what is using up your limits: which skills, subagents, plugins, and MCP servers, and warnings about habits such as very long conversations. Press d or w to switch between the last day and the last week. The breakdown is approximate and counts only sessions on this computer, not your phone or claude.ai.
/cost and /stats are other names for /usage, and /usage-credits opens the usage-credit settings.

On claude.ai, the same information is in Settings > Usage. Ways to use fewer tokens (such as /clear between tasks) are covered in Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code.






Deeper dive: Things that cost extra even on a subscription





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Fable models on your plan · Fast mode · Code Review pricing
These are billed through usage credits (pay as you go), not your plan’s included usage:

Fable models on Pro and on Team Standard seats. (On Max and Team Premium seats, Fable can use up to half of the weekly limit; beyond that it needs usage credits.)
Fast mode in Claude Code (research preview): Opus up to 2.5× faster at a higher per-token price.
Code Review (research preview), the automatic pull-request reviewer on Team and Enterprise plans.

In interactive sessions, Claude Code asks for your consent before a Fable request bills usage credits.









Deeper dive: Older models and Claude Mythos





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Models overview · Claude Platform release notes

Older models such as Fable 5, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 remain available on the API. Old models are eventually retired: for example, Sonnet 4.5 leaves the API on November 30, 2026. Programs that name a retired model stop working, so developers watch the deprecation announcements.
Claude Mythos 5.1 is offered by invitation only to vetted cybersecurity and biology research groups. Fable 5.1 is the same underlying model with extra safeguards.

text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Matching
Match each model with its description.








Model

Description




1. Claude Fable 5.1

A. The fastest and smallest current model


2. Claude Opus 5.5

B. The most capable model available to everyone, for the hardest and longest tasks


3. Claude Sonnet 5.5

C. Anthropic’s suggested starting point for most work, including long agentic coding


4. Claude Haiku 4.5

D. “The best combination of speed and intelligence”









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → D, 4 → A.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which current model has the smallest context window?

Claude Fable 5.1
Claude Opus 5.5
Claude Sonnet 5.5
Claude Haiku 4.5







Suggested answer





d. Haiku 4.5 has a 200K-token context window. Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and Sonnet 5.5 all have 1M tokens.





Question 3 · True or false
Your chats on claude.ai and your Claude Code sessions draw from separate usage limits.






Suggested answer





False. claude.ai, the desktop and mobile apps, and Claude Code all draw from one shared pool of usage. Heavy chatting leaves less for Claude Code, and the other way around.





Question 4 · Short answer
What does the effort setting control? List the five effort levels from lowest to highest.






Suggested answer





Effort controls how much work Claude puts into each response: how carefully it reasons and checks its work. Higher effort is more thorough but slower and uses more tokens. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh (“Extra high”), and max.





Question 5 · Fill in the blank
Inside a Claude Code session, the command ________ shows your plan’s usage bars and what is using up your limits.






Suggested answer





/usage (/cost and /stats are other names for the same command).





Question 6 · Multiple choice
How does the shorter of the two usage limits reset?

Every hour, on the hour
On a rolling 5-hour window
Every day at midnight in your time zone
Once a month, on your billing date







Suggested answer





b. Every plan has a limit that resets on a rolling 5-hour window. Paid plans also have a weekly limit, which resets at a fixed day and time assigned to your account. Options a, c, and d are not how Claude’s limits work.






Medium

Question 7 · Scenario
Maria has a Pro plan. At 3 p.m., in the middle of a Claude Code session, she sees a message that she has reached her usage limit. List her options.






Suggested answer






Wait until the limit resets (the message says when).
Upgrade to a bigger plan (Max 5x or Max 20x).
Turn on usage credits to keep working, paying as she goes at API rates, ideally with a monthly spending cap.
Use a free limit reset if she has been given one (Settings > Usage on the web or in Claude Desktop).

To stretch her limits afterwards she can use a smaller model or lower effort for routine work, and start fresh conversations between tasks.





Question 8 · Find the bug
Sam has a Pro plan. For a class project he added this line to his ~/.bashrc file:
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
Now he sees API charges on his Console bill whenever he uses Claude Code. Explain what is happening and how he can fix it.






Suggested answer





Because ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set in every new terminal, Claude Code offers to use the key, and once Sam approved it, Claude Code uses the API key instead of his Pro subscription, so he is billed per token. Fix: delete the line from ~/.bashrc, run unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or open a new terminal), start Claude Code again, and check /status to confirm that his claude.ai subscription is the active sign-in. If the class project needs the key, he can set it only in that project’s own environment instead of in ~/.bashrc.





Question 9 · Short answer
What is the difference between a usage limit and a length limit?






Suggested answer





A usage limit controls how much you can use Claude over a period of time (the 5-hour and weekly allowances, shared across all apps and Claude Code). A length limit is the context window: how long one conversation can get before it no longer fits. Hitting a usage limit means waiting, upgrading, or paying for more; hitting a length limit means starting a new conversation (or letting Claude summarize the old one).





Question 10 · Multiple choice
Which of these will use up your plan’s limits fastest?

A short question to Sonnet 5.5 at low effort
A long Claude Code session on Fable 5.1 at max effort, with several sessions running in parallel
Asking Haiku 4.5 to summarize a one-page PDF
One web search on claude.ai







Suggested answer





b. It combines everything that uses limits quickly: a long conversation, the most demanding model, the highest effort, and parallel sessions. Options a, c, and d are short, single tasks.





Question 11 · Scenario
Suggest a model (and, where it applies, an effort level) for each task, and give a reason.

Rename a variable everywhere in one file.
Plan a risky change that touches most of a large, unfamiliar codebase.
A program that sorts 10,000 short customer emails into categories through the API, as cheaply as possible.







Suggested answer






A fast model such as Sonnet 5.5 (or the default model) at low effort: it is a simple, mechanical change that you will review anyway.
Opus 5.5 at high or xhigh effort, or Fable 5.1 if that still falls short: the task needs deep reasoning, and mistakes are expensive.
Haiku 4.5: the fastest and cheapest model, built for simple, high-volume work.

Other reasonable choices are fine if the reasoning matches the task’s difficulty, speed needs, and cost.





Question 12 · Short answer
What is a model alias in Claude Code? Give an example, one advantage, and one reason a developer might use a full model ID instead.






Suggested answer





An alias is a short name that points to the current version of a model family, for example opus (which points to Opus 5.5 on October 6, 2026), sonnet, haiku, or fable. Advantage: you don’t have to remember version numbers, and you get the newest version automatically. A full ID such as claude-opus-5-5 pins one exact version, so behavior doesn’t change when the alias moves to a newer model.





Question 13 · Predict the output
Two students run /usage in Claude Code. One is signed in with a Pro subscription; the other uses a Console API key. Describe what each one sees.






Suggested answer






Pro subscription: usage bars for the plan’s limits (current session and week) with reset times, plus a breakdown of what is using the limits (skills, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, and warnings about habits like very long conversations). Any session dollar estimate on the screen is not what a subscriber pays.
API key: the session’s token counts and an estimated dollar cost at API prices, with no plan usage bars. The real bill is in the Claude Console.







Hard

Question 14 · Compare
Should each of these use a subscription or the API? Explain.

A student who wants to use Claude Code for coursework this semester.
A startup building a customer-support chatbot for its website, used by thousands of customers.







Suggested answer






Subscription (for example Pro). It has a predictable monthly price, covers both the Claude apps and Claude Code, and the usage limits protect the student from a surprise bill.
API. The chatbot is the startup’s own software calling Claude, which requires an API key; a personal subscription can’t be used inside a product. Costs grow with use, so the startup should pick the cheapest model that does the job well, set spending limits, and monitor usage in the Console.






Question 15 · Long answer
Anthropic says that “tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.” Explain what this means and give an example.






Suggested answer





Instead of jumping up to a more capable (slower, more expensive) model, or down to a faster, less capable one, you can often keep the same model and change how hard it thinks. Lower effort makes routine work faster and cheaper; higher effort gives more thorough reasoning on hard steps.
Example: if Opus 5.5 at its default medium effort misses an edge case in a tricky bug fix, first try high or xhigh on Opus 5.5 before switching to Fable 5.1. If simple edits feel slow, try low effort before switching to a faster model.





Question 16 · Scenario
Maria compares two numbers: the usage breakdown in /usage on her laptop, and Settings > Usage on claude.ai. Claude.ai says she has used much more of her weekly limit than her laptop’s breakdown suggests. She also uses Claude a lot on her phone. Explain the difference.






Suggested answer





The breakdown in /usage is approximate and is calculated only from Claude Code sessions on that computer. It doesn’t include her phone, claude.ai, or other devices. Her plan’s limit is one shared pool across all of them, so claude.ai, which shows the whole account, reports more. (The plan usage bars come from her account, so for “how much is left,” trust the bars and Settings > Usage.)





Question 17 · Scenario
A blog post from June 2026 says, “Pro includes Fable at no extra cost.” But when Sam, who has a Pro plan, picks Fable 5.1 in October 2026, Claude Code says it requires usage credits. What is the most likely explanation, and how should Sam handle conflicting information like this in general?






Suggested answer





Plans change. According to Anthropic’s Help Center, a promotion that let Pro users use the earlier Fable 5 model within their limits ended in July 2026, and Fable 5.1 was never included in Pro. On Pro, Fable models now run on usage credits; on Max (and Team Premium seats) they are part of the plan, up to half of the weekly limit.
In general: check the date of what you read, prefer the official pages (claude.com/pricing and support.claude.com), and trust what your own account shows today over an older blog post.





Question 18 · Long answer
A friend on a tight budget wants to use Claude Code all semester. Give advice about choosing a plan and about keeping usage and costs under control.






Suggested answer





A good answer covers most of these points:

The Free plan does not include Claude Code, so a paid plan (usually Pro) or pay-per-use API billing is needed.
First check whether the university offers Claude for Education.
Pro has usage limits, which act like a built-in budget; upgrade to Max only if the limits regularly get in the way.
If turning on usage credits, set a monthly spending cap.
Stretch the limits: use the default or a smaller model and lower effort for routine tasks, /clear between unrelated tasks, and avoid running many sessions at once.
Make sure no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set by accident, so Claude Code uses the subscription.
Check /usage regularly, and check prices on claude.com/pricing, since they change.






Question 19 · Hands-on
Start a Claude Code session in any project folder and run:
/usage
/model
/effort status
Write down: (1) your usage bars and reset times, (2) the biggest contributors in the usage breakdown, if any, (3) your current model, and (4) your current effort level. Then close the /model picker without changing anything (press Esc).






Suggested answer





Answers depend on your account. A good answer reports the session and weekly percentages with their reset times; names any skills, subagents, plugins, or MCP servers in the breakdown (a new user may have none); names the model (on a paid plan the default is Opus 5.5 unless you changed it); and gives the effort level (for Opus 5.5 the default is medium). If you signed in with an API key, you see token counts and an estimated cost instead of usage bars.

text:
40.3 The changelog: what changed, and when
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code changelog · Claude Code repository on GitHub
A changelog is a list of every change made to a piece of software, grouped by version number, newest first. Claude Code’s changelog is in two places:

https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog: the docs version, which adds the release date to each version.
https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md: the original file on GitHub (same entries, no dates).

Version numbers have three parts, such as 2.1.291. New versions come out very often: 2.1.290 was released on October 5, 2026, and 2.1.291 the next day. Here is the 2.1.291 entry from the docs:
2.1.291 · October 6, 2026
 * Fixed a regression in 2.1.290 where cloud sessions could drop answers to permission prompts
 * Fixed a regression in 2.1.288 where the last messages of a session could be lost when quitting
How to read an entry:

Each line starts with a verb. Added means a new feature; Changed means something now works differently (read these carefully); Improved and Fixed are improvements and bug fixes; Removed means a feature is gone. A regression is something that used to work and broke in a newer version.
Some lines begin with a tag, such as [VSCode] or Windows:, meaning they apply only there.

To compare with your own copy, check which version you have:
claude --version
Output:
2.1.291 (Claude Code)
Inside a session, /release-notes opens the changelog in a version picker. Search the changelog for a feature’s name when a tutorial or an AI answer doesn’t match your screen: you may be on a different version, or the feature may have been renamed. For example, the changelog for version 2.1.144 (May 19, 2026) says that /extra-usage was renamed /usage-credits.

40.6 Give the docs to an AI: .md pages and llms.txt
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code Docs · Claude Platform docs

Add .md to the end of a docs page’s address to get the page as plain Markdown text, for example https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog.md. This works on all four sites. Plain text is easy to save, search, or hand to an AI (“read this page first, then answer”). Many pages also have a Copy page button.
llms.txt is an index of every page on a site, one line each, made for AI tools: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt and https://platform.claude.com/llms.txt.

Because the .md version is plain text, you can search it from the terminal with the tools from Wildcards, Pipes, and Searching:
curl -sL https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog.md | grep -n "usage-credits" | head -5
This downloads the changelog and shows the first five lines that mention usage-credits, each with its line number.

section: 40.7 When the docs aren’t enough: a recipe
text:
40.7 When the docs aren’t enough: a recipe
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Troubleshooting · Claude Code issues on GitHub
The docs are good but not always complete, and answers from AI models about Claude Code are often outdated: a model learns from data collected months before you use it, while Claude Code changes every week. When you can’t find an answer, or don’t trust the one you found, work through these steps:

Note your setup: claude --version, your operating system, and how you signed in (/status shows your version and account).
Search the official docs: use the search box or Ask Assistant, then check the reference pages (Commands, CLI reference, Settings).
Search the changelog for the feature’s name, to find out when it was added or changed.
Ask Claude Code itself. Treat the answer as a lead, not as proof.
Search GitHub issues at github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues for your exact error message. Issues show known bugs and workarounds, but comments there are not official answers.
Check the community (the official Claude Discord, forums, blog posts) last, and look at the date of everything you read.
Test it yourself in a safe place, such as a practice folder or a new Git branch. What your version actually does wins.
Write down what you found, with the date and version.

An example of why several sources matter: an older tutorial tells you to run claude --remote "fix the bug". claude --help doesn’t list --remote, but it does list --cloud. The cloud sessions docs page explains that --remote is the older, deprecated (being phased out) spelling of --cloud. Yet on October 6, 2026, searching the changelog for --cloud finds nothing: not every change gets a changelog entry.
To report a bug yourself, use /bug inside Claude Code or open a GitHub issue. For account and billing problems, contact Anthropic support through the Help Center instead.






Deeper dive: Connect the docs to Claude Code as an MCP server





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Connect to MCP servers
The Claude Code docs also run an MCP server (a service that gives Claude extra tools; see MCP Servers) with full-text search over the docs. The official MCP quickstart uses it as its first example:
claude mcp add --transport http claude-code-docs https://code.claude.com/docs/mcp
After that, you can ask: “Use the claude-code-docs server to look up what MCP_TIMEOUT does.” The quickstart also shows how to remove it again with claude mcp remove claude-code-docs.
