title: 40  40.  Navigating the Claude Documentation (and Keeping Up)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a changelog? Where can you find Claude Code’s changelog? Give both locations.






Suggested answer





A changelog is a list of all the changes made to a piece of software (new features, changes, and bug fixes), grouped by version, newest first. Claude Code’s changelog is at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog (with release dates) and in the file CHANGELOG.md in the GitHub repository https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code (same entries, without dates).





Question 2 · Matching
Match each question with the site that answers it best.








Question

Site




1. How do I cancel my Pro subscription?

A. code.claude.com/docs


2. What does the /rewind command do?

B. platform.claude.com/docs


3. How much does Sonnet 5.5 cost per million tokens through the API?

C. support.claude.com


4. How does an admin set up Claude Tag in Slack?

D. claude.com/docs









Suggested answer





1 → C (account and billing questions go to the Help Center), 2 → A (Claude Code), 3 → B (API prices and models), 4 → D (Claude Tag is documented on claude.com/docs).





Question 3 · Write the command
Write the command that shows which version of Claude Code is installed on your computer.






Suggested answer





claude --version
It prints something like 2.1.291 (Claude Code). Inside a session, /status also shows the version.





Question 4 · True or false
The CHANGELOG.md file on GitHub shows the release date of every version.






Suggested answer





False. The GitHub file lists versions and their changes but no dates. The changelog page in the docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) is generated from that file and adds the release dates.





Question 5 · Multiple choice
A tutorial mentions a / command you have never seen. Which docs page lists every command you can type inside a Claude Code session?

CLI reference
Commands
Glossary
What’s new







Suggested answer





b. The Commands reference lists every built-in / command and bundled skill. The CLI reference (a) covers options for the claude command itself (such as --model), the Glossary (c) defines terms, and What’s new (d) highlights only the most notable features of each week.





Question 6 · Short answer
Claude Code suddenly stops answering, and so does claude.ai. Which website tells you whether Anthropic is having an outage?






Suggested answer





The status page, https://status.claude.com. It shows the current state of claude.ai, the API, Claude Code, and other services. (The older address status.anthropic.com redirects there.)






Medium

Question 7 · Scenario
A tutorial from early 2026 tells Maria to type /extra-usage to buy more usage, but she can’t find that command. Which two official sources should she check, and what will she find?






Suggested answer






The Commands reference page, which lists /usage-credits and notes that it was previously called /extra-usage.
The changelog: searching it for extra-usage shows that version 2.1.144 (May 19, 2026) renamed “extra usage” to “usage credits” and /extra-usage to /usage-credits.

The tutorial is simply older than the rename.





Question 8 · Short answer
Here are four real lines from the changelog for version 2.1.290 (October 5, 2026):
- Added `claude attach <name>` and `claude logs <name>`: part of a session name works in place of the id
- Changed the Bash tool to ask for permission before running `pyright`, which is no longer treated as a read-only command
- [VSCode] Fixed the branch switch dialog offering to switch when it could not check for uncommitted changes
- Fixed `/rewind` not listing a prompt sent while Claude was still working

Which line is a new feature?
Which line could change what you see during a normal session, and how?
Which line applies only to one surface, and how can you tell?







Suggested answer






The first line (“Added …”): claude attach and claude logs now accept part of a session name.
The second line (“Changed …”): pyright is no longer treated as a harmless read-only command, so, depending on your permission mode, Claude Code may now ask you before running it, where before it ran without asking.
The third line: the [VSCode] tag means it applies only to the VS Code extension.






Question 9 · Write the command
Write one terminal command that downloads the plain-text (Markdown) version of the Claude Code changelog and shows only the lines that mention teleport, with line numbers.






Suggested answer





curl -sL https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog.md | grep -n "teleport"
Adding .md to the page’s address returns plain Markdown. curl -sL downloads it quietly, following redirects, and grep -n prints matching lines with their line numbers. (Adding | head limits the output to the first few matches.)





Question 10 · Compare
How is the weekly What’s new digest different from the changelog? Why shouldn’t you rely on What’s new alone?






Suggested answer





What’s new is a selective weekly summary of the most notable features, with demos and explanations. The changelog is the complete list of changes in every version, including small fixes. What’s new skips most changes, and it can lag behind: on October 6, 2026, its newest digest covered September 7–11, while the changelog listed a version released that same day.





Question 11 · Multiple choice
A developer’s program uses an older Claude model through the API and wants to know when that model will be retired. Where should she look?

The Claude Code changelog
The Claude Platform release notes and model deprecation pages on platform.claude.com/docs
The Claude apps release notes in the Help Center
The What’s new weekly digest







Suggested answer





b. API changes, new models, and model retirements are announced in the Claude Platform release notes, with details on the platform docs’ model deprecation page. The Claude Code changelog (a) and What’s new (d) cover Claude Code, and the apps release notes (c) cover claude.ai and the apps.





Question 12 · Short answer
What does adding .md to the end of a docs page’s address do, and why is it useful when you work with an AI?






Suggested answer





It returns the page as plain Markdown text instead of a web page with menus and scripts (for example https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview.md). Plain text is easy to save, search with tools like grep, or give to an AI so that it answers from the current official page instead of from its (possibly outdated) training data.





Question 13 · Compare
What is the difference between running claude --version in your terminal and typing /release-notes inside a Claude Code session?






Suggested answer





claude --version prints the version number you have installed (for example 2.1.291 (Claude Code)) and exits. /release-notes works inside a session and opens the changelog in a version picker, so you can read what changed in a particular version, or in all of them.






Hard

Question 14 · Ordering
Put these steps for answering a Claude Code question in the order recommended on this page:

Test it yourself in a practice folder or a new Git branch
Search the official docs and the reference pages
Note your version, operating system, and how you signed in
Search GitHub issues for the exact error message
Search the changelog for the feature’s name
Write down what you found, with the date and version







Suggested answer





c → b → e → d → a → f.
Start by knowing your own setup (c), then go to the most authoritative source (b), find when things changed (e), look for known bugs (d), confirm on your own machine (a), and record the result (f). Asking Claude Code itself and checking the community fit between e and a, as leads to verify.





Question 15 · Scenario
An AI chatbot tells Sam: “To start a cloud session from your terminal, run claude --remote "update the README".” How can Sam check whether this advice is current, and what will he find?






Suggested answer





He can run claude --help, which lists --cloud (to create a cloud session) but not --remote. The cloud sessions page in the docs explains that --remote is the older, deprecated spelling of --cloud. So the advice is out of date; the current command is:
claude --cloud "update the README"
(On October 6, 2026, searching the changelog for --cloud finds nothing, a good example of why you check several sources and test.)





Question 16 · Long answer
Give two reasons why answers from AI models about Claude Code are often out of date, and describe two habits that protect you.






Suggested answer





Reasons:

A model learns from data collected up to its training cutoff, often months before you use it, so it doesn’t know about recent versions.
Claude Code changes very quickly (often a new version every day), so commands, flags, and defaults are renamed or redesigned, and old tutorials that the model learned from describe old behavior.

Habits: give the AI the current official page (for example the .md version), or ask Claude Code itself, which reads the latest docs; check the answer against the reference pages and the changelog; check your version with claude --version; and test in a safe place before relying on it.





Question 17 · Scenario
Maria reads about a feature in the Claude Code docs, but it doesn’t appear in her Claude Code. claude --version prints 2.1.250. Suggest the most likely explanation and what she should do.






Suggested answer





The docs describe the latest version, and hers is older (2.1.291 was current on October 6, 2026). The feature was probably added after 2.1.250. She should search the changelog for the feature’s name to see which version added it, then update Claude Code (see Installing Claude Code). If her version is already new enough, the feature may depend on her plan, sign-in, or surface; the docs page usually states such requirements.





Question 18 · Long answer
Rank these sources from most to least reliable for “How does feature X work in Claude Code today?”, and explain your ranking:

A GitHub issue comment from another user
The official docs page for feature X
A blog post from last year
The changelog entry for the version that added X
An answer from an AI chatbot that has no access to the web







Suggested answer





A reasonable ranking:

The official docs page: written by Anthropic and kept current.
The changelog entry: official and dated, but brief, and later versions may have changed the feature again.
The GitHub issue comment: useful for real-world bugs and workarounds, but not official, and possibly wrong.
The blog post from last year: may have been right then, but Claude Code changes weekly.
The chatbot without web access: answers from training data that may be months old, and can confidently invent details.

Whatever the ranking, the final check is testing it yourself on your own version.





Question 19 · Scenario
Sam wants Claude Code to answer questions about Claude Code using the current official documentation instead of guessing. Describe three ways to do this.






Suggested answer






Just ask Claude Code. The docs say Claude has built-in access to the latest Claude Code documentation; it may use its built-in claude-code-guide subagent for such questions.
Give it the page: paste a docs address ending in .md, or point it to https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt so it can find the right page.
Connect the docs MCP server: claude mcp add --transport http claude-code-docs https://code.claude.com/docs/mcp gives Claude a search tool over the docs.

In every case, Sam should still check important answers against his own version.





Question 20 · Hands-on
Choose one Claude Code feature mentioned in this book (for example /usage, plan mode, or /loop). Find (1) its page in the official docs, (2) the changelog entries that mention it (search the .md version with grep), and (3) any open GitHub issues about it. Write a five-line summary that includes the date and your Claude Code version.






Suggested answer





Answers vary. A good summary:

names the feature and links to its docs page;
quotes or summarizes one or two changelog lines, with their versions or dates;
mentions whether there are open issues (and that issues are not official answers);
states your own version (claude --version) and the date you checked;
notes anything the docs left out that you discovered by testing.

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
text:
41.1 What you need
This page gets Claude Code onto your computer, logs you in, and checks that everything works. It takes about ten minutes. Your first real working session is on the next page.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Advanced setup · Authentication

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
text:
A supported computer. macOS 13.0 or later; Windows 10 version 1809 or later (or Windows Server 2019+); or a common Linux such as Ubuntu 20.04+. At least 4 GB of RAM, a 64-bit processor, an internet connection, and a location in one of Anthropic’s supported countries.
An account that includes Claude Code. A paid Claude subscription (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise) or a Claude Console account (the developer account that is billed per use of the API). The free claude.ai plan does not include Claude Code. Plans and prices are compared in Claude Models, Plans, and Usage Limits.
A terminal. Mac users use the Terminal app. Windows users should have Git for Windows installed (see Getting Bash on Your Computer). It is optional for Claude Code but recommended: it provides Git Bash, which Claude Code uses for its Bash tool (the tool Claude uses to run shell commands). Without it, Claude Code runs commands through PowerShell instead.







Prefer buttons to a terminal?



Claude Code also comes as a desktop app and in other places (see Claude Code Beyond the Terminal). This course uses the terminal version, because that is where you see exactly what Claude does.

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
text:
41.2 Install Claude Code
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Advanced setup · Terminal guide for new users
The recommended way to install is Anthropic’s native installer: a small script that downloads the claude program and keeps it up to date automatically.

MacWindows (Git Bash)Linux



Open Terminal (Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter).
Paste this line and press Enter:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
curl downloads the installer from claude.ai, and the pipe | hands it to bash, which runs it. When it finishes you see Claude Code successfully installed!
If the output also shows Setup notes saying that ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH, run the command shown there (the same fix is under Fixing common problems below). The installer does not change your PATH itself. Then close the Terminal window and open a new one.



The installer runs in PowerShell, not in Git Bash. (The curl ... | bash command on the Mac tab is for Mac, Linux, and WSL only.)

Press Win+X and choose Windows PowerShell or Terminal. The prompt starts with PS, for example PS C:\Users\sam>. Do not pick an entry that ends in “(x86)”.
Paste this line and press Enter (you do not need to run as Administrator):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
irm downloads the installer and iex runs it. When it finishes you see Claude Code successfully installed!
If the output also shows Setup notes saying that the install folder is not in your PATH, add it first (see Fixing common problems below). Then close all terminal windows. From now on, open Git Bash to use Claude Code, like every other command in this book.

If your window is the older Command Prompt (CMD; the prompt has no PS), use this command instead:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd


Use the same command as on a Mac. If you use WSL (Linux inside Windows), run it inside your WSL terminal, and later start claude there too.
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash









Piping a download into a shell



Bash Scripts (and Using AI at the Command Line) warns you never to run curl ... | bash on something you don’t understand, because it runs a script from the internet with your permissions. This case is fine because it is the official installer published in Anthropic’s own documentation. Still, copy it from the official docs (or this page) and check that the address is exactly https://claude.ai/....








Deeper dive: Other ways to install






Homebrew (Mac): brew install --cask claude-code. This “cask” follows the stable release channel (typically about a week behind), and by default it does not update itself: run brew upgrade claude-code now and then.
WinGet (Windows, in PowerShell): winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode. Also no automatic updates by default: run winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode.
npm: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code (needs Node.js 22 or later). Never use sudo with it. The native installer is preferred.
Linux package managers: signed apt, dnf, and apk repositories exist; see the setup docs.
Native Windows vs WSL: Claude Code runs natively on Windows (what this book uses) or inside WSL 2. Only WSL 2 supports Claude Code’s sandbox (see Permissions, Modes, and Safety).

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
text:
41.3 Check that it worked
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Advanced setup
Open a new terminal window (Git Bash on Windows) and run:
claude --version
Output:
2.1.291 (Claude Code)
Your number will be higher, because Claude Code updates often. For a fuller health check, run:
claude doctor
claude doctor prints read-only diagnostics about your installation and settings (problems found and suggested fixes) without starting a session. If either command says claude is not found, jump to Fixing common problems below.

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
section: 41.4 Start Claude Code and log in
text:
41.4 Start Claude Code and log in
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Authentication · Quickstart
Claude Code always works in a folder, so start it inside a project folder, not in your home directory. For now, make an empty practice folder:
mkdir -p ~/Documents/claude-practice
cd ~/Documents/claude-practice
claude
The first launch shows a few setup screens (their exact order and wording can change between versions):

Pick a color theme with the arrow keys and Enter.
Log in. Choose your account type (a Claude subscription or a Console account). A browser window opens; sign in there. If the browser doesn’t open, press c to copy the login address and paste it into your browser. If the browser shows a code instead of sending you back, paste the code into the terminal where it says Paste code here if prompted. When you see Login successful, press Enter.
Trust the folder. Claude Code asks whether you trust the files in this folder. Answer yes for your own folders (more on this on the next page).

You are now at the Claude Code prompt. Type /exit and press Enter to leave for now.
Your login is saved (in the macOS Keychain on a Mac, in a credentials file inside C:\Users\sam\.claude on Windows), so you won’t log in every time. Inside a session, /login switches accounts and /logout signs you out.






Watch out for an old ANTHROPIC_API_KEY



If the environment variable ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set on your computer (see Environment Variables), Claude Code asks once whether to use that key. If you say yes, it uses the key, and your usage is billed to that API account instead of your subscription. Run /status inside Claude Code to see which login is active. To go back to your subscription, run unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and delete the export line from your ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc.

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
text:
41.5 Updating
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Advanced setup

The native installer updates automatically in the background. A new version takes effect the next time you start claude.
To update right now, run claude update.
Homebrew and WinGet installs do not update themselves by default (see the deeper dive above).
By default you are on the latest release channel. You can switch to stable (about a week older, skipping releases with major problems) in /config under Auto-update channel.

Claude Code changes almost every week. When a tutorial (or an AI answer) does not match what you see, check your version and the changelog, as explained in Navigating the Claude Documentation.

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
section: 41.6 Where Claude Code lives on your computer
text:
41.6 Where Claude Code lives on your computer
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Advanced setup · Troubleshoot installation and login








What
Mac and Linux
Windows




The claude program (launcher)
~/.local/bin/claude
C:\Users\sam\.local\bin\claude.exe


The downloaded versions
~/.local/share/claude/
C:\Users\sam\.local\share\claude\


Your settings, session history, and more
~/.claude/
C:\Users\sam\.claude\


Global configuration file
~/.claude.json
C:\Users\sam\.claude.json



All of these are hidden (their names start with a dot; see Files, Folders, and Paths). Projects can also have their own .claude folder; what goes in each folder is covered in The .claude Folders and Settings Files.






Deeper dive: Uninstalling





Remove the program and its downloaded versions:

MacWindows (Git Bash)


rm -f ~/.local/bin/claude
rm -rf ~/.local/share/claude
(Homebrew installs: brew uninstall --cask claude-code.)


In PowerShell:
Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin\claude.exe" -Force
Remove-Item -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.local\share\claude" -Recurse -Force
(WinGet installs: winget uninstall Anthropic.ClaudeCode.)



Your settings and history stay behind in ~/.claude and ~/.claude.json. Deleting those (rm -rf ~/.claude and rm ~/.claude.json) removes all your settings, permission rules, MCP server configurations, and session history, so only do it when you really want a clean slate. The VS Code extension and the desktop app also use ~/.claude.

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
text:
41.7 Fixing common problems
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Troubleshoot installation and login



What you see
What it means and what to do




command not found: claude (Mac), bash: claude: command not found (Git Bash), or 'claude' is not recognized (PowerShell)
The shell can’t find the program: its folder isn’t on your PATH yet (Environment Variables). First open a new terminal window. If that doesn’t help, add the folder to your PATH (below).


'irm' is not recognized
You are in CMD, not PowerShell. Open PowerShell, or use the CMD command.


The token '&&' is not a valid statement separator
You ran the CMD command in PowerShell. Use the PowerShell command (the one starting with irm).


'bash' is not recognized ... or A parameter cannot be found that matches parameter name 'fsSL'
You ran the Mac/Linux command in PowerShell. Use the Windows command.


syntax error near unexpected token '<', or a 403 error
The download returned a web page instead of the installer: your country may not be supported, or a network or proxy is blocking it. Retry later, or try Homebrew/WinGet.


Claude Code does not support 32-bit Windows
You opened “Windows PowerShell (x86)”. Open the entry without “(x86)”.


Anything else
Run claude doctor, then check the troubleshooting page in the docs.



To add the install folder to your PATH:

MacWindows (Git Bash)


echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc


In PowerShell, run these two lines, then close every terminal and open a new Git Bash window:
$currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', 'User')
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', "$currentPath;$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin", 'User')









Deeper dive: Windows, Git Bash, and the PowerShell tool





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Advanced setup · Tools reference
On Windows, Claude Code can run shell commands with two tools: the Bash tool (which uses Git Bash) and the PowerShell tool. With Git for Windows installed and a claude.ai or Console login, both are on by default, and Claude treats PowerShell as its main shell, so you may see Claude run PowerShell commands such as Get-ChildItem instead of ls. If you would rather have Claude stick to Bash (matching this book), you can turn the PowerShell tool off by setting CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL to 0 in your user settings file, ~/.claude/settings.json:
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL": "0"
  }
}
If Claude Code reports that it can’t find Git Bash, set CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH the same way, to the path of bash.exe (by default C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe). Settings files are explained in The .claude Folders and Settings Files.

title: 41  41.  Installing Claude Code
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Which of these accounts can not be used to log in to Claude Code?

A Claude Pro subscription
The free claude.ai plan
A Claude Console (API) account
A Claude Team subscription







Suggested answer





b. The free claude.ai plan does not include Claude Code. Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise subscriptions (a and d) include it, and a Claude Console account (c) works too, billed per use of the API.





Question 2 · Short answer
What command checks that Claude Code is installed, and what does a working installation print?






Suggested answer





claude --version. A working installation prints a version number followed by (Claude Code), for example 2.1.291 (Claude Code).





Question 3 · True or false
Claude Code cannot run on Windows unless Git for Windows is installed.






Suggested answer





False. Git for Windows is optional but recommended. With it, Claude Code uses Git Bash for its Bash tool. Without it, Claude Code runs shell commands through PowerShell instead.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. claude --version

A. Signs you out (typed inside a session)


2. claude doctor

B. Installs a newer version right now


3. claude update

C. Prints read-only diagnostics about your install and settings


4. /login

D. Prints the installed version number


5. /logout

E. Logs in or switches accounts (typed inside a session)









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → C, 3 → B, 4 → E, 5 → A.
Note that claude --version, claude doctor, and claude update are typed at the normal shell prompt, while /login and /logout are typed inside a running Claude Code session.





Question 5 · Short answer
Name the hidden folder and the hidden file in your home directory where Claude Code keeps your settings, session history, and global configuration.






Suggested answer





The folder ~/.claude/ and the file ~/.claude.json. Both are hidden because their names start with a dot, so you need ls -a to see them.






Medium

Question 6 · Write the command
Maria has a Mac. Write the command she types in Terminal to install Claude Code with the native installer.






Suggested answer





curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
curl downloads the installer script and | bash runs it.





Question 7 · Write the command
Sam has Windows. In which program should he run the installer, and what command does he type?






Suggested answer





In PowerShell (not Git Bash, not CMD):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
After it finishes, he closes his terminals and uses Claude Code from a new Git Bash window.





Question 8 · Find the bug
Sam pastes curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash into PowerShell and gets A parameter cannot be found that matches parameter name 'fsSL'. What went wrong, and what should he do?






Suggested answer





He ran the Mac/Linux install command in PowerShell. In PowerShell, curl is a different command that doesn’t understand the -fsSL options. He should run the Windows command in PowerShell instead: irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex.





Question 9 · Scenario
Sam types irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex and sees 'irm' is not recognized as an internal or external command. His prompt looks like C:\Users\sam>. What is going on, and what are his two options?






Suggested answer





His prompt has no PS, so he is in CMD, not PowerShell, and CMD doesn’t know irm. He can either open PowerShell and run the same command there, or stay in CMD and run the CMD installer: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd.





Question 10 · Scenario
Maria installs Claude Code and, in the same Terminal window, types claude. She gets zsh: command not found: claude. What should she try first, and what should she do if that doesn’t work?






Suggested answer





First, close the window and open a new terminal: a window that was already open keeps the PATH it started with. If claude is still not found, the install folder isn’t on her PATH yet (the installer’s Setup notes say so; it doesn’t change the PATH itself), so she adds it:
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
Then check with claude --version.





Question 11 · Short answer
Maria installed Claude Code with Homebrew (brew install --cask claude-code). Will it update itself? If not, what command updates it?






Suggested answer





No. Homebrew installs don’t auto-update. She updates with brew upgrade claude-code. (Only the native installer updates automatically in the background. The claude-code cask also follows the stable channel, which is typically about a week behind the latest release.)





Question 12 · Multiple choice
You started claude for the first time and the browser didn’t open for the login. What can you do?

Nothing; Claude Code only works if a browser opens automatically
Press c to copy the login address and paste it into a browser yourself
Reinstall Claude Code
Run claude --version







Suggested answer





b. Pressing c at the login prompt copies the login URL so you can open it in any browser. Reinstalling (c) or checking the version (d) doesn’t help with login, and (a) is wrong because the copy option exists exactly for this case.






Hard

Question 13 · Scenario
Last semester Maria added export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... to her ~/.zshrc for a class project. Now she has a Claude Pro subscription. On her first launch, Claude Code asks whether to use an API key. What happens if she says yes, how can she check which login is in use, and how does she switch back to her subscription?






Suggested answer





If she approves the key, Claude Code uses that API key instead of her subscription, so usage is billed to the API account (and if that old key’s organization is disabled, requests may even fail). Inside Claude Code, /status shows which authentication method is active. To switch back she runs unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and deletes the export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... line from ~/.zshrc so it doesn’t come back in new terminals, then starts claude again.





Question 14 · Long answer
Explain, using the idea of the PATH variable, why the shell can’t find claude right after a successful install in some cases, and why opening a new terminal window is part of the fix.






Suggested answer





When you type a command name, the shell searches the folders listed in the PATH environment variable, in order, for a program with that name. The installer puts the launcher in ~/.local/bin (Windows: C:\Users\sam\.local\bin). If that folder isn’t in PATH, the shell can’t find claude even though the file exists. The installer doesn’t change your PATH; its Setup notes tell you to add the folder yourself (a line in ~/.zshrc on a Mac, or the user PATH on Windows). A terminal window reads its PATH when it starts, so a window that was already open keeps the old PATH even after that change; a new window reads the updated one.





Question 15 · Compare
Compare installing with the native installer and with Homebrew/WinGet. Which one does the official documentation recommend, and what is the main practical difference for a student?






Suggested answer





The docs recommend the native installer. Its main advantage is automatic background updates: you always have a recent version (it uses the latest channel by default). Homebrew and WinGet installs don’t update themselves, so you must remember to run brew upgrade claude-code or winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode; the Homebrew claude-code cask also follows the slower stable channel. Because Claude Code changes weekly, an outdated version is a common reason why your screen doesn’t match the docs.





Question 16 · Short answer
This book warns you not to run curl ... | bash commands you don’t understand. Why is curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash acceptable, and what should you check before running it?






Suggested answer





Piping a download into bash runs a script from the internet with your permissions, so it is only safe when you trust the source. This command is the official installer, published in Anthropic’s own documentation. You should copy it from the official docs (or a source that quotes them) and check that the address is exactly https://claude.ai/install.sh, not a look-alike site or a copy from a random forum.





Question 17 · Scenario
Sam (Windows, with Git for Windows installed) notices that Claude Code sometimes runs commands like Get-ChildItem instead of ls. Why does this happen, and what setting could he change if he wants Claude to use Bash?






Suggested answer





On Windows, Claude Code has both a Bash tool (using Git Bash) and a PowerShell tool. With a claude.ai or Console login, the PowerShell tool is on by default and Claude treats PowerShell as its main shell, so it may use PowerShell commands such as Get-ChildItem. Setting the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_USE_POWERSHELL_TOOL to 0 (for example in the env section of ~/.claude/settings.json) turns the PowerShell tool off, so Claude uses the Bash tool.





Question 18 · True or false
To remove Claude Code completely, including your settings and session history, it is enough to delete ~/.local/bin/claude.






Suggested answer





False. ~/.local/bin/claude is only the launcher. The downloaded versions live in ~/.local/share/claude/, and your settings and history live in ~/.claude/ and ~/.claude.json (projects may also have their own .claude folder and .mcp.json). Deleting the settings removes all your permission rules, MCP configurations, and session history, so do it only on purpose.






Challenge

Question 19 · Hands-on
Install Claude Code on your own computer. Then (a) run claude --version and write down the version, (b) run claude doctor and note any warnings, (c) start claude in ~/Documents/claude-practice, log in, and run /status to see which account and model you are using. Finally, list the files in your home directory with ls -a and find the .claude folder and .claude.json file.






Suggested answer





A good answer reports the version number (for example 2.1.291 (Claude Code) or newer), any claude doctor warnings and what they suggested, and the account, login method, and model shown by /status. In the ls -a listing you should see .claude (a folder) and .claude.json (a file), which were created when you installed and first started Claude Code. If something failed, describe the error message and which row of the “Fixing common problems” table it matched.

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.1 Before you start
This page walks you through a complete first session: starting Claude Code in a project, asking about the code, making a change, reviewing it, committing it with Git, and coming back later. Along the way you learn the handful of keys you will use every day.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Quickstart
You need Claude Code installed and logged in (Installing Claude Code) and a small project to work on. We use git-tutorial-project from Your First Repository: a tiny website with README.md, css/style.css, and src/index.html. It should be a Git repository with at least one commit, so Git can undo anything that goes wrong (What Is Version Control?).
Download the Git practice project (zip)
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.2 Start a session
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Quickstart · Choose a permission mode
Claude Code works on the folder you start it in, called its working directory. So first cd into the project, then start claude:
cd ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project
claude --permission-mode manual
Why --permission-mode manual? Recent versions of Claude Code start in auto mode, where a separate safety model reviews actions instead of you, so Claude edits most files and runs most commands without asking. For your first session, Manual mode is better: Claude asks before every edit and every command that could change something, so you see each step. (You can also start with plain claude and press Shift+Tab once to switch from auto to Manual.) Modes are explained in Permissions, Modes, and Safety.
What you see:

The trust question (first time in a folder only). Claude Code asks whether you trust this folder, because a project can contain settings that change what Claude Code does. Say yes for your own projects; look around first in a project you downloaded from a stranger. Don’t start Claude Code in your home directory: trust is never saved there, so you get asked every time.
A header showing the Claude Code version, the model (with its effort level), and the working directory.
The prompt box, where you type. Before you type, it may show a grayed-out example prompt.
A status bar under the prompt box that shows the permission mode, for example ⏸ manual mode on or ⏵⏵ auto mode on.

Type ? on an empty prompt to see the keyboard shortcuts. Want a guided tour? The /powerup command offers short interactive lessons.
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.3 Ask about the project
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Common workflows
Start by asking questions in plain English. Claude reads the files it needs; you don’t have to paste anything:
what does this project do?
explain the folder structure, then tell me how the HTML page loads the CSS file
To point Claude at a specific file, type @ and start typing its name; a menu suggests matching paths (Tab or Enter accepts one). The file’s content is added to the conversation:
explain @src/index.html line by line for a beginner
Reading files inside the project doesn’t need your permission, even in Manual mode, so these answers come right away.
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.4 Make a first change
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Configure permissions · Checkpointing
Now ask for a small, specific change:
in @src/index.html, replace "Under construction!" with one sentence introducing me: Maria, a business student learning web development
Claude shows the edit it wants to make as a diff (lines starting with - are removed, lines starting with + are added; see Viewing History and Undoing Changes) and, because you are in Manual mode, asks for permission. The prompt offers to approve this edit once, to allow edits for the rest of the session, or to say no. Choose Yes. If you choose No (or press Esc), you can tell Claude what to do differently.
Then review what changed:

Type /diff to see the changes in your working tree, file by file.
Or run Git yourself in shell mode: a message that starts with ! runs as a command in your shell, and its output is added to the conversation:

! git diff
Don’t like the result? Tell Claude what to change (“make it shorter and more formal”). Or press Esc twice on an empty prompt to open the rewind menu and restore the code to how it was before a message you sent (a checkpoint). Rewind has limits, covered on the safety page; Git is your real safety net.
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.5 Commit with Git
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Quickstart · Common workflows
Claude Code can run Git for you. Ask it in plain English:
what files have I changed?
commit my changes with a short, descriptive message
Claude runs commands such as git status, git diff, git add, and git commit. Read-only commands like git status run without asking; in Manual mode it asks before git add and git commit. Read each command before you approve it. By default, Claude Code adds a Co-Authored-By line naming Claude to its commit messages. Check the result yourself:
! git log --oneline -3
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.6 Essential keys
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Interactive mode



Key
What it does




Enter
Send your message


Shift+Enter
New line without sending (works in most terminals, including Apple’s Terminal and Windows Terminal)


\ then Enter, or Ctrl+J
New line without sending, in any terminal


Esc
Stop Claude mid-response; it keeps the work done so far. On a permission prompt, Esc means “No”


Esc Esc
On an empty prompt: open the rewind menu. With text typed: clear it


Shift+Tab
Cycle through permission modes


Ctrl+C
Interrupt. If nothing is running, clears your input; a second press exits


Ctrl+D twice
Exit Claude Code


Up arrow
Recall earlier prompts


@
Mention a file or folder, with path suggestions


! at the start
Shell mode: run a command yourself, for example ! git status


/ at the start
Open the menu of commands and skills (Essential Slash Commands)


? on an empty prompt
Show the keyboard shortcuts


Ctrl+O
Toggle the detailed transcript, which shows every tool call


Ctrl+V (Mac) or Alt+V (Windows)
Paste an image from the clipboard (in iTerm2 on a Mac: Cmd+V)



You can also type while Claude is working: your message is queued, and Claude reads it as soon as its current step finishes. That is a gentle way to steer; Esc is the emergency brake.






Deeper dive: Showing Claude a screenshot





Screenshots of error messages or web pages are often the fastest way to explain a problem. Copy a screenshot to the clipboard (Mac: Cmd+Ctrl+Shift+4, then drag; Windows: Win+Shift+S) and paste it into the Claude Code prompt with Ctrl+V on a Mac or Alt+V on Windows. It appears as [Image #1] in your message. You can also drag an image file into the terminal window, or just give Claude the image’s path (“look at ~/Desktop/error.png”).
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.7 Ending and coming back
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Manage sessions
A conversation with Claude Code is a session. Claude Code saves every session automatically (as a file under ~/.claude/projects/), tied to the folder you started in.







To…
Do this




Leave Claude Code
Type /exit (or press Ctrl+D twice)


Reopen the most recent session in this folder
claude --continue (short: claude -c)


Pick an older session from a list
claude --resume (short: claude -r)


Switch sessions without leaving Claude Code
/resume


Start a fresh conversation
/clear (the old one can still be resumed)


Give a session a name you can resume by
claude -n portfolio-intro, or /rename portfolio-intro inside



Then claude --resume portfolio-intro brings that session back. A brand-new session starts with a fresh, empty conversation: Claude does not see your earlier conversations unless you resume one. Instructions you want in every session belong in a CLAUDE.md file (CLAUDE.md and Memory).
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
42.8 A sample first session
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Quickstart
Here is a simplified version of the whole session. Lines starting with $ are typed in the shell, lines starting with > are typed in Claude Code, and square brackets describe what happens on screen (the exact wording varies by version).
$ cd ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project
$ claude --permission-mode manual

> what does this project do?

  [Claude lists the folder and reads a few files, then answers:]
  This is a small personal portfolio website. src/index.html is the
  page, css/style.css styles it, and README.md describes the project.

> in @src/index.html, replace "Under construction!" with one sentence
  introducing me: Maria, a business student learning web development

  [Claude shows the edit as a diff and asks permission. You choose Yes.]
  -    <p>Under construction!</p>
  +    <p>Hi, I'm Maria, a business student learning web development.</p>

> /diff
  [A list of changed files opens. You check index.html, then press Esc.]

> commit my changes with a short, descriptive message

  [Claude runs git status and git diff, then asks permission to run
   git add and git commit. You read the commands and choose Yes.]
  Committed: "Replace placeholder text with a personal introduction"

> /exit
crumbs: 42  42. Your First Claude Code Session

title: 42  42.  Your First Claude Code Session
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
Why do you cd into a project folder before typing claude?






Suggested answer





Because Claude Code works on the folder you start it in (its working directory). That folder decides which files Claude can read and edit without extra permission, which CLAUDE.md and project settings load, and where the session is saved.





Question 2 · Matching
Match each key with what it does in Claude Code.



Key

What it does




1. Esc

A. Run a shell command yourself


2. Esc Esc (empty prompt)

B. Cycle permission modes


3. Shift+Tab

C. Mention a file


4. @

D. Stop Claude mid-response


5. ! at the start

E. Open the commands menu


6. / at the start

F. Open the rewind menu









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → F, 3 → B, 4 → C, 5 → A, 6 → E.





Question 3 · True or false
claude --continue shows you a list of all your old sessions to choose from.






Suggested answer





False. claude --continue (or -c) reopens the most recent session in the current folder. claude --resume (or -r), or /resume inside a session, opens the list to pick from.





Question 4 · Short answer
Give two ways to leave Claude Code.






Suggested answer





Type /exit, or press Ctrl+D twice. (Pressing Ctrl+C twice when nothing is running also exits: the first press clears the input, the second exits.)





Question 5 · Multiple choice
The first time you start Claude Code in a folder, it asks whether you trust the folder. Why?

To check that you have a paid plan
Because a project can contain settings that change what Claude Code does, so you should only trust folders whose contents you know
To decide which model to use
Because Claude Code can only read trusted files







Suggested answer





b. A project folder can include Claude Code settings (for example permission rules), and Claude Code holds some of them back until you trust the folder. It has nothing to do with your plan (a) or the model (c), and it is not a list of readable files (d).






Medium

Question 6 · Write the command
Write the two commands Maria types to start Claude Code in ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project so that Claude asks before every edit and command.






Suggested answer





cd ~/Documents/git-tutorial-project
claude --permission-mode manual
(Starting with plain claude and pressing Shift+Tab once, which switches from auto mode to Manual mode, also works.)





Question 7 · Scenario
Halfway through a task you see Claude editing the wrong file. What do you press right away, and what do you do next?






Suggested answer





Press Esc to stop Claude immediately; the running action is canceled and Claude waits for you. Then explain what you actually want (“don’t touch style.css; only change index.html”). If an unwanted edit already happened, press Esc twice on an empty prompt to open the rewind menu and restore the code, or undo it with Git.





Question 8 · Write the prompt
Write a prompt that asks Claude to explain the CSS file to a beginner, making sure Claude looks at exactly that file.






Suggested answer





explain @css/style.css to me as a beginner: what does each rule do?
The @css/style.css mention adds that file’s content to the conversation.





Question 9 · Predict the output
Inside Claude Code you type ! git status. What happens, and does Claude need your permission to run it?






Suggested answer





The ! puts the message in shell mode: git status runs directly in your shell (you typed it, so there is no permission prompt), its output is shown and added to the conversation, and Claude then responds to that output.





Question 10 · Scenario
Sam wants to write a three-line prompt, but every time he presses Shift+Enter in his terminal, the message is sent. What can he do?






Suggested answer





Use a method that works in any terminal: type \ and then press Enter, or press Ctrl+J, to start a new line without sending.





Question 11 · Write the command
Yesterday Maria named a session portfolio-intro. Write (a) the shell command that reopens it, and (b) what she types if she is already inside another Claude Code session.






Suggested answer






claude --resume portfolio-intro (from the project folder).
/resume portfolio-intro (or /resume alone to pick from the list).






Question 12 · True or false
After you type /clear, the previous conversation is deleted for good.






Suggested answer





False. /clear starts a new conversation with an empty context, but the previous one stays saved, and you can return to it with /resume.





Question 13 · Short answer
Name two ways to show Claude Code a screenshot of an error message.






Suggested answer





Any two of: copy the screenshot to the clipboard and paste it with Ctrl+V (Mac) or Alt+V (Windows); drag the image file into the terminal window; or give Claude the image’s path in your message.






Hard

Question 14 · Explain why
Recent versions of Claude Code start in auto mode, where a safety model approves most actions. Why does this page suggest starting your first session in Manual mode anyway?






Suggested answer





In Manual mode Claude asks before every edit and every command that could change something, so you see each step of how an agent works: which files it reads, what edits it proposes (as diffs), and which commands it wants to run. That builds the habit of reading actions before approving them. In auto mode most of this happens without prompts, which is convenient once you know what to expect, but it hides the learning, and the safety model is not a guarantee.





Question 15 · Scenario
Claude edited src/index.html with its edit tool, then ran mv css/style.css css/main.css in the shell. You open the rewind menu and restore the code to before that message. What gets restored, and what doesn’t? How can you undo the rest?






Suggested answer





Rewind restores src/index.html, because checkpoints track edits made with Claude’s file-editing tools. It does not undo the mv, because changes made by shell commands are not tracked. Undo the rest yourself: git status shows that css/style.css was deleted and css/main.css is new, and moving the file back (mv css/main.css css/style.css) fixes it. Git is what lets you see and repair changes like this, which is why you work in a Git repository with committed work.





Question 16 · Scenario
In Manual mode, Claude runs git status and git diff without asking, but asks before git commit. Explain the difference.






Suggested answer





git status and git diff only read information, and Claude Code has a built-in set of read-only commands that run without a prompt. git commit changes the repository (it creates a new commit), so in Manual mode Claude Code asks before running it. That gives you a chance to read the commit command and message first.





Question 17 · Long answer
Describe, step by step, a complete first session that makes one small change to a project and commits it. At which steps are you, the human, responsible for checking Claude’s work?






Suggested answer





A good answer includes:

cd into the project (a Git repository with committed work) and start claude, ideally claude --permission-mode manual the first time.
Answer the trust question for your own folder.
Ask questions to understand the project (what does this project do?, @file mentions).
Ask for one small, specific change.
Check the proposed diff before approving it.
Review the result with /diff or ! git diff; ask for corrections or rewind if needed.
Ask Claude to commit; read the git add/git commit commands and the message before approving.
Verify with ! git log --oneline -3 (and by opening the page in a browser).
/exit; later resume with claude --continue or claude --resume.

You stay responsible for every approval and for checking that the result is correct.





Question 18 · Compare
Compare claude --continue with starting a fresh claude session. What does Claude know in each case?






Suggested answer





claude --continue reopens the most recent session in that folder with its full conversation history, so Claude still “remembers” what you discussed and did. A fresh claude session starts with an empty conversation: Claude only knows what Claude Code loads at startup (such as your CLAUDE.md files) and what it reads from your files again. Use a fresh session for a new, unrelated task and --continue to pick up unfinished work.






Challenge

Question 19 · Hands-on
Do the whole sample session yourself on git-tutorial-project in Manual mode: ask what the project does, change the paragraph in src/index.html, check the change with /diff, have Claude commit it, and verify with ! git log --oneline -3. Then exit, run claude --continue, and ask Claude “what did we change last time?”. Write down every permission prompt you saw and which option you chose.






Suggested answer





A good report lists the prompts in order: typically one edit prompt for src/index.html and one or more command prompts for git add and git commit (read-only commands such as git status and git diff ran without a prompt). It shows the new commit at the top of git log --oneline -3 (a plain git log also shows the Co-Authored-By line in the full message), and notes that after claude --continue Claude could describe the change, because the resumed session kept the conversation history.

title: 43  43.  How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools
text:
43.1 The agentic loop
When you ask Claude Code to fix a bug, it doesn’t just type an answer. It reads files, runs commands, checks the results, and tries again. This page explains the loop behind that behavior, the tools that make it possible, and how the other pieces you’ll hear about (MCP servers, skills, hooks, plugins…) fit together.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How Claude Code works
For every task, Claude works through three phases, over and over, until the task is done. The docs call this the agentic loop:
The phases blend together, and the loop adapts to the request. A question about your code may only need the first phase. “Fix the failing tests” might go like this:
Each step gives Claude new information that decides the next step. You are part of the loop too: you approve actions, you can type a correction while Claude works, and Esc stops it. An agent, in this sense, is a model plus tools plus this loop (see AI-Assisted Development).

title: 43  43.  How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools
text:
your prompt
     │
     ▼
 ┌────────────────┐
 │ gather context │ ◄───────────────┐   read files, search, check git
 └───────┬────────┘                 │
         ▼                          │
 ┌────────────────┐                 │
 │  take action   │                 │   edit files, run commands
 └───────┬────────┘                 │
         ▼                          │
 ┌────────────────┐  not done yet   │
 │ verify results │ ────────────────┘   run tests, read the output
 └───────┬────────┘
         ▼ done
   answer to you          (you can interrupt at any point with Esc)


Run the test suite to see what fails.
Read the error output.
Search for the relevant source files.
Read those files to understand the code.
Edit the files to fix the problem.
Run the tests again to verify the fix (and loop back if they still fail).

title: 43  43.  How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools
text:
43.2 The model and the harness
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How Claude Code works · Glossary
Two different things are working together:

The model (Claude: Opus, Sonnet, and so on) does the reasoning. When the docs say “Claude decides”, they mean the model.
The harness is Claude Code itself: the program around the model. It supplies the tools, decides what the model gets to see (its context), enforces your permission settings, runs the loop, and saves your sessions.

An analogy: the model is a brilliant consultant on a phone call; the harness is the office around them, with the keys to your filing cabinet, a person who carries out their requests, and rules about what needs your signature.
The model never touches your computer directly. It asks for an action; Claude Code checks your permissions, carries it out, and sends the result back:
 Claude (model)               Claude Code (harness)            your computer
 "Read src/index.html"  ───►  check permissions, run Read  ───►  the file
        ▲                                                           │
        └──────────── the file's contents come back as text ◄───────┘
crumbs: 43  43. How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools

title: 43  43.  How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools
text:
43.3 Tools: how Claude acts
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Tools reference
A tool is an action Claude can ask Claude Code to perform: read a file, edit code, run a shell command, search the web, start a helper agent. Without tools, a language model can only reply with text (see How Large Language Models Work). With tools, it can act. The main built-in tools, with their exact names:








Tool
What it does
Asks you first (Manual mode)?




Read
Reads a file (also images, PDFs, and notebooks)
No, inside the working directory


Edit
Changes part of a file by replacing exact text
Yes


Write
Creates a file, or overwrites a whole file
Yes


Bash
Runs a shell command
Yes, except a built-in set of read-only commands such as ls, cat, pwd, and git status


PowerShell
Runs a PowerShell command (mainly on Windows)
Yes


Glob, Grep
Find files by name pattern; search inside files
No, inside the working directory


WebFetch
Fetches a web page and extracts what Claude asked for
Yes, except some documentation sites


WebSearch
Searches the web
Yes


Agent
Starts a subagent (a helper with its own conversation)
No; the subagent’s own actions are checked


Skill
Runs a skill
Yes


AskUserQuestion
Asks you a multiple-choice question
No


ExitPlanMode
Presents a plan for your approval
Yes



The last column describes Manual mode. In auto mode, a safety classifier decides most of these instead of you (see Permissions, Modes, and Safety). The full list in the docs has more than forty tools, many for special situations; to see what your session has, ask Claude “What tools do you have access to?”
In the conversation, a tool call shows the tool and its target, for example Read(src/index.html) or Bash(git status) (some labels differ slightly from the official names). Press Ctrl+O to see every call in detail.






Deeper dive: Why you may not see Grep or Glob





On macOS, Linux, and WSL, Claude Code leaves the Glob and Grep tools out of the default set. Claude searches with find and grep through the Bash tool instead (Claude Code supplies its own built-in versions of both), so in your transcript you see Bash(grep ...) rather than Grep(...). On Windows, Glob and Grep are part of the default set. Similarly, the to-do checklist tools (TaskCreate, TaskList, …) are included by default only with older models and Haiku 4.5, not with the current Opus, Sonnet, and Fable models. Details like these change between versions, which is why the tools reference page is worth bookmarking.









Deeper dive: WebFetch reads a summary, not the page





WebFetch takes a URL and a question. It downloads the page and converts it to Markdown; then, for most pages, a separate model call answers the question about the page, and Claude receives that answer rather than the raw page. The docs list this as one of the safeguards against hidden instructions on web pages (prompt injection), but it makes WebFetch “lossy”: if the answer says the page doesn’t mention something, the question may simply not have asked about it. WebFetch also refuses localhost; Claude uses curl through Bash to reach a local web server.

title: 43  43.  How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools
section: 43.4 One mental model for all the pieces
text:
43.4 One mental model for all the pieces
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Extend Claude Code · Glossary · Plugins overview · Mods overview
People often mix up tools with the other things you can add to Claude Code. They are different kinds of things:
Claude Code (the harness)
├── the model (Claude) ...... reasons and decides which tool to call next
├── built-in tools .......... Read, Edit, Write, Bash, WebFetch, Agent, Skill, ...
├── MCP servers ............. connect outside services and add MORE tools
├── skills .................. instructions for a kind of task (loaded via the Skill tool)
├── subagents ............... helper agents with their own context (started via the Agent tool)
├── hooks ................... your commands that run automatically on events
├── CLAUDE.md ............... instructions loaded into every session
└── plugins ................. installable packages of skills, subagents, hooks, MCP servers, ...
    └── mods ................ plugins whose code runs inside Claude Code and customizes it



Piece
What it is
Example
Details




Tool
An action Claude can call
Read, Bash
this page


MCP server
A program that gives Claude extra tools (and data) from another service
a GitHub server with a “create issue” tool
MCP Servers


Skill
A SKILL.md file of instructions or knowledge; Claude loads it when relevant, or you run it as /name. It is not a new tool
a “write release notes” checklist
Skills


Subagent
A helper agent with its own context window and tools; it returns a summary
the built-in Explore subagent
Subagents


Hook
A handler (usually a shell command) that Claude Code runs at a fixed moment, such as right before or after a tool call; it can even block the call
run a code formatter after every edit
Hooks


Plugin
A package that bundles skills, subagents, hooks, MCP servers, and more, installed as one unit
a team’s code-review setup
Plugins


Mod
A plugin made of JavaScript or TypeScript code that runs inside Claude Code and changes how it looks and behaves
a pane that charts context usage
Mods



The most important difference: Claude chooses when to use a tool or a skill, but a hook always runs when its event happens, whatever Claude thinks. So “never edit .env” written in CLAUDE.md is a request, while a hook or a permission rule that blocks the edit is enforcement. Extending Claude Code: The Big Picture shows when to use which.

title: 43  43.  How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools
section: 43.5 Why it acts differently from a chat window
text:
43.5 Why it acts differently from a chat window
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How Claude Code works · Glossary
The same Claude models power ordinary claude.ai chats and Claude Code, yet Claude Code behaves very differently. The model is the same; the harness around it is not:

Tools. In a regular chat, Claude mostly works with what you type, upload, or connect. In Claude Code it can read your whole project, run your commands, and edit your files itself.
Context. Claude Code automatically tells the model about your environment: the working directory, operating system, shell, whether the folder is a Git repository (with its branch, status, and recent commits), and the instructions in your CLAUDE.md files.
System prompt. Before your conversation, Claude Code sends its own instructions on every request (the system prompt): how to use the tools, how to behave safely, and how to format answers for software work.
The loop. Claude Code keeps acting and checking until the task is done, instead of stopping after one reply.







Deeper dive: What fills Claude’s context at the start of a session





Before you type anything, Claude Code loads: its system prompt; Claude’s own auto memory notes from earlier sessions (the start of a MEMORY.md file); environment information and Git status; the names (not full descriptions) of any MCP tools; one-line descriptions of available skills; and your CLAUDE.md files. Every file Claude reads and every command output then adds more. All of this shares one context window, and when it fills up, Claude Code summarizes older parts. Run /context to see what is using space. Managing this is covered in Context, Models, Effort, and Usage.

title: 43  43.  How Claude Code Works: The Agentic Loop and Tools
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
Name the three phases of the agentic loop.






Suggested answer





Gather context, take action, and verify results. Claude repeats them until the task is done (and you can interrupt at any point).





Question 2 · Multiple choice
In the docs, what is the “agentic harness”?

The Claude model that does the reasoning
Claude Code itself: the layer around the model that provides tools, manages context, enforces permissions, and runs the loop
A safety belt that stops Claude from deleting files
The terminal window







Suggested answer





b. Claude is the model inside; Claude Code is the harness around it. The model (a) does the reasoning but has no access to your computer by itself. Permission checks are one job of the harness, not the whole thing (c), and the terminal (d) is just where you see it.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each built-in tool with what it does.



Tool

What it does




1. Read

A. Runs a shell command


2. Edit

B. Creates a file or overwrites a whole file


3. Write

C. Starts a subagent


4. Bash

D. Reads a file


5. WebFetch

E. Replaces exact text inside a file


6. Agent

F. Fetches a web page and extracts information









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → E, 3 → B, 4 → A, 5 → F, 6 → C.





Question 4 · True or false
Without tools, a language model can only respond with text.






Suggested answer





True. Tools are what make Claude Code an agent: they let Claude read files, run commands, edit code, and search the web. Each tool result then informs the next step.





Question 5 · Multiple choice
Which piece adds new tools that connect Claude to an outside service such as GitHub or a database?

A skill
A hook
An MCP server
CLAUDE.md







Suggested answer





c. An MCP server is a program that gives Claude extra tools (and data). A skill (a) gives instructions or knowledge, a hook (b) runs your command on an event, and CLAUDE.md (d) holds instructions loaded every session; none of these adds tools.






Medium

Question 6 · Ordering
Put these steps for “fix the failing tests” in a sensible order: (A) edit the source files, (B) run the tests again, (C) run the test suite, (D) read the relevant source files, (E) read the error output.






Suggested answer





C → E → D → A → B. Run the tests to see what fails, read the errors, read the code involved, edit it, and run the tests again to verify. If they still fail, the loop continues.





Question 7 · Matching
Match each piece with its description.








Piece

Description




1. Tool

A. Runs automatically at a lifecycle event, such as before a tool call


2. Skill

B. A package that bundles several of the other pieces


3. Hook

C. An action Claude can call


4. Subagent

D. Instructions or knowledge for a type of task, in a SKILL.md file


5. Plugin

E. A plugin whose code runs inside Claude Code and changes how it looks and behaves


6. Mod

F. A helper agent with its own context window that returns a summary









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → F, 5 → B, 6 → E.





Question 8 · Scenario
Your team wants a code formatter to run after every file edit, with no exceptions, even if Claude forgets. Which piece fits best, and why?






Suggested answer





A hook (one that runs after each edit tool call). Hooks are deterministic: Claude Code runs them every time the event happens. An instruction in CLAUDE.md or a skill only asks Claude to do it, and Claude might not.





Question 9 · Scenario
You keep pasting the same five-step checklist for writing release notes into the chat. Which piece fits best?






Suggested answer





A skill: a SKILL.md file holding the checklist. Claude can load it when it is relevant, or you can run it yourself as /release-notes (or whatever you name it). Its full text only loads when it is used, unlike CLAUDE.md, which is loaded into every session.





Question 10 · Predict
Maria, on a Mac, asks Claude to find every file that mentions “portfolio”. In the transcript she sees Bash(grep -rn "portfolio" .) instead of a Grep tool call. Why?






Suggested answer





On macOS, Linux, and WSL, Claude Code leaves the Grep and Glob tools out of the default tool set. Claude searches with grep and find through the Bash tool instead (Claude Code provides its own built-in versions of both). On Windows, the Grep and Glob tools are part of the default set.





Question 11 · Short answer
In Manual mode, which of these run without asking you: Read on a file in the project, Edit on a file in the project, Bash running ls, Bash running npm install?






Suggested answer





Read inside the project and Bash running ls run without asking (ls is in the built-in set of read-only commands). Edit and Bash running npm install ask first, because they change things.





Question 12 · Compare
What is the difference between the Edit and Write tools?






Suggested answer





Edit makes a targeted change: it replaces one exact piece of text in an existing file with new text. Write creates a new file or overwrites an entire file with the full content provided. For small changes to existing files, Claude uses Edit.






Hard

Question 13 · Long answer
The same Claude model powers a claude.ai chat and Claude Code. Explain why it behaves so differently in Claude Code.






Suggested answer





The model is the same, but the harness is different:

Tools: Claude Code lets the model read your project, run commands, and edit files itself; in a chat it mostly works with what you type, upload, or connect.
Context: Claude Code automatically adds information about your environment (working directory, OS, Git branch and status) and your CLAUDE.md instructions.
System prompt: Claude Code sends its own instructions about using tools, safety, and formatting for software work on every request.
Loop: Claude Code keeps gathering context, acting, and verifying until the task is done, instead of producing one reply.






Question 14 · Evaluate
A classmate says: “A skill is just another tool, like Read or Bash.” Is that right? Explain.






Suggested answer





Not quite. A tool is an action Claude can call. A skill is instructions or knowledge (a SKILL.md file) for a type of task. Skills don’t add new tool entries: Claude loads a skill through the existing built-in Skill tool, and the skill’s instructions then tell Claude how to use its ordinary tools for that task. (By contrast, an MCP server really does add new tools.)





Question 15 · Explain why
Why is the “verify results” phase so important, and how can you help Claude do it well?






Suggested answer





Without verification, the only thing deciding that the work is finished is Claude’s own belief, and code that looks plausible can still be wrong. Verifying (running tests, building the project, running the app, comparing a screenshot) gives Claude real evidence and lets it loop back and fix mistakes. You help by giving Claude a check it can run: tell it the test command, how to start the app, or what the correct output should look like.





Question 16 · Find the bug
A student wrote this in their notes. Find and fix the mistake: “Hook: Claude decides when it is useful and runs it, just like a skill.”






Suggested answer





Hooks are not chosen by Claude. A hook is deterministic: Claude Code runs it every time its lifecycle event happens (for example right before or after a tool call), whatever Claude thinks. Skills are the ones Claude decides to use (or you invoke with /name). Corrected note: “Hook: a handler that Claude Code runs automatically on a specific event; it can even block an action.”





Question 17 · Scenario
Claude uses WebFetch on a documentation page and reports that the page “does not mention Windows”. You are fairly sure it does. What might have happened, and what can you ask Claude to do?






Suggested answer





WebFetch does not give Claude the raw page: a separate model call answers the specific question Claude asked about the page, and Claude only receives that answer. If the question didn’t ask about Windows, the answer may leave it out, so the result is lossy. Ask Claude to fetch the page again with a more specific question (for example “list every mention of Windows”), or to download the raw page with curl.





Question 18 · Compare
When would you want a subagent rather than doing the work in your main conversation?






Suggested answer





When a side task would flood your main conversation with material you won’t need again, for example exploring dozens of files to answer one question. A subagent works in its own context window and returns only a summary, so your main context stays clean. It is also useful for running independent tasks in parallel or for a specialized helper with limited tools.






Challenge

Question 19 · Hands-on
In a practice project, ask Claude “What tools do you have access to?”. Then give it a small task (for example “find where the page title is set and change it to My Portfolio”) and press Ctrl+O to open the detailed transcript. List each tool call it made and label each one as gather context, take action, or verify.






Suggested answer





A typical answer: Claude’s tool list included Read, Edit, Write, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, Agent, Skill, and others (the exact list depends on your platform and version). For the task, the transcript might show Bash(ls ...) or a search (gather context), Read(src/index.html) (gather context), an edit to src/index.html (take action), and a final Read or git diff to check the result (verify). A good answer notes which calls asked for permission and which ran without asking.
