title: 47  47.  The .claude Folders and Settings Files
section: 47.5 Settings files and which one wins
text:
47.5 Settings files and which one wins
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Settings files and precedence
Settings are JSON keys that change how Claude Code behaves: which model it starts with, what it may do without asking, which environment variables to set, and much more. A key can be set in several places. When the same key is set in more than one, the higher level in this list wins:
Highest priority
 1. Managed settings   set by an organization's IT department; can't be overridden
 2. Command line       flags such as --model or --settings   (this session only)
 3. Project local      .claude/settings.local.json            (you, this project)
 4. Shared project     .claude/settings.json                  (everyone in the project)
 5. User               ~/.claude/settings.json                (you, every project)
Lowest priority

Lists combine. List settings such as permissions.allow are merged from all the files, so each file can add rules. Single values such as model come from the highest level that sets them.
Deny always wins. A permission rule that denies something blocks it even if a file at any other level allows it.
Start Claude Code in the project’s top folder. Claude Code reads .claude/settings.json from the folder you start it in, not from parent folders (unlike CLAUDE.md files, which also load from parent folders).

Notice the difference from CLAUDE.md: all CLAUDE.md files are loaded and read together, while settings files override each other key by key.
crumbs: 47  47. The .claude Folders and Settings Files

title: 47  47.  The .claude Folders and Settings Files
text:
47.6 An example settings.json
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Settings files and precedence · Configure permissions · All settings
Maria and Sam commit this small .claude/settings.json to their project:
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "model": "sonnet",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)"
    ],
    "ask": [
      "Bash(git push *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)"
    ]
  },
  "env": {
    "BASH_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS": "300000"
  }
}







Key
What it does




$schema
Optional. Lets editors such as VS Code autocomplete and check the file.


model
Sessions in this project start on the sonnet model (anyone can still switch with /model).


permissions.allow
Run any npm run ... script and any git diff command without asking. A * matches any text.


permissions.ask
Always ask before a git push.


permissions.deny
Stop Claude from reading .env and .env.something (files that hold secrets) with its file tools or commands like cat .env.


env
Environment variables for the session and the commands it runs: here, give slow commands 5 minutes (300,000 ms) instead of the default 2.



Rules are written as Tool or Tool(details). Unlike CLAUDE.md, these are enforced by Claude Code itself. When you answer “Yes, and don’t ask again” to a prompt for a command, Claude Code saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json for you. The full rule syntax and permission modes are on Permissions, Modes, and Safety; the official example settings files page has bigger examples.






Settings files are strict JSON



No comments (//) and no comma after the last item of a list or object. A mistake makes Claude Code show a Settings Error the next time it starts. And never put API keys or passwords in a settings file you commit.
crumbs: 47  47. The .claude Folders and Settings Files

title: 47  47.  The .claude Folders and Settings Files
text:
47.7 Checking and changing settings: /config and /status
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Settings files and precedence · Debug your configuration







Command
What it does




/config
Opens the Settings screen. Its Config tab has common personal options (theme, editor mode, verbose output, …) and saves your changes for you, mostly to ~/.claude/settings.json. You can also set one option directly: /config theme=dark.


/status
The Status tab: version, model, account, and a Setting sources line listing which settings files loaded.


/permissions
Lists every allow, ask, and deny rule and the file it came from; add or remove rules.


/context
Shows what fills the context window, including which CLAUDE.md files loaded.


claude doctor
Typed in the terminal (not in a session): checks your installation and finds invalid settings files.



Claude Code notices when you save a settings file and applies most changes, such as permissions, right away. A few keys are read only when a session starts; the ones you will meet are model and effort. To change those mid-session, use /model and /effort (Context, Models, Effort, and Usage).






Deeper dive: common mix-ups













Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




Your global permission rules are ignored
They are in ~/.claude.json
Move them to ~/.claude/settings.json


A value in .claude/settings.json seems ignored
The same key is set in .claude/settings.local.json, which wins
Check /status and your local file


Allow rules a teammate committed don’t work for you
Allow rules in .claude/settings.json apply only after you accept the “trust this folder” prompt (deny and ask rules apply right away)
Trust the folder when Claude Code asks


MCP servers in .mcp.json never load
The file is inside .claude/
Move it to the project root


A skill doesn’t show up
It is saved as .claude/skills/name.md
Use a folder: .claude/skills/name/SKILL.md



To check whether your configuration causes a problem, run claude --safe-mode. It starts a session with your customizations (CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, and more) turned off.
crumbs: 47  47. The .claude Folders and Settings Files

title: 47  47.  The .claude Folders and Settings Files
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Where do your personal settings for every project go?

.claude/settings.json
~/.claude/settings.json
~/.claude.json
.claude/settings.local.json







Suggested answer





b. ~/.claude/settings.json is the user settings file. .claude/settings.json (a) is the team’s file for one project, ~/.claude.json (c) holds app state that Claude Code manages (settings like permissions there are ignored), and .claude/settings.local.json (d) is personal but only for one project.





Question 2 · Write the command
You run ls in your home directory and don’t see the .claude folder. Why? Write a command that lists the contents of ~/.claude, including hidden items.






Suggested answer





Names that start with a dot are hidden, and plain ls doesn’t show them.
ls -a ~/.claude
(ls -a ~ would show .claude itself among your home folder’s hidden items.)





Question 3 · True or false
You should commit .claude/settings.local.json so your teammates get the same setup.






Suggested answer





False. .claude/settings.local.json holds your personal overrides for one project and should stay out of Git. Shared team settings go in .claude/settings.json, which you do commit.





Question 4 · Ordering
Put these settings levels in order from highest priority to lowest: user (~/.claude/settings.json), managed settings, shared project (.claude/settings.json), command line, project local (.claude/settings.local.json).






Suggested answer






Managed settings
Command line
Project local (.claude/settings.local.json)
Shared project (.claude/settings.json)
User (~/.claude/settings.json)

The more specific to you and this session, the higher it ranks, except that an organization’s managed settings beat everything.





Question 5 · Matching
Match each item with what it holds.








Item

Holds




1. .mcp.json (project root)

A. Your conversation transcripts and auto memory


2. ~/.claude.json

B. MCP servers shared by the team


3. .claude/rules/

C. App state such as your login and trusted folders


4. ~/.claude/projects/

D. Topic-specific instruction files


5. .claude/settings.local.json

E. Your personal setting overrides for one project









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → D, 4 → A, 5 → E.





Question 6 · Short answer
What does /status tell you about your settings?






Suggested answer





Its Status tab shows your version, model, and account, plus a Setting sources line that lists which settings files Claude Code loaded for this session (for example user settings and project local settings). It tells you which files loaded, not which file supplied each key.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the path
Write the full path of Sam’s user settings file as Git Bash shows it, and as Windows shows it. (Sam’s Windows user name is sam.)






Suggested answer






Git Bash: /c/Users/sam/.claude/settings.json (or ~/.claude/settings.json)
Windows: C:\Users\sam\.claude\settings.json






Question 8 · Predict
Maria’s settings files contain:

~/.claude/settings.json: "model": "opus"
.claude/settings.json: "model": "sonnet"
.claude/settings.local.json: "model": "haiku"

Which model does a session in this project start on if she types claude? Which if she types claude --model opus?






Suggested answer






claude: haiku. Project local beats shared project, which beats user.
claude --model opus: opus. The command line beats all three files, for that session only.






Question 9 · Find the bug
Sam saved this ~/.claude/settings.json, and Claude Code now shows a Settings Error at startup. Find the two problems and fix them.
{
  // use Sonnet to save money
  "model": "sonnet",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)",
    ]
  }
}






Suggested answer






// use Sonnet to save money is a comment; settings files are strict JSON and don’t allow comments.
There is a trailing comma after "Bash(git diff *)", the last item in the list.

Fixed:
{
  "model": "sonnet",
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run *)",
      "Bash(git diff *)"
    ]
  }
}





Question 10 · Write the JSON
Write a settings file that lets Claude run npm test (with or without extra arguments) without asking, and stops Claude from reading anything inside the project’s secrets/ folder.






Suggested answer





{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm test *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./secrets/**)"
    ]
  }
}
Bash(npm test *) matches npm test and npm test followed by anything (a trailing * also matches the bare command). Read(./secrets/**) matches every file under secrets/.





Question 11 · Scenario
Sam answers a permission prompt for npm run build with “Yes, and don’t ask again”. Where is that choice saved, and will his teammates get it when they pull from GitHub?






Suggested answer





Claude Code saves it as an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json in the project. That file is personal and kept out of Git (Claude Code adds it to Sam’s global Git ignore file), so his teammates won’t get it. To share the rule, he would add it to .claude/settings.json and commit that.





Question 12 · Predict
Maria’s user settings allow Bash(git push *). The project’s .claude/settings.json denies Bash(git push *). What happens when Claude tries to run git push origin main?






Suggested answer





It is blocked. Deny rules are checked before allow rules, and a deny from any level wins over an allow from any other level. Maria’s personal allow can’t override the project’s deny.





Question 13 · Scenario
Maria’s user settings allow Bash(git diff *), and the project’s .claude/settings.json (which she has trusted) allows Bash(npm run *). Which of these commands run without a prompt: git diff, npm run dev, npm install?






Suggested answer





git diff and npm run dev run without asking. List settings such as permissions.allow are merged across files, so both rules apply. npm install matches neither rule, so it goes through the normal permission check for the current mode (in Manual mode, Claude Code asks you).





Question 14 · Classify
For each file, say “commit” or “keep private”: CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, .claude/settings.json, .claude/settings.local.json, .mcp.json, .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md, ~/.claude/settings.json.






Suggested answer






Commit: CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .mcp.json, .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md
Keep private: CLAUDE.local.md, .claude/settings.local.json, ~/.claude/settings.json (it isn’t even in the project folder)







Hard

Question 15 · Scenario
Sam wants a deny rule for every project, so he opens ~/.claude.json and adds a "permissions" section. Claude ignores it. Explain why and what he should do.






Suggested answer





~/.claude.json is Claude Code’s app-state file (login, trusted folders, personal MCP servers, UI toggles). Settings such as permissions, hooks, and env are not read from it. Sam should put the rule in ~/.claude/settings.json, the user settings file inside the ~/.claude/ folder. The two names look alike but are different files in different places.





Question 16 · Scenario
A teammate committed .claude/settings.json with an allow rule for Bash(npm run *) and a deny rule for Read(./.env). Claude Code applies the deny rule as soon as Maria opens the cloned project, but applies the allow rule only after she accepts the “trust this folder” prompt. Why does it treat the two rules differently?






Suggested answer





Allow rules grant capability: they let Claude run commands without asking. A repository you just downloaded could contain anything, so Claude Code won’t let it grant itself extra power until you have looked at it and said you trust it (the trust prompt lists the rules it would turn on). Deny and ask rules only restrict what Claude can do, so applying them immediately can only make you safer.





Question 17 · Scenario
In the middle of a session, Sam changes "model": "sonnet" to "model": "opus" in the project’s .claude/settings.json. Claude keeps using Sonnet. Why, and how can he switch now?






Suggested answer





Claude Code reloads most settings when a file changes, but it reads model only when a session starts. The edit applies to the next session. To switch now he should run /model opus (which also saves Opus as his own default) or use the /model picker and press s for this session only.





Question 18 · Compare
Maria wants Claude to never run git push in her project. Compare writing “Never run git push” in CLAUDE.md with adding a deny rule Bash(git push *) to .claude/settings.json.






Suggested answer






CLAUDE.md is guidance: Claude reads it and usually follows it, but nothing enforces it, and it may be forgotten in a long session.
A deny rule is enforced by Claude Code: matching commands are blocked no matter what Claude decides. (Rules match the command as written, so a push written in an unusual way could slip past; hooks and sandboxing add stronger protection, see Permissions, Modes, and Safety.)

For “must never happen” rules, use the deny rule. CLAUDE.md is for “how we do things here”.





Question 19 · Write the JSON
The team’s .claude/settings.json sets "model": "sonnet", but Maria wants Opus for herself in this project without changing anything for her teammates. Which file should she edit, and what should it contain?






Suggested answer





.claude/settings.local.json in the project (personal, not committed, and higher priority than the shared file):
{
  "model": "opus"
}
Her user file ~/.claude/settings.json would not work: user settings rank below the project’s shared settings.





Question 20 · Long answer
Explain why Claude Code’s transcripts can be a privacy risk, and list three things you can do about it.






Suggested answer





Claude Code saves each conversation as a plain-text transcript under ~/.claude/projects/. Everything that passes through a tool is included: file contents Claude read, command output, pasted text. If Claude reads a .env file or a command prints a password, that secret is now stored, unencrypted, on your disk.
Things you can do:

Add deny rules such as Read(./.env) so Claude doesn’t read secret files in the first place.
Keep secrets out of prompts and pasted text.
Lower cleanupPeriodDays so transcripts are deleted sooner than the default 30 days.
Run claude purge <project-path> to delete what Claude Code saved about a project.







Challenge

Question 21 · Hands-on
Explore your own setup:

Run ls -a ~/.claude and identify three items from this page.
In a practice project, start Claude Code and run /status. Which setting sources are listed?
Create .claude/settings.json with a deny rule for Read(./notes.txt) (create a notes.txt file too), then ask Claude to read notes.txt. What happens?
Run /permissions and find your rule and the file it came from.







Suggested answer





Answers depend on your computer. Typically you will see items such as settings.json, projects/, and plugins/ in ~/.claude. After step 3, Claude Code blocks Claude’s attempts to read notes.txt with its Read tool (or with a command such as cat notes.txt) and reports that a deny rule blocked it, even if you ask directly. In /permissions, the rule appears with .claude/settings.json as its source. (Settings changes apply right away, so you don’t need to restart.)

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
48.1 The context window in practice
Four dials decide how well, how fast, and how expensively Claude Code works for you: the context Claude can see, the model doing the work, the effort it puts into thinking, and the usage it draws from your plan or budget. This page shows how to read and adjust each one.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Explore the context window · Best practices for Claude Code
The context window is Claude’s working memory for one session. It is measured in tokens, small chunks of text (see How Large Language Models Work); on current Claude models, a million tokens is roughly 555,000 words. It holds far more than your chat:
Current models have large windows (1 million tokens for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Fable 5.1; 200,000 for Haiku 4.5), but how full yours is still matters:
Run /context at any time to see a colored grid of what is using space, with suggestions for freeing some.
crumbs: 48  48. Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
Context window (one session)
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| Loaded before you type: Claude Code's instructions,        |
| CLAUDE.md, auto memory, skill descriptions, MCP tool names |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| Your messages and Claude's replies                         |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| Every file Claude reads and every command's output         |
| (often the biggest part, though you see only one line      |
| such as "Read auth.ts")                                    |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
| ... free space ...                                         |
+------------------------------------------------------------+


Quality drops as it fills. With lots of old, unrelated material, Claude may “forget” earlier instructions or make more mistakes.
Every message sends the whole conversation again. A one-line question at the end of an all-day session still counts the entire history against your usage.

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
48.2 Freeing up context: /compact, /clear, and friends
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Explore the context window · Commands
When the window gets close to full, Claude Code compacts automatically: it clears old tool output and then replaces the conversation with a summary. Your project’s CLAUDE.md and auto memory are reloaded from disk afterward, but details you only mentioned in the chat can be lost. That is why lasting rules belong in CLAUDE.md (CLAUDE.md and Memory).
You can also act yourself:








Command
What it does
Use it when




/context
Shows what fills the window
Claude seems confused, or usage is high


/compact
Summarizes the conversation so far to free space
At a natural break in a long task


/compact focus on the login bug
Same, but tells the summary what to keep
You know what matters for the next step


/clear
Starts a new conversation with an empty context (CLAUDE.md still loads)
You switch to an unrelated task


/btw <question>
Answers a side question that never enters the conversation
Quick lookups, e.g. /btw what does git stash do?


/rewind (or Esc twice on an empty prompt)
Goes back to an earlier point; can also summarize from there
A path went wrong



/clear costs nothing and is often the best move: old conversation crowds out what Claude needs next and costs tokens on every message. Run /rename first if you may want to come back to it later with /resume. For research that reads many files, ask Claude to “use a subagent”: the reading happens in a separate context window and only a summary comes back (Subagents).

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
48.3 Choosing a model
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Model configuration · Models overview
You usually pick a model with an alias, a short nickname that points to the currently recommended version of that model:








Alias
Model (Oct 2026)
Good for




opus
Claude Opus 5.5
Complex coding and reasoning; the default on Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise, and API accounts


sonnet
Claude Sonnet 5.5
Everyday coding; fast, and cheaper than Opus


haiku
Claude Haiku 4.5
Simple, quick tasks; the fastest and cheapest


fable
Claude Fable 5.1
The hardest, longest tasks; most capable but slower (on some plans it is billed to extra usage credits)


default
Your account’s default
Undoing your choice



A full model ID such as claude-opus-5-5 pins one exact version instead. For plans and prices, see Claude Models, Plans, and Usage Limits.
How to switch:

/model opens a picker. Enter switches and saves your choice as the default for new sessions; s switches for this session only. Typing /model sonnet switches directly (and saves it).
claude --model sonnet starts one session on that model.
"model": "sonnet" in a settings file sets the starting model (The .claude Folders and Settings Files).
/status shows which model you are using.

Pick your model at the start of a task. Switching mid-conversation works, but the next reply has to re-read the whole conversation without the usual speed-up from the prompt cache (see the deeper dive below), so that one reply is slower and uses more.
crumbs: 48  48. Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
48.4 Effort: how hard Claude thinks
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Model configuration
Current models think (reason step by step) before they answer, and decide for themselves how much. Effort sets how much thinking they lean toward. Higher effort means deeper reasoning, but slower answers and more tokens (thinking tokens are billed like output).







Level
When to use it




low
Quick back-and-forth, renames, first sketches you will review


medium
Everyday work with a clear scope; the default on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5


high
Bug fixing and work where edge cases matter; the default on most other models, including Fable 5.1


xhigh
Deeper reasoning, at higher cost


max
Very hard problems; may overthink, and lasts for the current session only




/effort opens a slider; /effort high sets a level directly; /effort auto clears the level you saved.
In the /model picker, the left and right arrow keys adjust effort.
claude --effort high sets it for one session.
Write ultrathink anywhere in a prompt to ask for deeper reasoning on that one turn only. (Phrases like “think hard” are just ordinary words.)

Haiku 4.5 doesn’t support effort levels. On Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and the Fable models, thinking can’t be turned off; effort is the control.
crumbs: 48  48. Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
48.5 Fast mode
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Speed up responses with fast mode
Fast mode (/fast) runs Claude Opus with a special high-speed setting: up to 2.5 times faster, same quality, but a higher price per token (for Opus 5.5, twice the normal API price). It is not a different model. It is a research preview, and on subscription plans it is paid only from usage credits (extra, pay-as-you-go money), never from your plan’s included usage. If you are on another model, turning fast mode on switches you to Opus.
For most students: leave it off. If you use it, turn it on at the start of a session, because the first fast turn re-processes the whole conversation at the fast price. A ↯ icon next to the prompt shows it is on; run /fast again to turn it off.







Option
Effect




Fast mode
Same quality, shorter wait, higher cost


Lower effort
Less thinking: faster and cheaper, but possibly lower quality on hard tasks

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
48.6 Checking your usage
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Manage costs effectively
There are two ways to pay for Claude Code (details on Claude Models, Plans, and Usage Limits):

Subscription (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise): a fixed monthly price with usage limits that reset over time. When you hit one, Claude Code tells you when it resets.
API key (Claude Console): you pay for every token.

Run /usage (also available as /cost and /stats) to see:

Session: tokens used in this session and an estimated cost. The dollar figure matters for API users; subscribers already have usage included.
Plan usage bars (subscribers): how much of your limits you have used.
A breakdown (subscribers) of what used your limits recently, such as skills, subagents, MCP servers, and /loop tasks. Press d or w to switch between the last 24 hours and the last 7 days.

/insights writes a report about how you work (where things go wrong, features to try), not just how many tokens you used.
crumbs: 48  48. Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
48.7 Using fewer tokens
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Manage costs effectively · Best practices for Claude Code

/clear between unrelated tasks.
Be specific. “Add input validation to the login function in auth.ts” reads far fewer files than “improve this codebase”.
Match the model to the job. Sonnet for routine work; Opus or Fable for hard problems.
Lower the effort for simple tasks.
Keep CLAUDE.md short (under about 200 lines); move rarely needed instructions into skills (Skills).
Turn off MCP servers you aren’t using (/mcp), and prefer command-line tools such as gh when one exists.
Send verbose work to a subagent, such as running a test suite or reading long logs.
Plan complex changes first (plan mode) and press Esc as soon as Claude heads the wrong way: rework is the most expensive kind of token.
Pick your model and effort at the start of a session.







Deeper dive: prompt caching (why some actions cost more)





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: How Claude Code uses prompt caching
Every message you send makes Claude Code send the entire conversation to the model again. Prompt caching lets the server reuse the part it has already processed (the unchanged beginning of the request). Re-reading cached text is faster and billed at a much lower rate. Claude Code handles this for you.
Some actions break the cache, so the next reply re-reads the whole conversation at the full price. The main ones are switching models and turning on fast mode for the first time in a conversation. Changing effort mid-session breaks it on most models too, but not on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, or Fable 5.1 when you use a Claude subscription or an API key. That is why the official advice is to choose your model and effort at the start, and to save /compact for natural breaks between tasks.
The cache also expires while you are away: after an hour on a subscription (five minutes once you are drawing on usage credits), and after five minutes by default with an API key. Your first message after a long break is slower and uses more.
Editing CLAUDE.md doesn’t break the cache, but the edit doesn’t reach the running session either. It loads after /clear, /compact, or a restart.









Deeper dive: more model options





As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Model configuration · Interactive mode

opusplan uses Opus while you are in plan mode and Sonnet once Claude starts implementing: strong planning, cheaper execution.
best picks Fable where it is available to you, otherwise Opus.
Option+P (Mac) or Alt+P (Windows) switches models without clearing what you have typed. (On a Mac, this needs your terminal’s “Use Option as Meta Key” setting turned on.)
/autocompact changes how full the window gets before automatic compaction, for example /autocompact 500k. By default, models with a 1 million token window compact at about 967,000 tokens.
crumbs: 48  48. Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code

title: 48  48.  Context, Models, Effort, and Usage in Claude Code
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is Claude Code’s context window? Name three kinds of things that fill it.






Suggested answer





It is Claude’s working memory for one session, measured in tokens. It holds (any three): Claude Code’s own instructions, your CLAUDE.md files, auto memory, skill descriptions, MCP tool names, your messages, Claude’s replies, the contents of every file Claude reads, and the output of every command it runs.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which command shows a breakdown of what is using your context window?

/usage
/context
/compact
/model







Suggested answer





b. /context shows a colored grid of what fills the window, with suggestions. /usage (a) shows tokens, cost estimates, and plan limits, not the contents of the window. /compact (c) summarizes the conversation, and /model (d) changes the model.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. /clear

A. Summarizes the conversation to free space, keeping its gist


2. /compact

B. Shows session tokens, estimated cost, and plan usage


3. /btw

C. Starts a new conversation with an empty context


4. /usage

D. Asks a side question that doesn’t enter the conversation


5. /effort

E. Sets how much Claude thinks









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → D, 4 → B, 5 → E.





Question 4 · True or false
Fast mode switches you to a smaller, faster model that is a bit less capable.






Suggested answer





False. Fast mode is not a different model: it runs Claude Opus with a high-speed configuration. Quality is the same; responses come up to 2.5 times faster, at a higher price per token.





Question 5 · Multiple choice
Which of these is not an effort level in Claude Code?

low
xhigh
turbo
max







Suggested answer





c. The levels are low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. There is no turbo level (for speed, there is fast mode, which is a separate setting).





Question 6 · Short answer
What is a model alias such as sonnet, and why is it handy?






Suggested answer





An alias is a short nickname for a model, such as opus, sonnet, haiku, or fable. It points to the currently recommended version of that model family and is updated over time, so you don’t have to remember exact version numbers. (A full ID such as claude-opus-5-5 pins one specific version instead.)






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
Write the command that starts a Claude Code session on Sonnet for that session only, without changing your saved default.






Suggested answer





claude --model sonnet
The --model flag applies only to the session it starts. (Inside a session, opening the /model picker and pressing s on the Sonnet row also switches for that session only.)





Question 8 · Scenario
Maria just finished fixing a bug in the login page. Next she wants Claude to write a README section about a completely different feature. What should she run first, and why?






Suggested answer





/clear. The bug-fixing conversation (files read, failed attempts, test output) has nothing to do with the README task. Keeping it would crowd the context window, can distract Claude, and makes every message cost more. /clear starts fresh for free, and CLAUDE.md still loads. If she might return to the bug session, she can /rename it first and later /resume it.





Question 9 · Write the command
Your session is long, and the next step is to finish the database migration. Write a command that frees up context while making sure the summary keeps the details of the migration.






Suggested answer





/compact focus on the database migration: which files changed and what is left to do
Any /compact followed by focus instructions about the migration is correct.





Question 10 · Predict
A long session is automatically compacted. Which of these will Claude still “know” afterward?

Rules in the project’s top-level CLAUDE.md
“Please always use single quotes in JavaScript”, typed in the chat two hours earlier
Auto memory notes







Suggested answer





1 and 3 for sure: the project’s CLAUDE.md and auto memory are reloaded from disk after compaction. Item 2 might survive in the summary, but it can be lost, because it was only given in the conversation. To make it last, add it to CLAUDE.md.





Question 11 · Short answer
What does including the word ultrathink in a prompt do? Does “think hard” do the same?






Suggested answer





ultrathink asks for deeper reasoning on that one turn, without changing your session’s effort setting. “Think hard” is not a special keyword: Claude Code passes it along as ordinary text.





Question 12 · Multiple choice
Sam has a Pro subscription and turns on fast mode. How is his fast-mode work paid for?

From his plan’s included usage, like everything else
Only from usage credits (extra pay-as-you-go money)
It is free during the research preview
Per token, through a separate Claude Console API account







Suggested answer





b. On subscription plans, fast mode is available only through usage credits and is not included in the plan’s usage, even if Sam has plan usage left. It is not part of included usage (a) and not free (c). Console (API) organizations pay for fast mode per token (d), but Sam is signed in with his Pro subscription.





Question 13 · Short answer
Why does switching models in the middle of a long conversation make the next reply slower and more expensive?






Suggested answer





Each message re-sends the whole conversation, and the prompt cache lets the server reuse what it already processed. Each model has its own cache, so after a switch the new model must process the entire conversation from scratch: one slow, full-price turn. That is why it’s best to pick the model at the start of a task.





Question 14 · Scenario
For each task, suggest a model alias and an effort level, and explain briefly:

Renaming a variable in three files.
Tracking down a tricky bug that only happens after a user’s session times out.







Suggested answer






sonnet at low effort (or haiku, which has no effort setting): a small, clear change you will review yourself; deep reasoning would waste time and tokens.
opus at high (or xhigh) effort: a bug fix where edge cases matter benefits from more reasoning and verification.

Other sensible combinations are fine if the reasoning matches the task’s difficulty.






Hard

Question 15 · Scenario
Sam keeps one Claude Code session open all day. He has used it for five different tasks, and Claude has read dozens of files. Now even short questions use a surprising share of his plan, and Claude seems to mix up details from earlier tasks. Explain both problems and give him three fixes.






Suggested answer





Every message sends the whole conversation again, so a huge context makes even a one-line question expensive. A context full of unrelated material also lowers quality: Claude can confuse or forget instructions from earlier tasks (the “kitchen sink” session).
Fixes (any three):

/clear between unrelated tasks (/rename first if he may want to resume).
/compact with focus instructions at natural breaks.
Ask Claude to use subagents for research that reads many files.
Check /context and /usage to see what is using space and usage.
Put lasting rules in CLAUDE.md instead of repeating them in chat.






Question 16 · Compare
Maria wants faster answers while she makes many small edits. Compare three options: turning on fast mode, lowering effort to low, and switching to Haiku.






Suggested answer






Fast mode: same Opus quality, up to 2.5 times faster, but a higher price per token, and on a subscription it is paid only from usage credits.
Lower effort: less thinking, so faster and cheaper; fine for simple edits, but quality can drop on hard tasks. Costs no extra money.
Haiku: the fastest and cheapest model, good for simple tasks, but less capable, with a smaller (200,000-token) context window and no effort setting.

For many small, simple edits on a student budget, lower effort (or Sonnet at low effort) is usually the best first choice; fast mode only if speed is worth extra money.





Question 17 · Scenario
Maria is on a Pro plan. /usage shows “Total cost: $4.20” for her session. Does she owe Anthropic $4.20? Explain.






Suggested answer





No. The session cost is an estimate that Claude Code computes from token counts at API list prices; it matters for API (pay-per-token) users. Her Pro usage is included in the subscription and counts against her plan limits, shown in the usage bars. She would pay extra only for things billed to usage credits (such as fast mode, or usage beyond her limits if she turned usage credits on).





Question 18 · Long answer
Describe a cost-conscious way to build a medium-sized feature with Claude Code, from planning to finishing. Mention at least four techniques from this page.






Suggested answer





A model answer:

Start a fresh session (/clear) and choose the model and effort at the start, for example the opusplan alias (Opus for planning, Sonnet for implementing) or Sonnet at medium.
Use plan mode to explore and agree on a plan before any code is written, so there is less expensive rework.
Write specific prompts that name the files and the expected result.
Ask Claude to use a subagent for wide research or for running long test suites, so the bulky output stays out of the main context.
Press Esc early if Claude goes the wrong way.
At a natural break, /compact with focus instructions; check /context and /usage now and then.
When the feature is done, /clear before starting anything unrelated.

A good answer explains why each step saves tokens (smaller context, fewer re-reads, less rework, no cache-breaking switches mid-task).





Question 19 · Scenario
/context for Sam’s session shows that before he typed anything, a large part of the window was already used: his CLAUDE.md is 900 lines long and six MCP servers he never uses are connected. What should he change, and why does it matter?






Suggested answer






Trim CLAUDE.md to the essentials (aim for under about 200 lines); move occasional instructions into skills or path-scoped rules. All of CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session.
Disable the unused MCP servers with /mcp (and prefer CLI tools such as gh where possible). Their tool names and instructions take space in every session.

It matters because this start-up material is sent with every request: it costs usage on every message, leaves less room for real work, and a crowded context makes Claude follow instructions less reliably.





Question 20 · True or false
If you edit your project’s CLAUDE.md in the middle of a session, Claude uses the new version from your very next message.






Suggested answer





False. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md when the session starts. The edit takes effect after /clear, /compact, or a restart. (The edit also doesn’t break the prompt cache, for the same reason: the running session isn’t using it yet.)






Challenge

Question 21 · Hands-on
In a practice project:

Start Claude Code and run /context before typing anything. Note how much is already used and by what.
Ask Claude to read and explain three files, then run /context again.
Run /compact and check /context a third time.
Run /usage (and press d and w if you are on a subscription).

Write three sentences on what you learned about what fills the context window.






Suggested answer





Your numbers will differ. Typically you will see that some space is used before you type anything (Claude Code’s instructions, tools, CLAUDE.md), that file reads grow the context quickly, and that /compact shrinks the conversation part while the start-up material remains. A good write-up connects this to habits: specific prompts, /clear between tasks, and subagents for heavy reading.

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
text:
49.1 The core workflow
Claude Code can read your files, run commands, and fix its own mistakes, but how much you get out of it depends on how you work with it. This page collects the habits that matter most, based on Anthropic’s official best practices.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Best practices for Claude Code
Planning adds overhead, so skip it for small, clear changes. If you could describe the change in one sentence (fix a typo, rename a variable), just ask for it.
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
text:
1. Explore  -->  2. Plan  -->  3. Implement  -->  4. Verify  -->  5. Commit
plan mode:       Claude        leave plan         tests, build,   clear message;
read and ask     writes a      mode; Claude       run the app;    you review
questions        plan; you     edits files        fix failures    the diff
                 review it

Explore in plan mode: press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows ⏸ plan mode on, or start with claude --permission-mode plan. Claude reads files and answers questions but doesn’t edit your files (Permissions, Modes, and Safety).
Plan: ask “which files need to change? Create a plan.” Press Ctrl+G to open the plan in your text editor and change it before approving.
Implement: approve the plan, and ask Claude to write tests, run them, and fix any failures.
Verify and commit: see the sections below.
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
section: 49.2 Give Claude a way to check its work
text:
49.2 Give Claude a way to check its work
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Best practices for Claude Code
This is the single most useful habit. Claude stops when the work looks done. If it has a check it can run (tests, a build, a linter, a screenshot to compare with a design), it can run the check, read the result, and keep fixing until the check passes. Without one, you are the only check, and every mistake waits for you to notice it.







Instead of…
Try…




“implement a function that validates email addresses”
“write a validateEmail function. Test cases: user@example.com is true, invalid is false, user@.com is false. Run the tests after implementing”


“make the dashboard look better”
“[paste screenshot] implement this design. Take a screenshot of the result, compare it to the original, list the differences, and fix them”


“the build is failing”
“the build fails with this error: [paste error]. Fix it and verify the build succeeds. Fix the root cause; don’t just hide the error”



Ask for evidence, not just “done”: the test output, the command it ran and what it returned, or a screenshot. The bundled /verify command goes one step further: it builds and runs your app to confirm a change really works.
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
text:
49.3 Be specific and give context
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Best practices for Claude Code · Prompt library
Claude can infer a lot, but it can’t read your mind.








Strategy
Vague
Specific




Scope the task
“add tests for foo.py”
“write a test for foo.py covering the case where the user is logged out. Avoid mocks.”


Point to an example
“add a calendar widget”
“look at how the existing widgets on the home page are built, and follow the same pattern for a calendar widget”


Describe the symptom
“fix the login bug”
“users say login fails after their session times out. Check the auth flow in src/auth/. Write a failing test that reproduces it, then fix it”



Give Claude the real material instead of describing it:

Type @ to mention a file: explain the logic in @src/utils/auth.js.
Paste a screenshot (Ctrl+V; Alt+V on Windows) or drag an image in. Screenshots of error pages and designs work well.
Paste the exact error message or log lines.
Pipe data in from the terminal: cat error.log | claude -p "explain this error".

For a bigger feature, let Claude interview you before it builds anything:
I want to build [brief description]. Interview me in detail using the
AskUserQuestion tool. Ask about implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and
tradeoffs. Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a
complete spec to SPEC.md.
Then start a fresh session to build it from SPEC.md, with a clean context focused only on implementation.
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
section: 49.4 Steer early and keep sessions focused
text:
49.4 Steer early and keep sessions focused
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Best practices for Claude Code · Checkpointing

Esc stops Claude mid-action. The work so far is kept, so you can redirect.
Type a correction and press Enter while Claude works; it reads your message after its current step.
Esc twice (on an empty prompt) or /rewind restores the code and/or the conversation to an earlier point. You can also just say “undo that”.
/clear between unrelated tasks (Context, Models, Effort, and Usage).
Corrected it twice and it’s still wrong? The context is now full of failed attempts. Run /clear and write a better first prompt that includes what you learned.
Use subagents for research: “use subagents to investigate how our login handles expired sessions” keeps all that file reading out of your main context (Subagents).
Name and resume sessions: /rename login-fix, then later claude --continue (the most recent session) or claude --resume (pick from a list).
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
text:
49.5 Git habits with Claude
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Checkpointing · Common workflows
Claude Code’s checkpoints let you rewind Claude’s file edits, but they only track changes made with Claude’s file-editing tools, not files changed by shell commands or other programs, and they can’t undo things outside your computer, such as a database change or a deployment. Git is your real safety net (What Is Version Control?):

Commit before a big change, so you have a clean point to return to.
Review the diff before you commit: git diff in the terminal, or /diff inside Claude Code. You can also ask: “review my uncommitted changes and flag anything that looks risky before I commit”.
Let Claude write the commit message: “commit these changes with a message that summarizes what I did”. Then read it.
Make small, frequent commits, so undoing one step is easy.
Get a second opinion: /code-review checks your current changes for bugs in a fresh context (Pull Requests and Code Review).
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
section: 49.6 Understanding a repository without changing it
text:
49.6 Understanding a repository without changing it
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Common workflows · Prompt library
To learn an unfamiliar project safely, start in plan mode:
cd ~/Documents/some-project
claude --permission-mode plan
Then ask the questions a new team member would ask:
give me an overview of this codebase: architecture, key directories, and how the pieces connect
trace what happens when a user logs in, from the front end to the database
which files would I need to touch to add a "remember me" checkbox? Don't edit anything yet.
For stronger guarantees (removing the editing tools entirely, or working on a read-only copy), see Permissions, Modes, and Safety.
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
section: 49.7 Keep Claude working until it’s done: /goal and /loop
text:
49.7 Keep Claude working until it’s done: /goal and /loop
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Keep Claude working toward a goal · Run prompts on a schedule
Normally Claude works until it thinks it is done and then waits for you. Two commands keep it going.
/goal <condition> sets a finish line. Claude starts working right away. After every turn, a separate small, fast model reads the conversation and judges whether the condition is met; if not, Claude starts another turn on its own. The goal ends when the condition is met, when the judge decides it is impossible, or when an error you have to fix stops the work. For example, to keep fixing bugs until the tests pass:
/goal npm test exits 0 with all tests passing; fix the code, not the tests; or stop after 20 turns
A good condition has one measurable end state, says how Claude should prove it, and names what must not change. The judge doesn’t run anything itself: it only reads what Claude showed in the conversation. Type /goal alone to see progress, and /goal clear to stop early.
/loop [interval] [prompt] re-runs a prompt on a schedule while the session stays open:
/loop 30m run the test suite and fix any new failures
Without an interval, Claude picks the wait itself (one minute to one hour). Without a prompt, it runs a built-in maintenance routine: continue unfinished work, tend to the current pull request, then hunt for bugs or simplify code. Press Esc to stop a self-paced loop. To stop a loop with a fixed interval, ask Claude to cancel it; otherwise it expires after seven days.









Next turn starts when…
Stops when…




/goal
The previous turn finishes
The condition is met or judged impossible, an error you must fix occurs, or you run /goal clear


/loop
A time interval passes
You stop it, or Claude decides the work is done



Both run only while your session is open, and every turn counts against your usage. Neither changes your permission mode: in Manual mode, Claude still stops to ask before actions that need approval. For jobs that should run even when your computer is off, see routines on Claude Code Beyond the Terminal.
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
text:
49.8 Common mistakes
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Best practices for Claude Code








Mistake
What happens
Fix




The kitchen-sink session
One session drifts across unrelated tasks; the context fills with noise
/clear between unrelated tasks


Correcting over and over
The context fills with failed attempts
After two failed corrections, /clear and write a better prompt


The over-long CLAUDE.md
Important rules get lost in the noise
Prune it; turn must-happen rules into hooks


Trusting without verifying
Plausible-looking code that misses edge cases
Always give Claude a check (tests, scripts, screenshots); if you can’t verify it, don’t ship it


Endless exploration
“Investigate X” with no limits reads hundreds of files
Scope the question, or use a subagent


Not reading the diff
You commit code you don’t understand
Review every diff; ask Claude to explain anything unclear









Deeper dive: a second Claude as reviewer





A fresh context reviews code better, because it isn’t attached to the code it just wrote. The official guide suggests a Writer/Reviewer pattern: one session implements a feature; a second session (or a subagent) reviews it, for example “review the rate limiter in @src/middleware/rateLimiter.ts for edge cases and race conditions”; then you paste the review back into the first session to fix the issues. Tell the reviewer to report only problems that affect correctness or the requirements: a reviewer asked to find gaps will usually find something, and chasing every comment leads to over-engineering.
crumbs: 49  49. Working Effectively with Claude Code

title: 49  49.  Working Effectively with Claude Code
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Ordering
Put these steps of the recommended workflow in order: Implement, Commit, Explore, Verify, Plan.






Suggested answer





Explore → Plan → Implement → Verify → Commit.
Exploring and planning first avoids solving the wrong problem; verifying before committing catches mistakes while they are cheap to fix.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
What does plan mode do?

Claude edits files immediately, without asking
Claude reads files and proposes a plan, but doesn’t edit your files until you approve
Claude only answers general questions and can’t read your files
Claude schedules the work to run later







Suggested answer





b. In plan mode Claude explores (reads files, answers questions) and writes a plan; edits stay blocked until you approve the plan. It doesn’t edit without asking (a), it can read your files (c), and scheduling is what /loop and routines are for (d).





Question 3 · True or false
Because Claude Code has checkpoints and /rewind, you no longer need Git.






Suggested answer





False. Checkpoints only track edits made with Claude’s file-editing tools. They don’t capture files changed by shell commands or other programs, and they can’t undo outside effects such as a database change or a deployment. Git records your whole project history and is the real safety net.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each action with what it does.








Action

What it does




1. Esc

A. Re-runs a prompt on a time interval


2. Esc twice (empty prompt)

B. Keeps Claude working until a condition is met


3. /clear

C. Stops Claude mid-action so you can redirect


4. /goal

D. Opens the rewind menu


5. /loop

E. Starts a new conversation with an empty context









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → E, 4 → B, 5 → A.





Question 5 · Short answer
Why is “give Claude a way to check its work” called the single most useful habit?






Suggested answer





Claude stops when the work looks done. With a check it can run (tests, a build, a linter, a screenshot comparison), it can see failures itself and keep fixing until the check passes. Without one, you become the only check, and every mistake waits for you to notice it.





Question 6 · Multiple choice
For which task is it most reasonable to skip plan mode?

Adding login with Google to an app you don’t know well
Changing how data flows through five different files
Fixing a typo in a button label
Choosing between two database designs







Suggested answer





c. If you can describe the change in one sentence, just ask for it. Planning pays off when you are unsure of the approach (a, d), when many files change (b), or when you don’t know the code well (a).






Medium

Question 7 · Rewrite
Rewrite these vague prompts to be specific and checkable:

“Fix the signup form.”
“Make the homepage look nicer.”







Suggested answer





Possible rewrites:

“When I submit the signup form with an email that already exists, the page shows a blank screen. The form is in src/app/signup/page.tsx. Write a failing test that reproduces it, fix it so the form shows ‘This email is already registered’, and run the tests.”
“[paste screenshot of the design] Make the homepage match this design. Take a screenshot of the result, compare it to the design, list the differences, and fix them.”

Good rewrites name the place, the symptom or goal, and a way to verify.





Question 8 · Write the command
Write a /goal that keeps Claude fixing code until npm test passes, without letting it change or delete the test files, and that stops after at most 15 turns.






Suggested answer





/goal npm test exits 0 with all tests passing; do not modify or delete any test files; or stop after 15 turns
It has one measurable end state (npm test exits 0), a constraint (test files unchanged), and a limit (15 turns).





Question 9 · Write the command
Write a /loop command that checks every 10 minutes whether the deployment has finished and reports what happened.






Suggested answer





/loop 10m check whether the deployment finished and tell me what happened
Here the interval (10m) comes first, followed by the prompt; a trailing clause such as “every 10 minutes” also works. The loop runs only while the session stays open.





Question 10 · Scenario
Sam has corrected Claude twice about how the app should calculate event capacity, and the result is still wrong. What does the official guide recommend, and why?






Suggested answer





Run /clear and start again with a better first prompt that includes what he has learned (for example the exact capacity rule and a test case). After two failed corrections, the context is cluttered with failed approaches; a clean session with a better prompt almost always does better than a long session full of corrections.





Question 11 · Write the command
Maria wants Claude to explain a classmate’s project without changing anything. Write the commands to open it in plan mode, and give one good first prompt.






Suggested answer





cd ~/Documents/classmate-project
claude --permission-mode plan
A good first prompt: “give me an overview of this codebase: architecture, key directories, and how the pieces connect.” (Any broad overview question works; she can then narrow down to specific parts.)





Question 12 · Find the bug
What is wrong with this goal, and how would you fix it?
/goal make the app better






Suggested answer





“Better” can’t be measured, so the judge can’t tell when the goal is met, and Claude can’t prove it. A good condition has a measurable end state, a stated check, and limits, for example:
/goal npm run lint reports no errors and npm test exits 0; do not change any test files; or stop after 20 turns





Question 13 · Multiple choice
How does the /goal judge decide whether your condition is met?

It runs your tests itself after every turn
It reads the conversation, including what Claude ran and the results it showed
It opens and inspects your files
It asks you after every turn







Suggested answer





b. A separate small, fast model reads the conversation after each turn. It doesn’t run commands (a) or read files (c) on its own, and it doesn’t ask you (d). That’s why the condition should say how Claude should prove it, for example “npm test exits 0”, so the evidence appears in the conversation.





Question 14 · Scenario
Claude just finished a new feature for Maria. List the Git habits she should follow before and after this point.






Suggested answer






Before starting the feature: commit, so there is a clean point to return to.
Now: review the changes with git diff (or /diff), and/or ask Claude to “review my uncommitted changes and flag anything risky”; optionally run /code-review.
Make sure the checks (tests, build) passed.
Ask Claude to commit with a message that summarizes the change, and read the message.
Keep commits small and frequent.







Hard

Question 15 · Scenario
Sam set /goal all tests pass. Claude made changes and wrote “All tests should pass now,” and the goal was marked as met, but npm test actually fails. How could this happen, and how should Sam write the goal instead?






Suggested answer





The judge doesn’t run the tests; it only reads the conversation. If the conversation contains no real test output, the judge has to rely on Claude’s claims. Sam should name the check so the evidence must appear, and ask for evidence, for example:
/goal npm test exits 0 and its output shows every test passing; do not modify the tests; or stop after 20 turns
He should still look at the final test output himself before trusting the result.





Question 16 · Compare
Which tool fits each job best: /goal, /loop, or a hook? Explain briefly.

Keep fixing a failing build until it succeeds.
Every 15 minutes, check whether a classmate has commented on your pull request.
In every session in this project, automatically run the linter whenever Claude finishes, with no exceptions.







Suggested answer






/goal: there is a clear, measurable end state (the build succeeds), and Claude should keep taking turns until it is reached.
/loop: the work repeats on a time interval (/loop 15m ...), while the session stays open.
A hook (for example a Stop hook in the project’s settings): it runs every time, in every session, no matter what Claude decides. /goal and /loop last only for the current session. See Hooks.






Question 17 · Long answer
Explain the Writer/Reviewer pattern and why a fresh context helps code review. What instruction should you give the reviewer, and why?






Suggested answer





One session (the writer) implements the change. A second session or a subagent (the reviewer) reviews it in a fresh context, and its findings go back to the writer to fix. The reviewer sees only the code and the requirements, not the reasoning that produced the code, so it is not biased toward what was just written and judges the result on its own terms.
Tell the reviewer to report only issues that affect correctness or the stated requirements. A reviewer asked to find problems will usually find some even when the work is fine, and fixing every comment leads to over-engineering (extra layers, unnecessary defensive code, tests for impossible cases).





Question 18 · Scenario
Maria plans to start /loop 15m run the test suite and fix any new failures before going to bed and close her laptop. List at least three things she should think about.






Suggested answer






The session must stay open. /loop runs only while Claude Code is running; closing the laptop (or the terminal) stops it.
Usage: every run sends the whole conversation and uses her plan’s usage, even when nothing changed.
Permissions: in Manual mode, Claude stops to ask before actions that need approval, so the loop can sit waiting all night. Unattended runs need pre-approved commands or auto mode, which reduces her oversight.
Review: she should still review every change in the morning (diffs, test output) before committing.
For work that must run while the computer is off, a cloud routine fits better (see Claude Code Beyond the Terminal).






Question 19 · Long answer
Describe how you would add a “forgot password” feature to the club-events site with Claude Code, using at least five habits from this page.






Suggested answer





A model answer:

Commit the current state (a clean point to return to).
Start a fresh session in plan mode; ask Claude to explore how login works now and which files a “forgot password” feature would touch.
Optionally have Claude interview you about edge cases (expired links, unknown emails), then write SPEC.md.
Ask for a plan, review it (Ctrl+G to edit), then approve.
Ask Claude to write tests for the new flow, implement it, and run the tests, or set a /goal such as “npm test exits 0 and the reset-password tests pass; don’t modify existing tests”.
Check the result yourself: run the app, try the flow, and look at the evidence Claude shows.
Review the diff (git diff or /diff), maybe run /code-review, then have Claude commit with a clear message.
/clear before starting the next, unrelated task.






Question 20 · Scenario
Sam types “investigate why the app is slow.” Claude reads more than 200 files and his context fills up before anything is fixed. What went wrong, and how could he ask better?






Suggested answer





This is the “endless exploration” mistake: an unscoped investigation makes Claude read everything, filling the context. Better options:

Scope it: “the events page takes 5 seconds to load. Check how src/app/events/page.tsx fetches data and find the slowest step.”
Give a target and a check: “make the events page load in under 1 second. Measure the load time before and after your change and show me both numbers.”
Use a subagent: “use a subagent to investigate why the events page is slow and report the top three causes”, so the file reading stays out of his main context.







Challenge

Question 21 · Hands-on
Pick a small practice project (for example the Git practice project). Commit its current state, then:

In plan mode, ask Claude to explain the project and propose one small improvement with a way to verify it.
Approve the plan and let Claude implement it, asking for evidence (output or a screenshot) that it works.
Use /rewind to undo Claude’s edits, then redo the change with a more specific prompt.
Review the diff, then have Claude commit with a clear message.

Write a short reflection: which habit made the biggest difference?






Suggested answer





There is no single right answer. A strong reflection describes the workflow you followed (explore, plan, implement, verify, commit), shows that you reviewed the diff and the evidence before committing, and explains how a more specific prompt or a verification step changed the result.

title: 50  50.  Claude Code Beyond the Terminal
text:
50.1 Same engine, many surfaces
This course uses Claude Code in the terminal, but Claude Code also runs in code editors, a desktop app, the cloud, your phone, GitHub, and Slack. This page is a tour: what each place is good for, what it needs, and which of your settings come along.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Platforms and integrations · Claude Code overview
Each place where you can use Claude Code is called a surface. In the docs’ words, Claude Code “runs the same underlying engine everywhere, but each surface is tuned for a different way of working.” For any surface, ask: where does the work run, and where do you watch and steer it?

title: 50  50.  Claude Code Beyond the Terminal
section: 50.2 In your code editor: VS Code and JetBrains
text:
50.2 In your code editor: VS Code and JetBrains
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Use Claude Code in VS Code · JetBrains IDEs

VS Code extension: a Claude Code panel inside VS Code (also in editors built on VS Code, such as Cursor), with inline diffs, @-mentions of files, and plan review. It bundles its own copy of Claude Code (typing claude in a terminal still needs the normal install), offers a subset of the slash commands, and shares conversation history with the CLI: claude --resume in a terminal can continue an extension conversation.
JetBrains plugin (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, and others; still labeled beta in the JetBrains Marketplace): it runs the claude command in the editor’s built-in terminal and shows Claude’s changes in the editor’s diff viewer. It does not include Claude Code, so install the CLI first.
From a separate terminal, the /ide command connects a running Claude Code session to your editor.
crumbs: 50  50. Claude Code Beyond the Terminal

title: 50  50.  Claude Code Beyond the Terminal
text:
50.3 The Desktop app’s Code tab
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Desktop application · Get started with the desktop app
The Claude Desktop app (Mac and Windows; Linux in beta) has a Code tab: Claude Code with buttons and panels instead of a terminal. It needs a paid plan, and you don’t have to install the CLI separately. Highlights:

Several sessions at once, listed in a sidebar, each optionally in its own copy of the project (a Git worktree; see Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents).
A visual diff view where you can comment on Claude’s changes, a preview pane for your running web app, a built-in terminal and file editor, and pull-request status.
For each session you choose Local (your computer), Cloud, or SSH (another computer you manage).

Typing /desktop in the terminal moves your session into the app (Mac and x64 Windows); /resume in the Code tab picks up terminal sessions. The app has no scripting mode (claude -p), and some terminal-only commands, such as /permissions, don’t work there.
crumbs: 50  50. Claude Code Beyond the Terminal

title: 50  50.  Claude Code Beyond the Terminal
text:
50.4 Cloud sessions at claude.ai/code
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Use Claude Code in the cloud · Get started with Claude Code in the cloud
A cloud session runs Claude Code on a virtual machine that Anthropic manages, not on your computer, so it keeps working after you close your laptop. You can start one at claude.ai/code, from the phone app’s Code tab, from the Desktop app (choose Cloud), or from your terminal:
claude --cloud "Fix the failing test in tests/test_login.py"

Claude clones your GitHub repository (the version on GitHub, not your local files, so push your commits first), works on a new branch, and pushes it. You review the changes and create a pull request.
A cloud session uses only what is in the repository, such as a committed CLAUDE.md, not your personal settings in ~/.claude.
Good for: parallel tasks, repositories you don’t have locally, and well-defined tasks that need little steering.
claude --teleport brings a cloud session’s branch and conversation into your terminal.
Plans: Pro, Max, Team, and some Enterprise seats. Cloud sessions use your normal plan limits; the virtual machine costs nothing extra.
crumbs: 50  50. Claude Code Beyond the Terminal

title: 50  50.  Claude Code Beyond the Terminal
section: 50.5 From your phone: the mobile app and Remote Control
text:
50.5 From your phone: the mobile app and Remote Control
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code on mobile · Remote Control
There is no separate Claude Code phone app: use the Code tab in the regular Claude app for iPhone or Android (/mobile shows a QR code to get it). From your phone you can:

start and check on cloud sessions, which run without your computer; or
use Remote Control to drive a session that runs on your own computer. Your files, tools, and MCP servers stay on your machine, and the phone (or any browser at claude.ai/code) is just a window into the session.

To turn on Remote Control, type /remote-control (or /rc) in a running session, or start with claude --remote-control. Your computer must stay on, with Claude Code running. It requires a paid plan sign-in (API keys don’t work); on Team and Enterprise plans an admin must enable it. Claude can send push notifications to your phone when it finishes or needs a decision.
crumbs: 50  50. Claude Code Beyond the Terminal

title: 50  50.  Claude Code Beyond the Terminal
section: 50.6 Driving your browser: the Chrome integration
text:
50.6 Driving your browser: the Chrome integration
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Use Claude Code with Chrome
With the Claude in Chrome extension installed, Claude Code (in the terminal or in VS Code) can open tabs, click, type, and read the browser’s console errors, which is perfect for testing the web app you’re building. Start with claude --chrome; /chrome changes its settings. It works with Chrome and Edge (not inside WSL), and it uses your real browser and your logins, so it can act on any site where you are signed in. You’ll try it in Letting Claude Use a Browser.

section: 50.7 On GitHub: GitHub Actions and Code Review
text:
50.7 On GitHub: GitHub Actions and Code Review
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions · Code Review

GitHub Actions: a workflow file in your repository runs Claude Code on GitHub’s servers when someone mentions @claude in an issue or a pull-request comment (or on a schedule). Claude can answer, write code, push commits, and open pull requests. Set it up with /install-github-app inside Claude Code (you need admin access to the repository). Runs use GitHub Actions minutes plus Claude usage (an API key or a subscription token).
Code Review (research preview, Team and Enterprise): a managed service in which several agents review every pull request and comment on the lines where they find problems. It is billed separately from the plan’s included usage. On any plan, /code-review reviews your changes locally.

More in Pull Requests and Code Review.

text:
50.8 In Slack
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code in Slack · Claude Tag

Claude Tag (Team and Enterprise, beta): @Claude in a channel acts as the organization’s shared teammate, for coding and non-coding work.
Claude Code in Slack (the earlier version, Pro and Max): mention @Claude with a coding task, and it starts a cloud session under your own account. It works only in Slack workspaces that are not connected to Claude Tag.
