title: 56  56.  Hooks: Running Your Own Commands Automatically
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
In one or two sentences, what is a hook in Claude Code?






Suggested answer





A hook is a command (usually a shell command) that Claude Code runs automatically at a specific point in a session, called a hook event, such as before a tool runs or when Claude finishes responding. It runs every time the event happens, without Claude deciding to run it.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which hook event runs before Claude uses a tool and can stop the tool call?

PostToolUse
PreToolUse
Notification
SessionStart







Suggested answer





b. PreToolUse fires before a tool call runs and can block it (for example with exit code 2). PostToolUse (a) fires after the tool already ran, so it can’t undo it. Notification (c) and SessionStart (d) can’t block anything.





Question 3 · True or false
If your CLAUDE.md file says “Never edit the .env file”, Claude Code guarantees that .env will never be edited.






Suggested answer





False. CLAUDE.md contains instructions that Claude reads and usually follows, but nothing enforces them. A PreToolUse hook (or a permission deny rule) is run by Claude Code itself and actually blocks the edit. The docs describe the CLAUDE.md line as a request and the hook as enforcement.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each hook event with when it fires.








Event

When it fires




1. SessionStart

A. Claude finishes responding


2. UserPromptSubmit

B. After a tool call succeeds


3. PostToolUse

C. A session begins or resumes


4. Notification

D. You submit a prompt, before Claude processes it


5. Stop

E. Claude Code needs your attention (permission, idle)









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → B, 4 → E, 5 → A.





Question 5 · Fill in the blank
To see a read-only list of all the hooks that are currently configured, type ________ at the Claude Code prompt.






Suggested answer





/hooks. It lists hooks by event and shows where each one is defined (user, project, or local settings, a plugin, …).





Question 6 · Multiple choice
Maria wants a notification hook that works in all of her projects, without sharing it with anyone. Which file should she put it in?

~/.claude/settings.json
.claude/settings.json in each project
.claude/settings.local.json in each project
CLAUDE.md







Suggested answer





a. User settings in ~/.claude/settings.json apply to all of her projects and stay on her computer. Option b would be committed and shared with the team, and it only covers one project at a time. Option c is personal but covers only one project. CLAUDE.md (d) holds instructions, not hook configuration.






Medium

Question 7 · Read the config
Explain in plain English what this configuration does, and when.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}






Suggested answer





After Claude successfully uses the Edit or Write tool (event PostToolUse, matcher Edit|Write), Claude Code runs a shell command. The command reads the event JSON from stdin, jq extracts the path of the file that was changed, and xargs passes that path to npx prettier --write, which reformats the file. It does not run after other tools such as Bash or Read.





Question 8 · Predict the outcome
Sam writes a PreToolUse guard script that prints Not allowed! to stderr and ends with exit 1 when Claude tries to run git push. What happens when Claude runs git push? How should Sam fix it?






Suggested answer





The push is not blocked. Exit code 1 is a non-blocking error: the action continues and the transcript only shows a hook error notice. Only exit code 2 blocks a tool call (or exit 0 with a JSON permissionDecision of "deny"). Sam should change exit 1 to exit 2.





Question 9 · Write the config
Write a complete settings file that, every time Claude finishes responding, appends the line Claude finished to the file ~/claude-stops.log.






Suggested answer





{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "echo 'Claude finished' >> ~/claude-stops.log"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
The event is Stop (Claude finished responding). Stop doesn’t support matchers, so the matcher group has only the "hooks" list. Writing "matcher": "" would also be fine (it is ignored).





Question 10 · Find the bug
This hook is supposed to log every file edit, but it never runs. Find the bug.
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "edit|write",
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "echo 'edited' >> ~/edits.log" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}






Suggested answer





Matchers are case-sensitive, and the tools are named Edit and Write with capital letters. "edit|write" matches no tool, so the hook never fires. Use "matcher": "Edit|Write".





Question 11 · Matching
Match each PreToolUse matcher with what it matches.








Matcher

Matches




1. "Bash"

A. Every tool call


2. "Edit|Write"

B. Only shell commands


3. ""

C. Every tool from an MCP server named github


4. "mcp__github__.*"

D. The Edit tool or the Write tool









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → C. (MCP tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool>, so mcp__github__.* matches all tools from the github server.)





Question 12 · Scenario
Your team wants everyone who works on the club website repository to get the same auto-format hook. You also want a personal hook that logs commands only on your machine. Where does each hook go?






Suggested answer






Team hook: the project’s .claude/settings.json, committed to git so every teammate gets it.
Personal hook: the project’s .claude/settings.local.json (git-ignored, just for you in this project), or ~/.claude/settings.json if you want it in all your projects.






Question 13 · Multiple choice
The protect-files.sh script on this page blocks an edit with echo "Blocked: ..." >&2 followed by exit 2. What happens to the Blocked: ... text?

It is thrown away
It is shown to Claude as the reason the edit was blocked
It is saved into the .env file
It is emailed to the project owner







Suggested answer





b. For PreToolUse, exit code 2 blocks the tool call and Claude Code passes the hook’s stderr text (>&2 sends it there) to Claude as feedback, so Claude can adjust its approach. Nothing is written to .env (c), and hooks don’t send email on their own (d).






Hard

Question 14 · Predict the output
With the protect-files.sh hook from this page installed, which of these edits are blocked? Explain any surprise.

.env.example
.gitignore
src/my.environment.ts
README.md







Suggested answer





The script blocks any path that contains one of the patterns .env, package-lock.json, or .git/.

.env.example - blocked (contains .env).
.gitignore - not blocked (the pattern is .git/ with a slash).
src/my.environment.ts - blocked, which is probably a mistake: the name contains .env inside .environment. Simple text matching can catch more than you intended.
README.md - not blocked.






Question 15 · Long answer
Why can’t a PostToolUse hook stop Claude from editing a protected file? Which event should you use instead, and why?






Suggested answer





PostToolUse fires after the tool call has succeeded, so the file is already changed; exit code 2 there only shows the stderr text to Claude. Use PreToolUse, which fires before the tool runs. Exiting 2 (or returning a JSON "deny") cancels the call, so the file is never touched.





Question 16 · Short answer
A PreToolUse hook exits with code 0 for a Bash call. Does that mean the command is approved and will run without asking you? Explain.






Suggested answer





No. Exit 0 only means “no objection”. The normal permission flow still applies: depending on your permission mode and rules, Claude Code may still show you a permission prompt (or deny the call). To actively approve, a hook must return JSON with "permissionDecision": "allow", and even that can’t override deny or ask rules in your settings.





Question 17 · Find the bug
Maria installed protect-files.sh as a PreToolUse hook, but Claude still edits .env freely and no error appears. When she tests the script by hand, she sees this:
$ echo '{"tool_name":"Edit","tool_input":{"file_path":".env"}}' | .claude/hooks/protect-files.sh
.claude/hooks/protect-files.sh: line 5: jq: command not found
$ echo $?
0
Explain what is going on and how to fix it.






Suggested answer





jq isn’t installed, so the line that extracts the file path fails and FILE_PATH is empty. An empty path matches none of the patterns, so the script reaches exit 0, which means “no objection”: the edit goes ahead. (Stderr from a hook that exits 0 only goes to the debug log, which is why no error appears.) The guard is silently switched off. Fix: install jq (on a Mac, brew install jq), then repeat the test and check that echo $? prints 2.





Question 18 · Scenario
Sam clones a classmate’s repository and wants to run claude -p "summarize this project" in it. Why could that be risky with respect to hooks, and what are two ways to reduce the risk?






Suggested answer





The repository’s .claude/settings.json can contain hooks, and hooks run shell commands with Sam’s full user permissions. In -p (non-interactive) mode, Claude Code doesn’t show the workspace trust prompt and treats the folder as trusted, so those hooks run immediately. To reduce the risk, Sam can:

read the repository’s .claude/ settings files first, and/or
disable hooks for that run: claude -p "summarize this project" --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'.






Question 19 · Compare
The protect-files.sh hook uses the matcher Edit|Write. Explain how Claude could still change .env without the hook noticing, and describe one way to close that gap.






Suggested answer





Claude can change files with shell commands through the Bash tool, for example echo "X=1" >> .env. Those calls don’t match Edit|Write, so the hook never runs. Ways to close the gap: also match Bash|PowerShell (on Windows, Claude often uses its PowerShell tool) and check what changed (the docs suggest git status --porcelain), add a Stop hook that scans the project once per turn, and add permission deny rules for sensitive files.






Challenge

Question 20 · Hands-on
Set up the desktop notification hook for your operating system in ~/.claude/settings.json. Confirm it appears in /hooks, trigger it, and then turn all hooks off with "disableAllHooks": true and confirm that the notification no longer appears. Write down what you did and what you saw.






Suggested answer





A good answer includes:

the exact JSON added (the Mac osascript version or the Windows powershell.exe version from this page), placed inside one "hooks" key;
a description of /hooks showing the hook under Notification;
how the notification was triggered (for example, Manual mode plus a request that needs permission, then switching windows and waiting about six seconds), and any fix needed (such as allowing Script Editor notifications on a Mac);
the "disableAllHooks": true line added to the same settings file, and the observation that the notification stopped. Remove that line afterwards to turn hooks back on.






Question 21 · Hands-on
In a practice project (for example the Git practice project Download the Git practice project (zip)), add a .env file containing API_KEY=test, install the protect-files.sh hook from this page, and test the script by hand. Then start Claude Code in the project and ask it to add a line to .env. What happens, and what does Claude say?






Suggested answer





A good answer shows:

the script saved in .claude/hooks/protect-files.sh, made executable on a Mac, and registered as a PreToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write in .claude/settings.json;
the hand test printing Blocked: .env matches protected pattern '.env' and exit code 2;
in Claude Code, the edit being blocked before it runs, with Claude reporting the Blocked: ... reason and suggesting another approach (it might try a different method, which is a good moment to notice the Bash gap from Question 19). If the edit goes through, check jq, the script path, and /hooks.






Question 22 · Hands-on
Ask Claude Code to write a hook for you: “Add a project hook that appends every Bash command you run to .claude/command-log.txt.” Before approving the change, read the JSON Claude proposes and identify the event, the matcher, and the handler. Then test it and look at the log file.






Suggested answer





A good answer names the parts of Claude’s proposal, which should look similar to the docs’ command-logging example: event PostToolUse (or PreToolUse), matcher Bash, and a command handler such as jq -r '.tool_input.command' >> ... that extracts the command from the JSON input. (On Windows, Claude often runs commands with its PowerShell tool, which a Bash matcher misses; Bash|PowerShell catches both.) It should note which settings file Claude edited (.claude/settings.json for a project hook), confirm the hook appears in /hooks, and show a few logged commands. Reviewing the proposal first matters because a hook runs with your permissions.
crumbs: 56  56. Hooks: Running Your Own Commands Automatically

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
57.1 What a subagent is
When Claude works on a big task, its context window fills up with everything it reads. A subagent lets Claude hand a side task to a helper that has its own, fresh context, and get back only a short summary. This page explains subagents, how to create your own, and the other ways Claude Code can run several agents at once.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Create custom subagents
A subagent is a separate AI assistant that Claude starts to handle one task. Each subagent runs in its own context window, with its own instructions (its system prompt), its own set of allowed tools, and its own permissions. When it finishes, it sends a summary back to the main conversation.
An analogy: a manager asks an intern to read 40 reports and come back with a one-page memo. The intern’s desk gets messy; the manager’s desk only receives the memo.
Why use subagents?
Subagents are not free: each one sends its own requests to the model, which count toward the same usage limits as your main conversation, and their results add to your main context.
Claude starts a subagent with its Agent tool. In the transcript, a delegation appears as a row with the subagent’s name and a short task description, such as code-reviewer(Review recent changes).
crumbs: 57  57. Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
Main conversation:  "Where do we call the payments API?"
   │
   ├──► Explore subagent  (its own context window: reads 60 files)
   │         │
   │         └── returns: "3 places: checkout.js, refund.js, ..."
   ▼
Main conversation continues, holding only the short answer


Keep the main conversation clean. Search results, logs, and file contents stay in the subagent’s context; only the summary comes back.
Specialize. A subagent with focused instructions (say, a code reviewer) does one job well.
Restrict what it can do. You can give a subagent fewer tools, for example no file editing.
Work in parallel. Several subagents can research different areas at the same time.
Control cost. A simple job can run on a faster, cheaper model such as Haiku.
crumbs: 57  57. Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
57.2 Built-in subagents
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Create custom subagents: Built-in subagents
Claude Code includes several subagents that Claude uses automatically when they fit the task:



Subagent
What it’s for
Tools




Explore
Fast searching and analysis of a codebase. Claude picks how thorough to be: quick, medium, or very thorough
Read-only (no Write or Edit)


Plan
Gathers context in plan mode before Claude presents a plan
Read-only


general-purpose
Complex, multi-step tasks that need both exploring and changing things
All tools available to subagents


Others
claude (a catch-all), statusline-setup (used by /statusline), and claude-code-guide (answers questions about Claude Code’s features)
Varies
crumbs: 57  57. Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
57.3 Using subagents
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Create custom subagents: Work with subagents

Automatically. Claude compares your request with each subagent’s description and delegates when one fits.
By asking. Plain English works:
Use a subagent to run the test suite and report only the failing tests with their error messages
Research the authentication, database, and API modules in parallel using separate subagents
By @-mention, which guarantees that a particular subagent runs. Type @ and pick it from the list, for example @"code-reviewer (agent)" look at the auth changes (or type @agent-code-reviewer).
For a whole session. claude --agent code-reviewer starts a session in which the main conversation itself takes on that subagent’s instructions, tools, and model.

In an interactive session, subagents run in the background by default, so you can keep working. A panel below the prompt shows the running ones, /tasks lists background work (including subagents that just finished), and if a background subagent needs permission for a tool call, the prompt appears in your main session with the subagent’s name.

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
57.4 Creating your own subagent
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Create custom subagents: Configure subagents
A custom subagent is a Markdown file. It starts with frontmatter (settings written in YAML between two --- lines), followed by the subagent’s instructions, which become its system prompt. Where you save the file decides who can use it (see The .claude Folders and Settings Files):








Folder
Available in
Tip




.claude/agents/ (in a project)
That project
Commit it so your team gets it too


~/.claude/agents/
All your projects
Personal helpers



Plugins can also provide subagents. This is the docs’ read-only code reviewer, saved as .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Expert code review specialist. Proactively reviews code for quality, security, and maintainability. Use immediately after writing or modifying code.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: inherit
---

You are a senior code reviewer ensuring high standards of code quality and security.

When invoked:
1. Run git diff to see recent changes
2. Focus on modified files
3. Begin review immediately

Review checklist:
- Code is clear and readable
- Functions and variables are well-named
- No duplicated code
- Proper error handling
- No exposed secrets or API keys
- Input validation implemented
- Good test coverage
- Performance considerations addressed

Provide feedback organized by priority:
- Critical issues (must fix)
- Warnings (should fix)
- Suggestions (consider improving)

Include specific examples of how to fix issues.
The most useful frontmatter fields (only name and description are required):



Field
Meaning




name
Unique name, such as code-reviewer


description
When Claude should use it. Claude reads this to decide; phrases like “use proactively” encourage automatic use


tools
Allowed tools, e.g. Read, Grep, Glob. If omitted, it gets all tools available to subagents


disallowedTools
Tools to take away, e.g. Write, Edit


model
sonnet, opus, haiku, fable, a full model ID, or inherit (same as the main conversation)


permissionMode
The permission mode it runs in, e.g. plan (ignored while your main session is in auto, acceptEdits, or bypassPermissions mode: the subagent then uses that mode)


isolation
worktree gives it its own copy of the repository (see Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents)



Field names must match exactly (disallowedTools, not disallowed-tools): Claude Code silently ignores fields it doesn’t recognize.
The easy way: ask Claude. Describe what you want and where to save it, then review the file it writes:
Create a personal code-improver subagent in ~/.claude/agents/ that scans files and suggests improvements for readability, performance, and best practices. It should explain each issue, show the current code, and provide an improved version. Make it read-only and have it use Sonnet.
Claude Code notices new and changed subagent files within a few seconds. The exception: if the agents folder didn’t exist when the session started, restart Claude Code. (Older tutorials show an interactive /agents wizard; in current versions /agents only prints a reminder to ask Claude or edit the files.)






Deeper dive: what a subagent can (and can’t) see





A subagent starts fresh. It does not see your conversation history, the files Claude already read, or the skills already used. It starts with:

its own system prompt (the Markdown body of its file) plus basic details such as the working directory;
the task message Claude writes when it delegates;
your CLAUDE.md files and a git status snapshot (the built-in Explore and Plan subagents skip both to stay fast and cheap);
any skills listed in its skills field.

So if you told Claude something only in the chat (“ignore the vendor/ folder”), a subagent won’t know it. Put lasting rules in CLAUDE.md, or ask Claude to include them when it delegates.

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
57.5 Subagent, skill, or main conversation?
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Choose between subagents and main conversation · Extend Claude Code: Compare similar features

Main conversation: back-and-forth work, quick targeted changes, or steps that share a lot of context (plan, build, test). A fresh subagent needs time to gather context.
Subagent: the task produces lots of output you don’t need to keep, it is self-contained and can return a summary, or you want to restrict its tools.
Skill: reusable instructions or a workflow that should run in your main conversation. (The two combine: a subagent can preload skills, and a skill can run in a subagent.)

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
section: 57.6 The bigger picture: running agents in parallel
text:
57.6 The bigger picture: running agents in parallel
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Run agents in parallel · Agent view · Agent teams · Dynamic workflows
Subagents are one of five ways Claude Code can work on several tasks at once:








Approach
What it is
Status




Subagents
Helpers inside one session that return a summary
Standard


Agent view
claude agents opens one screen to start, watch, and reply to full Claude Code sessions running in the background on your computer
Research preview


Agent teams
A “lead” session splits the work among teammate sessions that message each other and share a task list
Experimental, off by default


Dynamic workflows
A script Claude writes that runs dozens or hundreds of subagents and cross-checks their findings. Try the built-in /deep-research; watch runs with /workflows
Paid plans (on Pro, turn on in /config)


Projects
One ongoing conversation at claude.ai/code or in the desktop app that starts parallel sessions in the cloud
Public beta on Pro and Max



A few related tools: /subtask <task> starts a fork, a subagent that inherits your whole conversation instead of starting fresh; /fork copies the whole session into a new background session; and /background (or /bg) moves the current session to the background. When parallel agents edit files, git worktrees keep them from overwriting each other.






More agents, more usage



“Running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage.” The agent view docs give an example: ten background agents use your quota roughly ten times as fast as one. Start small, and try a big workflow on a small slice first.








Deeper dive: nesting, limits, and resuming






A subagent can start subagents of its own, by default up to three layers below the main conversation.
By default, at most 20 subagents can run at the same time in a session.
Claude can resume a finished subagent (for example, “continue that code review and now check the authorization logic”), and it picks up with its full history. The built-in Explore and Plan subagents can’t be resumed.
You can block a subagent with a permission deny rule such as "Agent(Explore)".

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
57.7 Key takeaways

A subagent does a side task in its own context window and returns a summary, keeping your main conversation clean.
Built-ins (Explore, Plan, general-purpose) work automatically; custom subagents are Markdown files in .claude/agents/ or ~/.claude/agents/.
The description tells Claude when to delegate; tools limits what the subagent can do.
Every extra agent uses more of your usage; parallel options range from subagents to agent view, agent teams, and workflows.
crumbs: 57  57. Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)

title: 57  57.  Subagents (and Running Agents in Parallel)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a subagent, and what does it send back to the main conversation?






Suggested answer





A subagent is a separate AI assistant that Claude starts to handle one task. It works in its own context window, with its own instructions, tools, and permissions, and when it finishes it sends a summary of its results back to the main conversation (not everything it read).





Question 2 · Multiple choice
What is the main benefit of having a subagent search 60 files instead of doing it in the main conversation?

The subagent is never charged against your usage limits
The search results stay in the subagent’s context, so your main context stays clean
The subagent can see more of your conversation history
The subagent always uses a more powerful model







Suggested answer





b. Only the summary comes back, so the main context window doesn’t fill up with search results. (a) is false: subagents’ requests count toward the same usage limits. (c) is false: a normal subagent starts fresh, without your conversation history. (d) is false: unless its settings say otherwise, a subagent normally uses the main conversation’s model, and you can set a cheaper one such as Haiku.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each built-in subagent with its job.








Subagent

Job




1. Explore

A. Answers questions about Claude Code’s own features


2. Plan

B. Complex multi-step tasks that explore and change things


3. general-purpose

C. Fast, read-only search and analysis of a codebase


4. claude-code-guide

D. Gathers context in plan mode before Claude presents a plan









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → B, 4 → A.





Question 4 · True or false
A normal (non-fork) subagent can see the whole conversation you’ve had with Claude so far.






Suggested answer





False. A normal subagent starts with a fresh context: its own system prompt, the task message Claude writes for it, your CLAUDE.md files (except Explore and Plan), and a git status snapshot. Only a fork (for example one started with /subtask) inherits the full conversation.





Question 5 · Fill in the blank
Project subagents are saved in the folder ________, and personal subagents that work in all your projects are saved in ________.






Suggested answer





.claude/agents/ (inside the project) and ~/.claude/agents/ (in your home folder).





Question 6 · Multiple choice
Which two frontmatter fields are required in a subagent file?

name and model
tools and description
name and description
model and tools







Suggested answer





c. Only name and description are required. Without tools, the subagent gets all tools available to subagents; without model, Claude Code picks the model by its default rules (normally the main conversation’s model).






Medium

Question 7 · Read the file
Read this subagent file and answer: (a) What is it called? (b) When will Claude use it? (c) Can it edit files with the Edit tool? (d) Which model does it use?
---
name: safe-researcher
description: Research agent with restricted capabilities. Use for questions about how the code works.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: haiku
---

Answer questions about the codebase. Quote file names and line numbers.






Suggested answer






safe-researcher. (b) When a request matches its description: questions about how the code works (or when you ask for it by name or @-mention it).
No. Its tools list only allows Read, Grep, and Glob, so Edit, Write, and Bash are not available. (d) Haiku, a fast, lower-cost model.






Question 8 · Write the prompt
Your test suite prints hundreds of lines. Write a prompt that keeps that output out of your main conversation.






Suggested answer





For example:
Use a subagent to run the test suite and report only the failing tests with their error messages
The subagent runs the tests in its own context and returns only the failures.





Question 9 · Write the file
Write a project subagent named test-runner that may only use Read, Grep, Glob, and Bash, runs on Haiku, and should be used after code changes to run the tests and summarize failures. Give the file’s path too.






Suggested answer





Path: .claude/agents/test-runner.md
---
name: test-runner
description: Runs the test suite and summarizes failures. Use proactively after code changes.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: haiku
---

Run the project's tests. Report only the failing tests, each with its error
message and the file it is in. Do not change any files.
Any clear system prompt is fine; the key parts are the path, the required name and description, the tools list, and model: haiku.





Question 10 · Scenario
For each situation, choose main conversation, subagent, or skill:

You and Claude are going back and forth to fine-tune the wording of a web page.
You want Claude to search a large codebase for every use of an old function and report the list.
You type the same 12-step release checklist into chat every week.







Suggested answer






Main conversation: lots of back-and-forth that shares context.
Subagent: a self-contained search with a lot of output; only the list needs to come back.
Skill: reusable instructions you can run again and again in your main conversation.






Question 11 · Predict
During a session, Maria asks Claude to create her first personal subagent in ~/.claude/agents/ (the folder didn’t exist before). When she then asks Claude to use it, Claude can’t find it. Why, and what should she do?






Suggested answer





Claude Code watches the agents folders for changes, but only folders that existed when the session started. Because ~/.claude/agents/ was created during the session, the new file wasn’t picked up. She should restart Claude Code; after that, edits are detected automatically.





Question 12 · Multiple choice
A tutorial says to “run /agents and use the wizard to create a subagent”. What actually happens in current versions of Claude Code?

/agents opens agent view
/agents prints a reminder to ask Claude or edit the agent files directly
/agents deletes all custom subagents
/agents lists the plugins you have installed







Suggested answer





b. The interactive wizard existed in older versions (v2.1.197 and earlier). Now /agents just reminds you to ask Claude or edit .claude/agents/ or ~/.claude/agents/. Agent view (a) is opened with claude agents from your shell, a different command despite the similar name.





Question 13 · Short answer
How can you make sure that your code-reviewer subagent (and not some other one) handles a request? Give two ways.






Suggested answer






@-mention it: type @ and pick it, e.g. @"code-reviewer (agent)" look at the auth changes (or @agent-code-reviewer). This guarantees that subagent runs for that task.
Run the whole session as that agent: claude --agent code-reviewer.

Naming it in plain English (“Use the code-reviewer subagent to …”) usually works too, but then Claude still decides.






Hard

Question 14 · Find the bug
Sam wants a reviewer that can’t change files, but it edits files anyway. Find the bug.
---
name: careful-reviewer
description: Reviews code without changing it. Use after code changes.
disallowed-tools: Write, Edit
---

Review the recent changes and list problems by priority.






Suggested answer





The field name is wrong. It must be disallowedTools (camelCase), exactly as in the docs. Claude Code silently ignores fields it doesn’t recognize, so disallowed-tools does nothing; with no tools field either, the subagent inherits all tools, including Write and Edit. Fix: disallowedTools: Write, Edit (or an allowlist such as tools: Read, Grep, Glob).





Question 15 · Long answer
The docs’ code-reviewer subagent has tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash and is described as read-only. Is it truly unable to change files? Explain.






Suggested answer





Not completely. It has no Edit or Write tool, but it does have Bash, and shell commands can change files (for example echo "x" >> file.txt or rm file.txt). It needs Bash to run git diff. What protects you is the permission system: such commands still go through permission checks and your deny rules. For a reviewer that truly can’t run commands, remove Bash from tools (and, if needed, give it the diff in the task instead).





Question 16 · Scenario
You tell Claude in the chat, “From now on, ignore everything in the vendor/ folder.” Later, an Explore subagent’s report is full of findings from vendor/. Explain why, and give a better way to make the rule stick.






Suggested answer





A subagent starts with a fresh context: it doesn’t see your conversation history, so it never saw the chat instruction. (Explore also skips CLAUDE.md files.) Better options: ask Claude to include the rule in the task it gives the subagent (“search, but ignore vendor/”), and put lasting rules in CLAUDE.md, which normal subagents do load. For Explore specifically, restating the rule in the delegation is the reliable route.





Question 17 · Compare
Compare subagents and agent teams: how do they communicate, who coordinates the work, and which costs more? Which one can you use without changing any settings?






Suggested answer






Subagents report their results back to the conversation that started them; the main agent manages all the work. They cost less because only summaries come back.
Agent teams: a lead session coordinates teammates that message each other directly and share a task list. Each teammate is a separate Claude session, so teams use significantly more tokens.
Subagents work out of the box. Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default (they must be turned on with a setting).






Question 18 · Scenario
A classmate on a Pro plan opens claude agents and dispatches ten tasks at once “to finish faster”. Then they hit their usage limit by lunchtime. Explain what happened and suggest a better approach.






Suggested answer





Each background session in agent view is a full Claude Code session that uses the subscription quota independently, so ten sessions use quota roughly ten times as fast as one. A better approach: dispatch only the tasks that are truly independent and important, start with one or two, use subagents (which return summaries) for side research, and check usage with /usage.





Question 19 · Scenario
Your team must check all 400 files of a codebase for the same security issue, and you want each finding double-checked. Which parallel approach from this page fits best, and what should you do before running it on everything?






Suggested answer





A dynamic workflow: Claude writes a script that runs many subagents (dozens to hundreds) and can have other agents cross-check the findings, which is too much for a handful of subagents in one conversation. Because a workflow can use many more tokens than a normal conversation, first run it on a small slice (for example one folder), watch the cost in /workflows, and then scale up. On a Pro plan, workflows must first be turned on in /config.






Challenge

Question 20 · Hands-on
In a practice Git repository, ask Claude to create a project code-reviewer subagent (read-only, using Sonnet). Review the file it writes, make a small change to a file, and then ask the subagent to review it with an @-mention. While it runs, look at /tasks. Report what you saw.






Suggested answer





A good answer includes:

the file .claude/agents/code-reviewer.md with name, a clear description, a tools list without Edit and Write, and model: sonnet, plus a short explanation of each field;
the prompt used, such as @"code-reviewer (agent)" review my last change;
what appeared in the transcript (a row like code-reviewer(...)) and in /tasks;
the summary the subagent returned, and a note on whether its feedback was useful and correct.






Question 21 · Hands-on
Ask the same research question twice: once normally (“Explain how this project is organized”) and once with “Use a subagent to …”. Run /context after each (in separate sessions, or after /clear) and compare how full your context window is. What do you notice?






Suggested answer





A good answer reports the /context numbers (or a description of them) for both runs and notices that, with a subagent, less of the main context window is used, because the files the subagent read stay in its own context and only its summary comes back. It may also note that the subagent version took a bit longer to start and that both runs used part of the plan’s usage.





Question 22 · Long answer
Design three custom subagents for a team web-app project (for example a test runner, a code reviewer, and a documentation writer). For each, write the frontmatter (name, description, tools, model), say where you would save it, and explain why you gave it those tools and that model.






Suggested answer





A good answer has three focused subagents, each saved in .claude/agents/ (so the team shares them through git), with descriptions that clearly say when to use each one. For example:

test-runner: tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, model: haiku. It needs Bash to run tests, but a cheap, fast model is enough to summarize failures.
code-reviewer: tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash (Bash for git diff), model: sonnet or inherit. No Edit/Write, because a reviewer should report, not change code.
docs-writer: tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, model: sonnet. It must create and edit Markdown files, but it doesn’t need Bash.

The explanation should follow “give each subagent only the tools it needs” and match the model to how hard the job is.

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
58.1 What a plugin is
Skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers each work on their own. A plugin packages several of them into one unit that you can install with one command, share with classmates, and keep up to date. This page covers what plugins are, where they come from, how to install and manage them, how to judge whether to trust one, and how to build a tiny plugin of your own.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Plugins overview
A plugin is a folder of components that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit. Think of an app on your phone: one install, and you get a bundle of features. The usual components are:
Plugins can also carry language servers (for code intelligence), output styles, color themes, and executable programs. Each part has a fixed place in the plugin’s folder:
The manifest (plugin.json) names the plugin. That name becomes a prefix on its skills and agents, such as /my-plugin:review, so two plugins can both have a review skill without colliding.
Do you need a plugin? Not to use these features yourself: a skill saved in ~/.claude/skills/, for example, already works in all your projects. Use a plugin to install a setup someone else built, or to share your own setup with teammates and several projects.

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
Skills: instructions Claude loads when relevant, which you can also run as / commands.
Agents: subagent definitions.
Hooks: commands that run at lifecycle events.
A hooks module: hooks written as JavaScript functions; a plugin that has one is a mod.
MCP servers: extra tools for Claude.


my-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json      <- the manifest: the plugin's name, description, version
├── skills/
│   └── review/
│       └── SKILL.md     <- a skill, run as /my-plugin:review
├── agents/
│   └── reviewer.md      <- a subagent
├── hooks/
│   └── hooks.json       <- hooks
└── .mcp.json            <- MCP servers

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
58.2 Marketplaces
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Anthropic’s marketplaces
A marketplace is a catalog of plugins: a repository or folder with a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file that lists plugins and where to fetch each one. It’s a catalog, not a store. You add a marketplace once, then install plugins from it as plugin-name@marketplace-name, for example commit-commands@claude-plugins-official.
Anthropic publishes three general-purpose marketplaces:










Official
Community
Demo




Name (after @)
claude-plugins-official
claude-community
claude-code-plugins


GitHub repository
anthropics/claude-plugins-official
anthropics/claude-plugins-community
anthropics/claude-code


What’s in it
Plugins Anthropic maintains, plus plugins from partners and other authors
Third-party plugins submitted to Anthropic
A few example plugins


How you get it
Added automatically the first time you start an interactive terminal session
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-code



Anthropic also has a few topic-specific marketplaces. Any marketplace without one of Anthropic’s reserved names is third-party, such as one a classmate or a company publishes on GitHub. Anthropic doesn’t review third-party marketplaces. To browse the official catalog on the web, see Claude Marketplace (a website, not a marketplace you add).

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
58.3 Installing and managing plugins
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Install and manage plugins
Inside Claude Code, /plugin opens the plugin panel. Press Tab to move between its tabs: Discover (plugins from your marketplaces; type to search), Installed, Marketplaces, and Errors.
To install the official commit-commands plugin (commands for committing, pushing, and opening pull requests):
/plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
This doesn’t install right away. It opens the plugin’s details, which list what it will add (“Will install”) and, for official plugins, a Context cost estimate. Then you choose a scope:








Scope
Who gets the plugin
Recorded in




User
You, in every project on this computer
~/.claude/settings.json


Project
Everyone who works in this repository
.claude/settings.json (committed)


Local
You, in this repository only
.claude/settings.local.json



The install summary tells you whether the plugin is active now or whether to run /reload-plugins. Its skills then appear under its name: type / and look for /commit-commands:commit.
The same actions work from your shell (Mac Terminal or Git Bash), without starting a session:
claude plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
claude plugin list
claude plugin disable commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
claude plugin enable commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
claude plugin uninstall commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
claude plugin install uses user scope unless you add --scope project or --scope local. A plugin installed from the shell loads in your next session, or after /reload-plugins in an open one.

Disable vs uninstall. Disabling keeps the plugin installed but turns it off; uninstalling removes it. Both are also on the Installed tab.
Updates. Plugins from the official marketplace update automatically by default; for the community marketplace and third-party marketplaces, auto-update is off unless you turn it on. Update one by hand with claude plugin update <plugin>@<marketplace>. A running session keeps the old version until /reload-plugins or the next session.
Marketplaces. claude plugin marketplace add <owner>/<repo>, list, update, and remove manage marketplaces (inside a session, use /plugin marketplace ...). Removing a marketplace uninstalls every plugin you installed from it.







Deeper dive: plugins outside the terminal





In the desktop app’s Code tab, click + next to the prompt box, then Plugins. In VS Code, type /plugins in the Claude Code panel. The terminal, the desktop app’s local sessions, and the VS Code extension on one computer share the same settings files, so a user-scope plugin installed in one is available in the others. Cloud sessions (such as claude.ai/code) don’t load the plugins installed on your computer. Plugins you turn on in your claude.ai account can also sync into Claude Code; they show up with the ID <name>@synced.

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
58.4 What an enabled plugin costs
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Plugins overview: What an enabled plugin adds to your sessions
An enabled plugin is part of every session, not only the ones where you use it:

Context and usage. The name and description of each skill and agent Claude can use on its own sit in Claude’s context on every turn, so Claude knows they exist. That uses tokens and room in the context window even when nothing from the plugin runs.
Processes. Its MCP servers run, and its hooks fire on their events.

To check: look at the Context cost in the plugin’s details, run claude plugin details <name> in your shell (its Always-on line shows the tokens added to every session), and look for the Not used recently group on the Installed tab. Disable what you don’t use.

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
58.5 Trust and security
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Plugin security and trust






A plugin can run code as you



“A Claude Code plugin you install can execute arbitrary code on your machine with your user privileges.” This is true whichever marketplace it comes from.


What makes a plugin powerful also makes it risky:

Its hooks, MCP servers, and mod code run on your computer with your permissions, outside Claude Code’s sandbox. Your permission rules cover the tool calls Claude makes, not the code a plugin runs by itself.
Programs in its bin/ folder can be run by Claude’s Bash commands.
Its skills and agents enter Claude’s context as instructions, which shape what Claude does.
With auto-update on, the files you reviewed can change later.

Before installing, especially from a third-party marketplace:

Check where the marketplace comes from: claude plugin marketplace list prints each marketplace’s source.
Read the Will install list in the plugin’s details in /plugin.
Open the plugin’s source (Open homepage or View on GitHub) and read hooks/hooks.json (what each hook runs), .mcp.json (each server’s command or URL), and everything in bin/.
If you don’t understand it or don’t trust the author, don’t install it.

Marketplace names help a little: Claude Code accepts Anthropic’s official and community marketplace names only from github.com/anthropics/ repositories, so a stranger can’t publish a fake claude-plugins-official. But the name tells you who publishes the catalog, not what each plugin does.
To remove a plugin you no longer trust, run claude plugin uninstall <plugin> --scope <the scope you used>.

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
58.6 Create a minimal plugin
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Create a Claude Code plugin
This plugin has one component, a greeting skill. Run these commands in your shell (Mac Terminal or Git Bash), from a folder such as ~/projects:
mkdir -p my-first-plugin/.claude-plugin
mkdir -p my-first-plugin/skills/hello
Save the manifest as my-first-plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json:
{
  "name": "my-first-plugin",
  "description": "A greeting plugin to learn the basics",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "author": {
    "name": "Your Name"
  }
}
Save the skill as my-first-plugin/skills/hello/SKILL.md:
---
name: hello
description: Greet the user with a friendly message
disable-model-invocation: true
---

Greet the user warmly and ask how you can help them today.
(disable-model-invocation: true means only you can start this skill; Claude won’t run it on its own.) Check the files, then start Claude Code with the plugin loaded for this session only:
claude plugin validate ./my-first-plugin
claude --plugin-dir ./my-first-plugin
The first command should end with ✔ Validation passed. In the session, run /my-first-plugin:hello and Claude greets you. If you edit the files during the session, run /reload-plugins to load your changes.






Only plugin.json goes in .claude-plugin/



Put skills/, agents/, hooks/, and .mcp.json at the plugin’s top level, next to .claude-plugin/. Components saved inside .claude-plugin/ don’t load.


To share the plugin, you can send the folder (or a .zip), list it in a marketplace of your own (a GitHub repository with a marketplace.json), or submit it to Anthropic’s directory.






Deeper dive: other ways to start a plugin






claude plugin init my-tool scaffolds a starter plugin in ~/.claude/skills/my-tool/, which then loads in every session as my-tool@skills-dir.
If you already have skills, agents, or hooks under a project’s .claude/ folder, you can copy them into a plugin folder; hooks move from your settings file into hooks/hooks.json (same format).
Anthropic’s plugin-dev plugin (in the official marketplace) adds /plugin-dev:create-plugin, which walks you through designing and validating a larger plugin.

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
58.7 Key takeaways

A plugin bundles skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, and more under one name; a marketplace is a catalog you install plugins from.
Use /plugin (or claude plugin ... in your shell) to browse, install, disable, update, and uninstall; pick a user, project, or local scope.
Enabled plugins cost context and run processes in every session.
Plugins run code with your permissions: review them before installing.

title: 58  58.  Plugins and Marketplaces
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a Claude Code plugin? Name three kinds of components it can contain.






Suggested answer





A plugin is a folder of components that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit, named by a manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json). It can contain, for example, skills, agents (subagents), hooks, MCP servers, and a hooks module (which makes it a mod), as well as language servers, output styles, themes, and executables.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
What is a plugin marketplace?

A store where you pay for plugins with a credit card
A catalog (a marketplace.json file in a repository or folder) that lists plugins and where to fetch them
The ~/.claude/plugins/ folder on your computer
Another name for an MCP server







Suggested answer





b. A marketplace is a catalog, not a store (a). ~/.claude/plugins/ (c) is where Claude Code keeps installed plugin files, and an MCP server (d) provides tools; neither is a catalog.





Question 3 · Fill in the blank
Anthropic’s official marketplace is named ________, and Claude Code adds it automatically the first time you start an ________ terminal session.






Suggested answer





claude-plugins-official; interactive.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each file or folder in a plugin with what it provides.








Path

Provides




1. .claude-plugin/plugin.json

A. A subagent Claude can delegate to


2. skills/review/SKILL.md

B. Tools from an MCP server


3. agents/reviewer.md

C. The plugin’s name and description (the manifest)


4. hooks/hooks.json

D. Commands that run at lifecycle events


5. .mcp.json

E. A skill run as /<plugin>:review









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → A, 4 → D, 5 → B.





Question 5 · True or false
Plugins from Anthropic’s official marketplace run in a sandbox, so they can’t run code on your computer.






Suggested answer





False. Any installed plugin can execute code with your user privileges (through hooks, MCP servers, mod code, or bin/ programs), whichever marketplace it comes from. Hooks and MCP servers run outside Claude Code’s sandbox. Review plugins before installing them.





Question 6 · Multiple choice
In the /plugin panel, which tab shows the plugins you have installed and lets you enable, disable, update, or uninstall them?

Discover
Installed
Marketplaces
Errors







Suggested answer





b. Installed. Discover (a) lists plugins available from your marketplaces, Marketplaces (c) manages the catalogs themselves, and Errors (d) shows what failed to load and why.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
From your shell (not inside Claude Code), install the commit-commands plugin from Anthropic’s official marketplace so that it is enabled for everyone who works in the current repository.






Suggested answer





claude plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official --scope project
Without --scope project, claude plugin install uses user scope.





Question 8 · Short answer
After installing commit-commands, Sam types /commit, and the command menu suggests /commit-commands:commit. Why does the plugin’s skill have that longer name?






Suggested answer





Plugin skills are named /<plugin>:<skill>, with the plugin’s name as a prefix, so different plugins can have skills with the same name without colliding. (The / menu also finds a plugin skill by its short name, so typing /commit lists it and choosing it inserts the full name. If it doesn’t appear at all, the install summary may have asked him to run /reload-plugins.)





Question 9 · Scenario
Maria installs a formatting plugin at project scope and commits .claude/settings.json. Her teammate pulls the change. Is the plugin now working for the teammate? Explain.






Suggested answer





Not automatically. Project scope records in the committed .claude/settings.json that the plugin is enabled for the repository, but it doesn’t download the plugin to other machines. Each teammate still installs it once, for example with claude plugin install <name>@<marketplace> --scope project.





Question 10 · Short answer
What is the difference between disabling and uninstalling a plugin, and when would you choose each?






Suggested answer





Disabling turns the plugin off but keeps it installed, so you can switch it back on later (good for a plugin you use only sometimes, to save context and avoid running its servers and hooks). Uninstalling removes it (good when you no longer want it or no longer trust it).





Question 11 · Write the command
Inside a Claude Code session, add Anthropic’s community marketplace, then start installing a plugin named example-tool from it.






Suggested answer





/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community
/plugin install example-tool@claude-community
Note that the marketplace’s name is claude-community, not the repository name. The install command opens the plugin’s details, where you choose a scope.





Question 12 · Multiple choice
You are developing a plugin in the folder ./my-first-plugin. Which command starts Claude Code with that plugin loaded for this session only, without installing it?

claude plugin install ./my-first-plugin
claude --plugin-dir ./my-first-plugin
claude plugin validate ./my-first-plugin
claude --agent my-first-plugin







Suggested answer





b. --plugin-dir loads a plugin folder (or .zip) for one session. claude plugin install (a) installs from a marketplace by name. claude plugin validate (c) only checks the files, and --agent (d) runs a subagent as the session’s main agent.





Question 13 · Short answer
You are in a session started with --plugin-dir and you just edited your plugin’s SKILL.md. How do you load the change without restarting?






Suggested answer





Run /reload-plugins. It reloads the active plugins and reports what it loaded.






Hard

Question 14 · Find the bug
Sam’s plugin loads, but its skill never appears. Here is his layout. What is wrong?
my-plugin/
└── .claude-plugin/
    ├── plugin.json
    └── skills/
        └── hello/
            └── SKILL.md






Suggested answer





Only plugin.json belongs inside .claude-plugin/. Components saved there don’t load. Move skills/ up to the plugin’s top level, next to .claude-plugin/ (so the path is my-plugin/skills/hello/SKILL.md), then run /reload-plugins or restart.





Question 15 · Scenario
A classmate sends you a link to a third-party marketplace with a plugin that “makes Claude 10x faster”. List the steps you would take before installing it.






Suggested answer






Check who publishes the marketplace and where it comes from (after adding, claude plugin marketplace list prints the source).
Open the plugin in /plugin and read the Will install list.
Read the source: hooks/hooks.json (what each hook runs), .mcp.json (each server’s command or URL), and everything in bin/.
Optionally clone it and run claude --plugin-dir <folder> plugin details <name> to list its components.
Be skeptical of vague claims; if you don’t understand what it runs or don’t trust the author, don’t install it. If you do install it, consider the narrowest scope and remember it runs with your permissions.






Question 16 · Long answer
You installed eight plugins but use only two. Explain why the other six still cost you something, and how you would find and fix the problem.






Suggested answer





An enabled plugin is part of every session: the names and descriptions of its skills and agents sit in Claude’s context on every turn (using tokens and context space), its MCP servers run, and its hooks fire, even if you never use it. To find the cost, check claude plugin details <name> (the Always-on line), the Context cost shown in the details pane, and the Not used recently group on the Installed tab. Fix it by disabling (or uninstalling) the plugins you don’t use.





Question 17 · Predict
Someone creates a GitHub repository github.com/evil-dev/plugins whose marketplace is named claude-plugins-official, and tricks you into adding it. What does Claude Code do, and why?






Suggested answer





Claude Code refuses to load it. Anthropic’s official and community marketplace names are accepted only for marketplaces sourced from github.com/anthropics/ repositories, so a third-party marketplace can’t pretend to be Anthropic’s (the error says the marketplace is registered from an untrusted source). Note that this protects the name; it says nothing about whether a plugin in a genuine third-party marketplace is safe.





Question 18 · Compare
You have permission deny rules and the sandbox turned on. Does that protect you from a malicious hook inside a plugin? Explain.






Suggested answer





No. Permission rules and the sandbox cover the tool calls Claude makes. A plugin’s hooks and MCP server processes are run by Claude Code itself, with your full user permissions and outside the sandbox. A malicious hook could read or delete your files no matter what your deny rules say. The protection is to review the plugin (especially hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json, and bin/) before installing it.





Question 19 · Long answer
Plugins from the official marketplace auto-update by default, while third-party marketplaces don’t. Give one advantage and one risk of automatic updates for a plugin.






Suggested answer






Advantage: you get bug fixes, security fixes, and new features without doing anything.
Risk: the files you reviewed before installing can change on disk later, so a plugin that was safe could start running different code (for example if its author’s account is compromised). For third-party plugins, keeping auto-update off and updating deliberately (with claude plugin update <plugin>@<marketplace>) after a review is safer.







Challenge

Question 20 · Hands-on
Install commit-commands from the official marketplace at local scope in a practice Git repository. Before installing, note what the details pane says it will install and its context cost. Use /commit-commands:commit to commit a small change, then run claude plugin details commit-commands in your shell and finally disable the plugin.






Suggested answer





A good answer records:

the Will install list and the Context cost numbers (Every turn / When invoked) from the details pane;
the scope chosen (“Install for you, in this repo only”) and that the entry went into .claude/settings.local.json;
the commit Claude made (message and files) and a check with git log;
the Always-on token count from claude plugin details;
how the plugin was disabled (Installed tab or claude plugin disable commit-commands@claude-plugins-official).






Question 21 · Hands-on
Build my-first-plugin from this page, validate it, and run /my-first-plugin:hello. Then add a second skill, skills/explain/SKILL.md, that explains a file in plain English for a beginner, and load it with /reload-plugins.






Suggested answer





A good answer shows the folder tree, the plugin.json, both SKILL.md files, the ✔ Validation passed output, and the result of running /my-first-plugin:hello and /my-first-plugin:explain <file>. The second skill needs its own folder under skills/ with frontmatter (name, description) and instructions such as “Explain the file the user names in plain English for a beginner: what it does, its main parts, and how it fits into the project.”





Question 22 · Long answer
Your student team wants everyone to have the same two skills, one code-review subagent, and one formatting hook. Explain whether you would share them by committing them to the project’s .claude/ folder or by building a plugin, and why.






Suggested answer





Either can work; a good answer weighs them:

Project .claude/ folder: simplest for one repository. Everything is committed with the code, so teammates get it when they pull, and nothing has to be installed.
Plugin: better when the same setup is needed in several repositories, when you want versioned releases and updates, or when other people outside the repository should install it. It needs a marketplace (or a shared folder) and each person installs it.

For one team project, committing to .claude/ is usually enough; if the team starts several projects that need the same setup, package it as a plugin.

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
59.1 What a mod is
Hooks, skills, and MCP servers all work from outside Claude Code: they run a script or give Claude text or tools. A mod runs inside Claude Code, so it can change how Claude Code itself looks and behaves: add a panel beside the conversation, restyle the spinner, add an instant /command, or hold a risky command until you decide. This page explains what mods are, how to get and try them safely, and how to turn them off.
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Mods overview · Changelog
A mod is a plugin that contains JavaScript or TypeScript event handlers: functions that Claude Code calls when something happens, such as Claude being about to use a tool, you submitting a prompt, or part of the screen being drawn. The handler can watch the event, change it, or take it over. If plugins are like apps, mods are like browser extensions that change how the browser itself works.
Mods are brand new: Claude Code added them in version 2.1.287 on October 1, 2026. Expect details to change quickly, and check the docs.
A mod can:
crumbs: 59  59. Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
Draw an interface you can use: a pane (a panel beside the conversation in a wide fullscreen terminal, or above the prompt otherwise) or a band (a strip right above the prompt), with tabs, buttons, and text fields.
Redraw parts of Claude Code, such as tool-call rows, the spinner, or the dialog in which Claude asks you questions.
Step into a tool call: hold it while asking you a question, refuse it, or answer it without running the tool.
Add instant commands: a /command that runs your code right away, with no Claude turn, even while Claude is working.
Share data between its handlers: for example, count tool calls in one handler and show the count beside the spinner in another.







Two kinds of “hooks”



The mods docs call a mod’s handlers hooks too. To avoid confusion, they call the hooks from the Hooks page (shell commands configured in settings.json) settings hooks. Both kinds keep working side by side.
crumbs: 59  59. Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
59.2 Where mods run
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Mods overview: Where mods run
Mods are on by default in the Claude Code CLI (version 2.1.287 or later; check with claude --version) and in the Code tab of the Claude Desktop app (version 2.1.286 or later; check with /status). Their handlers run wherever the plugin loads, but drawing only shows up in some places:



Where you run Claude Code
Handlers run?
Drawings appear?




claude in a terminal (including an editor’s terminal)
Yes
Yes


Desktop app, Code tab (not WSL sessions)
Yes
Yes, mostly


VS Code extension’s chat panel
Yes
No


claude -p (non-interactive)
Yes
No


Cloud sessions
Yes, if the plugin reaches the session
No

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
59.3 Mods you already have
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Mods built into Claude Code
Some of Claude Code’s own features are built-in mods. Run /plugin, open the Installed tab, and look under Built-in:







Name in /plugin
What it does




cc-plugin-diff
Draws the pane for the /diff command (review the changes in your working tree)


cc-plugin-agents-md
Loads AGENTS.md files as project instructions


cc-plugin-plugin-authoring
Gives Claude the plugin-authoring skill for writing mods


cc-plugin-you-should-know
A side agent that watches while Claude works on longer tasks and shows you notes above the prompt. Off by default; turn it on with /plugin enable cc-plugin-you-should-know@builtin


cc-plugin-telemetry, cc-plugin-sec-default
Analytics records, and a guard that protects what an organization manages



You can’t uninstall built-in mods, but you can disable most of them in /plugin. The source code of several is public in the mods folder of the Claude Code repository.
crumbs: 59  59. Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
59.4 Getting more mods
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Create a mod · Mods overview: Get a mod

59.4.1 Ask Claude to make one
Describe the mod in a Claude Code session, for example:
make a mod that shows the current git branch above the prompt
Claude follows the built-in plugin-authoring skill (you can also load it yourself with /plugin-authoring) and writes the mod into a folder under ~/.claude/dev-mods/ named after the session’s ID. Because ~/.claude is a protected location, in Manual and acceptEdits modes you approve each file. When Claude saves the first file, Claude Code asks about hot reloading:

Enable for this session: the mod loads when Claude’s turn ends, and reloads after each turn that changes it.
Not now: nothing loads for now.

Check /plugin (Installed tab) to confirm it loaded. A mod Claude writes loads only in the session that made it, and Claude Code eventually deletes that folder. To keep it, copy its folder somewhere such as ~/mods/git-branch and start future sessions with claude --plugin-dir ~/mods/git-branch.


59.4.2 Try a sample mod
Anthropic shares sample mods, “as they are, without support”, in the claude-code-playground repository, for example token-weather (a forecast of your context window above the prompt), blast-radius (holds a risky command such as rm -rf and shows what it would change, with buttons to proceed or cancel), and replay-theater (a /replay command that steps through the file edits Claude made in the last turn). To try one for a single session:
git clone https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-playground.git
claude plugin validate claude-code-playground/claude-code/mods/token-weather
claude --plugin-dir claude-code-playground/claude-code/mods/token-weather
Inside the session, /plugin shows a dim line such as 1 mod active · token-weather. Mods also install from marketplaces exactly like other plugins: /plugin install <name>@<marketplace>.
crumbs: 59  59. Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
crumbs: 59  59. Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
59.6 Turning mods off
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Turn mods on or off · Check whether mods can load







To stop…
Do this




One mod
Disable or uninstall its plugin on the Installed tab of /plugin


Every installed mod, for one session
Start with claude --safe-mode (this also disables your other customizations)


Every installed mod, in every session
Add "disableAllHooks": true to ~/.claude/settings.json (this also stops your settings hooks and custom status line)



Built-in mods aren’t stopped by --safe-mode or disableAllHooks; disable them one by one in /plugin. An organization can also limit which mods load through its managed settings.
To check whether mods can load on your computer at all, run claude plugin test in your shell from a folder that contains no mod. no hooks module to load means mods can load (there was just nothing to test there); a message saying hooks modules are “turned off” means a setting, your organization, or Anthropic has switched them off.

text:
59.7 How mods compare
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Compare mods, settings hooks, skills, and MCP servers · Customize your status line




Mod
Settings hook
Skill
MCP server
Status line




What it is
Functions Claude Code calls inside its own process
A shell command, web request, or prompt run at a lifecycle event
A SKILL.md file of instructions Claude reads
An outside program or service that gives Claude tools
A script whose output is shown in a bar at the bottom of the screen


What it can change
Tool calls, prompts, commands, turns, and what the interface draws
Whether a tool call or prompt goes ahead, a call’s arguments and result, context for Claude
What Claude knows and does
Which tools Claude has
Only the text in its bar


Draws in the interface?
Yes
No
No
No
Only its own bar


What you write
JavaScript or TypeScript
A script plus a settings.json entry
Markdown
A server in any language
A script plus a statusLine setting (or ask /statusline)


Pick it when
You want a pane, a band, an instant command, or to rewrite an event
You want to block, allow, or log an event with a script
You keep pasting the same instructions
Claude needs to reach an outside system
You want an always-visible line, such as model, context use, or git branch



If a settings hook, skill, or MCP server already does what you need, the docs suggest comparing them before you write a mod; the simpler tool is usually the better choice. One plugin can hold a mod, settings hooks, skills, and MCP servers at once.
