title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
59.9 Key takeaways

A mod is a plugin with JavaScript or TypeScript handlers that run inside Claude Code and can draw panes, add instant commands, and step into tool calls.
Get mods by asking Claude (plugin-authoring), loading a sample with --plugin-dir, or installing from a marketplace; /plugin shows what is active.
Mods aren’t sandboxed and can override some permission checks: run claude plugin validate and trust the author before installing.
Turn mods off per plugin, per session (--safe-mode), or everywhere (disableAllHooks).
crumbs: 59  59. Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself

title: 59  59.  Mods: Customizing Claude Code Itself
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
In your own words, what is a mod, and how is it different from a settings hook?






Suggested answer





A mod is a plugin containing JavaScript or TypeScript event handlers that Claude Code calls inside its own process when events happen (tool calls, prompts, drawing the screen). A settings hook is a shell command (or web request or prompt) configured in settings.json that runs outside Claude Code at a lifecycle event. Because a mod runs inside Claude Code, it can do things settings hooks can’t, such as draw panes or add instant commands.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which of these can a mod do that a settings hook, a skill, and an MCP server cannot?

Give Claude extra instructions
Draw a pane with buttons inside Claude Code’s interface
Run a shell command after Claude edits a file
Give Claude tools for an outside service







Suggested answer





b. Only a mod can draw in Claude Code’s interface. Instructions (a) are what skills provide, running a command after an edit (c) is a typical settings hook, and tools for an outside service (d) come from an MCP server.





Question 3 · True or false
Mods run in a sandbox, so a mod can’t read the files in your home folder.






Suggested answer





False. Mods aren’t sandboxed. A mod runs with your permissions: it can read and write any file your account can, start programs, make network requests, and read secrets such as API keys. Even with sandboxing on, a process a mod starts runs outside the sandbox.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each built-in mod (as named in /plugin) with what it does.








Built-in mod

What it does




1. cc-plugin-diff

A. Loads AGENTS.md files as project instructions


2. cc-plugin-agents-md

B. Gives Claude the skill for writing mods


3. cc-plugin-plugin-authoring

C. A side agent that shows notes about things you might miss (off by default)


4. cc-plugin-you-should-know

D. Draws the pane for the /diff command









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → A, 3 → B, 4 → C.





Question 5 · Short answer
Mods need a recent version of Claude Code. Which command shows the version you have installed, and where in the /plugin panel can you see which mods a session loaded?






Suggested answer





claude --version shows your version (in the Desktop app’s Code tab, use /status). In /plugin, a dim line under the tabs lists the active mods, such as 1 mod active · first-mod; the Installed tab lists mods, including the built-in ones under Built-in.





Question 6 · Multiple choice
Where do a mod’s handlers run, but its panes and bands don’t appear?

claude in a terminal
The Code tab of the Desktop app
The VS Code extension’s chat panel
claude in VS Code’s built-in terminal







Suggested answer





c. In the VS Code extension’s chat panel (and in claude -p and cloud sessions), the mod’s handlers run but nothing it draws is shown. In a terminal (a), including an editor’s terminal (d), and in the Desktop app’s Code tab (b), drawings appear.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
A classmate shares a mod in the folder ./focus-timer. Write the command that lists what it does without running it, and name the two output lines you should read most carefully.






Suggested answer





claude plugin validate ./focus-timer
Read the hooks: line (which events the mod handles) and the calls: line (what it asks Claude Code to do, such as reading files, starting processes, or making network requests).





Question 8 · Read the output
claude plugin validate prints these lines for a mod. What does the mod react to, and what does it ask Claude Code to do?
  ❯ ./register.js hooks: tool.call, ui.render{component=Spinner}
  ❯ ./register.js calls: $.ui.invalidate






Suggested answer





It handles two events: tool.call (each time Claude is about to use a tool) and ui.render filtered to the Spinner (each time the spinner is drawn). Its only outside action is $.ui.invalidate, asking Claude Code to redraw the interface. It doesn’t read files, start processes, or use the network, so it looks low-risk (this is the tool-call counter from this page).





Question 9 · Matching
Match each goal with the best way to turn mods off.








Goal

Do this




1. Stop one misbehaving mod

A. Start Claude Code with claude --safe-mode


2. Troubleshoot today’s session with no mods (or other customizations)

B. Add "disableAllHooks": true to ~/.claude/settings.json


3. Keep every installed mod off in all future sessions

C. Disable or uninstall its plugin in /plugin









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → B. (Remember that option B also stops your settings hooks and custom status line, and none of them stop built-in mods.)





Question 10 · Write the commands
Write the shell commands to download Anthropic’s sample mods, check the replay-theater sample, and try it for one session only.






Suggested answer





git clone https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-playground.git
claude plugin validate claude-code-playground/claude-code/mods/replay-theater
claude --plugin-dir claude-code-playground/claude-code/mods/replay-theater
--plugin-dir loads the mod for that session only, without installing it.





Question 11 · Predict
On Monday, Maria asks Claude to make a mod and chooses Enable for this session. On Tuesday she starts a new session in another project and the mod isn’t there. Why, and how can she keep using it?






Suggested answer





A mod Claude writes is saved in that session’s folder under ~/.claude/dev-mods/ and loads only in the session that made it (and the folder is eventually deleted). To keep it, she should copy the mod’s folder somewhere permanent, such as ~/mods/my-mod, and start sessions with claude --plugin-dir ~/mods/my-mod (or publish it in a marketplace and install it).





Question 12 · Matching
Match each need with the best tool.








Need

Tool




1. Always see the model name and context percentage at the bottom of the screen

A. Mod


2. Run a formatter after every file edit

B. Skill


3. A pane with buttons that lists the files Claude changed

C. MCP server


4. Let Claude query your team’s database

D. Status line


5. Stop retyping your 10-step release checklist

E. Settings hook









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → E, 3 → A, 4 → C, 5 → B.





Question 13 · Short answer
While Claude writes a mod for you, Claude Code asks about hot reloading. What do Enable for this session and Not now each do?






Suggested answer





Enable for this session loads the mods Claude writes in this session when Claude’s turn ends, and reloads them after each turn that changes them, so you can try changes right away. Not now loads nothing for now; the files stay where Claude wrote them.






Hard

Question 14 · Long answer
How is it possible for claude plugin validate to list what a mod does without running it?






Suggested answer





A mod’s handlers can only reach outside their own code (draw, add a command, call a model, read a file, start a process, use the network) by calling the mods API, the $ object. Mods must write each on('event', ...) and each API call in full (for example $.ui.invalidate), so Claude Code can analyze the source code statically, without executing it, and list the events (hooks:) and the API calls (calls:). That is why the docs say a hook “has no other way” to do those things.





Question 15 · Scenario
Sam finds a mod on a random GitHub account that promises “no more annoying permission prompts”. He uses Claude Code on a personal Pro plan with no managed settings. Explain the specific risks.






Suggested answer





A mod runs with Sam’s permissions and isn’t sandboxed, so it could read his files and secrets (such as API keys), see every prompt, and make network requests. A mod that approves tool calls can approve calls that an ask rule or his own settings hooks would stop, and in auto mode its approvals skip the safety classifier. On a personal setup like his (no managed settings, not Team or Enterprise), it can even approve calls that his deny rules refuse. So “no more prompts” could mean Claude runs dangerous commands with no check. He should not install it unless he trusts the author and has read the code and the claude plugin validate output.





Question 16 · Compare
To stop a misbehaving mod, Maria adds "disableAllHooks": true to ~/.claude/settings.json. What else stops working, and what keeps running?






Suggested answer





Stops: every mod she installed, her settings hooks, and her custom status line. Keeps running: the built-in mods (such as the /diff pane), and the rest of the mod’s plugin, since the plugin stays installed and its skills, commands, agents, and MCP servers still load. Anything her organization manages also keeps running. To stop just one mod, disabling its plugin in /plugin is more precise.





Question 17 · Predict the output
With the tool-call counter mod from this page loaded via --plugin-dir, Claude makes 3 tool calls. Then Maria edits a comment in register.js (the mod hot-reloads), and Claude makes 1 more tool call. What does the spinner show during that last call, and why?






Suggested answer





It shows · tool calls: 1… after the spinner’s word (for example Thinking · tool calls: 1…). A reload runs register again, which starts the code fresh, so calls goes back to 0; the next tool.call makes it 1. (The docs point out this reset; keeping a value across reloads needs the mods API’s state feature.)





Question 18 · Troubleshoot
Sam installed a mod from his team’s marketplace, but nothing it promises appears. List four things he could check.






Suggested answer





Any four of:

his version: claude --version (mods need a recent version);
whether /plugin shows the mod in its mods active line and on the Installed tab (enabled, not disabled);
whether he started with --safe-mode or --bare, or set disableAllHooks, or his organization blocks mods;
whether he accepted the workspace trust prompt for the folder;
whether he ran /reload-plugins (or restarted) after installing from the shell;
whether he uses a surface that doesn’t draw, such as the VS Code chat panel;
claude plugin validate on the mod’s folder, claude plugin test from an empty folder, and the debug log from claude --debug.






Question 19 · Long answer
Your team wants Claude Code to refuse every git push --force. You could use a permission deny rule, a PreToolUse settings hook, or a mod. Compare the options and recommend one for a beginner team.






Suggested answer






A permission deny rule is the simplest: one line in settings, enforced by Claude Code.
A PreToolUse settings hook (exit 2 with a reason) can contain more logic and its reason is fed back to Claude; it needs a small script.
A mod can also refuse the call (its tool.call handler returns { deny: ... }) and could even show a pane with buttons, but it is JavaScript code running inside Claude Code with full permissions, which is more power and more risk than needed.

For a beginner team: a deny rule (optionally plus a settings hook for a helpful message). A mod makes sense only if you want an interactive interface, like the blast-radius sample.






Challenge

Question 20 · Hands-on
In a practice Git repository, ask Claude to “make a mod that shows the current git branch above the prompt”. Choose Enable for this session, try it, then turn it off in /plugin. Describe each step and what you saw.






Suggested answer





A good answer describes: the prompt; the file approvals (in Manual or acceptEdits mode, because ~/.claude is protected); the hot-reloading question and the choice made; the folder Claude used under ~/.claude/dev-mods/; seeing the branch name above the prompt (and checking it changes after git switch); the mod listed on the Installed tab of /plugin; and disabling it there. Bonus: running claude plugin validate on the mod’s folder and explaining its hooks: and calls: lines.





Question 21 · Hands-on
Clone Anthropic’s sample mods, run claude plugin validate on token-weather, and try it for one session with --plugin-dir. Before running it, write down what you expect it to do based on the validate output; afterwards, compare.






Suggested answer





A good answer shows the three commands (git clone ..., claude plugin validate .../token-weather, claude --plugin-dir .../token-weather), copies the hooks: and calls: lines and interprets them (which events it reacts to and whether it touches files, processes, or the network), confirms the mod active line in /plugin, and describes the context-window “forecast” it draws above the prompt as you work. It should end with a short judgment of whether the mod seemed safe and useful.





Question 22 · Long answer
Write a short “mod policy” (5-8 bullet points) for your student team: when a mod is allowed, how a teammate must review one before installing it, how to turn mods off, and what to do if a mod misbehaves.






Suggested answer





A good policy covers the main ideas of this page, for example:

Prefer a settings hook, skill, MCP server, or status line when one of them does the job; use a mod only when you need a pane, a band, an instant command, or to step into tool calls.
Install mods only from authors and marketplaces the team trusts (Anthropic’s samples or the team’s own marketplace).
Before installing, get the files and run claude plugin validate; read the hooks: and calls: lines and the code, and be extra careful with mods that read files, start processes, use the network, or approve tool calls.
Remember that mods aren’t sandboxed and can override ask rules (and, on personal plans, even deny rules), so never install a mod that promises to remove permission prompts.
Try a new mod for one session with --plugin-dir before installing it.
If a mod misbehaves: disable it in /plugin, use claude --safe-mode to troubleshoot, or set "disableAllHooks": true; then tell the team.

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.1 What is a branch?
So far, every commit you made went onto one straight line of history. Branches let you work on a new idea in a separate line of commits without disturbing the working version of your project, and merging brings the finished work back. Branches are the foundation of everything else in this part of the book: teamwork, pull requests, and running several AI agents at once.
Each commit remembers the commit that came before it, so your commits form a chain. A branch is simply a movable label that points at one commit: the newest commit of that line of work. When you commit on a branch, Git moves the label forward to the new commit automatically.
The branch you have used all along is called main. Nothing makes it special except a convention: main holds the working, “official” version of the project.
(Each letter is a commit; A is the oldest.)
Git also keeps a special label called HEAD, which means “the branch you are on right now”. When Git’s output says HEAD -> main, read it as “you are on main”.
Creating a branch is instant. Git does not copy your files; it only writes down a new label.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text: A---B---C   <- main
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.2 Why use branches?

Try ideas safely. If an experiment fails, delete its branch; main was never touched.
Keep main working. Half-finished work lives on its own branch until it is ready.
Work on several things at once. Use one branch per feature or bug fix and switch between them whenever you like.
Work with others (people or AI agents). Each one works on their own branch, and the branches are combined later (see the next pages).
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.3 Creating and listing branches
The examples continue Maria’s git-tutorial-project from the earlier Git pages (it is already on GitHub, see Putting Your Repository on GitHub). Her README says the contact page is next, so she’ll build it on a branch. Your commit IDs will be different, and Git’s messages can vary slightly between versions.
git branch lists your branches. The * marks the one you are on:
git branch
Output:
* main
To create a new branch and switch to it, use git switch -c (-c means “create”):
git switch -c add-contact-page
git branch
Output:
Switched to a new branch 'add-contact-page'
* add-contact-page
  main
The new branch starts at the commit you were on, so for now both labels point to the same commit:
A---B   <- main, add-contact-page (HEAD)
Branch names cannot contain spaces. Use short, lowercase words joined with hyphens that describe the work, such as add-contact-page or fix-login-bug.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.5 Switching branches changes your files
Watch what happens to the src folder when Maria switches back to main:
git switch main
ls src
Output:
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
index.html
contact.html is gone! It isn’t lost: it lives in the add-contact-page branch. When you switch branches, Git rewrites the files in your project folder to match that branch. Run git switch add-contact-page and contact.html comes back. (If a file is open in your editor, the editor shows the new version.)
The line Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main' compares your main with origin/main, Git’s record of where main was on GitHub the last time you pushed or pulled.






Commit before you switch



If you have uncommitted changes that switching would overwrite, Git refuses to switch:
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
    src/index.html
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting
Uncommitted changes that don’t clash are carried along to the other branch, which is confusing. The simple habit: run git status and commit before you switch.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.6 Merging a branch
To merge, first switch to the branch that should receive the work, then name the branch whose work you want to bring in. Maria is back on add-contact-page, so:
git switch main
git merge add-contact-page
Output:
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
Updating c0d14e5..14b4ab2
Fast-forward
 src/contact.html | 11 +++++++++++
 src/index.html   |  2 +-
 2 files changed, 12 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
 create mode 100644 src/contact.html

60.6.1 Fast-forward merge
main had no new commits since the branch started, so Git did the simplest possible thing: it slid the main label forward to D. This is called a fast-forward merge. No new commit is created.
A---B---C---D        <- main (HEAD), add-contact-page


60.6.2 Merge commit
Often both branches move. Maria creates a branch style-links, adds a rule to css/style.css that colors links dark blue, and commits (E). Then she switches back to main, updates the status line in README.md, and commits there too (F):
A---B---C---D-----F          <- main (HEAD)
             \
              '---E          <- style-links
Now Git can’t just slide a label forward. Instead, it creates a new commit:
git merge style-links
Git first opens your text editor with a ready-made message, Merge branch 'style-links'. Accept it by saving and closing the editor (in nano: Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X, as when you pulled on Cloning and Pulling). If you see a screen full of ~ symbols, Git opened the Vim editor: type :wq and press Enter. To skip the editor entirely, run git merge --no-edit style-links instead.
Output:
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 css/style.css | 4 ++++
 1 file changed, 4 insertions(+)
(ort is just the name of Git’s merging method.) The new commit M is a merge commit: it combines both lines of work and has two parent commits.
A---B---C---D-----F-----M    <- main (HEAD)
             \         /
              '---E---'      <- style-links
Git combined the two branches automatically because they changed different files. When two branches change the same lines, you get a merge conflict - that’s the next page, Merge Conflicts.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
section: 60.7 Seeing all branches as a graph
text:
60.7 Seeing all branches as a graph
git log --oneline --graph --all
Output (the oldest commits are cut off here):
*   c2c5ec0 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'style-links'
|\
| * aa25d8c (style-links) Make links dark blue
* | 2fcaf72 Update project status in README
|/
* 14b4ab2 (add-contact-page) Link to contact page from home page
* e5b1cce Add contact page
*   c0d14e5 (origin/main) Merge branch 'main' of https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project
|\
| * 0b2c2b7 Update README.md
* | b25b21a Increase line spacing
|/
* 647a9b5 Add project status to README
Read it from the bottom up. Each * is a commit, the lines on the left show where history splits and joins again, and the names in parentheses are branch labels. --all includes every branch, not only the one you are on. (The lower merge commit, c0d14e5, is the one Maria’s git pull created in Cloning and Pulling.)
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.8 Deleting a branch
Once a branch is merged, its label is no longer needed:
git branch -d add-contact-page style-links
Output:
Deleted branch add-contact-page (was 14b4ab2).
Deleted branch style-links (was aa25d8c).
Only the labels are deleted; the commits remain part of main’s history. As a safety check, git branch -d refuses to delete a branch whose commits have not been merged, and the error message tells you that git branch -D (capital D) forces the deletion. Use -D only when you really want to throw that work away.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.9 Pushing to GitHub
Everything so far happened only on Maria’s computer, as git status reminds her:
git status
Output:
On branch main
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 5 commits.
  (use "git push" to publish your local commits)

nothing to commit, working tree clean
A plain git push sends the updated main to GitHub:
git push
Output (progress lines such as Enumerating objects... omitted):
To https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git
   c0d14e5..c2c5ec0  main -> main
You can also push a branch before merging it, to back it up, to share it with teammates, or to open a pull request (see Pull Requests and Code Review). For example, Maria starts a branch add-footer, commits a page footer, and wants Sam to see it. The first push of a new branch needs -u origin and the branch name:
git push -u origin add-footer
Output (progress lines omitted):
To https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/git-tutorial-project.git
 * [new branch]      add-footer -> add-footer
branch 'add-footer' set up to track 'origin/add-footer'.
-u (short for --set-upstream) connects your local branch to the branch of the same name on GitHub, so from now on a plain git push or git pull works while you are on add-footer. On GitHub, the branch now appears in the branch menu of your repository.






Deeper dive: git checkout, the older way to switch branches





git switch was added in Git 2.23 (2019). Before that, one command, git checkout, did both switching and restoring files. You will still see it in older tutorials, Stack Overflow answers, and sometimes in AI answers:



Older command
Modern equivalent




git checkout main
git switch main


git checkout -b new-branch
git switch -c new-branch



Both styles work. This book uses git switch because its name says what it does. Also, many older repositories call their main branch master instead of main; it works exactly the same way.









Deeper dive: Putting work aside with git stash





Sometimes you are in the middle of something and need to switch branches now, but your work isn’t ready to commit. git stash saves your uncommitted changes on a hidden “shelf” and makes your working directory clean:
git stash
Output:
Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: c2c5ec0 Merge branch 'style-links'
Now you can switch branches freely. When you come back, git stash pop puts the changes back into your files (and removes them from the shelf); git stash list shows what is on the shelf. Stashes are easy to forget, so for anything you want to keep, a commit on your branch is usually the better choice.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.10 Branches and AI coding agents
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Quickstart · Run parallel sessions with worktrees
Before you let Claude Code make a large or risky change, put the work on its own branch. You can type git switch -c try-new-layout yourself or ask in plain English; the Claude Code quickstart suggests prompts such as create a new branch called feature/quickstart. If you like the result, merge the branch into main. If you don’t, switch back to main and delete the branch with git branch -D try-new-layout; main never changed.
Claude Code can also run several sessions at the same time, each in its own folder (a worktree) on its own branch. That is covered in Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
60.11 Key takeaways

A branch is a movable label pointing at a commit; HEAD marks the branch you are on.
git switch -c name creates a branch and switches to it; git switch name switches to an existing one; git branch lists them.
Switching branches rewrites the files in your folder, so commit first.
To merge, switch to the receiving branch and run git merge other-branch. If the receiving branch hasn’t moved, you get a fast-forward; otherwise Git creates a merge commit.
git branch -d name deletes a merged branch’s label; git push -u origin name publishes a new branch on GitHub.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 60  60.  Branches and Merging
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
In one or two sentences, what is a branch in Git?






Suggested answer





A branch is a movable label (a name) that points at a commit - the newest commit of one line of work. When you make a new commit on that branch, Git moves the label forward to the new commit.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which command creates a new branch named fix-typo and switches to it?

git branch fix-typo
git switch -c fix-typo
git switch fix-typo
git merge fix-typo







Suggested answer





b. -c tells git switch to create the branch first. git branch fix-typo (a) creates the branch but leaves you on your current branch. git switch fix-typo (c) only works if the branch already exists. git merge (d) combines branches; it doesn’t create one.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. git branch

A. Delete the label of a merged branch


2. git switch main

B. Show the history of every branch as a graph


3. git merge feature

C. List your branches and mark the current one


4. git branch -d feature

D. Move to the existing branch main


5. git log --oneline --graph --all

E. Bring the commits of feature into the current branch









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → E, 4 → A, 5 → B.





Question 4 · True or false
Creating a branch makes a complete copy of all your project files, so you should avoid creating many branches.






Suggested answer





False. A branch is just a small label that points at a commit. Creating one is instant and copies nothing, so it’s fine to create a branch for every feature, fix, or experiment.





Question 5 · Short answer
In the output of git branch, what does the * mean? And in the output of git log, what does HEAD -> main mean?






Suggested answer





Both tell you which branch you are currently on. In git branch, the * marks the current branch. In git log, HEAD -> main means HEAD (Git’s “you are here” marker) is pointing at the branch main.





Question 6 · True or false
To merge the branch add-faq into main, you should first switch to main.






Suggested answer





True. git merge brings the named branch’s work into the branch you are on. So you switch to the receiving branch (git switch main) and then run git merge add-faq.






Medium

Question 7 · Predict the output
Maria has only one branch, main. She runs:
git switch -c redesign
git branch
What does git branch print?






Suggested answer





  main
* redesign
Both branches exist, and the * shows she is now on redesign (Git lists branches in alphabetical order).





Question 8 · Write the command
You are on the branch add-faq, and its work is finished. Write the commands to merge it into main and then delete the add-faq branch.






Suggested answer





git switch main
git merge add-faq
git branch -d add-faq
You must be on main (the receiving branch) when you merge. After the merge, git branch -d safely removes the label, because its commits are now part of main.





Question 9 · Predict
Maria committed a new file, src/contact.html, on the branch add-contact-page. She has not merged it yet. She runs git switch main and then ls src. Is contact.html listed? Has her work been lost?






Suggested answer





No, contact.html is not listed, but nothing is lost. Switching branches rewrites the files in the project folder to match the branch you switch to, and main doesn’t contain that file yet. The file is safely stored in the add-contact-page branch; git switch add-contact-page brings it back.





Question 10 · Scenario
main points at commit B. Since creating feature from B, you made commits C and D on feature; nobody committed to main. You run git switch main and git merge feature. What kind of merge happens, and is a new commit created?






Suggested answer





A fast-forward merge. Because main hasn’t moved since the branch started, Git simply slides the main label forward to D. No new commit is created, and Git prints Fast-forward.





Question 11 · Scenario
This time, after you created feature, someone also added commit F to main, while feature has commit E. You merge feature into main. What does Git create, and where do the two branch labels point afterwards?






Suggested answer





Git creates a merge commit (call it M) with two parents, F and E, so it contains the work of both branches. Git opens your editor for the merge message (unless you use --no-edit). Afterwards main points at M; feature still points at E, because merging moves only the branch you are on.





Question 12 · Read the output
Use this output to answer the questions below.
*   c2c5ec0 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'style-links'
|\
| * aa25d8c (style-links) Make links dark blue
* | 2fcaf72 Update project status in README
|/
* 14b4ab2 Link to contact page from home page

Which branch are you on?
Which commit is the merge commit?
Which commit was made on style-links before the merge, and which one was made on main?







Suggested answer






main (HEAD -> main).
c2c5ec0, “Merge branch ‘style-links’”. Its two parent lines join at the |\ below it.
aa25d8c was made on style-links (it carries that label). 2fcaf72 was made on main while the branch was in progress. Both started from 14b4ab2.






Question 13 · Write the command
You created a branch add-footer and made two commits on it. Write the command that publishes this branch on GitHub for the first time, so that a plain git push works for it later.






Suggested answer





git push -u origin add-footer
origin is the GitHub remote, and -u (--set-upstream) connects your local add-footer to origin/add-footer, so later pushes and pulls on this branch need no extra arguments.





Question 14 · Multiple choice
After merging two branches into main on her laptop, Maria runs git status and sees Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 5 commits. What does this mean?

Five commits were lost during the merge.
GitHub has five commits that Maria doesn’t have yet.
Maria’s main has five commits that are not on GitHub yet; she should run git push.
Maria must delete five branches before she can push.







Suggested answer





c. origin/main is where main was on GitHub when Maria last talked to GitHub. “Ahead by 5” means her local main has five commits that GitHub doesn’t have, because merging happened only on her computer. git push sends them. Nothing was lost (a), it’s not GitHub that is ahead (b - that would say “behind”), and branches don’t block pushing (d).






Hard

Question 15 · Find the bug
Sam edited src/index.html on his branch but didn’t commit. When he runs git switch main, he gets:
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
    src/index.html
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting
Explain what Git is protecting him from, and give two different ways he could continue.






Suggested answer





src/index.html is different on main, so switching would overwrite Sam’s uncommitted edits with main’s version - and uncommitted work can’t be recovered. Git refuses instead of destroying his work. He can:

Commit the changes on his current branch (git add src/index.html, git commit -m "..."), then switch.
Stash them (git stash), switch, and later return and run git stash pop.

(If he doesn’t want the edits at all, git restore src/index.html discards them - permanently.)





Question 16 · Scenario
Maria runs git branch -d experiment and Git refuses, saying the branch is not fully merged. What does that mean, and what should she do if (a) she wants to keep the work, or (b) she is sure the experiment was a failure?






Suggested answer





It means experiment has commits that are not part of the branch she is on, so deleting the label would make that work hard or impossible to find again.

To keep the work: merge it first (git switch main, git merge experiment), then git branch -d experiment succeeds.
To throw it away: git branch -D experiment (capital D) forces the deletion. Its unmerged commits are then effectively lost, so be sure.






Question 17 · True or false
After a branch has been merged into main, running git branch -d on it deletes the commits that were made on that branch.






Suggested answer





False. Only the label is removed. The commits were merged into main and remain in its history (you can still see them with git log).





Question 18 · Compare
Compare a fast-forward merge with a merge that creates a merge commit: when does each happen, and how does the history look afterwards?






Suggested answer






Fast-forward: happens when the receiving branch (e.g. main) has no new commits since the other branch started. Git just moves the main label forward to the other branch’s latest commit. No new commit is created and history stays one straight line.
Merge commit: happens when both branches have new commits. Git creates a new commit with two parents that combines both lines of work. In git log --graph, history splits and joins again at the merge commit.

A good answer mentions the condition (has the receiving branch moved?), whether a new commit appears, and the shape of the history.





Question 19 · Long answer
You want Claude Code to try a risky redesign of your website, and you’re not sure you’ll like the result. Describe a branch-based way to work that keeps main safe. Include what you do if you like the result and what you do if you don’t.






Suggested answer






Commit (or otherwise clean up) your current work so git status is clean.
Create a branch for the experiment: git switch -c redesign (or ask Claude Code to create one), and let Claude make and commit its changes there.
Review and test the redesign (look at the diff, open the site).
If you like it: git switch main, git merge redesign, then git branch -d redesign and git push.
If you don’t: git switch main and git branch -D redesign. main never changed, so nothing needs to be undone.

A good answer stresses that all of Claude’s changes stay on the experiment branch until you decide to merge.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.1 When do conflicts happen?
Most merges happen automatically. But when two branches change the same lines of a file in different ways, Git can’t know which version you want, so it stops and asks you to decide. This is a merge conflict. Conflicts are a normal part of working with branches, teammates, and AI agents, and once you have resolved one or two, they are not scary.
Git merges files line by line:
The same thing can happen with git pull, because a pull ends with a merge (see Sharing a Repository). When a conflict happens, nothing is lost: Git keeps both versions and shows you exactly where they disagree.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
What the two branches changed
Result of the merge




Different files
Merged automatically


Different parts of the same file (with unchanged lines between them)
Merged automatically


The same lines (or lines right next to each other), in different ways
Conflict - you decide


One branch deleted a file, the other edited it
Conflict - you decide
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.2 A conflict, step by step
The easiest way to learn is to create a conflict on purpose. Maria continues from Branches and Merging. In src/index.html, her introduction line reads:
    <p>Hi, I'm Maria. I study business and build websites.</p>

She creates a branch new-intro, changes the page title to Maria Lopez - Portfolio, rewrites the intro line as <p>Hi, I'm Maria, a business student who builds websites.</p>, and commits.
She switches back to main, changes the same intro line differently, to <p>Hi, I'm Maria. I study business and love building websites.</p>, and commits again.

Both branches changed the intro line, so merging them conflicts:
git merge new-intro
Output:
Auto-merging src/index.html
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/index.html
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
The merge is now paused. Git is waiting for you.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.4 Resolving the conflict

Decide what the file should say. Keep your version, keep the other version, or combine them. Maria combines them:
    <p>Hi, I'm Maria, a business student who loves building websites.</p>
Delete all three marker lines (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) and save the file. A file that still contains markers is broken: the markers would appear on the web page. Before you stage the file, git diff --check lists any leftover markers (it also flags stray spaces at the ends of lines) and prints nothing when the file is clean:
git diff --check
Mark the file as resolved by staging it:
git add src/index.html
git status
Output:
On branch main
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit.
  (use "git push" to publish your local commits)

All conflicts fixed but you are still merging.
  (use "git commit" to conclude merge)

Changes to be committed:
 modified:   src/index.html
Finish the merge with a commit:
git commit
Git opens your editor with the message Merge branch 'new-intro' already filled in (plus some comment lines starting with #, which Git ignores). Save and close to accept it (in nano: Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).
Output:
[main cd24c15] Merge branch 'new-intro'

The history now shows the merge commit joining the two branches:
git log --oneline --graph
Output (older commits cut off):
*   cd24c15 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'new-intro'
|\
| * 0f4ca56 (new-intro) Update title and intro
* | ed29994 Reword intro
|/
*   c2c5ec0 (origin/main) Merge branch 'style-links'
Finally, Maria tests the page in her browser, deletes the merged branch (git branch -d new-intro), and runs git push.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.5 Changing your mind: git merge --abort
If a conflict is bigger than you expected, or you are not sure which version is right, you can cancel the whole merge before you commit it:
git merge --abort
This prints nothing; your files and branch go back to exactly how they were before you ran git merge, and git status shows a clean working tree again. You can talk to your teammate, then try the merge later.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.6 Conflicts when you pull
git pull downloads new commits and then merges them, so a teammate’s edit to the same lines produces the same kind of conflict, and you resolve it the same way (edit, git add, git commit). The only visible difference is that the bottom marker shows a long commit ID instead of a branch name, for example >>>>>>> 2d96bf5be8abfe33f58d30404c943a4cb773bfe6. Pulling in teams is covered in Sharing a Repository.






Deeper dive: Keeping one whole side of a file





If you know you want all of one version of a conflicted file, you don’t have to edit the markers by hand. To keep your current branch’s version of the whole file:
git restore --ours src/index.html
Or, to keep the incoming branch’s version instead:
git restore --theirs src/index.html
Then git add the file and git commit as usual. During a merge, “ours” is the branch you are on and “theirs” is the branch you are merging in. (Careful: during a rebase, Git swaps these two meanings.)
Many editors, including VS Code, also highlight conflict markers and offer one-click buttons to keep one side or both. They edit the same markers for you, so the steps afterwards (git add, git commit) are the same.









Deeper dive: Other kinds of conflicts






Modify/delete: one branch deleted a file that the other branch edited. Git reports CONFLICT (modify/delete) and git status shows, for example, deleted by them: css/style.css. Resolve it by keeping the file (git add css/style.css) or deleting it (git rm css/style.css), then commit.
Binary files such as images: Git can’t put markers inside a picture. Pick one version with git restore --ours or --theirs, then git add.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.7 Avoiding conflicts (and keeping them small)

Pull often and merge main into your branch regularly, so you find differences while they are small.
Keep branches short-lived and commits small and focused. A branch that lives for weeks drifts far from main.
Communicate. Agree on who is working on which files or features.
Don’t reformat whole files (or let an editor or AI do it) as part of an unrelated change. Changing the indentation of 300 lines creates 300 conflicting lines for everyone else.
Give parallel AI agents separate areas of the code (see Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents).
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.8 Getting help from Claude Code
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Prompt library · Quickstart
Claude Code can resolve conflicts for you. The Claude Code prompt library includes this prompt:
resolve the merge conflicts in this branch and explain what you kept from each side
Claude reads both versions, edits the files, and explains its choices. That explanation matters, because the AI only sees the code: it doesn’t know which change your team actually wanted. Before you commit Claude’s resolution:

Read the explanation and the changes. git diff HEAD shows everything the merge will change compared with your last commit, even in files Claude has already staged. Is each choice what the authors of both branches intended?
Make sure no markers are left with git diff HEAD --check. (Plain git diff --check misses markers in files that have already been staged with git add, which Claude may have done.)
Run the app or the tests and check the result in the browser.
If you want to review first, say so in the prompt, for example “…but don’t commit; I’ll review it first.”
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
61.9 Key takeaways

A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines differently (or one deletes a file the other edits). Nothing is lost.
Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your current branch’s version; between ======= and >>>>>>> other-branch is the incoming version.
To resolve: edit the file, remove all markers, git add the file, then git commit.
git merge --abort cancels a merge that you haven’t committed yet.
Pull often, keep branches short, and coordinate to avoid conflicts. Review any AI-made resolution before committing.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 61  61.  Merge Conflicts
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
When does Git report a merge conflict?

Every time you merge two branches.
When both branches changed the same lines of a file in different ways.
When a branch has more than three commits.
When you merge a branch that was pushed to GitHub.







Suggested answer





b. Git merges automatically whenever the changes don’t overlap. Only overlapping changes to the same lines (or a deleted-versus-edited file) need a human decision. Most merges don’t conflict (a), and the number of commits (c) or where a branch has been pushed (d) doesn’t matter.





Question 2 · Matching
Match each part of a conflict with its meaning.








Part

Meaning




1. <<<<<<< HEAD

A. Separates the two versions


2. Lines between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======

B. End of the conflict, naming the branch being merged in


3. =======

C. Your current branch’s version


4. Lines between ======= and >>>>>>>

D. Start of the conflict


5. >>>>>>> new-intro

E. The incoming branch’s version









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → C, 3 → A, 4 → E, 5 → B.





Question 3 · True or false
A merge conflict means that Git has lost part of your work.






Suggested answer





False. Git keeps both versions and writes them into the file between conflict markers. It only needs you to decide what the final version should be.





Question 4 · Fill in the blank
After editing a conflicted file and removing the markers, you mark the file as resolved with git ______ <file> and finish the merge with git ______.






Suggested answer





git add <file> and then git commit. Staging the file tells Git the conflict in it is resolved; the commit creates the merge commit.





Question 5 · Short answer
What does git merge --abort do, and when can you use it?






Suggested answer





It cancels the merge in progress and puts your files and branch back exactly as they were before you ran git merge. You can use it while the merge is paused by a conflict, before you have committed the merge.





Question 6 · True or false
Maria changes line 3 of README.md on her branch, and Sam changes line 40 of the same file on his. Merging the two branches will always produce a conflict.






Suggested answer





False. Git merges line by line. Changes to different, non-adjacent parts of the same file are combined automatically. Only overlapping changes conflict.






Medium

Question 7 · Ordering
Put these steps for handling a conflict in the right order:

A. Run git commit
B. Run git merge feature and see CONFLICT
C. Edit the file so it contains the right text, and delete the markers
D. Run git status to see which files are conflicted
E. Run git add on the fixed file







Suggested answer





B → D → C → E → A. Start the merge, find the conflicted files, fix each file (removing all markers), stage it, then commit to complete the merge.





Question 8 · Read the output
Sam is on main and runs git merge price-update. Part of menu.html now looks like this:
<<<<<<< HEAD
    <p>Coffee: $3.00</p>
=======
    <p>Coffee: $3.50</p>
>>>>>>> price-update
Which price is on main, and which is on price-update? If the new price is correct, what should this part of the file look like after resolving?






Suggested answer





$3.00 is on main (the HEAD section, between <<<<<<< and =======), and $3.50 is on price-update (between ======= and >>>>>>>). Resolved, the part should be just:
    <p>Coffee: $3.50</p>
with all three marker lines removed.





Question 9 · Write the resolution
Two teammates each added a different item at the end of the same list:
    <li>Home</li>
<<<<<<< HEAD
    <li>About</li>
=======
    <li>Contact</li>
>>>>>>> add-contact-link
Both links should stay. Write the resolved lines.






Suggested answer





    <li>Home</li>
    <li>About</li>
    <li>Contact</li>
Combining both sides is often the right answer when both people added something useful. The markers must be gone.





Question 10 · Short answer
During a conflict, where in the output of git status do you find the conflicted files, and what label does a file get when both branches changed it?






Suggested answer





Under the heading Unmerged paths, where each conflicted file is labeled both modified: (for example both modified:   src/index.html).





Question 11 · Write the command
You think you have removed all conflict markers from your files, but you want Git to double-check before you stage them. Which command lists leftover markers?






Suggested answer





git diff --check. It prints a line such as src/index.html:9: leftover conflict marker for each marker it finds and prints nothing when the files are clean. (Searching with grep -n "<<<<<<<" src/index.html also works.)





Question 12 · Scenario
In the middle of resolving a conflict in five files, Maria realizes she doesn’t understand Sam’s changes and wants to talk to him first. She hasn’t committed anything yet. What should she do?






Suggested answer





Run git merge --abort. It cancels the merge and restores her branch and files to the state before the merge, so she can talk to Sam and redo the merge later.





Question 13 · Scenario
Sam runs git pull and gets a conflict. The end marker in his file reads >>>>>>> 2d96bf5be8abfe33f58d30404c943a4cb773bfe6 instead of a branch name. Why, and does he resolve it differently from a branch merge?






Suggested answer





git pull downloads the new commits from GitHub and merges them, and Git labels the incoming side with the commit ID it is merging instead of a local branch name. The resolution is exactly the same: edit the file, remove the markers, git add it, and git commit.






Hard

Question 14 · Find the bug
After a conflict, Maria ran git add src/index.html and git commit immediately. Now her home page shows <<<<<<< HEAD and >>>>>>> new-heading as text. What went wrong, why didn’t Git stop her, and how should she fix it?






Suggested answer





She staged and committed the file without editing it, so the conflict markers were committed as ordinary text. Git doesn’t check file contents when you run git add: staging is how you tell Git the conflict is resolved. To fix it, she edits the file to the correct text, deletes the markers, checks with git diff --check, then git add src/index.html and commits the fix (for example git commit -m "Remove leftover conflict markers").





Question 15 · Long answer
Why can’t Git simply keep the newest change when two branches edit the same line? Use an example.






Suggested answer





Git doesn’t understand what the text means, and “newest” isn’t necessarily “right”. Example: Maria changes a price to $3.50 because of a supplier increase, and later Sam changes the same line to Coffee (large): $3.00 to add a size. Keeping only the newer line would silently undo Maria’s price change; the correct result might be Coffee (large): $3.50. Only a person who knows the intent of both changes can decide, so Git stops and asks.





Question 16 · Scenario
You asked Claude Code to “resolve the merge conflicts in this branch and explain what you kept from each side”. It says it’s done. List what you should check before committing the merge.






Suggested answer






Read Claude’s explanation and the actual changes (git status, and git diff HEAD, which also covers files Claude has already staged). Does each choice match what both authors intended? The AI only sees the code, not your team’s decisions.
Confirm that no conflict markers are left (git diff HEAD --check, which also checks files Claude has already staged).
Run the app or tests and check the affected pages.
Only then git add and git commit (or let Claude commit after your review).






Question 17 · Long answer
Three students are building one website together. Give four habits that will reduce merge conflicts, and briefly say why each one helps.






Suggested answer





Any four of these, with reasons:

Pull often / merge main into your branch regularly - you see others’ changes early, while differences are small.
Keep branches short-lived and commits small - less time to drift apart, and smaller conflicts when they happen.
Agree who works on which files or features - fewer people editing the same lines.
Don’t reformat whole files in unrelated changes - reformatting touches every line and conflicts with everyone.
Push finished work promptly - others build on the latest version.






Question 18 · Scenario
Two AI coding sessions worked in parallel on the same website. One added a dark theme to css/style.css; the other was asked to “clean up the CSS” and re-indented and reordered the whole file. Why is merging these two branches likely to be painful, and how could it have been avoided?






Suggested answer





The clean-up changed almost every line of css/style.css, and the dark theme also changed that file, so the two branches overlap nearly everywhere and the merge produces large conflicts that are hard to read. To avoid it: give parallel sessions separate files or areas, avoid whole-file reformatting while other work is in progress (or do it alone, merged quickly, before other branches start), and merge small changes often.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
62.1 Two ways to work together
Until now, only you pushed to your GitHub repository. This page covers the two ways to work on a repository with other people - collaborators on one shared repository, and forks - and the habits that keep a shared project running smoothly.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
Collaborators (one shared repository)
Fork (your own copy)




What it is
The owner invites people; everyone pushes to the same repository
You copy someone else’s repository into your own GitHub account


Who can push to the original?
Every collaborator
Only its owners; you propose changes with a pull request


Typical use
A class team project, a small team
Open-source projects, starter code from a course or tutorial, any repository you can’t push to
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
62.2 Adding collaborators
Maria (GitHub username maria-lopez) wants Sam to work on her git-tutorial-project. On GitHub she:

Opens the repository and clicks Settings (under the repository name).
In the Access section of the sidebar, clicks Collaborators.
Clicks Add people, types Sam’s GitHub username, picks him from the list, and confirms (Add NAME to REPOSITORY).

Sam receives an email invitation. Only after he accepts it can he push to the repository. (If you sign in to Git with a personal access token: GitHub doesn’t let fine-grained tokens push to a repository where you are a collaborator, so use browser sign-in or a classic token instead.) Then he clones it, just as on Cloning and Pulling:
git clone https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project.git
Output (progress lines omitted):
Cloning into 'git-tutorial-project'...
Sam now has the full project and history, with origin pointing at Maria’s repository. Every collaborator follows the same routine:

git pull before you start, so you have everyone’s latest work.
Work and commit (ideally on a branch, as on the next page).
git pull again just before you push.
git push.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
62.3 When your push is rejected
On Cloning and Pulling you saw that GitHub rejects a push when it has commits you don’t have, and that the fix is git pull, then git push. On a team this happens all the time, because everyone pushes to the same main.
Sam adds a “Team” section to the README, commits (“Add team section to README”), and pushes. Meanwhile Maria, who hasn’t pulled, adds max-width to css/style.css, commits (“Limit page width”), and pushes:
git push
Output (the hint: lines that follow are omitted):
To https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project.git
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project.git'
The two main branches have simply moved apart:
On GitHub:          A---B---S     (S = Sam's commit)
On Maria's laptop:  A---B---L     (L = Maria's commit)
A push may only add commits on top of what is already on GitHub. Pushing Maria’s main as it is would replace S with L and throw away Sam’s work, so Git refuses. Maria pulls and then pushes:
git pull
git push
Output (progress lines omitted):
From https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project
   cd24c15..6ea40b6  main       -> origin/main
Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
 README.md | 5 +++++
 1 file changed, 5 insertions(+)
To https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project.git
   6ea40b6..333e3a2  main -> main
Because both sides had new commits, and Git is set to merge when it pulls (the pull.rebase false setting from Installing and Configuring Git), the pull created a merge commit M. In between, Git opened the editor with the message Merge branch 'main' of https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project; Maria saved and closed it (in nano: Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X). Sam’s commit is now part of her main, so the push could simply add to GitHub’s branch:
A---B---L---M     <- main (Maria)
     \     /
      '-S-'       <- Sam's commit, from GitHub
If Sam and Maria had changed the same lines, the pull would have stopped with a conflict; she would resolve it as on Merge Conflicts and then push.
You may see either of two rejection messages. Both mean “GitHub has commits that your branch doesn’t include yet”, and both are fixed by pulling first:







Message
What it means




! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)
GitHub has commits you have never downloaded.


! [rejected] main -> main (non-fast-forward)
You downloaded them (with git fetch), but you haven’t merged them into your branch yet.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
62.4 git fetch vs. git pull
git fetch downloads new commits from GitHub and updates origin/main (Git’s record of GitHub’s main), but it doesn’t change your files or your own main. git pull is a fetch followed by a merge (or a rebase, if you configured that).



Command
Downloads new commits?
Changes your branch and files?




git fetch
Yes (updates origin/main)
No


git pull
Yes
Yes



Fetching first lets you look before you merge. After Maria’s push, Sam runs:
git fetch
git status
Output (progress lines omitted):
From https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project
   6ea40b6..333e3a2  main       -> origin/main
On branch main
Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 2 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.
  (use "git pull" to update your local branch)

nothing to commit, working tree clean
git log --oneline --graph --all would now show the two new commits on origin/main. When he is ready, Sam merges them, which is exactly the second half of a pull:
git merge origin/main
Output:
Updating 6ea40b6..333e3a2
Fast-forward
 css/style.css | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)






Deeper dive: Pulling with rebase instead of merge





Instead of creating a merge commit, git pull --rebase takes your new local commits and replays them on top of the commits it downloaded, so history stays one straight line. Before (you committed L locally while a teammate pushed T):
      .---L          <- main (your laptop)
     /
A---B---T            <- origin/main
After git pull --rebase:
A---B---T---L'       <- main
        ^
   origin/main
L' has the same changes as L but a new commit ID. Git prints Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main., and you can push. To make rebasing the default, set git config --global pull.rebase true instead of false.
Rebasing rewrites the commits being replayed, so only rebase commits that nobody else has yet (your unpushed local commits, which is exactly what git pull --rebase does). If a rebase hits a conflict, fix the file, run git add, then git rebase --continue (or git rebase --abort to undo it).
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
62.5 Forks
A fork is your own copy of someone else’s repository, made on GitHub and stored under your account. You can push to your fork freely; to suggest your changes to the original project, you open a pull request (next page). The original repository is usually called upstream.
A fork is not the same as a clone: a fork is a copy on GitHub; a clone is a copy on your computer. Usually you do both:
   ORIGINAL-OWNER/REPO on GitHub      <-- the original ("upstream")
        |                   ^
        | 1. Fork           | 5. Pull request
        v                   |
   YOUR-USERNAME/REPO on GitHub       <-- your fork ("origin")
        |                   ^
        | 2. git clone      | 4. git push
        v                   |
   REPO folder on your computer       <-- 3. branch, edit, commit
To fork, open the original repository on GitHub, click Fork, choose your account as the owner, and click Create fork. (The tutorial step Fork the repo and clone it does exactly this with the tutorial’s starter code.) Then clone your fork and add a second remote, conventionally named upstream, that points at the original:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/REPO.git
cd REPO
git remote add upstream https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/REPO.git
git remote -v
Output (progress lines omitted):
Cloning into 'REPO'...
origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/REPO.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/REPO.git (push)
upstream    https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/REPO.git (fetch)
upstream    https://github.com/ORIGINAL-OWNER/REPO.git (push)
Your fork doesn’t update itself when the original changes. To bring in the original’s new commits, fetch from upstream, merge, and push to your fork:
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main
git push
On GitHub, the Sync fork button on your fork’s page (then Update branch) does the same for the fork on GitHub; afterwards, run git pull on your computer. If you use the GitHub CLI, gh repo fork ORIGINAL-OWNER/REPO --clone creates the fork and clones it in one step (run git remote -v afterwards to see the remotes it set up).
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
62.6 Team etiquette

Pull before you start; push when you finish. The longer you wait, the further your copy drifts from everyone else’s.
Small commits with clear messages. Your teammates have to read them.
Use branches and pull requests instead of everyone committing straight to main (see Pull Requests and Code Review).
Never commit secrets such as API keys (see .gitignore and Keeping Secrets Out of Git).







Never force-push a shared branch



When a push is rejected, you may find advice (sometimes from an AI) to run git push --force. A force push makes GitHub’s branch match yours exactly, deleting any commits on GitHub that you don’t have, such as your teammate’s work from this morning. On a shared branch like main, always pull and then push instead. The variant git push --force-with-lease refuses if GitHub’s branch changed since you last fetched, but it still rewrites shared history. Repository owners can protect main on GitHub with branch protection rules, which by default block force pushes to the protected branch.



62.6.1 AI agents in a shared repository
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Manage multiple agents with agent view · How Claude remembers your project
Claude Code can run Git commands, including git push, so it should follow your team’s rules too. When Claude Code works in a background session in its own worktree, its built-in instructions are to commit its work and push its branch (opening a draft pull request when the task calls for it), but never to push to main or master, force-push, or merge. Write your team’s own rules in the project’s CLAUDE.md (for example “never push to main; never force-push”). The docs say your Git instructions take precedence: for example, if CLAUDE.md says you handle committing or pushing yourself, Claude leaves Git to you. Review what an agent changed before anything reaches a shared branch.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
62.7 Key takeaways

Collaborators share one repository and can all push; a fork is your own copy of someone else’s repository, and you contribute back with pull requests.
A rejected push (“fetch first” or “non-fast-forward”) means GitHub has commits you don’t. Fix it with git pull, then git push.
git fetch only downloads; git pull downloads and merges (or rebases).
In a fork, origin is your fork and upstream is the original; update with git fetch upstream and git merge upstream/main.
Never force-push a shared branch.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
62  62. Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks

title: 62  62.  Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
In which situation do you need a fork rather than being added as a collaborator?

You and two classmates are building your team’s project in a repository one of you owns.
You want to contribute a fix to a public open-source project whose owners you don’t know.
You want to work on your own repository from a second computer.
You want to see the history of your own project.







Suggested answer





b. You can’t push to a stranger’s repository, so you fork it, push to your fork, and open a pull request. A team project (a) is the classic case for collaborators. Working from a second computer (c) only needs git clone and git pull, and viewing history (d) needs git log.





Question 2 · True or false
As soon as Maria adds Sam as a collaborator on GitHub, Sam can push to her repository, even before he responds to the invitation.






Suggested answer





False. Sam receives an invitation and gets collaborator access only after he accepts it.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. git clone URL

A. Download new commits and merge them into your current branch


2. git fetch

B. Send your new commits to the remote


3. git pull

C. Copy a repository from GitHub to your computer


4. git push

D. Connect your clone to the original repository of a fork


5. git remote add upstream URL

E. Download new commits without changing your files or branch









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → A, 4 → B, 5 → D.





Question 4 · Short answer
What is origin/main?






Suggested answer





It is Git’s record (on your computer) of where the main branch on the remote origin (GitHub) was the last time you talked to GitHub with git fetch, git pull, or git push. It doesn’t update by itself.





Question 5 · True or false
git fetch changes the files in your working directory.






Suggested answer





False. git fetch only downloads new commits and updates origin/main. Your files and your own main stay the same until you merge (or pull).





Question 6 · Short answer
You forked a project and cloned your fork. By convention, what do the remotes origin and upstream point to?






Suggested answer





origin points to your fork on GitHub (YOUR-USERNAME/REPO), because that is what you cloned. upstream points to the original repository (ORIGINAL-OWNER/REPO), which you add with git remote add upstream URL.






Medium

Question 7 · Read the output
Maria runs git push and sees:
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project.git'
What happened, and what should she do?






Suggested answer





Someone (here, Sam) pushed commits to main on GitHub that Maria doesn’t have. Her push would have thrown them away, so Git refused. She should run git pull to download and merge Sam’s commits (resolving any conflict), then run git push again.





Question 8 · Write the command
Write the commands Maria uses to fix the rejected push in Question 7, and describe what might happen between the two commands.






Suggested answer





git pull
git push
Between them, the pull downloads Sam’s commit and merges it. Because both sides have new commits, it creates a merge commit and opens the editor for its message (accept it). If both of them changed the same lines, the pull stops with a merge conflict instead, which she must resolve (edit the file, git add, git commit) before pushing.





Question 9 · Read the output
After running git fetch, Sam sees this in git status:
Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 2 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.
What does this mean, and which command brings his main up to date?






Suggested answer





GitHub’s main has two commits that his local main doesn’t, and he has no new commits of his own, so a fast-forward is possible. git merge origin/main (or simply git pull) moves his main forward to match.





Question 10 · Compare
A rejected push can end with (fetch first) or with (non-fast-forward). What is the difference between the two situations, and what do you do in each?






Suggested answer






(fetch first): GitHub has commits that your computer has never downloaded.
(non-fast-forward): you have already downloaded them (for example with git fetch, so origin/main knows about them), but your branch doesn’t include them yet.

The fix is the same in both cases: git pull (merging GitHub’s commits into your branch, resolving any conflicts), then git push.





Question 11 · Write the command
Your fork already has an upstream remote. The original project has new commits on main. Write the commands to bring them into your local main and then update your fork on GitHub.






Suggested answer





git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main
git push
git push sends the result to origin, which is your fork. (Alternatively, use Sync fork on GitHub and then git pull.)





Question 12 · Ordering
Put these steps for contributing to an open-source project in order:

A. Push your branch to your fork
B. Click Fork on the original repository
C. Open a pull request to the original repository
D. Clone your fork to your computer
E. Create a branch and commit your changes







Suggested answer





B → D → E → A → C. Fork on GitHub, clone your fork, work on a branch, push the branch to your fork (origin), then open a pull request asking the original project to merge it.





Question 13 · Multiple choice
Which statement about git pull is correct?

It uploads your commits to GitHub.
It downloads new commits and then merges (or rebases) them into your current branch.
It only works in forked repositories.
It deletes your local commits and replaces them with GitHub’s.







Suggested answer





b. A pull is a fetch followed by a merge (or a rebase, if configured). Uploading is git push (a). Pull works with any remote (c), and it keeps your local commits (d); it combines them with the downloaded ones.






Hard

Question 14 · Short answer
Explain why Git refuses a push when GitHub’s main has a commit you don’t have. What would happen to that commit if Git allowed the push?






Suggested answer





A normal push may only add commits on top of the branch on GitHub (a fast-forward). Your main doesn’t contain the other person’s commit, so making GitHub’s main equal to yours would drop that commit from the branch - your teammate’s work would disappear from main. Git refuses so that you integrate the work first (git pull) and then push a history that includes both.





Question 15 · Scenario
Sam’s push to main is rejected. A classmate says, “Just use git push --force, it always works.” Explain what would happen to the team and what Sam should do instead.






Suggested answer





A force push makes GitHub’s main exactly match Sam’s local main, so every commit on GitHub that Sam doesn’t have - for example Maria’s latest work - is removed from the branch. Teammates’ later pulls would get confusing results, and the work may be lost. Instead Sam should run git pull (resolving any conflicts) and then a normal git push. Teams can also protect main on GitHub so force pushes are blocked.





Question 16 · Compare
Compare git pull (with merge) and git pull --rebase. What does each do with your local commits, and why is git pull --rebase considered safe while rebasing commits you already pushed is not?






Suggested answer






Merge: keeps your local commits as they are and adds a merge commit that joins them with the downloaded commits. History shows a split and a join.
Rebase: replays your local commits on top of the downloaded ones, giving a straight history without a merge commit. The replayed commits get new IDs.

Rebasing changes commit IDs. With git pull --rebase, only your unpushed commits are replayed - nobody else has them yet, so nothing breaks. Rebasing commits others already have would give them different versions of “the same” commits and cause confusion and duplicated work.





Question 17 · Read the output
Sam sees this in git status:
Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged,
and have 1 and 1 different commits each, respectively.
Explain what “diverged” means here and what Sam should do before pushing.






Suggested answer





Both sides moved since they last matched: Sam’s main has 1 commit that GitHub doesn’t have, and GitHub’s main has 1 commit that Sam doesn’t have. A push would be rejected (non-fast-forward). He should run git pull (merge, or git pull --rebase) to combine the two lines of work, resolve any conflicts, and then git push.





Question 18 · Long answer
You are setting up a shared repository for a three-person student team that will also use Claude Code. Write five short team rules for working with Git and GitHub, and explain one of them.






Suggested answer





A model answer:

Pull before you start and before you push.
Do your work on a branch and merge it through a pull request; nobody commits directly to main.
Never force-push a shared branch (and protect main on GitHub).
Keep commits small with clear messages; never commit secrets.
Put these rules in CLAUDE.md and review everything an AI agent changes before it is pushed or merged.

Explanation (for example, rule 3): a force push replaces GitHub’s branch with yours and silently removes teammates’ commits, so the team agrees to pull and merge instead.





Question 19 · Scenario
Your team lets Claude Code work on tasks in background sessions in your shared repository. According to the Claude Code docs (as of Oct 2026), what does such a session do with its finished work, which Git actions does it avoid, and how can your team add its own Git rules?






Suggested answer





A background session that edited files in its own worktree commits its work and pushes its branch (and may open a draft pull request when the task calls for it). It never pushes to main or master, never force-pushes, and never merges. The team can write its own Git rules in the project’s CLAUDE.md; the docs say your Git instructions take precedence. People still review the work before it is merged.

63.1 What is a pull request?
On a team, nobody should merge their own work into main without anyone else looking at it. A pull request is GitHub’s way of asking “please review my branch and merge it”. This page covers the standard team workflow, code review, and how Claude Code can help (you stay responsible for what gets merged).
A pull request (often called a PR) is a request, on GitHub, to merge one branch into another, usually a feature branch into main. Each pull request gets its own web page with:
The name comes from asking the project to “pull” your changes in. (GitLab calls the same thing a merge request.) Pull requests also work across forks: you push a branch to your fork and open a pull request to the original repository (see Sharing a Repository).

text:
63.2 The GitHub Flow
Most teams follow a simple routine called the GitHub Flow:
1. Branch      git switch -c add-projects-page
2. Commit      git add ... and git commit ...  (as often as you like)
3. Push        git push -u origin add-projects-page
4. Open a PR   on github.com, or with gh pr create
5. Review      teammates comment, approve, or request changes;
               new commits pushed to the branch update the PR
6. Merge       on github.com, or with gh pr merge
7. Clean up    delete the branch; git switch main; git pull
main only ever receives reviewed work, and every change has a page that explains why it was made.

text:
63.3 Steps 1-3: Branch, commit, and push
Next on the team’s list is a projects page (issue #1), and Sam takes the job. He starts from an up-to-date main, creates a branch, and commits his work there (“Add projects page”, “Link to projects page from home page”), exactly as on Branches and Merging:
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c add-projects-page
Then he pushes the branch to GitHub:
git push -u origin add-projects-page
Output (progress lines omitted):
To https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project.git
 * [new branch]      add-projects-page -> add-projects-page
branch 'add-projects-page' set up to track 'origin/add-projects-page'.
