title: 63  63.  Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
63.4 Step 4: Open the pull request
On github.com: open the repository. Right after a push, a yellow banner offers Compare & pull request; click it. Check the two branch menus: base is where the changes should go (main) and compare is your branch (add-projects-page). Write a title and a description, then click Create pull request. If the work isn’t finished yet but you want early feedback, open the menu next to that button and choose a draft pull request instead.
From the terminal: the GitHub CLI (gh, which you may have installed for signing in on Putting Your Repository on GitHub) can do the same:
gh pr create --title "Add projects page" --body "Adds src/projects.html and links it from the home page. Fixes #1"
gh prints the web address of the new pull request. Useful options:







Option
What it does




--fill
Use your commit messages for the title and description


--draft
Open it as a draft


--base main
Choose the branch to merge into (the default is the repository’s default branch)


--reviewer USERNAME
Ask a teammate to review it


--web
Finish creating it in your browser



Keep pull requests small (one feature or fix), and say what changed, why, and how to test it. Fixes #1 links the pull request to issue number 1 (see Issues below).

title: 63  63.  Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
63.5 Step 5: Review
Code review means a teammate reads the changes before they are merged. On the pull request page:

Open the Files changed tab to see the diff.
To comment on a line, hover over it and click the blue comment icon, type your comment, and click Start a review.
Click Review changes, write a summary, and choose one option: Comment (general feedback), Approve (ready to merge), or Request changes (must be fixed before merging). Then click Submit review.

To fix what a reviewer asked for, the author doesn’t open a new pull request. He just commits on the same branch and pushes again, and the pull request updates itself:
git push
Output (progress lines omitted):
To https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project.git
   c3d6678..d38fddc  add-projects-page -> add-projects-page
Reviewers can also work from the terminal: gh pr checkout 2 downloads pull request 2’s branch so they can run and test it, and gh pr review 2 --approve or gh pr review 2 --request-changes --body "Please fix the link" submits a review.
What to look for in a review:

Does it work and do what the description says? Run it.
Is it readable, small, and focused?
Any bugs, missing cases, or leftover debugging code?
Any secrets, such as API keys or passwords?

Review AI-written code just as carefully: it often looks polished even when it is wrong.

title: 63  63.  Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
63.6 Steps 6-7: Merge and clean up
When the pull request is approved, someone with write access clicks Merge pull request and then Confirm merge at the bottom of the pull request page, then clicks Delete branch, since the branch is no longer needed. (gh pr merge 2 --merge --delete-branch does the same from the terminal.)
GitHub did the merge, so everyone’s computer is now behind. Sam updates his main and deletes his local copy of the branch:
git switch main
git pull
Output (progress lines omitted):
Switched to branch 'main'
Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
From https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project
   9c2c605..8cf4abd  main       -> origin/main
Updating 9c2c605..8cf4abd
Fast-forward
 src/index.html    |  1 +
 src/projects.html | 14 ++++++++++++++
 2 files changed, 15 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 src/projects.html
(Before the pull, Git still thinks main is up to date: it only learns about the merge on GitHub when it fetches.)
git branch -d add-projects-page
git fetch --prune
Output:
Deleted branch add-projects-page (was d38fddc).
From https://github.com/maria-lopez/git-tutorial-project
 - [deleted]         (none)     -> origin/add-projects-page
git branch -d deletes his local branch; git fetch --prune removes his local record (origin/add-projects-page) of the branch that was deleted on GitHub. The history now shows the merge commit that GitHub created, named after the pull request:
git log --oneline --graph
Output (older commits cut off):
*   8cf4abd (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Merge pull request #2 from maria-lopez/add-projects-page
|\
| * d38fddc Clarify project name
| * c3d6678 Link to projects page from home page
| * 33260fe Add projects page
|/
* 9c2c605 Change heading to Our Portfolio






Deeper dive: The three merge buttons





The merge button has a menu with up to three methods (repository owners can turn some off):







Method
What lands on main




Create a merge commit
All of the branch’s commits, plus a merge commit (what Sam’s PR used)


Squash and merge
One single new commit containing all of the branch’s changes


Rebase and merge
The branch’s commits, replayed one by one on top of main, without a merge commit



Squashing keeps main’s history short (one commit per pull request); merge commits keep every step. One surprise after a squash merge: your local branch’s original commits are not on main, so git branch -d may refuse to delete the branch (“not fully merged”). Once you’ve confirmed on GitHub that the pull request was merged, git branch -D branch-name is safe.

title: 63  63.  Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
63.7 Issues and linking pull requests
GitHub issues are the project’s to-do and bug list. Each issue gets a number (#1, #2, …; pull requests share the same numbering). You can create one on the Issues tab or with gh issue create --title "Add a projects page".
Writing #1 in a pull request or comment links to issue 1. Writing a closing keyword such as Fixes #1, Closes #1, or Resolves #1 in the pull request’s description closes issue 1 automatically when the pull request is merged into the repository’s default branch (usually main).






Deeper dive: Protecting main





Repository owners can make the review process mandatory with branch protection rules (in the repository’s settings). A rule for main can, for example, require pull request reviews before merging, require status checks (such as automated tests run by GitHub Actions) to pass before merging, and, by default, it blocks force pushes to main. Automated checks are part of CI/CD (see Hosting and Deployment).

63.8 AI in the pull request workflow

63.8.1 Asking Claude Code to open a pull request
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Common workflows: Create pull requests · Best practices
Claude Code can do steps 1-4 for you. The docs suggest asking it directly (“create a pr for my changes”) or step by step:
summarize the changes I've made to the authentication module
create a pr
enhance the PR description with more context about the security improvements
Install the GitHub CLI and sign in (gh auth login); the docs note that Claude knows how to use gh to open pull requests, create issues, and read comments. Review the pull request Claude wrote before you ask anyone to review it, and ask Claude to point out potential risks. To find the Claude Code session that created a pull request later, run claude --from-pr 2 (with your PR number); it lists the sessions linked to that pull request so you can resume one.


63.8.2 Reviewing code with /code-review
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Code Review: Review a diff locally · Find bugs with ultrareview · Commands
Inside a Claude Code session:

/code-review reviews your branch’s commits plus any uncommitted changes for correctness bugs. It runs in the background and reports its findings in your conversation. Pass a pull request number to review a teammate’s PR (/code-review 2). You can also add an effort level from low (only the findings it is most confident about) to max (broader coverage), --fix to apply the findings to your files, or --comment to post them as comments on the GitHub pull request. /review is another name for the same command.
/code-review ultra runs a deeper review in the cloud (called ultrareview): a group of reviewer agents that verify each finding, taking roughly 5 to 10 minutes. It needs a claude.ai account; Pro and Max accounts get 3 free runs (a one-time allowance), after which each review is billed separately as usage credits.
/security-review checks your branch’s changes for security problems.

An AI reviewer is a useful second reader, especially for code an AI wrote, but it doesn’t replace a human review: someone on the team should still read and approve the pull request.


63.8.3 Claude on GitHub: @claude and automatic reviews
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Claude Code GitHub Actions · Code Review

Claude Code GitHub Actions. Running /install-github-app in Claude Code (you need admin access to the repository and a signed-in gh) installs the Claude GitHub App, stores a credential as a repository secret, and prepares a pull request that adds the workflow file. After you merge it, anyone with write access can mention @claude in an issue or pull request comment, for example @claude fix the TypeError in the user dashboard component, and Claude works on it and replies in the comment. Each run uses GitHub Actions minutes plus either API tokens or your Claude subscription.
Code Review. A managed service (research preview, for Team and Enterprise plans) that reviews pull requests automatically and posts findings as comments on the changed lines, marked Important, Nit, or Pre-existing. It never approves or blocks a pull request. Commenting @claude review on a pull request requests a review. It is billed separately from the plan (the docs say reviews average $15-25 each). On other plans, use /code-review locally.

63.9 Key takeaways

A pull request asks to merge a branch and gives the team a page to discuss, review, and check the change first.
GitHub Flow: branch → commit → push → pull request → review → merge → delete the branch → pull main.
Open PRs on github.com (Compare & pull request) or with gh pr create; review on the Files changed tab with Comment, Approve, or Request changes.

title: 63  63.  Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a pull request, and why do teams use them instead of merging directly into main?






Suggested answer





A pull request is a request on GitHub to merge one branch (for example a feature branch) into another (usually main), together with a page for discussing it. Teams use them so that someone reviews the change (and automated checks run) before it reaches main, which keeps main working and records why each change was made.





Question 2 · Ordering
Put the steps of the GitHub Flow in order:

A. Open a pull request
B. Merge the pull request
C. Create a branch
D. Push the branch to GitHub
E. Teammates review the changes
F. Commit your changes
G. Delete the branch and pull main







Suggested answer





C → F → D → A → E → B → G.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each review option with its meaning.








Option

Meaning




1. Comment

A. The changes must be fixed before the pull request is merged


2. Approve

B. General feedback, without approving


3. Request changes

C. The changes are ready to merge









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → A.





Question 4 · True or false
After a reviewer requests changes, the author must close the pull request and open a new one with the fixes.






Suggested answer





False. The author commits the fixes on the same branch and runs git push. The pull request updates automatically with the new commits.





Question 5 · Short answer
In a pull request, what are the base branch and the compare branch?






Suggested answer





The base branch is where the changes should be merged into (usually main). The compare branch is the branch that contains your changes (for example add-projects-page).





Question 6 · Multiple choice
Which text in a pull request’s description closes issue 7 automatically when the pull request is merged into the default branch?

See issue 7
#7 please
Fixes #7
Issue: seven







Suggested answer





c. A closing keyword (such as fix, fixes, close, closes, resolve, resolves) followed by #7 links the pull request and closes the issue when it is merged into the default branch. A plain #7 (b) only creates a link, and (a) and (d) don’t reference the issue at all.






Medium

Question 7 · Write the command
You finished your work on the branch fix-footer and committed it. Write the command that publishes the branch to GitHub for the first time, and the gh command that opens a pull request with the title “Fix footer year”.






Suggested answer





git push -u origin fix-footer
gh pr create --title "Fix footer year" --body "Updates the copyright year in the footer."
(Any reasonable --body works; --fill would use the commit messages instead.)





Question 8 · Scenario
Your pull request was merged on GitHub and its branch was deleted there. On your laptop, git status on main still says Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'. Is your main really up to date? What should you run?






Suggested answer





No. The merge happened on GitHub, and Git only learns about it when it fetches; “up to date” compares with the last known origin/main. Run git pull on main (which fetches and merges), then delete your local branch with git branch -d branch-name.





Question 9 · Multiple choice
A teammate opened pull request 14 and you want to run the code on your computer before approving it. Which command gets you the branch?

gh pr create 14
gh pr checkout 14
git clone 14
gh pr merge 14







Suggested answer





b. gh pr checkout 14 downloads the pull request’s branch and switches to it. gh pr create (a) opens a new pull request, git clone (c) needs a repository URL, and gh pr merge (d) would merge it without your testing.





Question 10 · Short answer
List four things a reviewer should check in a pull request.






Suggested answer





Any four, for example: it does what the description says (run and try it); the code is readable; there are no obvious bugs, missing cases, or leftover debugging code; no secrets (API keys, passwords) are included; the change is small and focused; tests or checks pass.





Question 11 · Compare
What is the difference between “Create a merge commit” and “Squash and merge” on GitHub’s merge button?






Suggested answer





Create a merge commit adds all of the branch’s commits to main plus a merge commit that joins them. Squash and merge combines all of the branch’s changes into one single new commit on main, so the individual commits of the branch don’t appear in main’s history.





Question 12 · Short answer
In a Claude Code session, what does /code-review review by default, and how do you make it review pull request 2 instead?






Suggested answer





By default it reviews your current branch’s commits (those not yet on the branch’s upstream) plus any uncommitted changes, looking for correctness bugs. To review pull request 2, pass its number: /code-review 2.





Question 13 · Read the output
After pulling, Sam sees:
*   8cf4abd (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Merge pull request #2 from maria-lopez/add-projects-page
|\
| * d38fddc Clarify project name
| * c3d6678 Link to projects page from home page
| * 33260fe Add projects page
|/
* 9c2c605 Change heading to Our Portfolio
Which merge method was used, how many commits were on the pull request’s branch, and who created the merge commit?






Suggested answer





Create a merge commit (there is a merge commit with two parents). The branch had three commits (33260fe, c3d6678, d38fddc). GitHub created the merge commit when someone clicked the merge button, which is why its message names pull request #2.






Hard

Question 14 · Scenario
Maria’s pull request was squash-merged. Back on her laptop she runs git switch main, git pull, and git branch -d add-about-page, and Git refuses, saying the branch is not fully merged. Is her work lost? What should she do?






Suggested answer





Her work is not lost: the squash merge put all of its changes on main as one new commit. But her branch’s original commits are not on main, so Git thinks the branch is unmerged. After confirming on GitHub that the pull request was merged (and that main now has the changes), she can safely force-delete the branch with git branch -D add-about-page.





Question 15 · Long answer
Your team requires a pull request for every change to main. Give three advantages and one cost of this rule.






Suggested answer





Advantages (any three): a second person catches bugs before they reach main; main stays working; automated checks run before merging; every change has a written explanation and discussion; team members learn from each other’s code.
Cost: it takes longer - work waits for a reviewer, and reviewing takes the reviewer’s time. (Keeping pull requests small reduces this cost.)





Question 16 · Scenario
You asked Claude Code to “create a pr” for your changes, and it did. What should you do before asking a teammate to review it, and how could AI review tools help without replacing your teammate?






Suggested answer





Read the pull request yourself: check the description matches what actually changed, look at the diff, run the code, and make sure nothing secret or unrelated was included; ask Claude to point out risks. You can run /code-review (or /code-review ultra for a deeper cloud review, at extra cost after the free runs) to catch bugs before the human review. The AI findings help, but they don’t approve anything - a teammate still reads and approves the pull request, and the team stays responsible for what is merged.





Question 17 · Compare
Compare Claude Code GitHub Actions (@claude) with the managed Code Review service: what does each do, who can use it, and how is it paid for?






Suggested answer






GitHub Actions (@claude): a workflow you install in your repository (for example with /install-github-app). When someone with write access mentions @claude in an issue or pull request comment, Claude works on the request (answers questions, changes code, pushes commits) and replies in a comment. It uses GitHub Actions minutes plus API tokens or your Claude subscription.
Code Review: a managed service (research preview for Team and Enterprise plans) that automatically reviews pull requests and posts findings on the changed lines (Important, Nit, Pre-existing), without approving or blocking. It is billed separately per review (averaging $15-25 according to the docs). Individual Pro or Max users can use /code-review locally instead.






Question 18 · Scenario
A teammate merged their own pull request into main one minute after opening it, without any review, and the site broke. Suggest two changes to the team’s process or repository settings to prevent this.






Suggested answer






Add a branch protection rule for main that requires an approving review (and passing status checks, such as automated tests) before a pull request can be merged.
Agree as a team that authors never merge their own pull requests without an approval, and that reviewers actually run the code. (Automated reviews such as /code-review or @claude can add a quick first check.)






Question 19 · Write the command
Pull request 5 has been approved. Write one gh command that squash-merges it and deletes its branch, then the Git commands you run on your laptop afterwards.






Suggested answer





gh pr merge 5 --squash --delete-branch
git switch main
git pull
If your local copy of the branch remains, delete it with git branch -D branch-name (capital D, because after a squash merge Git may consider it unmerged).

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.1 The problem: one folder, one branch at a time
AI coding agents can work on several tasks at the same time, but not safely in the same folder. Git worktrees give each task its own folder and branch, all connected to one repository. This page shows the Git commands, Claude Code’s built-in worktree support, ways to run several agents at once (including dynamic workflows), and what all this costs you in tokens and attention.
A project folder has exactly one branch checked out at a time. If two agents (or you and an agent) work in the same folder at once:
You could wait for one task to finish, or make a second clone of the repository. Worktrees are the lighter-weight solution.

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.2 What is a worktree?
A worktree is an extra working folder connected to the same repository. Each worktree has its own files and its own checked-out branch, but all worktrees share one history, one set of branches, and the same remotes. A commit made in one worktree is immediately visible from the others.
Documents/
├── git-tutorial-project/             <- branch main       (you)
│   └── .git/                         <- the one shared repository
└── git-tutorial-project-dark-mode/   <- branch dark-mode  (an AI agent)
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
64  64. Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.3 Creating and using a worktree
Maria wants an agent to build a dark color scheme while she keeps working on main. From her project folder, she creates a worktree next to it (..) on a new branch (-b dark-mode):
git worktree add ../git-tutorial-project-dark-mode -b dark-mode
git worktree list
Output:
Preparing worktree (new branch 'dark-mode')
HEAD is now at 8cf4abd Merge pull request #2 from maria-lopez/add-projects-page
/Users/maria/Documents/git-tutorial-project            8cf4abd [main]
/Users/maria/Documents/git-tutorial-project-dark-mode  8cf4abd [dark-mode]
(To use a branch that already exists, leave out -b: git worktree add ../git-tutorial-project-fix fix-typo.)
The new folder behaves like a normal project folder:
cd ../git-tutorial-project-dark-mode
git status
ls -a
Output:
On branch dark-mode
nothing to commit, working tree clean
.  ..  .env.example  .git  .gitignore  README.md  css  src
Notice what is missing: Maria’s .env file. A new worktree contains only the files Git tracks, so ignored files (.env, logs) and installed packages (such as a node_modules folder) are not there. Copy .env over and install dependencies in each new worktree.
Work in the worktree is normal Git work. The agent (or Maria) edits css/style.css there, commits “Add dark color scheme”, and pushes the branch with git push -u origin dark-mode. Back in her main folder, Maria can see the new commit right away, because both folders share one repository:
cd ../git-tutorial-project
git log --oneline --graph --all -3
Output:
* 06b7154 (origin/dark-mode, dark-mode) Add dark color scheme
*   8cf4abd (HEAD -> main, origin/main) Merge pull request #2 from maria-lopez/add-projects-page
|\
| * d38fddc Clarify project name
(-3 shows only the three newest commits.) One rule: a branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time. If Maria runs git switch dark-mode in her main folder, Git refuses with a message saying dark-mode is already used by the worktree at .../git-tutorial-project-dark-mode. To work on that branch, she uses that folder.

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.4 Removing a worktree
When the task is done, remove the worktree from the main folder:
git worktree remove ../git-tutorial-project-dark-mode
git branch
Output:
  dark-mode
* main
Removing a worktree deletes the folder, not the branch: dark-mode and its commits are still there, ready for a pull request (Pull Requests and Code Review). If the folder still has uncommitted or untracked files, git worktree remove refuses and suggests --force, which would delete those files. If you deleted a worktree’s folder by hand, run git worktree prune to make Git forget it.






Deeper dive: Worktrees vs. second clones vs. switching branches















Switch branches in one folder
A second clone
A worktree




Separate folder for each task
No
Yes
Yes


Tasks can run at the same time
No
Yes
Yes


History and branches
One repository
Two separate repositories; sync through GitHub
One shared repository; commits visible everywhere at once


Disk space
Least
Full copy of history
Only the files (history is shared)



In a linked worktree, .git is a small file that points to the main repository’s .git folder, which is why history is shared.

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.5 Claude Code’s built-in worktrees
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Run parallel sessions with worktrees · Common workflows
Claude Code can create the worktree for you. In your project folder, run:
claude --worktree dark-mode
(-w is the short form.) Claude Code creates a worktree in .claude/worktrees/dark-mode/ inside your repository, on a new branch named worktree-dark-mode, and starts the session there. Run the same command with a different name in a second terminal to start a second, isolated session. If you leave out the name, Claude Code makes one up. Good to know:

Setup. The repository needs at least one commit, and you should have run plain claude in the folder once to accept the folder-trust prompt. Add .claude/worktrees/ to your .gitignore, or the worktrees show up as untracked files in your main folder.
Starting point. By default the new branch starts from the repository’s default branch as it is on GitHub (usually main), not from the branch you are on. The worktree.baseRef setting can change this.
Ignored files. List files such as .env in a .worktreeinclude file at the project root (same pattern syntax as .gitignore), and Claude Code copies them into each new worktree. Dependencies still need installing; you can ask Claude to do it.
When you exit. If the worktree has no changes, Claude Code removes it (for an unnamed session) or asks you. If it has changes, Claude asks whether to keep or remove it; to come back later, run the claude --worktree <name> --resume command it prints.
Other ways in. You can ask Claude to “work in a worktree” in the middle of a session; claude --worktree "#2" creates a worktree from pull request 2 (quote it, because # starts a comment in Bash); and the desktop app has a worktree option for each new session.

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.6 Running several agents at once
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Run agents in parallel · Manage multiple agents with agent view · Commands
Claude Code offers several ways to run work in parallel. Worktrees keep their file edits apart:



Approach
What it is
How edits are kept apart




Several terminals, each claude --worktree NAME
You start and steer each session yourself
Each session has its own worktree


Agent view (claude agents)
One screen to dispatch and watch background sessions (research preview)
Each session moves into its own worktree before it edits files


Subagents
Helpers inside one session (see Subagents)
Optional: isolation: worktree


/batch <instruction>
Splits one large change into 5 to 30 units, shows you a plan, then runs one background subagent per unit
Each unit gets its own worktree


Dynamic workflows
A script Claude writes that runs many subagents (below)
Agents can work on isolated copies


Agent teams
Experimental and disabled by default
No worktrees; split the work by files



A background session in its own worktree commits its work and pushes its branch, and can open a draft pull request; agent view then shows the pull request number on that session’s row.

64.6.1 Dynamic workflows and /workflows
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows
A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that Claude writes to run many subagents for one big job, such as auditing every file in a folder or migrating dozens of files. A runtime executes the script in the background while your session stays free. Workflows are available on all paid plans; on Pro you first turn them on in the Dynamic workflows row of /config.

Start one by asking for it in your prompt (“use a workflow to …”) or by including the keyword ultracode, for example: use a workflow to migrate every component under src/components/ from JavaScript to TypeScript, working on each file in its own isolated copy. Depending on your permission mode, Claude Code shows the planned phases and asks you to approve the run (in auto mode, only the first time). /deep-research is a workflow that comes built in.
Watch it with /workflows: it lists running and finished runs; in a run you can see each phase and agent, press p to pause or resume, x to stop, and s to save the script.
Reuse it. A saved workflow goes in .claude/workflows/ (shared with everyone who clones the repository) or ~/.claude/workflows/ (just for you), and runs later as /<name>.
Mind the cost. One run can start dozens of agents and use far more tokens than doing the task in conversation. Claude Code shows a Large workflow warning for big runs; try a small slice (one folder) first.

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.7 Bringing the work back together
Parallel work only pays off when you can combine it:

Each task ends as a branch (one per worktree or session).
Review each branch’s changes and test them, exactly as you would review a teammate’s work.
Open a pull request per branch and merge them one at a time (Pull Requests and Code Review).
If two tasks edited the same lines, the second merge conflicts (Merge Conflicts).

The best parallel tasks are independent: different pages, files, or features. Two agents restyling the same CSS file will step on each other no matter how many worktrees you use.
crumbs: Git and GitHub: Working with Others
64  64. Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.8 Costs and attention
As of Oct 6, 2026 · Official docs: Manage multiple agents with agent view: Limitations · Manage costs effectively

Tokens multiply. Each session uses your plan’s usage on its own; the agent view docs say ten agents in parallel use your quota roughly ten times as fast as one.
Your attention is the bottleneck. Every branch needs reading, testing, and merging. Five unreviewed branches are not five finished features.
Start small. Two or three well-defined, independent tasks with a clear way to check the result beat ten vague ones.
Clean up. Merge or delete finished branches and remove old worktrees (git worktree list shows them all). Background sessions stop if your computer shuts down, and deleting a session in agent view deletes its worktree, so commit anything you want to keep.

64  64. Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
64.9 Key takeaways

A worktree is an extra folder with its own branch, sharing one repository (history, branches, remotes) with your main folder.
git worktree add ../folder -b branch creates one, git worktree list lists them, and git worktree remove ../folder deletes the folder but keeps the branch.
A new worktree has only tracked files: copy .env and install dependencies.
claude --worktree NAME starts Claude Code in its own worktree under .claude/worktrees/; agent view, /batch, and dynamic workflows (/workflows) run many agents with worktree isolation.
Parallel agents multiply token use and review work; choose independent tasks and bring results back through branches and pull requests.

title: 64  64.  Git Worktrees and Parallel AI Agents
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a Git worktree?






Suggested answer





An extra working folder connected to the same repository. It has its own files and its own checked-out branch, but it shares the repository’s history, branches, and remotes with the main folder.





Question 2 · True or false
Every worktree contains its own separate copy of the repository’s history, so a commit made in one worktree can’t be seen from the others until you push it.






Suggested answer





False. All worktrees share one repository. A commit made in any worktree is immediately visible from the others (for example with git log --oneline --graph --all), without pushing.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
Which command creates a worktree in the folder ../site-fix on a new branch named fix-nav?

git switch -c fix-nav ../site-fix
git worktree add ../site-fix -b fix-nav
git clone ../site-fix fix-nav
git worktree list ../site-fix fix-nav







Suggested answer





b. git worktree add <folder> -b <new-branch> creates the folder and the branch together. git switch (a) changes branches in the current folder, git clone (c) makes a separate repository, and git worktree list (d) only lists worktrees.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. git worktree add ../x -b x

A. Make Git forget worktrees whose folders were deleted by hand


2. git worktree list

B. Delete a worktree’s folder (the branch stays)


3. git worktree remove ../x

C. Create a new folder with a new branch


4. git worktree prune

D. Show every worktree, its commit, and its branch









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → B, 4 → A.





Question 5 · Short answer
Give two problems that can happen when two AI agents work in the same project folder at the same time.






Suggested answer





Any two: they edit the same files and overwrite each other’s changes; one agent switches branches and the files change under the other; a commit includes the other agent’s half-finished changes; tests run on a mix of both tasks’ code.





Question 6 · True or false
The same branch can be checked out in two worktrees at the same time.






Suggested answer





False. A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time. Git refuses with a message that the branch is already used by another worktree.






Medium

Question 7 · Predict the output
Sam’s project is in /c/Users/sam/Documents/shop on branch main (commit a1b2c3d). He runs git worktree add ../shop-cart -b new-cart and then git worktree list. Describe what the list shows.






Suggested answer





Two lines, one per worktree, each with its folder, its current commit, and its branch in brackets: the main folder (.../shop) at a1b2c3d [main], and the new folder (.../shop-cart) at the same commit a1b2c3d [new-cart], because a new branch starts at the commit you were on.





Question 8 · Scenario
Maria creates a new worktree and starts her app in it, but the app fails because .env (which holds her API key) is missing, even though .env exists in her main folder. Why, and what are two ways to fix it?






Suggested answer





A new worktree contains only files that Git tracks, and .env is ignored (it must never be committed), so it isn’t there. She can copy .env into the worktree by hand, or, when Claude Code creates the worktree, list .env in a .worktreeinclude file at the project root so Claude Code copies it automatically. (She also needs to install dependencies in the new folder.)





Question 9 · Write the command
Write the command that starts Claude Code in a new isolated worktree named pricing-page. Where does the worktree go, and which branch is it on?






Suggested answer





claude --worktree pricing-page
(or claude -w pricing-page). Claude Code creates it in .claude/worktrees/pricing-page/ inside the repository, on a new branch named worktree-pricing-page, and starts the session there.





Question 10 · Scenario
git worktree remove ../shop-cart fails with a message that the folder “contains modified or untracked files, use –force to delete it”. What does that mean, and what should you do before using --force?






Suggested answer





The worktree has changes that were never committed (or new files Git doesn’t track). Removing it would delete them, so Git refuses. First go into the folder, check git status, and commit (and push) anything you want to keep. Use git worktree remove --force only for changes you really want to throw away.





Question 11 · Scenario
In her main folder, Maria runs git switch dark-mode and Git refuses because dark-mode is already used by the worktree at .../git-tutorial-project-dark-mode. Explain the message and give two ways to continue.






Suggested answer





A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time, and dark-mode is checked out in the other folder. She can (1) simply cd into ../git-tutorial-project-dark-mode and work on the branch there, or (2) remove that worktree (git worktree remove ../git-tutorial-project-dark-mode, after committing its work) and then switch to the branch in her main folder.





Question 12 · True or false
Running git worktree remove deletes the worktree’s branch and all of its commits.






Suggested answer





False. It deletes only the folder. The branch and its committed work stay in the repository (and on GitHub, if pushed), ready to be merged or deleted separately.





Question 13 · Multiple choice
What does the /workflows command do in Claude Code?

Lists the GitHub Actions workflow files in .github/workflows/.
Opens a view of running and finished dynamic workflows, where you can watch their phases and agents, pause, stop, or save them.
Creates a new git worktree for every branch.
Shows your recent commits as a graph.







Suggested answer





b. /workflows is the progress view for dynamic workflows (p pauses or resumes, x stops, s saves the script). It has nothing to do with GitHub Actions workflow files (a), it doesn’t create worktrees (c), and the commit graph comes from git log --oneline --graph (d).





Question 14 · Short answer
When you dispatch a background session from agent view (claude agents) in a Git repository, how does Claude Code keep its file edits apart from your other sessions, and how do you get its work back?






Suggested answer





Before editing files, the session moves into its own worktree under .claude/worktrees/, so parallel sessions write to separate folders and branches. It commits its work and pushes its branch (and can open a draft pull request, shown on its row in agent view). You review the branch or pull request and merge it like any other.






Hard

Question 15 · Scenario
Maria has four tasks: (1) write the text of a new FAQ page, (2) fix a typo in the footer, (3) change all link colors in css/style.css, and (4) redesign the whole layout in css/style.css. She wants to run Claude Code sessions in parallel. Which tasks are good to run in parallel, which are not, and how should she bring the results together?






Suggested answer





Tasks 1, 2, and one of the CSS tasks touch different files, so they can run in parallel, each in its own worktree (claude --worktree faq, and so on). Tasks 3 and 4 both rewrite css/style.css, so running them at the same time would cause conflicts; do them one after the other (or combine them into one task). Each task ends as a branch: review and test it, open a pull request, and merge the pull requests one at a time, pulling main in between.





Question 16 · Long answer
A classmate says: “If one agent finishes a feature in an hour, ten agents in parallel will finish ten features in an hour.” Explain why that’s too optimistic.






Suggested answer






Usage: each session uses tokens on its own; ten parallel agents use your plan’s quota roughly ten times as fast, so you may hit limits (or costs) soon.
Review: someone has to read, test, and merge every branch; your attention becomes the bottleneck.
Conflicts: features often touch the same files, so later merges conflict and need careful resolution.
Quality: vague tasks produce work that must be redone. A few independent, well-defined tasks usually finish sooner than ten loosely defined ones.






Question 17 · Compare
Compare three ways to work on two tasks at once: switching branches in one folder, making a second clone, and adding a worktree.






Suggested answer






Switching branches: one folder, so only one task’s files exist at a time; tasks can’t run simultaneously.
Second clone: a separate folder and a separate repository; tasks can run at once, but commits must travel through GitHub (push and pull) to reach the other copy, and history is stored twice.
Worktree: a separate folder with its own branch, sharing one repository; tasks run at once, and commits are visible in every worktree immediately.






Question 18 · Scenario
Two Claude Code sessions ran in separate worktrees. Both changed the same heading in src/index.html, in different ways. Maria merged the first pull request without trouble. What will happen with the second one, and what should she do?






Suggested answer





Worktrees kept the edits apart while the sessions were working, but they don’t prevent overlapping changes. The second branch now conflicts with main on the heading line. She (or the session, with her review) brings the latest main into the second branch (pull main, then run git merge main while on the second branch), decides what the heading should say, removes the markers, commits, pushes, and then merges the pull request. In future, she should give parallel sessions tasks that touch different files.





Question 19 · Scenario
Sam is on the Pro plan and wants Claude Code to run a dynamic workflow that converts 40 files from JavaScript to TypeScript. What should he know and do before and during the run?






Suggested answer






On Pro, dynamic workflows must first be turned on in the Dynamic workflows row of /config.
Start it by asking for a workflow (or using the keyword ultracode), and read the planned phases when Claude Code asks him to approve the run.
A workflow can start many agents and use far more tokens than a normal conversation, so try it on a small slice (one folder) first.
Watch the run with /workflows, where he can pause or stop it.
Commit his own work first, then review and test the result like any other branch before merging.

title: 65  65.  Tutorial - intro
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a “full-stack” web application? Name its two parts and say what each part does.






Suggested answer





A full-stack app includes both:

a front end (client side): what users see and interact with in their browser - pages, buttons, forms, animations;
a back end (server side): the logic that runs on a server - databases, authentication (logging in), APIs, business rules.

The task app in this tutorial is a full-stack app because it has both.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Which of these is part of the front end of the task app?

The database that stores every user’s tasks
The “create task” button and form that the user clicks and fills in
The code on the server that checks whether a user is logged in
The business rules that decide what each user is allowed to do







Suggested answer





b. The front end is what runs in the browser: the pages, buttons and forms the user sees and uses. The database (a), the login check on the server (c) and the business rules (d) are back-end jobs that run on servers.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each feature of the task app with the technology this tutorial uses for it.



Feature

Technology




1. Storing tasks and other data

A. Stripe


2. Storing uploaded image files

B. Google OAuth


3. “Log in with Google”

C. Supabase’s PostgreSQL database


4. Automatic AI labels for tasks

D. The OpenAI API


5. Monthly subscription payments

E. Supabase storage “buckets”


6. The web pages the user sees

F. Next.js









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → B, 4 → D, 5 → A, 6 → F.





Question 4 · True or false
To complete this tutorial, you have to write all of the task app’s code yourself.






Suggested answer





False. The code is provided for free in a GitHub repository (https://github.com/pixegami/task-app). The hard part is understanding the project’s architecture and doing the setup and integration that get it running.





Question 5 · Short answer
Name four features of the task-management app you will build.






Suggested answer





Any four of:

user authentication (logging in), including “log in with Google”
creating and editing tasks
automatic AI-powered task labels
image attachments for tasks
user profiles with task statistics
monthly subscription plans paid through Stripe






Question 6 · Multiple choice
Which service does this page name for web hosting, i.e. for putting the website online?

Stripe
Vercel
Google Cloud
OpenAI







Suggested answer





b. Vercel. In this project, Stripe handles payments (a), Google Cloud provides the “log in with Google” feature (c), and OpenAI provides the AI that labels tasks (d).






Medium

Question 7 · Classify
For each item, say whether it belongs to the front end or the back end:

A drop-down menu for choosing a task’s label
The PostgreSQL database
The server code that decides whether a login is valid
An animation that plays when a page opens
An API that other programs call to get data







Suggested answer






Front end
Back end
Back end (authentication)
Front end
Back end

Rule of thumb: what the user sees and touches in the browser is front end; data, logins, APIs and business rules that run on a server are back end.





Question 8 · Multiple choice
The project includes automated “integration” tests. What are they for?

To make the website load faster
To make sure everything works, and that you don’t break the code when you make changes
To connect the app to Google, OpenAI and Stripe
To check that the pages look good on a phone







Suggested answer





b. Tests are code that automatically checks that the app works. You run them again after a change, so you find out quickly if you broke something. Option (c) is tempting because of the word “integration”, but connecting the services is the setup work; the tests only check that the connected pieces work together. Tests don’t make the site faster (a), and these tests check the app’s features, not how the pages look (d).





Question 9 · Short answer
The code for this project is free to download. Why does the page still call setup and integration “the hard part”? Give two reasons.






Suggested answer






You need to understand the architecture of the whole project: what the different parts of the code are for and how they fit together.
You need to get the project running online: create accounts with several services (Vercel for hosting, Supabase for the database and more, plus Google, OpenAI and Stripe) and connect them all with the right settings and keys.

The code alone does nothing until all of these pieces are set up and connected.





Question 10 · Scenario
You want to rewatch the part of the video where the presenter talks about “webhooks”, but the video is more than 35 minutes long. How can you use this page to jump straight to that spot?






Suggested answer





Expand the transcript (“click here to see the transcript”), press Ctrl+F (Windows) or Cmd+F (Mac) to open the browser’s find tool, and search for webhook. Then click the timestamp link on a matching line: the video opens at that moment.





Question 11 · True or false
In the finished app, the PostgreSQL database runs inside each user’s web browser.






Suggested answer





False. The database is part of the back end: it runs on Supabase’s servers (that is what “database hosting” means). The browser runs only the front end, which sends requests to the back end to read and save data.






Hard

Question 12 · Long answer
The page says you can use AI to generate code, “but it is important to understand how the whole project is architected so that you know how to speak with the AI.” Explain why, using an example of a change you might want to make to the task app.






Suggested answer





Model answer: suppose you want to add a due date to every task. If you know the architecture, you can tell the AI that this touches several parts: the database (a new column in the tasks table in Supabase’s PostgreSQL database), the front-end form and task list (Next.js), and any back-end code that creates or updates tasks. Understanding the architecture helps you:

give the AI clear, specific instructions and the right context;
notice when its answer is incomplete (for example, it changed the form but not the database);
know where to look when something breaks, and which outside service (Supabase, Google, Stripe, …) might need new settings.

A good answer gives a concrete change, names the parts of the project it touches, and explains how that knowledge leads to better prompts and better checking of the AI’s work.





Question 13 · Scenario
A friend wants to build an expense-tracking app. Users log in with their Google account, upload photos of receipts, have AI sort each expense into a category automatically, and pay a monthly fee for a premium plan. Using this tutorial’s technologies, what would handle each feature, and where would the expense records be stored?






Suggested answer






Log in with Google: Google OAuth (connected through Supabase’s authentication)
Receipt photos: Supabase storage buckets
AI categories: the OpenAI API, called from back-end code such as a Supabase edge function
Monthly fee: Stripe subscription payments
Expense records: the Supabase PostgreSQL database
The screens: a Next.js front end, hosted for example on Vercel

The same building blocks (login, data, files, AI, payments) show up in almost every app, which is why this tutorial is worth learning.





Question 14 · Short answer
The task app asks the OpenAI API to pick a label for each new task. Why should that call happen in back-end code (such as a Supabase edge function) and not in the JavaScript that runs in the user’s browser?






Suggested answer





Calling the OpenAI API requires a secret API key, and the calls are billed to your account. Anything sent to the browser can be read by the user (for example with the browser’s developer tools), so a key in front-end code could be copied and misused. Back-end code runs on a server that users can’t look inside, so the key stays secret. This is one way edge functions make the site “more secure”, as the page puts it.





Question 15 · Long answer
The task app is “just” a to-do list, yet the page says it demonstrates “all the core technologies needed for modern web development.” Explain why a simple to-do app is a good choice for learning, and list the core building blocks it demonstrates.






Suggested answer





The app’s features are simple, so you can focus on how the pieces fit together instead of on complicated business logic. Yet it uses the building blocks that almost every real web product needs:

a front end (Next.js) and a host that puts it online (Vercel)
a database (Supabase’s PostgreSQL) and file storage (Supabase buckets)
user authentication (Google OAuth)
server-side code (Supabase edge functions)
a third-party AI service (the OpenAI API)
payments (Stripe)
automated tests

Once you can set up and connect these, you can use AI to help you build your own, different projects on the same foundation.

title: 66  66.  Project Architecture
text:
66.3 Keeping notes - Setup checklist
Over the course of this tutorial we will have to address all of the following in order to setup this project to work. The following sections will go into more detail about each of these topics:

Clone the project from GitHub
Create Supabase project
Set up Google OAuth
Configure OpenAI API
Set up Stripe
Deploy edge functions
Test the application

Many of these steps require keeping track of numerous URLs, “keys” and other “configuration information” for your project. Often the “configuration information” is generated on one website (e.g. vercel, supabase, google cloud console, stripe) and must be copied to a different website or recorded in a specific file on your computer.
Keeping track of all this information can get VERY confusing. If you’re doing this kind of thing for the first time, it could help a lot to have one place (e.g. a Word document) that you use to keep notes and record all the configuration information you will need. This makes it much easier to review your setup and debug it when there are problems. In addition to the keys, urls, etc, it can be helpful to paste screenshots into this Word document to help you remember where you retrieved the info from and where you copied it to.
Keep in mind that much of this configuration information should be treated as “secret info” similar to your passwords. Therefore, treat this Word document as you would treat your passwords.

title: 66  66.  Project Architecture
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
In this project, which code runs in the user’s browser?

The PostgreSQL database
The client-side part of the Next.js web app (HTML, CSS and JavaScript), including the Supabase client library
The Supabase edge functions
Stripe’s payment processing







Suggested answer





b. The frontend is the code that runs in the browser: the client-side portion of the Next.js app, plus the client library it uses to talk to Supabase. The database (a) and the edge functions (c) run on Supabase’s servers, and Stripe (d) runs on Stripe’s own servers.





Question 2 · Matching
Match each part of the architecture with its job.








Part

Job




1. Vercel

A. stores the app’s data


2. Supabase PostgreSQL database

B. stores the uploaded image files (similar to Amazon S3)


3. Supabase storage

C. the web server that runs the server side of the Next.js app


4. Supabase edge functions

D. lets users log in with their Google account


5. Google Cloud (OAuth)

E. processes payments


6. OpenAI API

F. TypeScript functions that run on Supabase’s servers


7. Stripe

G. uses AI to pick a “tag” for each task









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → B, 4 → F, 5 → D, 6 → G, 7 → E.





Question 3 · True or false
In this project, Vercel stores the image files that users attach to their tasks.






Suggested answer





False. Image files go into Supabase’s storage system (similar to Amazon S3). Vercel is the web server that hosts the Next.js app.





Question 4 · Fill in the blank
Supabase edge functions are written in ______ and run on ______’s servers, using the ______ runtime environment instead of Node.js.






Suggested answer





TypeScript; Supabase; Deno.





Question 5 · Short answer
What is a “tech stack”? Name the main technologies in this project’s tech stack.






Suggested answer





A tech stack is the set of technologies an app is built from (languages, frameworks and services), together with where each part runs. This project’s tech stack:

Next.js, running partly in the browser and partly on Vercel’s web server
Supabase: PostgreSQL database, storage, authentication and edge functions
third-party services: Google OAuth, the OpenAI API and Stripe







Medium

Question 6 · Ordering
Put the setup checklist in the order the page gives:

Deploy edge functions
Set up Stripe
Clone the project from GitHub
Test the application
Create Supabase project
Configure OpenAI API
Set up Google OAuth







Suggested answer






Clone the project from GitHub
Create Supabase project
Set up Google OAuth
Configure OpenAI API
Set up Stripe
Deploy edge functions
Test the application

The logic: you need the code first; the Supabase project has to exist before other services can be connected to it; the edge functions use the OpenAI and Stripe keys, so they are deployed after those services are set up; and testing comes last, when everything is connected.





Question 7 · Short answer
Look at the architecture diagram. Which part of Supabase connects to Google OAuth, and which part connects to the OpenAI API and Stripe?






Suggested answer





Authentication connects to Google OAuth: Supabase’s login system lets users sign in with their Google account. Edge functions connect to the OpenAI API and Stripe: they are server-side code, so they can safely use those services’ secret keys.





Question 8 · Short answer
Why does the page recommend keeping one notes document (for example, a Word document) while you set up this project, and what should you put in it?






Suggested answer





Setup produces many URLs, keys and other configuration values. A value is often created on one website (Vercel, Supabase, Google Cloud console, Stripe) and must be copied to another website or into a specific file on your computer. Keeping everything in one place makes it much easier to review your setup and to debug problems.
Put in the keys, URLs and other configuration information, plus screenshots that show where you got each item and where you copied it to.





Question 9 · Multiple choice
Your setup notes document contains API keys and other configuration values. How should you treat it?

Commit it to your GitHub repository so you never lose it
Like your passwords: keep it private and don’t share it
Paste it into the project’s README so teammates can find it
Share it freely - configuration values are never secret







Suggested answer





b. Much of this information is secret, just like a password: anyone who has your secret keys could use your accounts. Options (a) and (c) would publish the secrets to everyone who can see the repository, and (d) is simply not true.





Question 10 · True or false
Supabase had no choice but to use Deno for its edge functions, because Node.js could not have been used for this.






Suggested answer





False. The page says that, in theory, Supabase could have used Node.js. Deno is often chosen as a runtime environment for TypeScript. Both Deno and Node.js are runtime environments: programs that run JavaScript code outside a browser.






Hard

Question 11 · Scenario
For each problem below, which part(s) of the architecture would you investigate first?

“Log in with Google” fails.
Tasks save correctly, but attaching an image to a task fails.
New tasks are saved but never get an AI tag.
The page for upgrading to a paid subscription doesn’t work.







Suggested answer






Supabase authentication and the Google OAuth setup in Google Cloud.
Supabase storage.
The edge functions and the OpenAI API (for example, a missing or wrong API key).
Stripe and the edge functions that work with it.

The diagram tells you which pieces work together for each feature, so you know where to start looking; your setup notes tell you which keys and URLs you entered where.





Question 12 · Long answer
Explain the difference between the frontend and the backend in this project. Why is the backend spread across several companies’ servers (Vercel, Supabase, Google, OpenAI, Stripe) instead of running on one computer?






Suggested answer





The frontend is the client-side part of the Next.js app (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) running in the user’s browser: what the user sees and clicks. The backend is everything that runs on servers: Vercel runs the server-side part of the Next.js app; Supabase runs the PostgreSQL database, file storage, authentication and edge functions; and Google, OpenAI and Stripe provide login, AI and payments.
The backend is spread out because each company specializes in one hard job. Instead of building your own login system, payment processing or AI model, you use theirs and connect them with keys and URLs. The trade-off is more accounts, keys and settings to manage - which is why setup is the hard part, and why the page recommends keeping careful notes.





Question 13 · Short answer
The diagram shows Next.js in two places: in the browser and on Vercel’s web server. Why?






Suggested answer





A Next.js web app has two portions. The client-side portion (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) is sent to the user’s browser and runs there. The server-side portion is JavaScript that runs in Node.js on the web server (Vercel). One Next.js project produces the code for both places.

title: 67  67.  Step 0: Install Node.js and npm
text:
67.1 What is Node.js?
In this project we will be using Node.js and the npm tool. Below we will explain what they are and how they are used. For now though, let’s first make sure that you have the necessary software installed.
Node.js is a Javascript runtime environment. In other words, it is a program that runs Javascript code.
JavaScript was originally created to run inside web browsers to make webpages more interactive - e.g. dropdown menus, popup menus, tell users that they didn’t fill out a form properly, etc. It is still used inside browsers in these ways and others. To run Javascript in a browser, you do NOT need Node.js.
Node.js is used to run Javascript code outside of a browser. In this way you can use Javascript to create any type of program. This made Javascript more similar to other languages such as Python, Java, R, etc. Node.js was the first successful Javascript runtime. Today there are others such as Bun and Deno. However Node.js is still very popular.
crumbs: 67  67. Step 0: Install Node.js and npm

title: 67  67.  Step 0: Install Node.js and npm
text:
67.2 What are Packages?
When developers build software, they often need to solve common problems: connecting to databases, handling dates and times, processing images, and so on. Rather than writing this code from scratch every time, developers create reusable bundles of code called packages (sometimes also called libraries).
If you’ve used R or Python, you’re already familiar with this concept: - In R, you might use packages like ggplot2 for visualization or dplyr for data manipulation - In Python, you might use pandas for data analysis or requests for making HTTP requests
JavaScript packages work the same way. For example, instead of writing complex code to handle dates, you could use a package like date-fns that someone else has already written and tested.
crumbs: 67  67. Step 0: Install Node.js and npm

title: 67  67.  Step 0: Install Node.js and npm
text:
67.3 What is a Package Manager?
A package manager is a tool that helps you install, update, and manage packages. When you use R, you might run install.packages("ggplot2"). In Python, you use pip install pandas. These commands use package managers to:

Download the package from a central repository
Install it in the right location on your computer
Keep track of which packages your project uses
Manage dependencies (packages that other packages need to work)
crumbs: 67  67. Step 0: Install Node.js and npm

title: 67  67.  Step 0: Install Node.js and npm
text:
67.4 What is npm (Node Package Manager)?
npm stands for “Node Package Manager”. It is package manager that comes with Node.js. When you install Node.js, npm comes with it automatically.
Later we will cover more about how to use npm. For now though we just want you to understand what it is. npm connects to a massive online repository containing hundreds of thousands of JavaScript packages. When you need a package, you simply run the following command from the CLI (e.g. Bash) to have npm download the package and make it available for your project to use.
npm install package-name
The npm registry is one of the largest package ecosystems in the world, with over a million packages available. This means that for almost any problem you’re trying to solve, someone has probably already created a package to help.

title: 67  67.  Step 0: Install Node.js and npm
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
What is Node.js?

A web browser
A JavaScript runtime environment: a program that runs JavaScript code outside a browser
A package of reusable JavaScript code
A database







Suggested answer





b. Node.js runs JavaScript programs outside a browser. It isn’t a browser (a); a package (c) is a bundle of code that other programs use; and Node.js is not a database (d).





Question 2 · True or false
After you install Node.js, you have to install npm separately.






Suggested answer





False. npm is installed automatically when you install Node.js. You only need to install Node.js.





Question 3 · Write the command
Write the command that checks whether npm (and therefore Node.js) is installed on your computer.






Suggested answer





npm -v
If npm is installed, this prints its version number. If you get an error instead (for example “command not found”), npm and Node.js are most probably not installed.





Question 4 · Short answer
What does “npm” stand for, and what is it used for?






Suggested answer





Node Package Manager. It installs and manages JavaScript packages for your projects, downloading them from the huge online npm registry.






Medium

Question 5 · Matching
Match each language with a command that installs a package for it.



Language

Command




1. R

A. pip install pandas


2. Python

B. npm install date-fns


3. JavaScript (Node.js)

C. install.packages("ggplot2")









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → B.





Question 6 · Short answer
A package manager does four jobs. List them.






Suggested answer






It downloads packages from a central online repository.
It installs them in the right location on your computer.
It keeps track of which packages your project uses.
It manages dependencies: packages that other packages need in order to work.






Question 7 · Multiple choice
Which of these does not need Node.js?

Making a drop-down menu work on a web page in your browser
Running npm install to download packages
Running a JavaScript program from the terminal, outside the browser
Using JavaScript to build a program that isn’t a web page, the way you might use Python or R







Suggested answer





a. JavaScript inside a web page is run by the browser itself, so no Node.js is needed. npm (b) comes with Node.js and needs it in order to run, and (c) and (d) are exactly what Node.js was created for: running JavaScript outside a browser.





Question 8 · Short answer
Why do developers use packages instead of writing all of their code themselves? Give an example from the page.






Suggested answer





Many problems come up again and again (handling dates and times, connecting to databases, processing images), and someone has already written and tested code that solves them. Using a package saves time and avoids bugs. Examples: date-fns for dates in JavaScript, pandas in Python, ggplot2 in R.





Question 9 · True or false
Node.js is the only JavaScript runtime environment.






Suggested answer





False. Today there are others, such as Bun and Deno. Node.js is still very popular, and it is the one this tutorial uses.






Hard

Question 10 · Scenario
Sam installs Node.js on his Windows laptop. In the Git Bash window he had opened before the installation, he types npm -v and gets an error saying the command was not found. What should he try, and why might it help?






Suggested answer





He should close that terminal, open a new one, and run npm -v again (the page tells you to do exactly this after installing). A terminal that was already open may not know about programs installed after it started: for example, the installer may have updated the PATH (the list of folders where the shell looks for commands), and a terminal reads that setting when it starts. If a new terminal still can’t find npm, he should ask an AI assistant or a knowledgeable person for help.





Question 11 · Scenario
Package A needs package B in order to work. You run npm install A. What will npm do about package B, and why is that helpful?






Suggested answer





B is a dependency of A. Managing dependencies is one of a package manager’s jobs, so npm also downloads and installs B (and anything B itself needs). You don’t have to hunt down and install every required package by hand, and A won’t fail because a piece is missing.





Question 12 · Long answer
Explain how Node.js, npm and a package (such as date-fns) relate to each other. Use an analogy with R or Python.






Suggested answer





Model answer:

Node.js runs JavaScript programs outside the browser, just as R runs R code and Python runs Python code on your computer.
A package such as date-fns is a reusable bundle of code that someone else wrote and tested, like ggplot2 in R or pandas in Python.
npm is the package manager: it downloads packages from the online npm registry and installs them for your project, like install.packages() in R or pip in Python. npm comes bundled with Node.js.

Together: npm installs the packages, your code uses them, and Node.js runs the JavaScript. A good answer explains all three roles and how they work together.

68.1 Fork the repo
“cloning” a public github repo means taking a copy of that repo The bulk of the code for this project is provided in a github repo. We will now “clone” that repo that we have our own copy of the repo.
This section assumes that you have already created your own account on github. If you haven’t please do so now.
Open Software allows for a developer to take someone else’s software and modify it in their own way. Often developers take a github repository from another developer and continue to develop in their own way. The original developer has their version of the software and the new developer has their own (different) version of the software. This is known as “forking” a repo. The word fork comes from “a fork in the road” - i.e. the two repos started out the same but will continue in different directions.
We need to take our own copy of the repo for the original developer. To do so,

section: 68.2 Clone your repo to get a copy on your computer
text:
68.2 Clone your repo to get a copy on your computer
Once you have a copy of the repo on your github account, you can then “pull down” a copy of that repo to your local computer that you will be developing on. This is known as “cloning” a repo from github. This allows you to work on your local git repo and then eventually “push” the changes that you’ve made back to your personal github’s account copy of the repo.
To clone the repo to your local computer - do the following:

Go to https://github.com/pixegami/task-app
Click the “fork” button to create your own copy of the repo.
Then go to your own github repo and copy YOUR copy’s URL.
Open your Terminal and type the following command to create a new folder with your own copy of the repo. Replace the words URL_FOR_YOUR_REPO with the URL you copied in the previous step.
git clone URL_FOR_YOUR_REPO

You can now cd into the folder for your project and start Claude Code there by typing claude (see Your First Claude Code Session). You can also open the folder in any editor of your choice (e.g. VS Code).

title: 68  68.  Step 1: Fork the repo and clone it
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
What does it mean to fork a repository on GitHub?

To download a copy of the repository to your own computer
To make your own copy of someone else’s repository in your own GitHub account
To delete a repository from GitHub
To combine two repositories into one







Suggested answer





b. A fork is a copy on GitHub, in your own account. Downloading a copy to your computer (a) is cloning. Forking doesn’t delete (c) or combine (d) anything.





Question 2 · Short answer
Where does the word “fork” come from, and what does it say about the two repositories?






Suggested answer





It comes from “a fork in the road”. The original repository and your fork start out the same and then continue in different directions: the original developer keeps working on their version, and you work on yours.





Question 3 · True or false
You need your own GitHub account before you can fork the task-app repository.






Suggested answer





True. A fork is created inside your own GitHub account, which is why the page asks you to create an account first.





Question 4 · Write the command
Your fork’s URL is https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/task-app. Write the command that copies it to your computer.






Suggested answer





git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/task-app
Use your real GitHub user name in place of YOUR-USERNAME, and run the command from the folder where you want the project to live.






Medium

Question 5 · Ordering
Put these steps in the right order:

Run git clone with your fork’s URL
Create a GitHub account (if you don’t have one yet)
cd into the new project folder and start Claude Code (or open the folder in your editor)
Click Fork on https://github.com/pixegami/task-app
Go to your own copy of the repository on GitHub and copy its URL







Suggested answer






Create a GitHub account (if you don’t have one yet)
Click Fork on https://github.com/pixegami/task-app
Go to your own copy of the repository on GitHub and copy its URL
Run git clone with your fork’s URL
cd into the new project folder and start Claude Code (or open the folder in your editor)






Question 6 · Compare
Compare forking and cloning: where does each copy live, how do you make it, and what is it for?






Suggested answer














Fork
Clone




Where the copy lives
On GitHub, in your account
On your computer


How you make it
The Fork button on GitHub
git clone URL in the terminal


What it’s for
Your own online version of the project, which you control and can push to
The local copy you actually work on; you push your changes from it back to your fork








Question 7 · Multiple choice
Which URL should you use with git clone in this tutorial?

https://github.com/pixegami/task-app (the original repository)
The URL of your fork in your own GitHub account
The URL of the YouTube video
https://supabase.com







Suggested answer





b. Cloning your fork connects your local repository to your own copy on GitHub, so you can push your changes there. If you cloned the original (a), your local copy would be connected to pixegami’s repository, which you are not allowed to push to. Options (c) and (d) are web pages, not Git repositories.





Question 8 · Short answer
What does git clone URL create on your computer, and where?






Suggested answer





A new folder containing a copy of the repository: all of the project’s files plus its Git history. The folder is named after the repository (here task-app), and it is created inside the folder you are in when you run the command (your current working directory).





Question 9 · True or false
After you fork a repository, any changes the original developer makes later show up in your fork automatically.






Suggested answer





False. After the fork, the two repositories are separate and go their own ways (“a fork in the road”). If you want the original’s later changes, you have to bring them into your fork on purpose (see Sharing a Repository: Collaborators and Forks).






Hard

Question 10 · Scenario
Sam skipped the fork and cloned https://github.com/pixegami/task-app directly. Everything works on his laptop, but when he tries to git push his changes, the push fails with a permission error. Why? How can he fix it?






Suggested answer





His local repository is connected to pixegami’s original repository, and only its owner (and people the owner allows) can push to it. To fix it, Sam should fork the repository on GitHub and then either:

point his local repository at his fork: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/task-app, or
clone his fork into a new folder and copy his changes over.

After that, git push sends his changes to his own copy on GitHub.





Question 11 · Short answer
Why does the tutorial have you fork the repository first, instead of just cloning the original?






Suggested answer





The fork gives you your own copy on GitHub that you control. You can push the changes you make on your computer to it (so your work is backed up and can be shared), and your version can go in its own direction without affecting the original developer’s repository, which you couldn’t push to anyway. (Later in the tutorial, a hosting service such as Vercel can deploy the app from your own GitHub repository.)





Question 12 · Scenario
Maria’s working directory is ~/Documents. She runs git clone with her fork’s URL and then immediately types claude in the same terminal. What did she forget, and why does it matter?






Suggested answer





She forgot to cd into the new project folder first:
cd task-app
The page says to cd into the project folder and start Claude Code there. Started in ~/Documents, Claude Code would be looking at her whole Documents folder instead of the project. She should exit Claude Code, run cd task-app (and check with pwd), then start claude again. The same goes for an editor: open the task-app folder itself.

69.1 How to use a npm package in my Node.js project?
There are many “packages” of JavaScript code that have been developed by organizations or individual developers which are then shared with the Node.js community. These packages offer developers of new software to get a running start and avoid needing to write generally useful code from scratch.
Node.js includes a tool, npm. Which stands for the “Node Package Manager” tool. This tool is used to install and manage these packages (as we’ll see below). Therefore technically these packages are known as npm packages (and not Node.js packages).
The code for all npm packages can be found online at https://www.npmjs.com/. To see the Javascript code for a package. Search for the package, then click on the name of the package and click the “code” button.
To use a package in your project, you must do both of the following:

List the name of the package in the package.json file.
This file should be in the top folder (i.e. “root folder”) for the project.
(See more about the exact format of the package.json file below).
Run the npm install command in the terminal from the root folder for the project.
The npm install command downloads the packages that are used by this project into a folder named node_modules. (We’ll discuss this command more below).

69.2 More about the package.json file
Every project that uses Node.js and npm

should contain a file named package.json in the top (i.e. root) folder for the project
might also contain a file named package-lock.json

For now, let’s focus on the package.json file (we’ll explain the package-lock.json file later). Click on the link below to see the full package.json file for our task-app project is shown below. The file is in JSON format. We won’t give a full tutorial on JSON format here but it is relatively easy to see that the information in the file is structured and is laid out in sections. 69.2.1 package.json - the dependencies section
The following is the contents of the dependencies section for our task-app project. The dependencies section lists the npm packages that are needed to run the project. We’ll explain the exact format of the lines you see below.
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@radix-ui/react-checkbox": "^1.1.2",
    "@radix-ui/react-dialog": "^1.1.2",
    "@radix-ui/react-label": "^2.1.0",
    "@radix-ui/react-popover": "^1.1.2",
    "@radix-ui/react-select": "^2.1.2",
    "@radix-ui/react-slot": "^1.1.0",
    "@radix-ui/react-toast": "^1.2.2",
    "@supabase/ssr": "^0.5.2",
    "@supabase/supabase-js": "^2.47.10",
    "class-variance-authority": "^0.7.1",
    "clsx": "^2.1.1",
    "date-fns": "^3.6.0",

    "next": "14.2.16",
    "react": "^18",
    "react-day-picker": "^8.10.1",
