    "tailwindcss-animate": "^1.0.7"
  },
}
The following is the first line in the dependencies section:


    "@radix-ui/react-checkbox": "^1.1.2",`

Let’s explain this piece by piece:

@radix-ui is the name of the organization that developed the package.
Organizations that create many different npm packages may choose to use register their organization name with the npm package registry, https://www.npmjs.com/, to make it easier to find and identify their packages.
react-checkbox is the name of the package
^1.1.2 refers to the version number of the package that should be used. (see more about package version numbers below)
The ^ before the version number has special meaning which is described below.

Some packages do not list an organization name. For example the following entry in our file is for a package named “class-variance-authority” but the entry in packages.json doesn’t list an organization:

    "class-variance-authority": "^0.7.1",

Packages that don’t have an organization name are often packages that were developed by individual developers and aren’t necessarily associated with any organization.

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
section: 69.3 run npm install to in stall the packages
text:
69.3 run npm install to in stall the packages
To install these packages, run the following command from the top level folder (i.e. the “root” folder) in the project. This command creates a new folder named “node_modules” and downloads the code for each package into that folder.
npm install
Note: You may see warnings when you run this command saying that some of the packages that you are trying to install have been deprecated. This is not a problem for us now. This usually happens because the packages listed in the package-lock.json files (which we discuss below) file are out of date. Keep reading …
crumbs: 69  69. Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
text:
69.4 npm package version numbers
Every time an npm package is updated by the developers of the package a new “version number” is created for that new version of the package. When someone uses a package to write their software, they should record the version number of of the package that was used. This is important because sometimes later versions of the package might not work with the software that was written to use an older version of the package.
Package updates (and hence version numbers) fall into one of the following categories:

MAJOR updates: new features that are not necessarily totally compatible with existing software that used older versions of this package.
MINOR updates: new features that are intended to be backward-compatible with older versions
PATCH fixes: ie. bug fixes that are intended to be backward-compatible with older versions

The npm package version numbers reflect the type of changes that were made to the package since the last version. THe version numbers in the form: MAJOR_NUMBER.MINOR_NUMBER.PATCH_NUMBER
For example the version number 0.7.1 has

MAJOR_NUMBER 0
MINOR_NUMBER 7

PATCH_NUMBER 1

When a new version of a package is released, the major, minor and patch numbers in the version number are updated accordingly.
crumbs: 69  69. Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
section: 69.5 using a “^” before a version number (e.g. “^1.1.2”)
text:
69.5 using a “^” before a version number (e.g. “^1.1.2”)
It is common for version numbers to be listed with “special characters” that direct npm to install possibly later versions of the package than the specified version.
For example, a caret, i.e. ^, before a version number, e.g. ^1.1.2 , directs npm to install “this version or a later version that has the same MAJOR number”. This is often desired since versions of a package that have the same MAJOR version number should be compatible with each other.
For example the following line:
    "@radix-ui/react-checkbox": "^1.1.2",`
indicates that this project requires version 1.1.2 or later of the package. However, this will only install the latest 1.X.X version. It will NOT install any version from 2.0.0 or later.
The logic for this is that the original developer of our project probably developed the code for the project using version 1.1.2 of the package. If in the future a new improved version 1.1.3 would be released to fix some bugs in the package then that version should be used instead of 1.1.2. The same would be true if even later versions of the package would be release such as 1.1.4 or 1.1.5 or even 1.2.0 - the latest of any 1.X.X version would be used.
However, if a new MAJOR version is released, e.g. 2.0.0 then that would NOT be used when doing npm install for this project. The reason is that a new MAJOR version is not guaranteed to work with code that was written for a prior MAJOR version number of the package.
crumbs: 69  69. Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
section: 69.6 package-lock.json records the exact version numbers that were used
text:
69.6 package-lock.json records the exact version numbers that were used
As mentioned earlier, in theory, PATCH and MINOR updates to a package shouldn’t break code built and tested with an earlier version that shares the same MAJOR number. In practice, though, that’s not always true. To minimize potential issues, it’s best to install the project using the exact same package versions as those used by the original developer. Doing so ensures you’re working in the same environment and helps you avoid unexpected differences in behavior.
For this reason, when npm installs a package into the project, it records the EXACT version number that was installed into a file named package-lock.json. If the package-lock.json file exists then npm will install whatever version is registered in the package-lock.json file. However, if there is no package-lock.json file in a project then the rules stated above regarding which package is installed are followed. To be clear:
npm install will do the following:

If a package-lock.json file exists then the versions recorded in that file are downloaded to the node_modules folder.
If there is no package-lock.json file in the project then the versions of the packages as indicated in the package.json file are downloaded to the node_modules folder. Note that these could be later versions than the actual numbers listed in the file. For example if the package.json file lists version ^1.7.3 then the latest version number that still has a 1 in the first position will be installed. (see above for more info about version numbers in the package.json file)
crumbs: 69  69. Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
section: 69.7 Deprecated warning messages when doing npm install
text:
69.7 Deprecated warning messages when doing npm install
You may have noticed above that when you ran npm install, you got warning messages saying that one or more packages have been “deprecated”. In npm, a deprecation warning can refer either to an entire package or, more commonly, to a specific version of a package. In most cases, it means that the maintainers recommend upgrading to a newer version because the version being installed is outdated, has known issues, or has been superseded. This could happen if the package-lock.json file that was in the git repo has versions of packages that had later releases of new versions after the package-lock.json was created.
This generally should not be a problem for a learning tutorial. However, if you are planning on using this code in “production” it is recommended that you delete the package-lock.json file and re-run npm install. This should install the later versions of those packages that may have fixed some bugs. Hoewver, be aware the the original developer did not use these new package versions and therefore the code you have might not work 100% as expected and you might need to spend a little time debugging and testing the application.
crumbs: 69  69. Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
section: 69.8 Additional rules for package version numbers in package.json file
text:
69.8 Additional rules for package version numbers in package.json file
Above we discussed version numbers that start with a ‘^’. There are other types of “special characters” that affect which version of a package is actually installed. Below are the common forms with brief examples.
The following is a quick reference table. These are explained in more detail below.










Form
Example
Meaning






Exact
1.2.3
Only that version




Caret
^1.2.3
Non-breaking updates (same major)




Tilde
~1.2.3
Patch updates (same minor)




X-range
1.2.x, *
Wildcards




Hyphen
1.2.3 - 1.4.0
Inclusive range




Comparators
>=1.2.3 <2
Logical AND/OR with |   |




Pre-release
^2.0.0-rc.1
Includes matching prereleases




Tag
"latest", "next"
Registry dist-tag




Alias
npm:pkg@^1
Install another package under this name




Local file
file:../dir
From local disk




Workspace
workspace:*
Workspace package reference




Link
link:../dir
Symlink to local dir




Tarball URL
https://…/pkg.tgz
Install from remote tarball




Git
github:user/repo#tag
From VCS (branch/tag/commit)






69.8.1 1) Exact version number (no extra special characters)

1.2.3

{ "dependencies": { "lodash": "1.2.3" } }


69.8.2 2) Caret range (^) — allow non-breaking updates (same major) - discussed above
The idea of the ^ is to only allow newer versions that will not break existing code. In general this means it allows for newer versions that have the same major number. For example:

^1.2.3 → >=1.2.3 <2.0.0

However, if the major version is 0 (e.g. 0.2.3) the caret works a little differently. A major version 0 is intended to signal that the package is still experimental or under active development. Because the package is not considered stable, even small changes—like a minor or patch update—may break existing code.
For this reason, npm’s version range rules become more restrictive for major-zero versions: the ^ will only allow updates that keep the left-most non-zero digit the same. This prevents accidentally upgrading to a version that might introduce breaking changes. For example:

^0.2.3 → >=0.2.3 <0.3.0 (major=0 is special)

{ "dependencies": { "lodash": "^4.17.21" } }


69.8.3 3) Tilde range (~) — allow patch updates (same minor)

~1.2.3 → >=1.2.3 <1.3.0

{ "dependencies": { "lodash": "~4.17.0" } }


69.8.4 4) X-range / wildcard

1.2.x, 1.x, *

{ "dependencies": { "lodash": "1.2.x" } }


69.8.5 5) Hyphen range

1.2.3 - 1.4.0 → >=1.2.3 <=1.4.0

{ "dependencies": { "lodash": "4.17.0 - 4.17.21" } }


69.8.6 6) Comparator sets

Use >, >=, <, <= and combine with spaces (AND) or || (OR):

>=1.2.3 <2.0.0
^1.2 || ^2.0


{ "dependencies": { "lodash": ">=4.17.0 <5" } }


69.8.7 7) Pre-releases

Append identifiers like -alpha.1, -beta, etc.
Pre-release … Must match explicitly. A prerelease like ^2.0.0-beta.1 will not include the final 2.0.0 version unless the range explicitly allows it (per npm’s semver rules).

{ "dependencies": { "react": "^19.0.0-rc.0" } }


69.8.8 8) Tags (dist-tags)

Named pointers published to the registry: latest, next, beta, etc.

{ "dependencies": { "typescript": "next" } }


69.8.9 9) Aliases (npm:)

Install one package as another name.

{ "dependencies": { "lodash": "npm:lodash-es@^4.17.21" } }


69.8.10 10) Local paths

file: to a directory or tarball on disk.

{ "dependencies": { "my-lib": "file:../my-lib" } }


69.8.11 11) Workspace references (workspace:)

For npm workspaces; pin to a workspace package.

{ "dependencies": { "ui": "workspace:*" } }


69.8.12 12) Local links (link:)

Symlink to a local folder (similar to npm link).

{ "dependencies": { "tooling": "link:../tooling" } }


69.8.13 13) Tarball URLs

Remote .tgz URL.

{ "dependencies": { "mypkg": "https://example.com/mypkg-1.2.3.tgz" } }


69.8.14 14) Git references

Full or shorthand; may include #branch, #tag, or #commit.

{
  "dependencies": {
    "lib-ssh": "git+ssh://git@github.com/user/repo.git#main",
    "lib-https": "git+https://github.com/user/repo.git#v1.2.3",
    "gh-short": "github:user/repo#abc1234",
    "gl-short": "gitlab:user/repo#v1.0.0",
    "bb-short": "bitbucket:user/repo#develop"
  }
}
crumbs: 69  69. Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
text:
69.9 Alternatives to npm
The npm is the tool used to install and manage these packages. However there are other competing “package manager” tools for “npm packages”. Currently available package manager tools are listed below. There are pros/cons to using each one:

npm – default with Node.js; biggest ecosystem. Slower than others.
Yarn – fast installs; good caching. Old v1 now legacy.
Yarn Berry – no node_modules; great for managing many packages together. Complex setup.
pnpm – space-efficient; strict resolution. Some tools misbehave.
Bun – ultra-fast; includes runtime. New and less stable.

If you’re just starting out, I recommend using npm (it’s most popular). However, don’t be surprised if some other tutorials that you see mention other package managers. All package managers for Javascript have similar capabilities and features.

69.10 Alternatives to Node.js
Similarly there are Javascript “runtime” environments other than Node.js. Again - if you’re just starting out, I recommend that you use Node.js but be aware of the existance of the others.

Deno – modern and secure; runs JavaScript and TypeScript easily. Not all Node tools work yet.
Bun – very fast and all-in-one (includes tools for testing and building). Still quite new.
Cloudflare Workers – runs small apps close to users for speed. Can’t use all Node features.
Workerd – the open-source engine behind Cloudflare’s system. Mainly for advanced use.

title: 69  69.  Step 2: Installing the Node.js packages with npm
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What two things must you do to use an npm package in your project?






Suggested answer






List the package (its name and version) in the package.json file in the project’s root (top) folder.
Run npm install in the terminal, from the project’s root folder. It downloads the packages listed in package.json.






Question 2 · Multiple choice
Where does npm install put the code of the packages it downloads?

In package.json
In a folder named node_modules
In package-lock.json
On npmjs.com







Suggested answer





b. npm install creates the node_modules folder and downloads each package’s code into it. package.json (a) only lists the packages the project needs, package-lock.json (c) records the exact versions that were installed, and npmjs.com (d) is the online registry the packages are downloaded from.





Question 3 · Matching
Match each part of the line "@radix-ui/react-checkbox": "^1.1.2" with its meaning.








Part

Meaning




1. @radix-ui

A. the version number


2. react-checkbox

B. “this version or a later one with the same MAJOR number”


3. 1.1.2

C. the organization that developed the package


4. ^

D. the name of the package









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each kind of package update with its description.








Update

Description




1. MAJOR

A. bug fixes, intended to be backward-compatible


2. MINOR

B. new features that are not necessarily compatible with software written for older versions


3. PATCH

C. new features, intended to be backward-compatible









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → A.





Question 5 · True or false
You should run npm install from the project’s root (top) folder, where package.json is.






Suggested answer





True. npm install works from the list of packages in the project’s package.json, which lives in the root folder, and it creates the node_modules folder there.





Question 6 · Short answer
Which file records the exact version of every package that npm install installed?






Suggested answer





package-lock.json. (package.json, by contrast, usually lists a range of allowed versions, such as ^1.1.2.)






Medium

Question 7 · Short answer
For the version number 2.13.4, what are the MAJOR, MINOR and PATCH numbers? If the next release is 3.0.0, what kind of update is that, and what does it warn you about?






Suggested answer





MAJOR = 2, MINOR = 13, PATCH = 4. 3.0.0 is a MAJOR update: it is not necessarily compatible with software written for version 2, so code that worked with 2.13.4 might break.





Question 8 · Multiple choice
Imagine a package named example-lib with these versions published: 1.0.9, 1.1.2, 1.4.0 and 2.0.0. Your package.json says "example-lib": "^1.1.2", and there is no package-lock.json. Which version does npm install install?

1.0.9
1.1.2
1.4.0
2.0.0







Suggested answer





c. ^1.1.2 means “1.1.2 or later, with the same MAJOR number (1)”, and npm installs the latest version that fits: 1.4.0. Version 1.0.9 (a) is older than 1.1.2; 1.1.2 (b) is allowed but is not the latest; and 2.0.0 (d) is a new MAJOR version, which the ^ doesn’t allow.





Question 9 · Predict
Same package and versions as in the previous question, but now the project does have a package-lock.json, and it records example-lib version 1.1.2. Which version does npm install install, and why?






Suggested answer





1.1.2. When a package-lock.json file exists, npm installs the exact versions recorded in it. That way you get the same versions the original developer used and tested, even though a newer 1.x.x version exists.





Question 10 · Write the range
Write the range of versions that each entry allows:

~1.2.3
^1.2.3
1.2.3







Suggested answer






>=1.2.3 <1.3.0: patch updates only (same MINOR number)
>=1.2.3 <2.0.0: minor and patch updates (same MAJOR number)
Exactly 1.2.3, and nothing else






Question 11 · Short answer
Look at the dependencies section of the project’s package.json. Which package is pinned to one exact version, and how can you tell?






Suggested answer





next (the Next.js framework): "next": "14.2.16". Its version has no ^ or other special character in front of it, so npm installs exactly 14.2.16. Every other package in that section has a ^ in front of its version.





Question 12 · Classify
According to the page, which of these tools are package managers, which are JavaScript runtimes, and which one is both? npm, Yarn, pnpm, Node.js, Deno, Bun.






Suggested answer






Package managers: npm, Yarn, pnpm
Runtimes: Node.js, Deno
Both: Bun (the page lists it as a package manager that “includes runtime”, and also as a runtime)

For beginners, the page recommends sticking with Node.js and npm.





Question 13 · Scenario
You run npm install and see several warnings saying that some packages are deprecated. What does that mean, and do you need to stop the tutorial?






Suggested answer





A deprecation warning means the package’s maintainers recommend upgrading, usually because that version is outdated, has known issues, or has been replaced by something newer. Here it happens because the project’s package-lock.json lists versions that have since been replaced by newer releases. For a learning tutorial this is generally not a problem: the packages still get installed, so you can keep going. (A warning is not an error. If npm stops with an error, that is a different problem, and you need to fix it.)






Hard

Question 14 · Short answer
The project lists "class-variance-authority": "^0.7.1". Which versions does the ^ allow here? Why is the rule different when the MAJOR number is 0?






Suggested answer





Only >=0.7.1 <0.8.0, that is, 0.7.x versions from 0.7.1 up. A MAJOR number of 0 signals that the package is still experimental or under active development, so even a MINOR update might break code. For such versions the ^ keeps the left-most non-zero number (here the 7) the same, instead of only the MAJOR number.





Question 15 · Long answer
package.json already says which versions are allowed. Why does a project also need package-lock.json?






Suggested answer





The ranges in package.json (such as ^1.1.2) allow later versions. In theory, MINOR and PATCH updates shouldn’t break anything; in practice they sometimes do. package-lock.json records the exact versions that were installed and tested. When it exists, npm install installs exactly those versions, so everyone who installs the project (you, a teammate, a server) gets the same environment as the original developer. Without it, two people who install at different times could get different versions and see different behavior.





Question 16 · Scenario
Maria’s copy of the task app works. Sam deleted package-lock.json “to clean up” and ran npm install again; now one feature behaves differently on his computer. What is the likely cause, and how can he fix it?






Suggested answer





Without the lock file, npm followed the ^ ranges in package.json and installed the latest allowed versions, which can be newer than the ones the original developer used. One of those newer MINOR or PATCH versions probably changed how something works.
Fix: get the original package-lock.json back (it is part of the Git repository, so git restore package-lock.json brings it back) and run npm install again to get the exact recorded versions.





Question 17 · Scenario
Sam opens a new terminal, which starts in his home folder, and runs npm install right away. He gets an error that mentions package.json. What went wrong, and how does he fix it?






Suggested answer





He ran npm install in the wrong folder. npm needs the project’s package.json, which is in the project’s root folder, not in his home folder. He should cd into the project’s root folder (for example cd ~/Documents/task-app), check with ls that package.json is there, and run npm install again.

title: 70  70.  Step 3: Storing your private info (env files, etc)
text:
70.1 More about the .env files
Private information such as passwords and API Keys (which we will discuss later) should never be stored in git because git repositories are often shared with other people. For similar reasons, passwords, API keys, etc. should also never by typed directly into Javascript code or code of any other programming language.
A typical web project requires different passwords, API keys, etc to allow integration with external services. In this project we will be integrating your NextJS app with Supabase, Google OAuth and the Chatgpt API. Each one of these integrations requires some sort of “secret” info (password, API Key, etc) to authenticate (i.e. login) to the remote system.
Much of this “secret” information will be stored in files whose filenames include “.env”. Remember that the .gitignore file identifies the files in your project that should never be committed to git. The .env files are prevented from being committed to git by referencing them in the .gitignore file.
In this project, we will need two different .env files. You will need to modify the contents of these .env files with the API keys that you generate for your Supabase account and other accounts.
The developer of this tutorial created one .env.example file. This is just an example file. It doesn’t contain real info. It should be copied into the locations for the .env files that we will be using.
For now, we will just copy the .env.exapmle file in the two locations. We will come back later and modify these files and explain more about them.
You need to create two local .env files for environment variables. These files will contain API keys and configuration that you’ll add throughout this tutorial. Note that the File names must be exact:

crumbs: 70  70. Step 3: Storing your private info (env files, etc)

title: 70  70.  Step 3: Storing your private info (env files, etc)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · True or false
It’s fine to store passwords and API keys in your git repository, so that your teammates can find them easily.






Suggested answer





False. Secrets should never be stored in git, because git repositories are often shared with other people. For the same reason, they should never be typed directly into your code either.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Where should you keep an API key for this project while you develop on your computer?

Typed directly into a JavaScript file
In a .env file, such as .env.local, that is listed in .gitignore
In the project’s README, so teammates can find it
In .env.example







Suggested answer





b. .env files hold the secrets, and because they are listed in .gitignore, git never commits them. A key typed into code (a) or into the README (c) ends up in git and is shared with everyone who can see the repository. .env.example (d) is part of the repository, so it must contain only example values, never real ones.





Question 3 · Short answer
The page says each integration needs “secret” information to authenticate to the remote system. What does “authenticate” mean here, and what kinds of secret information are used?






Suggested answer





To authenticate means to prove who you are, basically to log in, to the other system (Supabase, Google, OpenAI, …). The secret information is a password, an API key or something similar. Whoever has it can act as you on that service, which is why it must be kept secret.





Question 4 · Short answer
What is the .env.example file for?






Suggested answer





It is an example (template) file created by the project’s developer. It shows which settings the project needs, but it doesn’t contain real information. You copy it to create your real .env files, and later you fill in your own keys.





Question 5 · Short answer
What does the .gitignore file do, and how does it protect your .env files?






Suggested answer





.gitignore lists the files in the project that should never be committed to git. Because the .env files are referenced in .gitignore, git ignores them, so your secrets stay on your computer and out of the shared repository.






Medium

Question 6 · Write the command
You are in the project’s top-level folder. Write the two commands that create the project’s two .env files from the example file.






Suggested answer





cp .env.example .env.local
cp .env.example supabase/.env
cp copies a file: the first name is the original, the second is the new copy.





Question 7 · Short answer
Which two .env files does this project need, and what is each one for?






Suggested answer






.env.local: for the Next.js application
supabase/.env: for the Supabase functions

The page stresses that the file names must be exact, dots included: a file with a slightly different name won’t be found where the project expects it.





Question 8 · True or false
.env.example contains your real API keys, so it must never be committed to git.






Suggested answer





False. .env.example contains only example values, no real information. It is part of the repository (it came with the code you cloned), so that everyone can see which settings they need to fill in. Your real keys go into .env.local and supabase/.env, which are not committed.





Question 9 · Scenario
Maria runs cp .env.example .env.local and then ls, but .env.local isn’t in the list. Did the command fail?






Suggested answer





Probably not. Files whose names start with a dot are hidden, and a plain ls doesn’t show them. ls -a shows hidden files too, including .env.local. (Also, cp prints nothing when it succeeds; an error message would mean that something went wrong.)






Hard

Question 10 · Find the bug
Sam typed:
cp .env.example .env.locale
What’s wrong, and why could it cause two different problems?






Suggested answer





The file name is wrong: it must be exactly .env.local.

The project looks for .env.local, so it won’t find the settings Sam puts in his misnamed file.
The .gitignore rules may not cover a file named .env.locale, so if he later commits everything, his secrets could end up in git.

Fix: rename the file with mv .env.locale .env.local.





Question 11 · Scenario
Sam is in his home folder when he runs cp .env.example supabase/.env. He gets an error saying that .env.example doesn’t exist (“No such file or directory”). Why, and how does he fix it?






Suggested answer





.env.example and supabase/.env are relative paths, so they are looked up starting from the current working directory: his home folder, where those files don’t exist. As the page says, he must first cd into the project’s top-level folder (for example cd ~/Documents/task-app) and then run the command again.





Question 12 · Scenario
Two weeks later, Maria has filled in .env.local with her real keys. To be “safe”, she runs cp .env.example .env.local again. What happens? Can git help her undo it?






Suggested answer





cp overwrites an existing file without asking, so her real keys are replaced by the example values. Git can’t bring them back: .env.local is listed in .gitignore, so git never saved a copy of it. She has to enter the values again, from her setup notes or by getting them again from each service’s website. Lesson: copy .env.example only once, when you first create the files.





Question 13 · Long answer
Why should secrets never be typed directly into your code? What does keeping them in .env files give you instead?






Suggested answer





Code files are committed to git and shared: with teammates, on GitHub, and sometimes with the whole world. A key typed into code is therefore effectively published. Keeping secrets in .env files means:

the real values live only in files that .gitignore keeps out of git;
the code itself can be shared safely, because it contains no secrets;
each person (or computer) can use their own keys without changing the code.

title: 71  71.  Step 4 - Optional: Preview the Frontend
text:
Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is the point of this optional step? What will you be able to do, and what won’t work?






Suggested answer





It lets you see the app’s frontend before any backend is connected. The “front end boilerplate” commit uses placeholder backend logic, so you can click around and explore the user interface (UI), but nothing really works: the app isn’t connected to Supabase or any of the other services yet.





Question 2 · Short answer
What is a commit hash, and where do you find the one you need for this step?






Suggested answer





A commit hash is the unique ID of a commit (a saved snapshot of the project): a long string of letters and numbers. You find it on the repository’s commits page on GitHub: scroll down to the bottom, where the oldest commits are, find the front end boilerplate commit and copy its hash.





Question 3 · Write the command
Which command starts the development server so that you can see the app?






Suggested answer





npm run dev
Run it from the project’s top-level folder. It starts a local version of the site and prints a local address that you open in your browser.






Medium

Question 4 · Multiple choice
You have Git version 2.43. Which command takes your project back to the commit whose hash starts with abc1234?

git switch --detach abc1234
git clone abc1234
npm run abc1234
git commit abc1234







Suggested answer





a. On Git 2.23 or later, git switch --detach followed by the hash checks out that commit (the older git checkout abc1234 also still works). git clone (b) copies a whole repository from a URL, npm run (c) runs a script from package.json, and git commit (d) saves a new snapshot.





Question 5 · Ordering
Put these steps in order:

Run npm run dev
Copy the commit hash
Open the repository’s commits page on GitHub
Run git switch - to go back to the latest code
Check out the commit with git switch --detach <hash>
Click around and explore the UI







Suggested answer






Open the repository’s commits page on GitHub
Copy the commit hash
Check out the commit with git switch --detach <hash>
Run npm run dev
Click around and explore the UI
Run git switch - to go back to the latest code






Question 6 · Matching
Match each task with the right command.








Task

Command




1. Go to an old commit (Git 2.23 or later)

A. git checkout main


2. Go to an old commit (older Git)

B. git switch --detach <hash>


3. Go back to the main branch (Git 2.23 or later)

C. git checkout <hash>


4. Go back to the main branch (older Git)

D. git switch main









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → D, 4 → A.





Question 7 · True or false
In the front end boilerplate version, creating a task saves it in your Supabase database.






Suggested answer





False. That version has only placeholder backend logic. You can click around the UI, but it isn’t connected to Supabase or any other service, so nothing is really saved.






Hard

Question 8 · Short answer
Why does the page give different commands depending on your Git version?






Suggested answer





git switch was added in Git 2.23 (2019). Older versions only have git checkout, which does several jobs, including switching branches and checking out old commits. Newer versions understand both commands; git switch is clearer because its name says what it does.





Question 9 · Scenario
Maria previewed the boilerplate and forgot to switch back. She carries on with the next tutorial steps, but even after she connects the backend, the app still doesn’t really do anything. What happened, and how can she fix it?






Suggested answer





She is still on the old front end boilerplate commit, which only has placeholder backend logic, so the code she is running doesn’t use the backend she set up. Fix: stop the development server (Ctrl+C), run git switch - or git switch main (on older Git: git checkout - or git checkout main), and start the server again with npm run dev.





Question 10 · Short answer
To get back to the latest code, you can run git switch - or git switch BRANCH_NAME. What does the - mean, and when is naming the branch the safer choice?






Suggested answer





- means “go back to where I was just before”, like cd - for folders. Naming the branch (for example git switch main) is safer when you aren’t sure what you did last: if you switched more than once, - takes you back only one step, which may not be your main branch. In this repository the main branch is called main (other projects may use master); git branch lists your branches.

title: 72  72.  Step 5: Setup Supabase
text:
72.1 Remote vs. Local Supabase
Supabase is an online service that gives you the tools you need to store and manage data for your app. It includes:
Supabase can run remotely (hosted online by Supabase) and/or locally (running on your own computer). For beginners, remote Supabase is far easier. Everything happens in your browser, and nothing must be installed or configured. Local Supabase is mainly for advanced users and developers who want to test everything on their own computer before uploading to the Internet. Having a local copy of supabase also allows you to develop your app during times that you don’t have access to the Internet.
In this tutorial we will use remote Supabase only, so you do not need to install a local copy or manage anything technical on your machine.

72.2 Sign Up for Supabase

Go to the Supabase website
Sign up for a free account
Create a new project

text:
72.4 Get Your API Keys
Once your project is created:

Edit the .env.local file. It currently looks like this:

# You will need a .env.local file for local dev server (localhost)
# You will need a .env.test.local file for running the integration tests.

# Create the those files, and add the following variables.
# The local files are ignored by default.

# In .env.local and .env.test.local:
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL="https://XXXX.supabase.co"
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY="XXXX"

# In addition to that, you also need .env.test.local with these variables:
SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY="XXXX"
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY="sk_test_XXX"
STRIPE_PRICE_ID="price_XXX"
STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET="whsec_XXX"```

Delete the bottom few lines and top few lines so that the file now looks like this:
# In .env.local and .env.test.local:
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL="https://XXXX.supabase.co"
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY="XXXX"
Go to Project Settings (Gear button at bottom left of screen) → Data API
 Copy the URL.
Modify the following line in the .env.local file to reflect the URL that you copied.
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL="https://XXXX.supabase.co"
Click on the API Keys section.
Copy the anon public key.

Modify the following line in the .env.local file to reflect the URL that you copied.
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY="XXXX"

title: 72  72.  Step 5: Setup Supabase
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Multiple choice
Which of the following is not one of the Supabase features listed on this page?

A database for storing structured data
Authentication, so users can sign in to your app
File storage in the cloud
Processing credit card payments







Suggested answer





d. Supabase gives you a database, authentication, file storage and edge functions. Payments are not a Supabase feature; in this project they are handled by a separate service, Stripe. Options a, b and c are all on the page’s list.





Question 2 · Short answer
What are Supabase edge functions?






Suggested answer





Small pieces of code that run on servers close to your users (on Supabase’s servers, not in the user’s browser). In task-app, edge functions do jobs such as asking the OpenAI API to pick a tag for a task and talking to Stripe.





Question 3 · True or false
In this tutorial, you install and run your own copy of the Supabase server on your computer.






Suggested answer





False. The tutorial uses remote Supabase only: Supabase runs the server online, and you set it up through your browser. Running Supabase locally is mainly for advanced developers.





Question 4 · Short answer
When you create a new Supabase project, which three things does this page say you need to choose or set?






Suggested answer






A project name.
A database password (save it somewhere safe; you’ll need it later).
A region (choose the one closest to your users).







Medium

Question 5 · Multiple choice
Most of your app’s users will be in New York. Which region should you pick for your Supabase project?

The region closest to you, the developer
The region closest to your users, such as an East US region
Any region; the choice makes no difference
Whichever region is listed first in the menu







Suggested answer





b. The page says to choose the region closest to your users. Data that travels a shorter distance arrives faster, so the app responds more quickly. Where you, the developer, are located (a) matters less than where your users are, and the region does make a difference (c). The order of the menu (d) means nothing.





Question 6 · Short answer
Give two reasons why a developer might run Supabase locally (on their own computer) instead of using only the remote version.






Suggested answer






To test everything on their own computer before uploading it to the Internet.
To keep working on the app when they don’t have Internet access.

The price is that local Supabase must be installed and configured, which is why this tutorial uses remote Supabase.





Question 7 · Fill in the blank
Your Supabase project URL is https://qzvbnmtrewplkjhgfdsa.supabase.co. Write the complete line in .env.local that stores it.






Suggested answer





NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL="https://qzvbnmtrewplkjhgfdsa.supabase.co"
Keep the variable name and the quotes exactly as they are, and replace the whole placeholder https://XXXX.supabase.co with your real URL.





Question 8 · Short answer
The original file also contains SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_PRICE_ID and STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET. According to the comments in the file, why can you delete those lines from .env.local?






Suggested answer





.env.local is used by the local development server, which only needs the two NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_... lines. The other variables are only needed in a separate file, .env.test.local, which is used for running the project’s integration tests.





Question 9 · True or false
Even though your project is a Git repository, it is OK to type your real Supabase values into .env.local.






Suggested answer





True. As the comment in the file says, the “local” env files are ignored by default: the project’s .gitignore file lists them, so Git never commits them. That is exactly why real values go into .env.local and not into .env.example, which is committed. Still, treat the file as private.






Hard

Question 10 · Scenario
Sam starts the app, but nothing that needs Supabase works. His .env.local contains:
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL="https://XXXX.supabase.co"
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY="XXXX"
What went wrong, and how does he fix it?






Suggested answer





He never replaced the placeholders that came from the example file, so the app is trying to reach a Supabase project that doesn’t exist. He needs to copy his own project’s URL and key from his Supabase dashboard into these two lines and save the file. Restarting the development server (npm run dev) makes sure the app picks up the new values.





Question 11 · Short answer
The page tells you to save your database password securely. Why is this password so important? Give two reasons.






Suggested answer






You’ll need it later in the tutorial, so you must be able to find it again.
It is the password to your project’s database. Anyone who has it could connect to the database directly and read or change all of your app’s data, so treat it like any other important password: keep it out of Git and don’t share it.






Question 12 · True or false
Two classmates clone the same task-app repository from GitHub. Because the Supabase project URL is stored in the repository, both copies of the app automatically use the same Supabase project.






Suggested answer





False. The repository only contains .env.example, with placeholders such as https://XXXX.supabase.co. Each student creates their own Supabase project and puts its URL in their own .env.local. That file is ignored by Git, so it never goes into the repository, and each copy of the app talks to its own project.

title: 73  73.  Step 5a: Supabase CLI command
text:
73.1 Installing the Supabase CLI
The supabase CLI is a command that you can run from your terminal to control and configure your Supabase server. The name of the command is appropriately “supabase”.
While, you can configure and manage your remote supabase server directly from the supabase website, it is often easier to use the supabase CLI command to perform much of the configuration and management of the supabase server.
Do not confuse the supabase CLI command with the supabase server. These are different products. Both can be installed locally.
There is more than one way to install the supabase CLI:
In the previous section you setup a Supabase project on the Supabase website. Supabase has many different features (database, authentication, edge functions, storage buckets, etc). You can configure most of what you need to configure by “clicking around” on the website. However, there are some things that cannot be done on the website. For these things we must use the “supabase CLI tool”.
In addition, using the supabase CLI command can often be easier and more efficient than accessing the same functionality via the Supabase website.

73.2 Using Supabase CLI via npx
There are different options for installing/running the supabase CLI command. The simplest and easiest way to use the supabase command is to use the npx command to run the supabase command. npx (Node Package Executer) comes with Node.js. While the npm (Node Package Manager) tool can be used to download and install packages on your computer, the npx package is used to download and run the code from an npm package without actually “installing” the package on your computer.

section: 73.3 Installing Supabase CLI on your computer
text:
73.3 Installing Supabase CLI on your computer
NOTE: remember that the supabase CLI is NOT the same as the supabase server. In this section we are discussing installing the supabase CLI on your local computer - not the supabase server. 

In this tutorial we will be using npx to run the supabase CLI. However there are some benefits to acutally “installing” the supabase command on your computer. If you use npx to run the supabase CLI, then every time you run the npx supabase command, the latest copy of the supabase npm package is downloaded to your computer. If you don’t have access to the Internet, things become more complicated. For this and other reasons, some people prefer to install the supabase CLI on their computer. You can do so by using one of the options listed below. Note that if you do install supabase on your computer then the command would simply be

supbase ...(other options)...

instead of

npx supabase ...(other options)....

See official instructions for how to install here: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/cli/getting-started The following summarizes your options to install locally:

Install the supabase CLI command as an npm package. To do so, run the following command from the root (top level folder) for your project:
npm install supabase --save-dev
NOTE: installing using the -g option to npm is no longer supported
You can also install the supabase CLI command on Mac by using the Homebrew package manager or on Windows by using the Scoop package manager. See the instructions here https://github.com/supabase/cli?tab=readme-ov-file to learn more about this option.
You can also download the actual program files from here: https://github.com/supabase/cli/releases. Be aware that this page lists “pre-release” versions as well as “release” versions. The “pre-release” versions may have the latest fixes and modifications but are not supported. For example, at the time of this writing the latest “release” version is 2.58.5 but there are “pre-release” versions 2.58.6, 2.59.*, 2.60.1, 2.60.2 Use the pre-release versions if you want the absolute latest features but be aware that they may not have been fully tested.

text:
73.4 How to use the supabase command via npm and npx
IMPORTANT: If you are using supabase cli via npm then you should prefix all uses of the supabase command with “npx” (see examples below). For example, the following command will show you which version of the supabase cli you are using:
npx supabase --version
The following gives you a very short summary for how to use the supabase command
npx supabase --help
npx is the Node Package eXecution command. This command can be used to run (or eXecute) a command that is installed as an npm package.

73.4.1 supabase ‘sub-commands’
The supabse command has numerous “sub commands”. For example:

npx supabase db is used to work with the Supabase database.
Run npx supabase db --help to get help specific to the db sub-command.
npx supabse functions is used to work with Supabase “edge functions”.
Run npx supabase functions --help to get help specific to the db sub-command.
etc.

The full official reference for how to use the supabase CLI command is here: https://supabase.com/docs/reference/cli/introduction There are many options and the official reference can be overwhelming. We will walk you through an introduction of using the supabase CLI command in this tutorial.

73.5 Login in to Supabase
Run the following command:
npx supabase login

You should see the following: Hello from Supabase! Press Enter to open browser and login automatically.
Press Enter and a browser will open and display a code. Copy the code.
Go back to the terminal and enter the code and press Enter
You should now be logged into supabase.

title: 73  73.  Step 5a: Supabase CLI command
text:
73.7 Find your project’s reference ID
In the next step we will “link” the project on your computer to your Supabase project that you setup on the Supabase website. To do so, you will need to know your “project ref”. It is listed in the output of the npx supabase projects list command (see above). For example, the REFERENCE ID for the 2nd project listed above is bvysrsysihcpsomfkyja.
The project reference ID is also part of your project’s URL. You can find your project URL in your Supabase dashboard URL. It looks something like this: https://app.supabase.com/project/bvysrsysihcpsomfkyja The part after /project/ is your project ref, ie. in the example above this would be bvysrsysihcpsomfkyja. However, your own project-ref will obviously be different.

73.7.1 Link your project
Once you have identified your project ref, open your terminal, and navigate to your project directory. Then run the following command where “YOUR_PROJECT_REF” is replaced with your actual project ref. This command creates a connection between your local machine and your cloud project so that future commands from the CLI will knows which project you’re working with.
npx supabase link --project-ref YOUR_PROJECT_REF
For example, given the example above the command would be: The ouput shown below is what I got when I ran the command. This indicates that my project is linked with the remote supabase server. The WARNING that you see is harmless. Click on the link below to understand more about this warning message.

npx supabase link --project-ref bvysrsysihcpsomfkyja
Initialising login role...
Connecting to remote database...
Finished supabase link.
WARNING: Local database version differs from the linked project.
Update your supabase/config.toml to fix it:
[db]
major_version = 17






click for an explanation of the WARNING message





Developers often run a local version of the Supabase server that allows them to develop their project without having Internet access. When the developer wants to synchronize the work that they did on their local computer with the remote Supabase server, they can link their project to the remote project (as we did here) and then run the command npx supabase push to “push” their work to the remote server. For this to work correctly, the supabase version that is installed locally must be compatible with the supabase version on the remote server.
We decided that for simplicity, we will not use a local installation of the Supabase server. However, when this git repo was originally developed, the developer did have a local Supabase server installed on his computer. The file config.toml that is in the supabase folder stores configuration information for the local Supabase server. When this project was originally developed, the supabase/config.toml file got committed to git.
The warning message is simply saying that the recorded version of the local Supabase server not compatible with the version for remote Supabase server. However, as we said above, we are not using an actual local Supabase server. Therefore we can ignore this message. Alteratively, we can change the contents of the supabase/config.toml file by modifying the lines in the supabase/config.toml that record the local supabase version to read as follows:
[db]
major_version = 17







73.7.2 Test the link
You can run the following commands to test that your link has been established correctly.
The following should show all Supabase projects your CLI account has access to:
npx supabase projects list
The following should show whether your local directory is currently linked to a Supabase project:
npx supabase link status

text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · True or false
The Supabase CLI and the Supabase server are the same product.






Suggested answer





False. The CLI is a command (supabase) that you run in your terminal to configure and manage a Supabase project. The server is the Supabase system itself (database, authentication, storage and so on). In this tutorial the server runs remotely, on Supabase’s computers, and only the CLI runs on your computer.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
How do you type Supabase CLI commands in this tutorial?

supabase <command>
npx supabase <command>
npm supabase <command>
node supabase <command>







Suggested answer





b. The tutorial runs the CLI through npx, so every command starts with npx supabase. Plain supabase (a) only works if you installed the CLI in another way, for example with Homebrew or Scoop. npm (c) is for installing and managing packages, and node (d) runs JavaScript files.





Question 3 · Short answer
What is the difference between npm and npx?






Suggested answer





npm (Node Package Manager) downloads and installs packages. npx runs a command that comes from an npm package, without you having to install that command on your computer yourself. Both come with Node.js.





Question 4 · Write the command
Write the command that shows which version of the Supabase CLI you are using.






Suggested answer





npx supabase --version





Question 5 · Short answer
You can configure most of Supabase by clicking around on the Supabase website. Give two reasons why the tutorial uses the CLI anyway.






Suggested answer






Some things can’t be done on the website at all; they need the CLI.
For many tasks, typing one command is easier and faster than clicking through many screens.







Medium

Question 6 · Matching
Match each command with what it does.








Command

What it does




1. npx supabase login

A. Lists all Supabase projects your account can access


2. npx supabase projects list

B. Connects your project folder to one Supabase project online


3. npx supabase link --project-ref <ref>

C. Shows help for the database sub-command


4. npx supabase db --help

D. Connects the CLI to your Supabase account


5. npx supabase --help

E. Shows a summary of all CLI commands and options









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → A, 3 → B, 4 → C, 5 → E.





Question 7 · Short answer
Name two places where you can find your project’s reference ID (the “project ref”).






Suggested answer






In the REFERENCE ID column of the output of npx supabase projects list.
In the web address of your project’s Supabase dashboard: it is the part after /project/.

(It is also the first part of your project URL, https://<project-ref>.supabase.co.)





Question 8 · Write the command
Your project ref is kplmnoqrstuvwxyzabcd. Write the command that links your project folder to this Supabase project. In which folder should you run it?






Suggested answer





npx supabase link --project-ref kplmnoqrstuvwxyzabcd
Run it from your project’s top-level folder (the one that contains the supabase folder).





Question 9 · Ordering
Put these steps in the order you would do them.

Run npx supabase link --project-ref <ref>
Run npx supabase login and enter the code shown in the browser
Create a project on the Supabase website
Test the link, for example by running npx supabase projects list again
Run npx supabase projects list and copy your project’s REFERENCE ID







Suggested answer





c → b → e → a → d.
You need a project before it has a ref, the CLI must be logged in before it can list your projects, you need the ref to link, and you test at the end.





Question 10 · Scenario
An AI chatbot tells you to run supabase functions --help. Your terminal answers command not found. Why, and what should you type instead?






Suggested answer





In this tutorial the CLI is not installed as a stand-alone supabase command; you run it through npx. Type:
npx supabase functions --help
AI tools often assume that supabase is installed, so add npx in front of the supabase ... commands they give you.





Question 11 · True or false
The recommended way to install the Supabase CLI is npm install -g supabase.






Suggested answer





False. As the page notes, installing the CLI with npm’s -g (global) option is not supported. Instead you can run it with npx (as this tutorial does), install it into your project with npm install supabase --save-dev (run in the project’s top-level folder), or use Homebrew (Mac) or Scoop (Windows).





Question 12 · Short answer
The CLI’s GitHub releases page lists a “release” version and several newer “pre-release” versions. Which should a beginner use, and why?






Suggested answer





The latest regular release. Pre-release versions may have the newest features and fixes, but they are not supported and may not be fully tested.






Hard

Question 13 · Scenario
After running npx supabase link, you see:
WARNING: Local database version differs from the linked project.
Update your supabase/config.toml to fix it:
[db]
major_version = 17
What does the warning mean, why can you ignore it in this tutorial, and how could you make it go away?






Suggested answer





The file supabase/config.toml stores settings for a local Supabase server. The original developer ran one, and the file he committed to Git records a different database version than the one your remote project uses. Because this tutorial doesn’t run a local Supabase server, the mismatch doesn’t matter. To make the warning go away, edit supabase/config.toml and set major_version = 17 in its [db] section.





Question 14 · Scenario
You run npx supabase projects list. Before the list of projects, the output says Cannot find project ref. Have you run supabase link? Is something broken? What does the message mean?






Suggested answer





Nothing is broken; the list of projects is still printed. The message means that the folder you are in is not linked to a Supabase project yet, so the CLI doesn’t know which project “this” folder belongs to. Commands that work on your project need that link. Fix it by running npx supabase link --project-ref <your-project-ref> from the project’s top-level folder.





Question 15 · Short answer
Why should you run npx supabase link from your project’s top-level folder rather than from, say, your home folder?






Suggested answer





The CLI works with the supabase folder inside your project, which holds config.toml, the database migrations and the edge functions. Linking records which online project belongs to this project folder, so later commands run from that folder (for example, pushing the database or setting secrets) know where to send their changes. From your home folder, the CLI wouldn’t find your project’s supabase folder.





Question 16 · Scenario
A teammate says: “I already ran npx supabase login, so the CLI knows which project to work on.” Is that right? Explain.






Suggested answer





Not quite. login only connects the CLI to your Supabase account, and one account can have several projects (npx supabase projects list shows them all). link is the step that tells the CLI which of those projects belongs to the current project folder. You need both.

title: 74  74.  Step 6: setup authentication (Google OAuth)
text:
74.1 Create a Google Cloud Project
This step connects your Supabase project with Google’s OAuth 2.0 service so users can log in using their Google accounts.
OAuth stands for “Open Authentication”. It is a standard that website owners can use to integrate with 3rd party services, such as Google, Github, etc, so that the users of the website can use their Google/Github/etc password to login.
From the perspective of our website, task-app, the code to do all this is run on the Supabase Servers. Therefore we will have to configure the Supabase Servers with the info necessary to make this happen.
In addition will will need to setup a Google Cloud Project here: https://console.cloud.google.com/. This is where you will need to setup Google to recognize your app and allow your users to login using their google accounts.
See this page for more information about setting up Google’s OAuth 2.0 service. https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/

74.3 Add your basic app info:
Whether this is the first time you are configuring Google OAuth, you should see one of the screens similar to those shown below.NOTE that if you have already started to configure Google OAuth before, you may need to click on the Branding option in the left hand menu (2nd choice from the top- see the blue oval in the picture).

You may see this





or may see this



74.3.1 App name
A name for your app (users will see this)


74.3.2 User support email
email for users to contact you with questions


74.3.3 Authorized domains
Under Authorized domains, add the domain used by your Supabase project. For example: bysrsyzsihcpsomfkyja.supabase.co You can get this from your Supabase dashboard. If you have been following this tutorial in order this info should also be in the .env.local file if you have in your top level folder for your project.


74.3.4 Audience
Under “Audience” choose External
This will allow you app to be viewed from anywhere in the world. However, your app must undergo review by Google before being allowed to use Google OAuth2 externally. Until then you can setup “test users” with google accounts. Only the specified “test users” will be allowed to “sign in with google” until your app has been reviewed by Google.
You will setup the test users later.
NOTE: You can only choose “Internal” if you’ve setup an organization with Google.


74.3.5 Developer Contact Information
Type an email address for Google to contact you for technical issues.


74.3.6 Click “Save”
Save and continue through the remaining steps.

title: 74  74.  Step 6: setup authentication (Google OAuth)
text:
74.4 Get Your OAuth Credentials

Return to APIs & Services → Credentials.
Click as below to create an OAuth 2.0 Client ID.

Choose Web application as the application type.
 You need to give a name to the application (Web client 1” in the screenshot below). This name is only used internal to the Google Cloud environment to refer to the application that you are setting up. This name will not appear anywhere to your users.
You then need to setup the URIs (i.e. URLs) that the Supabase servers will be contacted with from Google to indicate that the login was successful. You need to get this info from your Supabase configuration. This info was also saved in your .env.local file

Add your Supabase callback URL under Authorized redirect URIs: https://[your-project-ref].supabase.co/auth/v1/callback
You can get your-project-ref by doing one of the following:

logging into your Supabase account and getting this info from the Supabase settings.
You also can retreive it from the .env.local file that you had setup earlier. That file contained a line such as :

NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=“https://dfdqbazsihcpsomfkyja.supabase.co”

In this example dfdqbazsihcpsomfkyja is your-project-ref. Therefore the Authorize redirect URI for this example is:

https://dfdqbazsihcpsomfkyja.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback

Obviously you will have a different project-ref and therefore a slightly different URL.

Click “Create button”
After creation, copy your Client ID and Client Secret. You WILL NOT BE ABLE TO GET THESE CODES AGAIN FROM GOOGLE. Store these codes in a safe place. DO NOT store these code in any files that will be committed to git.

title: 74  74.  Step 6: setup authentication (Google OAuth)
text:
74.5 Configure Google Auth in Supabase

Open your Supabase dashboard.
Navigate to Authentication → Providers.
Select Google.
Paste your Client ID and Client Secret.
Click Save to enable Google login for your project.


With this configuration complete, Supabase can now handle secure login flows using Google OAuth.

title: 74  74.  Step 6: setup authentication (Google OAuth)
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
In plain English, what does setting up Google OAuth let the users of task-app do?






Suggested answer





It lets them sign in to task-app with the Google account they already have (“Sign in with Google”), instead of creating a new username and password just for your app.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
On which website do you register your app with Google and create its OAuth credentials?

The Supabase dashboard (supabase.com)
The Google Cloud console (console.cloud.google.com)
The OpenAI platform (platform.openai.com)
The Stripe dashboard (stripe.com)







Suggested answer





b. You create a Google Cloud project in the Google Cloud console and set up OAuth there. The Supabase dashboard (a) is where you paste the credentials afterwards. OpenAI (c) and Stripe (d) have nothing to do with Google sign-in.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
When you create the OAuth client ID, which application type do you choose?

Web application
Desktop app
Android
iOS







Suggested answer





a. task-app is a website that runs in the browser, so you choose Web application. The other types are for programs installed on a computer (b) or on a phone (c, d).





Question 4 · True or false
The name you give your OAuth client (for example “Web client 1”) is shown to your users when they sign in with Google.






Suggested answer





False. That name is only used inside Google Cloud to identify the client. What users see comes from the consent screen information, such as the App name.





Question 5 · Matching
Match each consent-screen setting with its purpose.








Setting

Purpose




1. App name

A. Your Supabase project’s domain, such as <project-ref>.supabase.co


2. User support email

B. Who the app is for: External (people with any Google account) or Internal (only your own organization)


3. Authorized domains

C. The name users see when they sign in with Google


4. Audience

D. An address Google uses to contact you about technical issues


5. Developer contact information

E. An address your users can write to with questions









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → E, 3 → A, 4 → B, 5 → D.






Medium

Question 6 · Write the URL
Maria’s .env.local contains:
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL="https://mqhzrtlkdbvcpweoaxsn.supabase.co"
What exactly should she enter under Authorized redirect URIs?






Suggested answer





https://mqhzrtlkdbvcpweoaxsn.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback
Her project ref is mqhzrtlkdbvcpweoaxsn. The redirect URI is her Supabase project URL followed by /auth/v1/callback.





Question 7 · Multiple choice
After Google creates your OAuth client, where do you paste the Client ID and Client Secret?

Into .env.local, as NEXT_PUBLIC_... variables
Into the Google provider settings in your Supabase dashboard (in the Authentication section)
Into supabase/config.toml
Into the project’s README file, so teammates can find them







Suggested answer





b. Supabase runs the sign-in code, so Supabase needs the credentials: select the Google provider, paste both values and save. Option a would put the secret into code that is sent to every visitor’s browser. supabase/config.toml (c) holds settings for a local Supabase server and is committed to Git, and so is the README (d), so both would publish your secret.





Question 8 · Short answer
Why are the Google credentials given to Supabase rather than written into the Next.js code of task-app?






Suggested answer





The code that handles “Sign in with Google” runs on Supabase’s servers: Supabase talks to Google, receives the result and then logs the user in to task-app. So Supabase is the one that needs the Client ID and Client Secret. This also keeps the secret on a server instead of in code that runs in the user’s browser.





Question 9 · Ordering
Put these steps in the right order.

Paste the Client ID and Client Secret into the Google provider settings in Supabase and save
Create a Google Cloud project
Create an OAuth client ID (type: Web application) with your Supabase callback URL as an authorized redirect URI
Fill in the consent screen information (app name, support email, authorized domain, audience, contact email)
Copy the Client ID and Client Secret right away and store them in a safe place







Suggested answer





b → d → c → e → a.
You need a Google Cloud project first. Google wants the consent screen set up before it lets you create the client. The secret must be copied the moment the client is created, and the values go into Supabase last.





Question 10 · Short answer
In one or two sentences, what is the redirect URI for?






Suggested answer





It is the address Google sends the user back to after a successful sign-in: here, your Supabase project’s callback address (.../auth/v1/callback), so that Supabase can finish logging the user in. Google only sends users to addresses on this approved list.





Question 11 · Multiple choice
Under Audience, the page tells you to choose External. Why not Internal?

Internal is only available if you have set up an organization with Google
Internal apps only work on Android phones
Internal apps cannot be used with Supabase
Internal hides the app name from users







Suggested answer





a. Internal limits sign-in to members of your own Google organization, and you can only choose it if you have one. A class project has no such organization and is meant for ordinary Google users, so External is the right choice. Options b, c and d are not true.






Hard

Question 12 · Scenario
Your Audience is External and your app is still in the testing stage. You added your own Google account as a test user, and you can sign in. Your friend tries to sign in, and Google blocks them. Why, and how can you let your friend test the app?






Suggested answer





While the app is in this testing stage, only the Google accounts listed as test users may sign in, and your friend isn’t on the list. Add your friend’s Google account (email address) as a test user in your app’s OAuth settings in Google Cloud (look for Test users), then have them try again.





Question 13 · Find the bug
Sam’s sign-in fails with Google’s error redirect_uri_mismatch. The authorized redirect URI he entered is:
https://bvcxzlkjhgfdsapoiuyt.supabase.co/auth/callback
What is wrong, and how does he fix it?






Suggested answer





The address is missing /v1. It must be exactly:
https://bvcxzlkjhgfdsapoiuyt.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback
Google compares the address that Supabase sends with your list character by character, so any difference (a missing part, a wrong project ref, http instead of https) causes this error. Sam should correct the URI in his OAuth client’s settings in Google Cloud and save.





Question 14 · Scenario
You created the OAuth client, but you closed the window without copying the Client Secret. What now?






Suggested answer





As the page warns, you can’t get the secret again from Google: it is shown in full only once, when it is created. Create a new client secret for the client (or a new OAuth client) in Google Cloud, store it in a safe place, and paste it into the Google provider settings in Supabase. Next time, copy it the moment it appears.





Question 15 · True or false
When a user signs in with Google, task-app receives the user’s Google password and checks it.






Suggested answer





False. The user types their password only on Google’s own sign-in page. Google then sends the user back to the redirect URI (your Supabase project) with proof that the sign-in succeeded. Neither task-app nor Supabase ever sees the Google password; that is one of the main benefits of OAuth.





Question 16 · Short answer
The page says never to store the Client ID and Client Secret in a file that will be committed to Git. Why does that matter, and where should you keep them instead?






Suggested answer





Git repositories are often shared (or even public on GitHub), and anything you commit stays in the project’s history. Someone with your Client Secret could pretend to be your app when talking to Google. Keep the values in a safe, private place (for example, your private notes for this tutorial or a password manager) and in the Supabase dashboard, which is where they are actually used.

text:
75.2 Create a “project” (optional)
All OpenAI API keys are associated with a “project”. You automatically have one “Default Project”. However, it can be helpful to create a new OpenAI “project” for every website or other product you are creating.
OpenAI “projects” allow for more control as to how your API Keys are used.
When you use a “project” …

you can have several people in your team share the API Key
you can set more fine grained permissions as to how the project can use the key

See here for more info about Open AI projects: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9186755-managing-projects-in-the-api-platform
To create a project, do the following:

75.2.1 Click settings (gear) button



75.2.2 Select “projects”



75.2.3 Click “create”



75.2.4 Give your project a name
crumbs: 75  75. Step 7: Set Up OpenAI API

title: 75  75.  Step 7: Set Up OpenAI API
text:
75.3 Create API keys

75.3.1 Click API Keys



75.3.2 Click Create new secret key.



75.3.3 Key Owner - “YOU” or a “SERVICE ACCOUNT”
When creating the key you need to specify whether the key is owned by “you” or by a “service account”. See more explanation below.
 
API Keys that are owned directly by “you” are useful when you are performing experiments with AI or just getting to understand how things work. In addition some 3rd part websites ask you to upload an OpenAI API key so that the work that they do for you is billed to YOUR OpenAI API key - i.e. the service doesn’t pay for the AI processing it does on your behalf, you do. It makes sense for these types of keys to be owned by “You”.
However, when creating software products that use API Keys it’s recommended to create a “Service Account” for that product and have the key be owned by that service account. The use of the key can then be tracked to your product’s “service account”.

Setting permissions for keys owned by “You”
If you create a key that is owned by “You” (see above) then you are given the opportunity to set permissions that govern what is and what isn’t allowed to be done with the key. This is especially important if you are going to be using your API Key to access 3rd party services. You can restrict the API Key to only allow some features to ensure that the 3rd party service doesn’t abuse the use of the key (as use of the API key would be charged to you).
If you create a key that is owned by a “Service Account” (as recommended for this project) then you can set permissions


Setting permissions for keys owned by a “Service Account”
By contrast, the permissions for a key that is owned by a “Service Account” are governed by the service account’s “role”. To change what the key can do, you must change the service account’s roles/permissions, not the key. We’ll see below (after saving the key) how to modify the permissions for such a key.



75.3.4 Copy the key immediately — you won’t be able to see it again.
When you click “create secret key” (see above) you will be shown the actual key. Copy the key immediately and save it — you won’t be able to see it again.
The key should be treated in the same way as a password. (In the following screenshot the API Key is purposely obscured). It is secret information which should never be divulged to anyone outside of your organization. Even within your organization, only people who have a “need to know” should be given access to the actual key value. Therefore do NOT commit this to git because git repos are often shared with people who should not have access to this type of info.

In the next section we will explain how to store this API Key in the supabase/.env file. This is because the communication with OpenAI will be done via a Supabase Edge Function. Much of the other “secret” information that we will be using in this tutorial will also be stored in .env files (see the section above that describes more about .env files).
For now, I recommend that for the purposes of this tutorial, you also store all of the secret info in a Word document (or similar). This is NOT the recommended approach for actual software development projects. However, as you are learning it can be helpful to have one file that stores all of the “secret information” in one place. You can store notes and screenshots in this file that help you remember where you got the information (e.g. OpenAI) and what it will be used for.
