title: 75  75.  Step 7: Set Up OpenAI API
section: 75.4 Setting permissions for keys owned by a “Service Account”
text:
75.4 Setting permissions for keys owned by a “Service Account”
How to adjust permissions:
Go to Organization → Admin keys / Service accounts.
Select the service account.
Modify its assigned roles/permissions.
All keys for that service account will now reflect those updated permissions.
If you’d like, I can outline how to set up a more restrictive service account.

75.4.1 Store as Supabase Secret
You’ll configure your Edge Functions to read OPENAI_API_KEY from the Supabase environment.

Install Supabase CLI (if you haven’t already)
(see the chapter above about the Supabase CLI)
Link your local project to your Supabase project (if you haven’t already)
(see the chapter above about the Supabase CLI)
Run the following command to set the secret in Supabase, where “your-openai-key” is the tet of the key that you just got from openai
supabase secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY=your-openai-key
Confirm that the key was set:
You can run the following command to confirm that there is an OPENAI_API_KEY set to some value. However, the “DIGEST” that is shown here is NOT the actual key. This is done for security reasons. You can delete the key and reset it but you cannot see the actual value for the key.

npx supabase secrets list
NAME           | DIGEST                                                           
----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------
 OPENAI_API_KEY | 661627b246146bfd00805f19997db43c066fba3002fabe2ed6a9922c8db29f87 

You can also use the supabase website dashboard (Project Settings → API → Secrets) to see the same info.
crumbs: 75  75. Step 7: Set Up OpenAI API

title: 75  75.  Step 7: Set Up OpenAI API
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · True or false
Every OpenAI API key belongs to a project, and every account automatically has a “Default Project”.






Suggested answer





True. You can use the Default Project, or create more projects, for example one for each website or product you build.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
When can you see the full value of a new OpenAI API key?

Any time, on the API keys page
Only once, right after you create it
Whenever you run npx supabase secrets list
After you ask OpenAI’s support team







Suggested answer





b. OpenAI shows the key only once, when you create it, so copy it immediately. Later, the API keys page (a) only shows a shortened version, secrets list (c) only shows a digest, and there is no way to get the key back (d): if you lose it, you create a new key.





Question 3 · Short answer
Why should an API key be treated like a password? Give two reasons.






Suggested answer






Anyone who has the key can use OpenAI through your account, and that usage is charged to you.
It is secret information that only people who need it should see. That is why it must never be committed to Git: repositories are often shared with people who shouldn’t have it.






Question 4 · True or false
Keeping all of your project’s secret keys in a Word document is the recommended approach for real software projects.






Suggested answer





False. The page suggests a private notes document only while you are learning, to keep track of where each value came from and what it is for. In real projects, secrets are kept in places designed for them, such as .env files that are never committed and secret storage like Supabase secrets.






Medium

Question 5 · Multiple choice
You are creating the key that task-app itself will use. According to the page, who should own this key?

You, because you are the developer
A service account created for the product
The first user who signs up for task-app
It doesn’t matter; all keys behave the same







Suggested answer





b. For software products, the page recommends a key owned by a service account, so that the key’s use can be tracked to that product (and the key isn’t tied to one person’s own account). Keys owned by “You” (a) suit your own experiments. Option c makes no sense, and d is wrong: the owner affects how use is tracked and how permissions are managed.





Question 6 · Short answer
Why might you create a separate OpenAI project for each website or product you build?






Suggested answer





Projects give you more control over how your keys are used. With one project per product, each product gets its own keys, you can set permissions for that project, you can give the right teammates access, and the use of each product’s keys stays separate.





Question 7 · Scenario
A third-party website asks you to paste in your OpenAI API key so it can do AI work for you. What should you keep in mind, and how can you limit the risk?






Suggested answer





The AI work the site does will be billed to your OpenAI account. Create a separate key just for that site (owned by “You”) and use its permissions to allow only the features the site needs, so the key can’t be used for anything else. If you stop using the site, delete that key.





Question 8 · Write the command
Your new key is sk-abc123. Write the command that stores it as a Supabase secret named OPENAI_API_KEY.






Suggested answer





npx supabase secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-abc123
In this tutorial the Supabase CLI runs through npx, so the command starts with npx supabase.





Question 9 · Predict the output
You run npx supabase secrets list and see a row with the name OPENAI_API_KEY and the digest 661627b246146bfd.... Is the digest your OpenAI key? What does this output tell you?






Suggested answer





No. The digest is a scrambled “fingerprint” of the value, not the key itself: for security reasons, Supabase never shows the actual value. The output only confirms that a secret named OPENAI_API_KEY is set on your project. If you need a different value, you can delete the secret and set it again, but you can never read it back.





Question 10 · Short answer
Why is the OpenAI key stored as a Supabase secret rather than in .env.local?






Suggested answer





The code that talks to OpenAI runs in a Supabase Edge Function, on Supabase’s servers, so the key must be available there. secrets set stores the key in your Supabase project, where the function can read it. As a bonus, the key stays on a server and never reaches the users’ browsers.





Question 11 · Ordering
Put these steps in the right order.

Run npx supabase secrets list to confirm that the secret is set
Click Create new secret key and choose the key’s owner
Run npx supabase secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY=...
Open the API keys page on the OpenAI platform
Copy the key immediately and save it in a safe place







Suggested answer





d → b → e → c → a.






Hard

Question 12 · Scenario
You accidentally pushed a file containing your OpenAI key to a public GitHub repository. What should you do, and why isn’t deleting the file from the repository enough?






Suggested answer






Delete the leaked key on the OpenAI API keys page right away, so it stops working.
Create a new key.
Store the new key in Supabase with npx supabase secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY=<new key> (setting a secret again replaces its old value).

Deleting the file isn’t enough: the key is still in the Git history, someone may already have copied it, and anyone who uses it runs up charges on your account.





Question 13 · Scenario
You run npx supabase secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY=... and get the message Cannot find project ref. Have you run supabase link? What went wrong, and how do you fix it?






Suggested answer





Your project folder isn’t linked to your Supabase project yet (or you ran the command from a different folder), so the CLI doesn’t know which project should get the secret. Go to your project’s top-level folder, run npx supabase link --project-ref <your-project-ref>, and then run the secrets set command again.





Question 14 · Find the bug
To save time, a classmate skips the Edge Function and calls OpenAI directly from the app’s browser code, with this line in .env.local:
NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
Explain the problem.






Suggested answer





In Next.js, variables whose names start with NEXT_PUBLIC_ are built into the JavaScript that is sent to every visitor’s browser. Anyone could find the key there (for example, with the browser’s developer tools) and use OpenAI at your expense. Secret keys must stay on a server; that is why this project calls OpenAI from a Supabase Edge Function and stores the key as a Supabase secret.

text:
76.1 Create Stripe Account
Stripe will handle subscriptions and billing. You’ll run in Test Mode while developing.

title: 76  76.  Step 8: Set Up Stripe
text:
Go to https://stripe.com.
Sign up for a new account or log in.

title: 76  76.  Step 8: Set Up Stripe
text:
76.2 The Stripe Sandbox
When you first start using Stripe you will be in “Sandbox” mode. This means that real cards are never charged. However, you can use “fake” credit cards (see below) to make sure that your code works.

title: 76  76.  Step 8: Set Up Stripe
text:
76.3 Get API Keys
Click on the “Home” menu (you should be there when you start).
The API keys should be listed (search for API on the page).


Add the publishable key to your Next.js environment:
# .env.local
NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=your-publishable-key
Store the secret key in Supabase (for Edge Functions):
npx supabase secrets set STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key
If you have a separate dev/prod project, repeat this setup per environment (we do not in this tutorial).


76.3.1 Create a Product

In Stripe dashboard, go to Product Catalog > All Products.
Click + Create product.
Fill in:

Name (e.g., “Pro Plan”)
Optional description and image.

Under Pricing, create a price:

Recurring
Billing period: Monthly
Amount: e.g., $10

Save the product and its price.
Copy the Price ID (e.g., price_12345...).
Add the Price ID to your app’s config (e.g., environment variable or constants file), for example: .env.local
NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PRICE_ID=your-price-id



76.3.2 Get Webhook Signing Secret
You’ll use a webhook to let Stripe notify your app about subscription changes.

Go to Developers → Webhooks in Stripe.
Click + Add endpoint.
For now, you can use a temporary URL (you’ll update it later), such as: https://mybogusurl.com/ 
Under Select events to send, add:

checkout.session.completed
customer.subscription.updated
customer.subscription.deleted

Save the endpoint.
Stripe will show a Signing secret (e.g., whsec_...). Copy it.
Store it as a Supabase secret:
supabase secrets set STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=your-webhook-secret

title: 76  76.  Step 8: Set Up Stripe
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · True or false
While you work in the Stripe sandbox, real credit cards are charged.






Suggested answer





False. In the sandbox, real cards are never charged. You test your code with fake test credit card numbers instead.





Question 2 · Short answer
In your own words, what is a webhook, and what does task-app use one for?






Suggested answer





A webhook is a web address (URL) that you give to Stripe so that Stripe can notify your app automatically when something happens: Stripe sends a message to that address. task-app uses it so that Stripe can tell the app about subscription changes, such as a completed checkout or a cancelled subscription.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
Which Stripe value does the page put in .env.local (under a NEXT_PUBLIC_ name) for the Next.js app?

The secret key
The publishable key
The webhook signing secret
Your Stripe account password







Suggested answer





b. The publishable key is designed to be public, so it is safe to use in code that runs in the browser. The secret key (a) and the webhook signing secret (c) are stored as Supabase secrets instead, and your account password (d) never goes into any project file.





Question 4 · Matching
Match each Stripe value with its description.








Value

Description




1. Publishable key

A. Looks like price_12345...; identifies the price a customer subscribes to (for example, $10 per month)


2. Secret key

B. Looks like whsec_...; lets your code check that a webhook message really came from Stripe


3. Price ID

C. Safe to use in code that runs in the browser


4. Webhook signing secret

D. Can do anything with your Stripe account through Stripe’s API; must stay on a server









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.






Medium

Question 5 · Write the command
Stripe shows you the signing secret whsec_9f8e7d. Write the command that stores it as a Supabase secret named STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET.






Suggested answer





npx supabase secrets set STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_9f8e7d
Remember that in this tutorial every Supabase CLI command starts with npx supabase.





Question 6 · Multiple choice
You want a “Pro Plan” that costs $10 every month. Which price settings match?

One-off, $10
Recurring, billing period Monthly, $10
Recurring, billing period Yearly, $10
One-off, $120







Suggested answer





b. A subscription needs a recurring price, and monthly billing at $10 matches the plan. One-off prices (a, d) charge only once, and a yearly billing period (c) charges once a year.





Question 7 · Matching
Match each webhook event with when Stripe sends it.








Event

When Stripe sends it




1. checkout.session.completed

A. A customer’s subscription ends (for example, it is cancelled)


2. customer.subscription.updated

B. A customer finishes paying on Stripe’s checkout page


3. customer.subscription.deleted

C. Something about a subscription changes (for example, its plan or status)









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → A.





Question 8 · Short answer
Why is it fine to enter a made-up address such as https://mybogusurl.com/ when you first create the webhook?






Suggested answer





The real address, the Supabase Edge Function that will receive Stripe’s messages, doesn’t exist yet. You need the signing secret now, so you create the webhook with a temporary URL and replace it later, once the function is deployed. Until then, Stripe’s notifications go nowhere useful.





Question 9 · Short answer
When a user clicks to upgrade to the Pro Plan, how does Stripe know what to charge them? What role does the Price ID play?






Suggested answer





When the app starts a Stripe checkout, it tells Stripe which price the customer is buying by sending the Price ID (for example, price_12345...). That ID points to the price you created (recurring, monthly, $10), so Stripe knows how much to charge and how often.






Hard

Question 10 · Scenario
While testing, you complete Stripe’s checkout page successfully, but task-app still shows you on the free plan. The webhook endpoint in Stripe still points to https://mybogusurl.com/. Explain what is going on and how to fix it.






Suggested answer





task-app finds out about a completed payment through the webhook (the checkout.session.completed event). Stripe is sending that message to the made-up address, so the app never hears about the payment and never upgrades you. Fix: update the webhook endpoint in Stripe to the real URL of your deployed webhook Edge Function, and make sure that the endpoint’s signing secret is the one stored in STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET.





Question 11 · Short answer
Why does Stripe give each webhook a signing secret? What could happen if the app accepted webhook messages without checking it?






Suggested answer





A webhook address is a public URL, so anyone could send messages to it. Stripe signs every message using the signing secret, and your function uses the same secret to check that the message really came from Stripe and wasn’t changed. Without that check, an attacker could send a fake “checkout completed” message and get the paid plan for free.





Question 12 · Long answer
The page mentions repeating this setup for each environment if you have separate development and production setups. Suppose task-app goes live and starts charging real customers. What has to be set up again, and why?






Suggested answer





Real payments happen in Stripe’s live mode, which is completely separate from the sandbox. You need:

the live publishable key and secret key,
the product and its price created again for live use (with a new Price ID),
a live webhook endpoint that points to your function, with its own signing secret.

Then you update your app’s settings (.env.local or your hosting settings) and the Supabase secrets with these live values. Sandbox keys and IDs can’t be used for real payments.

title: 77  77.  Step 9: Set Up Supabase Database
text:
77.0.1 Run Database Migrations
Your project ships with migrations that define the database schema and policies.
crumbs: 77  77. Step 9: Set Up Supabase Database

title: 77  77.  Step 9: Set Up Supabase Database
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a database migration?






Suggested answer





A file of SQL commands that changes the structure of a database in a controlled, repeatable way, for example by creating tables or security policies. task-app’s migrations, in the supabase/migrations/ folder, define its whole database: the schema (the tables and their columns) and the policies.





Question 2 · Write the command
Write the command that sends the project’s migrations to your remote Supabase database.






Suggested answer





npx supabase db push
(In this tutorial, Supabase CLI commands start with npx.)





Question 3 · Short answer
According to the page, which folder should you be in when you run that command, and why?






Suggested answer





The project’s root (top-level) folder: the folder that contains supabase/config.toml. The CLI works with that project’s supabase folder, which holds the configuration and the migration files in supabase/migrations/.





Question 4 · True or false
Row Level Security (RLS) lets the database decide, row by row, which data each user may read or change.






Suggested answer





True. With RLS turned on, the database checks rules called policies before it returns or changes rows. In task-app, the policies make sure that users can only work with rows whose user_id matches their own user ID.






Medium

Question 5 · Predict the output
db push lists eight migrations, from 0_init_profile.sql to 7_init_stripe_integration.sql. Which one is applied first, and why does the order matter?






Suggested answer





0_init_profile.sql. Migrations run in order (here, by the number at the start of each file name), because later migrations build on earlier ones. For example, the tasks table created in 1_init_tasks.sql refers to the profiles table, so the profiles must be set up first.





Question 6 · Short answer
During db push you see:
NOTICE (42710): extension "uuid-ossp" already exists, skipping
Is this an error that you need to fix?






Suggested answer





No. It is only a notice: the migration asks for the uuid-ossp extension to be installed if it isn’t already, it was already there, so that step was skipped and the migration continued. Real problems are labeled ERROR, like the message that follows it on the page.





Question 7 · Find the bug
The push stops with:
ERROR: function uuid_generate_v4() does not exist (SQLSTATE 42883)
Which file do you change, what do you change, and what do you do next?






Suggested answer





In supabase/migrations/1_init_tasks.sql, replace the call uuid_generate_v4() with gen_random_uuid(), a function built into PostgreSQL that also creates a random ID. Save the file and run npx supabase db push again.





Question 8 · Short answer
How can you check that the migrations worked?






Suggested answer





First, the command must finish without any ERROR messages. Then open the Table Editor in the Supabase dashboard and confirm that the tables (such as tasks) exist.





Question 9 · Matching
Match each kind of access with what the RLS policies described on this page allow.








Who

What the policies allow




1. A signed-in user

A. Can bypass the restrictions where needed (system operations)


2. An anonymous (not signed-in) visitor

B. Can read and update only rows whose user_id is their own user ID


3. The service role

C. Cannot access private data









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → C, 3 → A.






Hard

Question 10 · Scenario
After fixing 1_init_tasks.sql, you run npx supabase db push again. Will 0_init_profile.sql be applied a second time? Explain.






Suggested answer





No. Supabase keeps a migration history table in your remote database. Every migration that is applied successfully is recorded there, and later pushes skip the migrations that are already recorded. 0_init_profile.sql succeeded the first time, so the second push only offers the migrations that haven’t been applied yet, starting with 1_init_tasks.sql.





Question 11 · Long answer
Why do projects define their database with migration files instead of having each developer create the tables by clicking around in the Supabase dashboard? Give at least two reasons.






Suggested answer






Migrations are files, so they are stored in Git with the rest of the code: changes have a history and can be shared and reviewed.
Anyone can rebuild exactly the same database with one command (npx supabase db push): a teammate, a new Supabase project, or the production database. That is how you set up the entire task-app database without creating a single table by hand.
Changes are applied in a fixed order, which avoids the mistakes that are easy to make when clicking by hand and hard to repeat exactly.






Question 12 · Scenario
Imagine the migrations had created the tasks table but forgot to turn on RLS for it. What risk would that create for task-app’s users?






Suggested answer





Without RLS, the database would not check who is asking, so the rule “users can only read and update their own rows” would not be enforced. Other users, and possibly even visitors who aren’t signed in, could read or change everyone’s tasks. Turning on RLS and adding policies is what keeps each user’s data private.
crumbs: 77  77. Step 9: Set Up Supabase Database

title: 78  78.  Step 10: Set Up Supabase Storage Bucket
text:
78.0.1 Create Storage Bucket
You’ll store task images in Supabase Storage.
crumbs: 78  78. Step 10: Set Up Supabase Storage Bucket

title: 78  78.  Step 10: Set Up Supabase Storage Bucket
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a Supabase Storage bucket, and what does this app keep in it?






Suggested answer





A bucket is a named container for files in Supabase Storage - think of it as a top-level folder in a cloud drive. This app keeps the images that users attach to their tasks in it.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
The page tells you to make the bucket Public. What does that setting mean?

Anyone on the internet can upload files to the bucket
Anyone who has a file’s URL can view that file
Anyone can delete files from the bucket
Only the user who uploaded a file can view it







Suggested answer





b. “Public” is about viewing: anyone who has a file’s URL can open it without signing in. Uploading (a) and deleting (c) are still controlled by the bucket’s policies - on this page, only signed-in users can upload, and users can delete only their own images. Option d describes a private setup, which the page suggests considering for production.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
The bucket allows only the file types image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif and image/webp. Which of these files would be rejected? (Assume every file is under the size limit.)

team-photo.jpg
logo.png
budget-report.pdf
celebration.gif







Suggested answer





c. A PDF is not an image, so it is not on the allowed list. JPEG (a), PNG (b) and GIF (d) images are all allowed. Labels such as image/png are called MIME types: a standard way of naming what kind of data a file contains.





Question 4 · True or false
The only way to create the storage policies is to click through the policy builder in the Supabase dashboard.






Suggested answer





False. The page gives two options: use the policies that come with the project’s migration files (the SQL files in supabase/migrations/), or create them with the dashboard’s policy builder.






Medium

Question 5 · Matching
Match each setting or policy with what it does.








Setting or policy

What it does




1. Public bucket

A. Only signed-in users can add files


2. Private bucket + signed URLs

B. A user can remove only their own images


3. Upload policy

C. Anyone who has a file’s URL can view it


4. Delete policy

D. Files can be viewed only through special links that the app hands out









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → A, 4 → B.
A signed URL is a link to one private file that works only for a limited time. That is why a private bucket gives you more control.





Question 6 · Short answer
The page says to give the bucket the name “your code expects”. Why must the bucket’s name match the name used in the code, and what happens if it doesn’t?






Suggested answer





The app finds the bucket by its name: the code says, in effect, “upload this file to the bucket called X” and “show the image stored in bucket X”. If your bucket’s name is different (even by one character), the app is asking for a bucket that doesn’t exist, so uploads fail (typically with a “Bucket not found” error) and images don’t appear. To find the name the code expects, search the project’s code and its migration files (supabase/migrations/) for the bucket name.





Question 7 · Scenario
Maria tries to attach a 3 MB photo of a whiteboard (a PNG file) to one of her tasks. The bucket’s size limit is 1 MB. What should happen? Is this a bug?






Suggested answer





The upload should be rejected, ideally with a clear error message, and the photo should not be saved. That is not a bug - it’s the size limit doing its job. Maria can shrink or compress the photo to under 1 MB and try again. (The next step, “Run the Application”, asks you to test exactly this.)





Question 8 · Scenario
When a signed-in user tries to upload an image from the app, the upload fails with an error like “new row violates row-level security policy”. Based on this page, what is most likely missing, and how could you fix it?






Suggested answer





The upload policy - the rule that allows authenticated (signed-in) users to add files to the bucket - is missing or wrong. Supabase checks the bucket’s policies on every upload and refuses anything they don’t allow. Fix it by adding the upload policy, either from the project’s migration policies or with the dashboard’s policy builder. It is also worth confirming that the user really is signed in.






Hard

Question 9 · Long answer
The page says to enforce the file-size limit “in your upload UI and/or server-side logic”. Explain what each of these two places adds, and why a check only in the upload page (the UI) is not enough.






Suggested answer






A check in the UI (the upload page in the browser) gives instant, friendly feedback (“File must be under 1 MB”) before the file is even sent.
A server-side check (for example, the bucket’s own size limit in Supabase) is enforced no matter how the request arrives.

A UI-only check is not enough because the browser is under the user’s control: someone can skip your web page and send files straight to Supabase (for example, with a short script), or tamper with the page’s code. Only a check on the server can’t be bypassed. Best practice is both: the UI for convenience, the server for protection.





Question 10 · Scenario
Suppose the app saves each image under a path that starts with the uploader’s user ID, for example maria-user-id/whiteboard.png (in real life the ID is a long random string). Explain how a delete policy can use that path so that Sam cannot delete Maria’s image.






Suggested answer





When someone asks to delete a file, the policy compares the first folder in the file’s path with the user ID of the person making the request (Supabase knows who is signed in). Maria’s image is stored under her ID, so when Sam - signed in with a different ID - tries to delete it, the two don’t match and Supabase refuses. When Maria deletes it, they match and the delete is allowed. This is the “match user_id in … path” idea from the page.





Question 11 · Compare
The page calls a public bucket “simpler for tutorials” but suggests a private bucket with signed URLs for production. Imagine the app adds a feature where employees upload photos of expense receipts. Which option would you choose, and why? Mention one downside of your choice.






Suggested answer





A private bucket with signed URLs. Receipts can contain sensitive information (names, amounts, the last digits of a card). In a public bucket, anyone who gets hold of an image’s URL - for example from a forwarded email - can view it without signing in. With a private bucket, the app first checks who is asking and then hands out a signed URL that stops working after a short time.
Downside: more work. The app has to create a signed URL every time it shows an image, and old links stop working once they expire. For harmless images in a class project, a public bucket is fine.

title: 79  79.  Step 11: Deploy Supabase Edge Functions
text:
79.0.1 The Three Functions
Edge Functions are serverless handlers for AI, billing, and webhooks.
Location in project: supabase/functions/
crumbs: 79  79. Step 11: Deploy Supabase Edge Functions

title: 79  79.  Step 11: Deploy Supabase Edge Functions
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is a Supabase Edge Function, and in which folder of the project is the code for the three functions kept?






Suggested answer





An Edge Function is a small piece of back-end code that runs on Supabase’s servers - not in the user’s browser and not on your laptop - whenever something calls its URL. The page calls them serverless handlers: you write the function and Supabase takes care of running it, so you never set up or manage a server yourself. The code lives in supabase/functions/, with each function in its own subfolder.





Question 2 · Matching
Match each function with its job. One job on the right does not belong to any of the three functions.








Function

Job




1. The AI task-creation function

A. Receives event notifications from Stripe and updates the subscription status in the database


2. The Stripe session function

B. Asks OpenAI to suggest a label for a task and saves the task


3. stripe-webhook

C. Stores the images that users upload




D. Sends the user to a Stripe checkout page, or to Stripe’s customer portal if they already subscribe









Suggested answer





1 → B, 2 → D, 3 → A.
C is not an edge function’s job: images are stored in the Supabase Storage bucket you set up in the previous step.





Question 3 · True or false
After you deploy a function, you can keep editing its file in supabase/functions/ on your laptop, and the live function on Supabase updates automatically.






Suggested answer





False. Deploying uploads a copy of your code to Supabase. The live function changes only when you deploy again (for example with npx supabase functions deploy stripe-webhook). Until then, Supabase keeps running the old copy.





Question 4 · Multiple choice
A function you deployed is returning errors. Where does this page tell you to look for the error messages?

The function’s Logs tab under Edge Functions in the Supabase dashboard
The supabase/migrations/ folder on your computer
The Google Cloud Console
The .env.local file







Suggested answer





a. The function runs on Supabase’s servers, so its runtime errors are recorded in its logs there. The migrations folder (b) holds database changes, the Google Cloud Console (c) holds the Google sign-in settings, and .env.local (d) holds settings for the Next.js app - none of them record what happens when the function runs.






Medium

Question 5 · Write the command
Write the command that deploys only the stripe-webhook function. In which folder should you be when you run it?






Suggested answer





npx supabase functions deploy stripe-webhook
Run it from the project root - the top-level folder of the project, which contains the supabase/ folder. This tutorial runs the Supabase CLI through npx; if you installed the CLI another way, type supabase functions deploy stripe-webhook instead.





Question 6 · Write the URL
Your Supabase project ref is abcdefghijklmnopqrst. What is the URL of your deployed stripe-webhook function? (This is the URL you give to Stripe.)






Suggested answer





https://abcdefghijklmnopqrst.supabase.co/functions/v1/stripe-webhook
The pattern is https://[your-project-ref].supabase.co/functions/v1/ followed by the function’s name.





Question 7 · Matching
Match each secret or credential with what it is used for.








Secret or credential

Used for




1. OPENAI_API_KEY

A. Proving which signed-in user is calling the AI task-creation function


2. STRIPE_SECRET_KEY

B. Checking that an incoming webhook event really came from Stripe


3. STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET

C. Letting the AI task-creation function ask OpenAI for a label


4. The user’s JWT

D. Letting the Stripe session function create checkout sessions









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → D, 3 → B, 4 → A.
A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed “ID badge” that the app sends along with a request to show which signed-in user is making it.





Question 8 · Multiple choice
A user who already has a subscription clicks “Manage Subscription”. According to the page, what does the Stripe session function do?

Creates a second subscription for the same user
Returns a link to Stripe’s customer portal, where the user can manage the existing subscription
Deletes the user’s account
Calls OpenAI to recommend a subscription plan







Suggested answer





b. For a new subscriber, the function creates a Stripe Checkout session (the payment page). For someone who already subscribes, it returns a customer portal link instead, so they can manage what they already have. It doesn’t create duplicates (a) or delete accounts (c), and calling OpenAI (d) is the AI task-creation function’s job.






Hard

Question 9 · Long answer
Explain why JWT verification must be turned off for stripe-webhook, and why doing so does not let just anyone fake a payment.






Suggested answer





With JWT verification on, Supabase lets a call through to a function only if it carries a valid JWT. That makes sense for the other two functions, which the app calls on behalf of a signed-in user. But stripe-webhook is called directly by Stripe’s servers, and Stripe doesn’t send a JWT - so Supabase would turn away every Stripe event before your code even ran.
It’s still safe because the function does its own check: Stripe signs every event, and the function verifies that signature using STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, which only you and Stripe know. A fake “payment succeeded” message sent by anyone else won’t carry a valid signature, so the function rejects it.





Question 10 · Scenario
You deployed all three functions and pointed Stripe at the stripe-webhook URL. Now Stripe reports that every delivery to your endpoint fails with HTTP status 401 (Unauthorized), and the function’s logs show none of the messages your code would print. What did you most likely forget, and how do you fix it?






Suggested answer





You forgot to turn off JWT verification for stripe-webhook. Stripe’s requests carry no JWT, so Supabase answers “401 Unauthorized” before your function’s code runs. Fix: in the Supabase dashboard, open the stripe-webhook function, go to its Details tab, switch off JWT verification in the function configuration, and save. (The exact wording of this switch in the dashboard may differ slightly from the page.)





Question 11 · Scenario
When you set up Stripe, you entered a temporary webhook URL (https://mybogusurl.com/). You deploy the functions but skip the section “Update Stripe Webhook URL”. Then you buy a subscription with a test card. What happens, and how do you fix it?






Suggested answer





The payment itself succeeds on Stripe’s checkout page, but Stripe sends its notification to the bogus URL, so your stripe-webhook function never hears about it. The database is never updated, and the app doesn’t treat the user as a subscriber. Fix: in the webhook settings in the Stripe Dashboard, change the endpoint URL to https://[your-project-ref].supabase.co/functions/v1/stripe-webhook and save.





Question 12 · Ordering
Put these steps in the order this page does them:

A. Change the endpoint URL in Stripe to the deployed stripe-webhook URL
B. Deploy the three functions with the Supabase CLI
C. Turn off JWT verification for stripe-webhook
D. Check in the Supabase dashboard that all three functions appear, and look at their logs







Suggested answer





B → D → C → A.
Deploying (B) has to come first: until a function is deployed, there is nothing to check (D), no setting to switch off (C) and no URL to give Stripe (A).

title: 80  80.  Step 12: Run the Application
text:
80.0.1 Start the Development Server
Now that the backend is configured, you can run the Next.js app locally.
From your project root:
The app usually runs at http://localhost:3000.
If you’re using pnpm or yarn, adjust accordingly.

title: 80  80.  Step 12: Run the Application
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What does each of these two commands do?
npm install
npm run dev






Suggested answer






npm install downloads all the packages the project needs (they are listed in package.json) into the node_modules folder.
npm run dev starts the Next.js development server, which runs the app on your own computer so you can use it in your browser.






Question 2 · Short answer
Once the development server is running, which address do you usually open in your browser? What does localhost in that address mean?






Suggested answer





http://localhost:3000. localhost means “this computer”: the app is served from your own machine, not from the internet, so only you can open it. The 3000 is the port - the numbered “door” on your computer that the app is listening at.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
You reach the Stripe checkout page while testing. What should you enter?

Your own credit card - the amount is small
The card number 4242 4242 4242 4242, any future expiry date and any 3-digit CVC
The card number 1234 5678 9012 3456 and any past expiry date
Nothing - checkout can’t be tested on localhost







Suggested answer





b. 4242 4242 4242 4242 is a Stripe test card: with any future expiry date, any 3-digit CVC and any billing info, it simulates a successful payment, and no real money moves. Don’t use a real card for testing (a). Option c is not a test card, and the expiry date must be in the future. Option d is wrong: this page has you test checkout while the app runs locally.





Question 4 · True or false
Once you have signed in with Google and landed on the dashboard, there is nothing else to check for sign-in.






Suggested answer





False. The page also asks you to look in the Supabase dashboard under Auth → Users to verify that your user was created. Checking both sides - the app and the back end - confirms that the data was really saved, not just that the page looked right.






Medium

Question 5 · Matching
After each test action, where can you confirm in Supabase that it worked? One place on the right is not used.



Test action

Where to check




1. Sign in with Google

A. The tasks table


2. Create a task

B. The storage bucket that holds task images


3. Upload an image to a task

C. The Users list under Auth




D. The Google Cloud Console









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → B.
D is not part of Supabase: the Google Cloud Console is where you set up “Sign in with Google”, not where your app’s users are recorded.





Question 6 · Ordering
Put the steps for testing a subscription in the right order:

A. Enter the test card 4242 4242 4242 4242, a future expiry date and any 3-digit CVC
B. Click “Manage Subscription”
C. Check that premium-only features have unlocked
D. Confirm you are on a Stripe-hosted checkout page that shows the right product and price
E. Complete checkout and return to the app







Suggested answer





B → D → A → E → C.





Question 7 · Short answer
What is a protected route, and how would you check that signing out really protects it?






Suggested answer





A protected route is a page of the app that only signed-in users may see - for example, the dashboard with your tasks. To check it: sign out, then try to open the dashboard directly by typing its address (for example http://localhost:3000/dashboard) into the browser. You should be sent back to the login page instead of seeing any tasks.





Question 8 · Short answer
Why does the page ask you to try uploading an invalid file type or a very large file on purpose?






Suggested answer





To test the app’s error handling - what happens when things go wrong. The app should refuse the file and show a clear message, not crash or save the file anyway. Real users will sometimes pick the wrong file, so the “unhappy path” needs testing just as much as the normal one.






Hard

Question 9 · Scenario
You create a task. It shows up in your list and as a new row in the tasks table, but even after you refresh the page, no AI label ever appears. Which part of the system is the most likely problem, and what would you check?






Suggested answer





The task was saved, so sign-in and the database work. What’s missing is the AI labeling, which the AI task-creation edge function does by calling OpenAI with OPENAI_API_KEY. Check:

the function’s Logs in the Supabase dashboard (Edge Functions) for an error message;
that the OPENAI_API_KEY secret is set in your Supabase project (npx supabase secrets list shows the names of the secrets that are set);
that the OpenAI key is valid and your OpenAI account has API credit.






Question 10 · Scenario
Checkout on Stripe’s page succeeds and you are sent back to the app, but the premium features do not unlock. Which part of the system is responsible for recording the payment in your database? Name three things you would check.






Suggested answer





The stripe-webhook edge function. After checkout, Stripe sends an event to that function, and the function updates the user’s subscription status in the database. If premium doesn’t unlock, that event probably never arrived or was rejected. Any three of:

the webhook’s endpoint URL in Stripe is https://[your-project-ref].supabase.co/functions/v1/stripe-webhook (not the temporary URL from the Stripe setup step);
JWT verification is turned off for stripe-webhook;
the STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET stored in Supabase matches the signing secret that Stripe shows for that endpoint;
the function’s Logs in Supabase, and the delivery attempts listed for the endpoint in the Stripe Dashboard.






Question 11 · Long answer
You are “running the app locally”, yet signing in, saving tasks and paying all work. Explain which parts of the system run on your computer and which run somewhere else while you test at http://localhost:3000.






Suggested answer





Only the Next.js app runs on your computer (started with npm run dev). Everything else is in the cloud:

Supabase - the database, the sign-in system, the storage bucket and the edge functions - runs on Supabase’s servers, in the project you created on the Supabase website;
Google handles the “Sign in with Google” step;
OpenAI suggests the task labels (called by an edge function);
Stripe hosts the checkout page and sends webhook events to your edge function.

So “running locally” means your computer serves the app’s pages, and those pages talk over the internet to all of these services. That’s why the app needs an internet connection and the right keys in .env.local even when it runs locally.

title: 81  81.  Step 13: Deploy to Production
text:
81.0.1 Deploying the Frontend
Once everything works locally, you can deploy the frontend.
Recommended: Vercel
Vercel is tightly integrated with Next.js and offers smooth deployments.
After deployment:
Alternative Options
If you prefer other providers:
Configuration will be similar: point to your repo and set env vars.

title: 81  81.  Step 13: Deploy to Production
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What does it mean to deploy to production? Why can’t other people use your app at http://localhost:3000?






Suggested answer





Deploying to production means putting the app on servers on the internet so that real users can reach it at a public web address (Vercel gives you one). Production is the live version that real users use. localhost means “this computer”, so http://localhost:3000 only works on your own machine, and only while your development server is running.





Question 2 · Multiple choice
Why does the page recommend Vercel for deploying this app?

Vercel is the only host that can run a Next.js app
Vercel is tightly integrated with Next.js, so deployments are smooth
Vercel also hosts the app’s database and edge functions
Vercel replaces Stripe for handling payments







Suggested answer





b. Vercel is the company that makes Next.js, and its hosting is built around it. Option a is false: the page lists Netlify, AWS Amplify and Render as alternatives. Option c is false: the database and edge functions stay on Supabase - this page deploys only the front end. Option d is false: Stripe still handles payments.





Question 3 · True or false
With the method on this page, your code must be in a Git repository (for example on GitHub) before Vercel can deploy it.






Suggested answer





True. Step 1 is to push your code to a Git repository. Vercel then imports the project from that repository and builds the app from it.





Question 4 · Short answer
Stripe test keys start with pk_test_ and sk_test_. What do the matching live keys start with, and what do pk and sk stand for?






Suggested answer





Live keys start with pk_live_ and sk_live_. pk stands for publishable key (safe to use in the browser) and sk for secret key (must be kept secret, on a server).






Medium

Question 5 · Short answer
Your .env.local file works perfectly on your laptop. Why doesn’t Vercel get the values in it automatically, and what do you need to do instead?






Suggested answer





.env.local is listed in .gitignore, so it is never committed or pushed to GitHub - that is exactly what keeps your keys out of the repository. Vercel builds the app from the GitHub repository, so it never sees the file. You have to enter each variable (NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY and so on) in the environment variable settings of your Vercel project. If you add or change a variable after a deployment, redeploy so that the new value is used.





Question 6 · Multiple choice
Variables whose names start with NEXT_PUBLIC_ are built into the JavaScript that is sent to every visitor’s browser. Which of these values must never go into a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable?

The Supabase project URL
The Supabase anon key
The Stripe publishable key (pk_...)
The Stripe secret key (sk_...)







Suggested answer





d. Anyone who visits your site can read a NEXT_PUBLIC_ value. The Supabase URL (a), the anon key (b) and the publishable key (c) are designed to be safe in the browser. The secret key gives full access to your Stripe account (for example, issuing refunds or reading customer data), so it must stay on a server. In this project it is stored as a Supabase secret that the edge functions use.





Question 7 · Matching
When you go live, different settings live in different places. Match each item with where you set it.








Item

Where




1. NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY for the live site

A. Supabase secrets, used by the edge functions


2. The live Stripe secret key (sk_live_...)

B. Supabase’s Auth settings (Site URL and allowed redirect URLs)


3. Your production web address, so that sign-in can return users to it

C. The live-mode webhook settings in the Stripe Dashboard


4. The endpoint that sends Stripe’s events to your stripe-webhook function

D. The environment variables of your Vercel project









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → A, 3 → B, 4 → C.
The Next.js app on Vercel reads its NEXT_PUBLIC_... variables from Vercel. The edge functions read the Stripe secret key from Supabase secrets (that’s where you stored it with npx supabase secrets set when you set up Stripe). Sign-in redirects are controlled by Supabase Auth. Webhook endpoints are set up in Stripe, and live mode has its own endpoints, separate from test mode.





Question 8 · Short answer
Vercel reports that the deployment succeeded and your home page loads. According to the page, what should you test next, and why isn’t “the page loads” enough?






Suggested answer





Visit the production URL and test login, task creation and the subscription flow there. A page that loads only proves the front end is online. Each of those flows depends on other services - Supabase, Google sign-in, OpenAI (through an edge function) and Stripe - and on settings that are different in production (web addresses, environment variables, keys). Any of them can be wrong even when the page looks fine.






Hard

Question 9 · Scenario
On your live Vercel site you click “Sign in with Google” and choose your account - and then you land on http://localhost:3000 instead of your live site. What’s wrong, and how do you fix it?






Suggested answer





Supabase’s Auth settings still only know about your local address. After Google signs you in, Supabase sends you back only to addresses it has been told are allowed; when the requested address isn’t allowed, it falls back to the Site URL, which is still http://localhost:3000.
Fix: in Supabase’s Auth URL settings, set the Site URL to your production address and add the production address to the allowed redirect URLs (for example https://your-app.vercel.app/**, where ** means “any page on this site”). Also make sure http://localhost:3000/** is on the redirect list, so that sign-in still works when you develop locally.





Question 10 · Long answer
In this tutorial you created only one Supabase project, and you use it both for developing on your laptop and for the live site. The page talks about using “your production Supabase project URL” and keys. What does that suggest bigger teams do, and what is one risk of using a single project for everything?






Suggested answer





Bigger teams usually keep separate Supabase projects: one (or more) for development and testing, and one for production that holds real users’ data. Each project has its own URL and keys, so .env.local points at the development project while Vercel points at the production project. With a single project, your Vercel variables simply use the same URL and anon key as .env.local.
The risk: everything you do while developing - creating junk test tasks, running automated tests, trying out a new migration - happens in the same database that real users rely on. A broken experiment can break or clutter the live app.





Question 11 · Scenario
You switch Stripe to live mode and replace the test keys with live keys, but you skip “update webhook endpoints/secrets”. Real customers pay successfully, yet their accounts never become premium. Explain why, and what you should do.






Suggested answer





Live mode is separate from test mode. The webhook endpoint you created, and its whsec_... signing secret, belong to test mode. In live mode, either no endpoint sends events to your stripe-webhook function at all, or - once you create one - it has a different signing secret from the test one stored in Supabase, so the signature check fails. Either way, your database never hears about the payments.
Fix: create a live-mode webhook endpoint that points to https://[your-project-ref].supabase.co/functions/v1/stripe-webhook (with the same events as before), then store its signing secret in Supabase:
npx supabase secrets set STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...

title: 82  82.  Step 14: Extending the functionality
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Matching
Match each folder with what it holds.








Folder

What it holds




1. app/

A. Reusable pieces of the user interface (React components)


2. components/

B. Migration files that define the database: tables, columns and policies


3. hooks/

C. The Next.js routes and pages


4. supabase/functions/

D. The integration test suite


5. supabase/migrations/

E. Client-side logic and the code that talks to Supabase


6. tests/integration/

F. Edge functions (back-end logic)









Suggested answer





1 → C, 2 → A, 3 → E, 4 → F, 5 → B, 6 → D.





Question 2 · Short answer
According to the start of this page, the finished app already has six capabilities. Name four of them.






Suggested answer





Any four of: authentication and user management; a Postgres database with row level security (RLS); file storage for images; AI-powered task labeling; subscription billing with Stripe; edge functions for serverless back-end logic.





Question 3 · True or false
The code in supabase/functions/ runs in the user’s web browser.






Suggested answer





False. That folder holds the edge functions: back-end code that runs on Supabase’s servers. The parts users see and click on are built from app/, components/ and hooks/.





Question 4 · Multiple choice
The page calls the project a “full-stack SaaS application”. What does SaaS mean?

Software as a Service: software people use over the internet, usually for a subscription fee
Server and Application Storage System: a kind of database
Secure Authentication as a Service: a login provider such as Google
Static and Simple Site: a website with no back end







Suggested answer





a. SaaS is software that customers use online instead of installing it, usually paying a subscription - which is what the Stripe subscription in this app supports. The other three are made-up expansions.






Medium

Question 5 · Short answer
For each change below, which folder would you mainly work in?

Change how the box that shows a single task looks, everywhere it appears.
Add a new “Reports” page with its own web address.
Store a new yes/no value for each task, reminder_sent, in the database.
Add back-end code that sends emails through an email service, using a secret API key.







Suggested answer






components/ - shared pieces of the user interface.
app/ - pages and routing.
supabase/migrations/ - a new migration file that adds the column.
supabase/functions/ - a new edge function. The email service’s API key belongs in Supabase secrets, not in the code.






Question 6 · Multiple choice
You want every task to have a new estimated_minutes column. Following the page, what is the best way to make this change?

Add the column by clicking around in the Supabase Table Editor
Create a new migration file in supabase/migrations/ that adds the column, then push it to the database
Add the column name to .env.local
Add the column inside a React component in components/







Suggested answer





b. A migration file records the change as code that is saved in Git, so the same change can be applied the same way to every copy of the database - a teammate’s, a test project, production. (You push it with npx supabase db push, as in the database step.) A change made by clicking (a) works once but leaves no record, so other copies of the database fall out of step. .env.local (c) holds settings, not the structure of the database, and React components (d) only display data.





Question 7 · Short answer
The app’s database uses row level security (RLS). In plain English, what does RLS do in this app, and what must you remember about RLS when a migration adds a brand-new table?






Suggested answer





RLS is a set of rules inside the database that decides, row by row, who may see or change which data. For example, each user can see and edit only their own tasks, even though everyone’s tasks are stored in the same table. A new table needs its own RLS policies (a migration can add them, as the page says). Without the right policies, users either can’t use the new table at all, or - if RLS is left switched off - may be able to see each other’s data.






Hard

Question 8 · Long answer
The page says to create new migration files. Why shouldn’t you instead edit an old migration file, such as supabase/migrations/1_init_tasks.sql, that has already been applied to your database?






Suggested answer





The database keeps a list of the migrations it has already run. When you push (npx supabase db push), only migrations that are not yet on that list are applied. If you edit a file that already ran, it won’t run again, so your change never reaches your database - while anyone who sets up the project from scratch later gets the edited version. The copies end up different. A new migration file is applied once, in order, everywhere. (Fixing a migration that failed and was never applied, as in the database step, is a different situation.)





Question 9 · Long answer
Plan the “email notifications for due tasks” idea. Using the folders on this page, describe what you would add or change, and where. A good answer covers at least three folders.






Suggested answer





A model answer:

supabase/migrations/: a new migration that adds what you need to store - for example, whether a reminder was already sent for each task, or each user’s email preferences (plus RLS policies for any new table).
supabase/functions/: a new edge function that finds tasks that are due and sends the emails through an email service. The service’s API key is stored as a Supabase secret, never in the code. Something must run this function regularly (a scheduled job), because no user clicks a button to start it.
app/ and components/: a settings option where users can turn reminders on or off.
hooks/: the client logic that saves the user’s choice in Supabase.
tests/integration/: a test that checks that due tasks get a reminder.






Question 10 · Compare
The page suggests building a mobile app with React Native or Expo. Which parts of the current system could the mobile app reuse, and which part would you have to build again?






Suggested answer





The back end can be reused: the same Supabase project with its sign-in system, its database (with the RLS rules), its storage bucket and its edge functions, including the AI labeling. The mobile app would simply talk to the same Supabase project. What you would build again is the front end - the screens and client logic, written with React Native or Expo instead of the Next.js code in app/, components/ and hooks/.

text:
83.1 Troubleshooting
A few quick checks for common problems.

83.1.1 Environment Variables Not Loading

Verify the filenames:

Local Next.js: .env.local
Supabase: supabase/.env (if applicable) and Supabase secrets.

Restart the dev server after any env changes.
Confirm the variables are defined in:

The Next.js runtime (console.log(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_... )).
Supabase dashboard (for secrets).




83.1.2 Authentication Errors

Ensure your OAuth redirect URIs match exactly in:

Google Cloud Console (OAuth credentials).
Supabase Auth settings.

Make sure the Supabase Site URL matches your local and production URLs.
Inspect the browser network tab for auth-related errors.



83.1.3 Edge Functions Failing

Check that all required secrets are set (OPENAI_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET).
In Supabase:

Open Edge Functions → Logs to see runtime errors.

Make sure code imports are correct and dependencies are installed.



83.1.4 Stripe Webhook Not Working

Confirm JWT verification is disabled for stripe-webhook.
Double-check the webhook URL in Stripe:

It must match the function URL exactly (including https).

Ensure the Signing secret in Supabase matches the current secret shown in Stripe.
Use Stripe’s Send test event to debug.



83.1.5 Database Errors

Ensure supabase db push ran successfully without errors.
Check that RLS policies allow the operation you’re trying.
Confirm that the user is authenticated when performing actions that require auth.
Inspect Supabase logs or use the SQL editor to run queries manually.

title: 83  83.  Step 15: Automated Testing and Troubleshooting
text:
Practice Questions

Easy

Question 1 · Short answer
What is an integration test, and what is its advantage over clicking through the app yourself after every change?






Suggested answer





An integration test is a small program that checks that several parts work together - here, the app’s code with your real Supabase project (database, storage, edge functions). Because the tests are automated, one command re-runs all of them after every change, the same way every time. Clicking through by hand is slow, and it’s easy to forget a step.





Question 2 · Write the command
Write the command that runs all of the project’s automated tests.






Suggested answer





npm test
Run it from the project root.





Question 3 · Multiple choice
Which file holds the environment variables for the Next.js app when you run it on your own computer?

.env.local
package.json
.gitignore
README.md







Suggested answer





a. The troubleshooting checklist names .env.local for local Next.js. package.json (b) lists the project’s packages and scripts, .gitignore (c) lists the files Git should ignore (including .env.local itself), and README.md (d) is documentation.





Question 4 · True or false
It’s fine to point the integration tests at your production Supabase project, the one that holds real users’ data.






Suggested answer





False. The tests create, change and delete real records (users, tasks, files) in whatever project they are pointed at. That is why the page says the integration tests usually run against a separate test environment, and that the test settings should be kept separate from production credentials.






Medium

Question 5 · Write the command
The project contains the test file tests/integration/3_storage.test.ts. Following the pattern on this page, write the command that runs only this file.






Suggested answer





npm test -- tests/integration/3_storage.test.ts
The -- tells npm to pass everything after it on to the test tool, instead of treating it as an option for npm itself.





Question 6 · Short answer
A test fails with a timeout the first time you run the tests, then passes when you run them again right away. What is a likely cause, and what does the page suggest?






Suggested answer





A cold start: an edge function that hasn’t been used for a while needs a moment to start up, so the first request can be slow enough to hit the test’s time limit. On the second run the function is already “warm” and answers quickly. The page suggests running the tests again, and checking that your edge functions are deployed and reachable from the test environment.





Question 7 · Multiple choice
Your deployed edge functions need keys such as OPENAI_API_KEY. Where do they read these values from?

The supabase/.env file on your laptop
The secrets stored in your Supabase project (set with npx supabase secrets set ...)
The environment variables of your Vercel project
The .env.local file







Suggested answer





b. Deployed functions run on Supabase’s servers, which can’t read files on your laptop - not even supabase/.env (a). The values must be stored in the Supabase project as secrets. Vercel’s variables (c) and .env.local (d) are for the Next.js app, not for edge functions. To see which secrets are set, run npx supabase secrets list (it shows their names, not their values).





Question 8 · Matching
Match each symptom with the section of the troubleshooting checklist you would turn to first.








Symptom

Checklist section




1. On the live site, after signing in with Google you land on localhost

A. Database Errors


2. Saving data fails with an error that mentions a “row-level security policy”

B. Edge Functions Failing


3. Stripe test payments succeed, but nothing changes in your database

C. Environment Variables Not Loading


4. AI labels stopped appearing, and the function’s logs show errors

D. Authentication Errors


5. You added a new key to .env.local, but the app still behaves as if it isn’t there

E. Stripe Webhook Not Working









Suggested answer





1 → D, 2 → A, 3 → E, 4 → B, 5 → C.






Hard

Question 9 · Scenario
You deleted your old Stripe webhook endpoint and created a new one with the correct URL. Stripe now delivers events to your stripe-webhook function, but the database is never updated, and the function’s logs show a signature-verification error. What’s wrong, and how do you fix it?






Suggested answer





Every Stripe webhook endpoint has its own signing secret (whsec_...). Your new endpoint got a new secret, but Supabase still holds the old one in STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, so the function can’t verify the signatures and rejects every event. Fix: copy the new endpoint’s signing secret from the Stripe Dashboard and store it in Supabase:
npx supabase secrets set STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...
This is the checklist item “Ensure the Signing secret in Supabase matches the current secret shown in Stripe”.





Question 10 · Scenario
Clicking “Sign in with Google” takes you to a Google error page that says Error 400: redirect_uri_mismatch. What is the most likely cause, and what exactly would you compare?






Suggested answer





The Authorized redirect URI saved in Google Cloud Console doesn’t exactly match the callback address that Supabase uses. Compare the URI in your OAuth credentials in Google Cloud Console with Supabase’s callback URL, which has the form https://[your-project-ref].supabase.co/auth/v1/callback. They must match character for character: look for a wrong project ref, http instead of https, a typo in /auth/v1/callback or an extra / at the end.





Question 11 · Scenario
Maria signs in and opens the dashboard, but her task list is empty. In the Supabase Table Editor you can see rows in the tasks table that belong to her. Using the “Database Errors” checklist, what two things would you check, and why might there be no error message at all?






Suggested answer





Check that (1) the app’s request really is made as the signed-in user - a request without Maria’s sign-in information counts as anonymous - and (2) the RLS policies on tasks allow users to read their own rows. With row level security, rows you aren’t allowed to see are simply left out of the results, so the app gets an empty list instead of an error. The Table Editor shows the rows because the Supabase dashboard looks at the data with full admin rights, which RLS does not limit.

title: 87  87.  Measures of well designed programs
text:
The following are some metrics that can be used to see if a program is designed well:

Cyclomatic Complexity: Measures independent execution paths in a function. Lower is better.
Code Coverage: % of code exercised by automated tests. Aim ≥ 80%.
Coupling and Cohesion:

Coupling: how interdependent modules are (lower is better)
Cohesion: how focused a module’s responsibilities are (higher is better)

Lines of Code (LOC) per Method/Class: Monitors size; excessively large methods or classes often signal poor abstraction.
Maintainability Index: Combines LOC, complexity, and comment density into a single score.
Defect Density: Bugs per thousand lines of code; fewer indicates higher-code quality.
Technical Debt Ratio: Estimated “remediation cost” vs. development cost; lower ratios are healthier.
Static Analysis Warnings: Number/severity of linter or analyzer alerts per 1,000 LOC.
Code Churn: Frequency and volume of changes; high churn may signal instability or unclear design.
Documentation Coverage: Ratio of documented public APIs to total; measures how well the codebase is described.
